News.title: Russians claim scientist who ‘died of plague after breaking test tube’ suffered mystery ‘pneumonia’ as 200 in isolation
News.content:
Next

RUSSIA has claimed the scientist thought to have died of plague after breaking a test tube had a mystery strain of pneumonia.

Health chiefs broke their silence today amid rising public panic to dismiss fears of another pandemic – as nearly 200 people remain in quarantine.



Lab worker Daria Shipilova, 28, died after falling desperately ill in Shelekhov, Siberia from what some reported to be bubonic plague.

Now, reports say that 189 people are in isolation – 114 are in one hospital, 63 in another, and another 12 are at the Anti-Plague Research Institute.



Health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor have tried to ease tensions by saying that Daria’s diagnosis was just “pneumonia of unknown origin”.

But experts are clearly flummoxed over the cause of her infection.

She was said to have become ill after breaking a test tube at Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute where she worked earlier this week.

Three out of six hospitals in the nearest city Irkutsk are reported to be maintaining strict quarantine restrictions as a result.

University classes have been cancelled and workers at a giant aluminium smelter have been ordered to wear masks.

Three-week quarantine restrictions are also active at a nearby children’s hospital and at least one maternity hospital.



Relatives have been barred from wards with claims medical staff are privately “talking about plague” even though it has not officially been diagnosed.

The case has even been compared to the situation in China when Covid broke out.

There are fears that Russia is also covering up a major disease outbreak, with Rospotrebnadzor failing to even mention that Daria had died.



Officials said extensive tests on samples from the young scientist did not detect microorganisms linked to her work at the anti-plague institute.

They also claimed a probe found no accidents involving dangerous pathogens and a broken test-tube at the high-security laboratory.

Daria was said to have become infected after a tube containing the bacterium Yersinia pestis, triggering fears of pneumonic plague.

The highly dangerous lung form of the disease is caused by the same bacterium responsible for the medieval Black Death.

Putin’s chief infectious diseases doctor Anna Popova rushed 2,600 miles from Moscow to Irkutsk in Siberia to take personal charge of the emergency – but has remained silent.



Meanwhile, regional governor Igor Kobzev has refused to name what he called a “dangerous infectious disease”, as he cancelled mass events.

Residents expressed fury at his failure to explain the killer disease, while antibiotics have already run out in the region.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Officials insist the wider epidemiological situation remains stable, but have failed to explain why there is such a serious clampdown in place.



The last registered case of the plague in Russia was in 2016, where a 10-year-old boy who was skinning a marmot carcass became infected.

News.title: We live in UK’s ‘poshest’ area loved by Love Islanders where corner shops flog £4k drinks – but it’s all about to change
News.content:
POSH PADS We live in UK’s ‘poshest’ area loved by Love Islanders where corner shops flog £4k drinks – but it’s all about to change







Next

CELEBRITIES, Love Islanders and royals are spotted on the daily in the UK’s “poshest” area where even corner shop items cost thousands of pounds.

Flats cost up to £9million and come complete with spas, gyms, saunas and 24 hour security- but residents say it is all about to change as they are about to be charged thousands extra a year.



Battersea Power Station in South West London has become one of the fanciest postcodes in the UK with the average flat costing £1.5million – being dubbed the “poshest” area in the UK.

Since a £9billion transformation the area has become a gentrified haven, complete with a 289,283 square foot shopping centre, for the city’s flush and famous locals.



Residents boast to have caught glimpse of big names in the area including Gordon Ramsey, Romeo Beckham and Jesse Tyler Ferguson.

One local florist even said they’ve seen the King of Dubai walking around with armed police.



Even shopping at the corner shop costs a bomb with £4,000 bottles of red wine stocked on the shelves.

Battersea General Store, a Nisa partner corner shop in disguise, has everything a loaded Lover Islander might need.

They’ve got all sorts from Japanese whisky, kefir matcha and even mega sized Stanley pitchers.

Even the olive oil is just shy of £40, but most eye watering is the rare £4,250 Petrus Pomerol red wine.

Jay Jay, a worker at the joint, told The Sun: “All the celebrities are friendly, absolutely no snobbery.



“I can’t tell you who comes in here though, I’ve got to respect their privacy.

“They buy the high end stuff you can’t get in other places like special cereal.”

Just down the street is Feel Good, a coffee van where locals come to get their caffeine fix.



Barista Moe told The Sun he’s seen loads of celebrities wandering around.

He said: “We get lots of Love Islanders, there are loads of reality TV stars.

“We’ve had Gordon Ramsey pop up a few times and Romeo Beckham showed his face as well.

“There was also Jesse Tyler Ferguson from Modern Family and Jane Wall.

“From Love Island we’ve seen Casey O’Gorman, Luke T and Charlie Frederick.



“Casey ordered a flat white.”

Love Islanders Arabella Chi and Layla Al-Momani have both previously lived in the area.

The shopping centre draws in visitors from across the UK and even hosts the country’s biggest Zara.



One shopper, Vanessa, said: “It’s quite posh round here, it’s a little bit sterile.

“But I’m enjoying it, I like the Zara and on the whole it’s a nice experience.”

Connor works nearby and said: “It seems like a certain type of lifestyle. It doesn’t have much character because it’s all new builds.

“I haven’t seen any celebrities but apparently people have seen Harry Styles“

But trouble is brewing for residents as council tax is set to be ramped up along with service charges for living in Battersea Power Station flats.



Wandsworth Council is set to nearly double council tax rates from April 2027.

They say the hike will foot the bill for government funding cuts.

This means some residents of the multi-million Battersea Power Station flats, many of which fall into band H, will have to cough up an extra £1,916 a year.



This would mean an extra £7,500 annually for some Battersea residents.

The Sun spoke to estate agents Adam and Alex who reckon celebrities will stay put despite the ramping costs.

Adam said: “The area has brought in a lot of foreign investors and has created an amazing community.

“It’s better than it being a wasteland.”

Alex said: “My problem is I wouldn’t recognise a celebrity even if they walked past me.



“The council tax rise will only bring it into line with what other people pay, but it will be a big jump up for residents here.

“I just don’t know what it means, we both live in Wandsworth so we’re concerned about it.

“But the bigger aspect of these blocks isn’t council tax, it’s service charges.

“After Covid they’ve gone up because skilled workers have left the country since Brexit.

“It’s gone up by almost 50 per cent since Covid, that’s the problem not the council tax.”



Some locals were unhappy about the increase in costs.

One anonymous resident said: “It’s lovely, it’s very nice and very safe but it’s very busy these days and is becoming a bit too commercialised.

“It attracts way too many people.

“The council tax is doubling sadly which isn’t ideal but there’s not too much we can do about it.

“At least for the service charge you get bang for your buck with gyms, spas, pools and all that sort of stuff.



“Jenna Jackson’s agent lives here so we see Jenna working out in the gym.

“We used to live in Chelsea which is nice as well but we like the power station so won’t move out.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I’ve heard of many people leaving the city because of the rising cost, some have lived here for seven years.”

The Sun has contacted Wandsworth Council for comment.

News.title: Moment massive bear strolls through farmer’s market before clambering on stall and devouring baked goods
News.content:
Next

THIS is the unbelievable moment a massive bear wanders through a farmer’s market before jumping onto stalls and devouring baked goods.

Stunned shoppers stopped to gawk at the giant predator as it took a stroll through downtown Aspen and looked for a quick bite to eat.



Shocking footage showed the bear eventually settle for Louis Swiss Bakery’s array of artisanal baked goods spread out across three tables.

Standing on its hind legs, it sniffed around the array of pastries, sourdough loaves and baguettes not commonly found in the Colorado wilderness.



The bear began chowing down on its decadent morning snack before eventually being shooed away by police.

One clip showed it clamber onto one of the fold out tables before scampering away down the pavement.

The bear then wandered into a small park and scaled a tree outside of the ski resort’s Moncler store as an officer tried to gesture it away.

It eventually complied with police and went on its way, having only made a dent in the bakery stall’s stock.

Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) quipped: “Fat bear fall is here,” while warning locals of the predators starting to bulk up for their winter.

The agency continued: “Its real name is hyperphagia, but you can also call it a bear’s fall bulk, the great fall feast, or gorging oneself in hopes of getting the perfect winter bod.



“During this period, Colorado’s bears will spend up to 20 hrs/day trying to eat up to 20,000 calories!”

Black bears are omnivores who like to chow down on berries, nuts and insects, and are taught to forage by their mothers.

The CPW recorded a significant number of bear sightings and conflicts this year, with 6,129 encounters reported from January to mid-August.



Widespread drought in the area has caused natural resources such as berries and acorns to diminish, forcing bears to venture into human settlements in search of food, The Denver Post reported.

It comes after a hilarious video showed a family of four bears skillfully climb into a car in a brazen bid to steal snacks.

Wild footage showed five black bears approach the parked vehicle in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, before the mama bear simply opened the door.

Three cubs follow her inside one by one to rummage around, as a fourth saunters towards the vehicle.

The mama can then be seen carefully carrying a plastic bag of items in her mouth as she leaves the vehicle with her four children in tow.



The jaw-dropping footage was recorded by local Kathie Gentry who had just arrived at a women’s retreat with her church.

Kathie said that she and her friends were “startled” when the mama and her four cubs emerged from the nearby trees.

To the women’s surprise, the bears opened the door and entered the car, which belonged to Kathie’s friend.

One of the women tried beeping her horn to scare the bears, but they ignored it.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The bears walked off with one of the welcome bags, before later ditching it in the parking lot as it only had a single bag of potato chips inside.



Kathie said: “We were thankful they didn’t come to my car next, considering I had snacks and chocolate that I’m sure they would have enjoyed!”

News.title: Two kids aged 7 and 8 die after being electrocuted at fun run as 2 others rushed to hospital
News.content:
FUN-RUN TRAGEDY Two kids aged 7 and 8 die after being electrocuted at fun run as 2 others rushed to hospital







Next

TWO KIDS have died after being electrocuted at a fun run as two others are rushed to hospital.

The horror unfolded during a Color and Bubble Fun Run at a Cauayan City high school in the Philippines on Saturday morning.

The children, aged 7 and 8, were students at Cauayan South Central School and were tragically pronounced dead at the scene, reports Inquirer.net.

Two other children – aged 9 and 6 – were raced to Cauayan Medical Specialist Hospital and Cauayan District Hospital respectively.





The nine-year-old sustained injuries to his arm and hands but was later discharged.

Meanwhile, the six-year-old remains in hospital with their condition currently unknown.

The shocking incident is said to have been reported shortly before 6.30am that morning.

It’s reported the four children were playing near to a bubble-blowing machine when they were electrocuted.



Investigations remain ongoing into the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The country’s Department for Education said in a statement that it “expresses its deepest sympathies to the families and school community mourning the tragic loss of two learners”.

It read: “DepEd is taking the necessary steps to establish the facts surrounding the incident and is coordinating with the local government and law enforcement authorities.

“A fact-finding investigation is underway, including a review of the activity, safety measures, equipment used, and the roles of those involved.



“Appropriate action will be taken based on the findings.

“We ask everyone to respect the privacy of the affected children and their families and to refrain from sharing unverified information, names, photographs or videos”.

Cherry Ramos, Cauayan City Schools Division Superintendent, added they were “deeply saddened by the tragic incident”.

“We mourn the loss of two learners and extend our deepest sympathies to their families and our sincere concern and support to those affected,” she said.

Ramos said school officials are cooperating with the ongoing investigation.



She added: “We ask for compassion and understanding for the bereaved families and all those affected, and for their privacy to be to be respected during this difficult time.”

News.title: Man dies after being pulled from the sea ‘by five heroic locals’ at popular UK beach
News.content:
BEACH TRAGEDY Man dies after being pulled from the sea ‘by five heroic locals’ at popular UK beach







Next

A MAN has died after he was pulled from the sea at a popular UK beach.

Witnesses say a man was “dragged” out of the water by five people at Durley Chine Beach, Bournemouth, in Dorset this afternoon.

Influencer James Edward Lees helped in the rescue by running to get a defibrillator as others, including an off-duty cop, administered CPR to the man.

He told the Bournemouth Echo: “It’s really scary… I ran to get the defibrillator.





“It’s absolutely heart-breaking, I literally had to drag him out the water.”

Mr Lees added: “That is the scariest thing to see.

“I was just sitting over there minding my own business, and I saw the situation happening just there.

“I phoned the ambulance; they’re busy. Luckily, loads of people phoned. It took a few mins to get through to the ambulance and it took a little bit of time to explain where we are.

“I ran all the way up to get the defibrillator; I’ve never run so fast in my life.

“We’ve got the ambulance here now. I’m just giving them their space.

“But it’s absolutely shocking, it’s really frightening, it’s awful, absolutely awful. I hope he’s going to be okay.”Dorset Police have confirmed the man has died.

Local reports say emotions were running high at the scene with people visibly upset and shocked, with some saying they are struggling to process events.



Around 10 emergency vehicles attended, along with the coastguard and ambulance crews.

A helicopter could also be seen circling above the area.

A spokesperson for Dorset Police said: “We received a report at 4.13pm on Sunday, October 4 of a man requiring medical attention at Bournemouth beach near to the pier.

“Emergency services attended and, very sadly, the man was pronounced dead at the scene.

“His family is aware. His death is not being treated as suspicious.



“Our thoughts are with the man’s family and friends at this very difficult time.”

News.title: Man, 24, fighting for life after being found shot outside police station in early hours of the morning
News.content:
SHOOTING PROBE Man, 24, fighting for life after being found shot outside police station in early hours of the morning







Next

A MAN is fighting for his life after being found shot outside a police station in the early hours of the morning.

Officers were scrambled to reports of a shooting at around 3.45am on Saturday in Wembley, London.



Cops said a 24-year-old man was later found outside Wembley police station with gunshot injuries.

The man was raced to hospital where he is understood to be in critical condition.



No arrests have yet been made as cops launch an investigation into the shocking incident.

The Met Police has urged any witnesses or anyone with information to come forward.



Detective Superintendent Tony Bellis said: “We are investigating a firearms incident in Wembley, which has left a 24-year-old man in a critical condition.

“Officers were called to reports of a shooting at 03:45hrs on Saturday, October 3 on Douglas Avenue.

“Later, a man was found outside Wembley Police Station suffering from gunshot wounds.

“Police administered emergency first aid and he was later taken to hospital by the London Ambulance Service, where he remains.



“Enquiries remain ongoing and no arrests have been made at this stage.

“I understand this has caused concern in the local community in Wembley, there will be an increased police presence in the area in the coming days.

“I would urge anyone who has any information, or as in the area at the time, to call police on 101 quoting reference 1115/ЗOСТ. Information can also be provided anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.”

The Sun has contacted London Ambulance Service for comment.

News.title: Russia vows ‘massive strikes’ on Ukraine as German leader visits Kyiv after Putin blasts bridge for second time in 24hrs
News.content:
Next

RUSSIA has vowed to launch “massive strikes” on Kyiv as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visits the Ukrainian capital.

A giant fireball explosion hit the city’s key Northern Bridge today after an attack by a long-range Russian drone.



Shocking pictures appeared to show cars on the crossing being hit, with drivers navigating flames and blast craters.

Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed that emergency services were deployed to the scene, bringing traffic towards Kyiv‘s right bank to a standstill.



It was the second strike in two days on the Northern Bridge, coming amid a campaign by Putin to disrupt life in the city.

Kyiv is now reportedly preparing pontoon bridges across the Dnipro River in case Russia destroys the existing bridges.

The Kremlin has until now mostly avoided attacking the city when senior Western leaders or officials have visited.

A defiant Merz arrived by train today for talks with Volodymyr Zelensky, despite the Russian Foreign Ministry warning Westerners to avoid travelling to Ukraine.

The German Chancellor was accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and executives from German defence and energy companies.

Merz confirmed that Germany will give €1billion (£850m) in military aid plus €350million (£297m) for energy repairs at a press conference today.



He also signed a joint Ukrainian-German agreement to produce drones and long-range weapons.

Writing on X, Merz said: “Germany is helping Ukraine. But Ukraine is also helping us – with its expertise, for example in drone defence, but also with contracts worth billions for German industry.

“Today we signed agreements to that effect. This partnership is not a one-way street.”



It comes as Russia said it will intensify its military strikes on Kyiv and the rest of Ukraine.

The threat came after Zelensky said yesterday that Ukraine would double down on attacking Russia’s oil refineries.

The Kremlin said that the Ukrainian leader “bears full personal and political responsibility” for the fresh strikes.

Washington has meanwhile proposed that the warring nations hold fresh peace talks within weeks, according to Zelensky.

He said that a “trilateral meeting at the technical level” has been suggested by the Americans in the hopes of finally reaching a breakthrough.



US negotiators including Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff have made several unsuccessful attempts to reach a peace deal.

Zelensky said: “Yesterday, I spoke with the American negotiating team.

“Today, the American side is in contact with both Ukraine and Russia and is proposing a trilateral meeting at the technical level by the end of October.



“Yesterday, I confirmed to them that our side is ready to support holding such a meeting by the end of October. There is no new information here.”

He added: “We are open to the United Arab Emirates or another country proposed by the American side.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I know they will propose this to the Russian side as well, or may have already done so.

“We will wait for the response. We respond positively to negotiations.”

News.content:

'KIDNAP' PROBE Man, 19, arrested on suspicion of child abduction after boy, 13, vanished for four days







Next

A MAN has been arrested on suspicion of child abduction after a teenage boy vanished for four days.

Kairo, 13, was reported missing after they were last spotted leaving an address in Bournemouth, Dorset on Wednesday morning.

Dorset Police launched an urgent search for the teenager after he vanished from the Windham Road area at around 8.40am.

But in an update on Sunday, the force said officers had safely located the 13-year-old.





A 19-year-old man, from Christchurch, has now been arrested in connection with the incident.

He currently remains in police custody with enquiries into the incident ongoing.

News.title: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' motion
News.content:
Green Party members have adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, in a move that has divided senior figures at the top of the party.

The party's joint deputy leaders have been at odds over the subject, with Mothin Ali backing the move, and Rachel Millward describing the wording as "problematic".

Activists endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of members at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1022 votes to 813.

Discussion about the vote has dominated the conference, and exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under leader Zack Polanski and its MPs elected at the last election.

The motion adopted by Green members defines Zionism as an ideology in support of "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

"The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it says.

It has attracted criticism from some Jewish groups, including the Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council.

In a letter to the party sent ahead of the vote, the organisations said Zionism was an anti-racist movement, adding that "modern Zionism was formed in part as a response to antisemitism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."

The letter also raised concerns about the safety of Jewish members in the Green Party, as well as the implications for Jewish institutions in areas represented by the Greens.

Israel's Foreign Ministry said the motion went beyond "the boundaries of legitimate political debate" and was "a stain on the history of the United Kingdom".

Debate about the motion, as well as the conflict in Gaza, has featured heavily during the conference, which is taking place after a surge in its membership in the wake of Polanski's election as leader in September last year.

Speaking after the vote, Lubna Speitan, the Green member behind the motion, argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression".

"We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions," she added.

Polanski himself did not vote in the debate, having left the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here.

News.title: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch
News.content:
Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and a 100 page statement on her guiding principles., external

"I believe in common sense, people working hard and being rewarded for that effort," she told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.

She added that welfare should be a "safety net, not a lifestyle".

The Tory leader is trying to ensure her party stands out in a crowded political field. The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in the opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than that of her party, has characterised Reform leader Nigel Farage as a "grumpy grandpa" and she told Laura Kuenssberg that Labour leader Andy Burnham is "the cheesy uncle who does all the dad jokes".

She described herself as a "no-nonsense mum".

Asked if her plan for benefit cuts and a massive increase in prison places was a return to the "nasty party" of the past, she said: "It's the common sense party. That's what we're doing.

"And, quite frankly, if we were doing so well the old way, then why did we have such a terrible issue in 2024?"

In her essay The Right Way - a deliberate echo of an essay written by Margaret Thatcher in 1976, external entitled The Right Approach - Badenoch says the last Conservative government failed because it did not know what it stood for.

Despite the party's rhetoric during its 14 years in power, she said: "We did little to reverse the structural changes Labour had made which took the country in the wrong direction.

"The result was that the state grew by stealth."

The essay says the "next Conservative government will have one central principle: business, not government, creates growth".

The Tories would achieve growth through tax cuts, cutting red tape and reducing the size of the civil service back to pre-pandemic levels, the essay says.

And it adds: "What is really missing from politics and government today is people prepared to say no.

"Political parties now need to recruit those who have the stomach to say no to good causes when the resources simply are not there to do everything."

News.title: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues
News.content:
The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.

The measures include plans for longer opening hours, as well as an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.

A museum spokesperson said the public response to the 11th Century embroidery had been "extraordinary", but acknowledged that some visitors had waited longer than they would have wanted.

Some people reported waits of up to two hours, while hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early last week due to a private event.

Some ticket holders took to social media to complain about the disruption.

One disappointed visitor said the trip had been a "big event" they had looked forward to, while another wrote she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux Tapestry, and bought tickets only to be turned away after queuing.

The museum later apologised to those who had been unable to enter and said they would be issued refunds and priority booking slots for a rearranged time.

From Monday, visitors will be offered an audio guide with more information about the embroidery, while additional signage and seating will be provided for those queuing to reach the main exhibition.

The museum said it planned to introduce longer opening hours to prevent queues building during the day and allow people with later bookings more time to view the exhibition.

Details of the extended hours have not yet been disclosed.

News.title: Glastonbury 2027 tickets sell out in 42 minutes
News.content:
Tickets for Glastonbury Festival 2027 sold out in 42 minutes, organisers have said.

Thousands of people joined the online queue at 09:00 BST in the hope of securing tickets to the festival at Worthy Farm in Somerset, which returns from 23 to 27 June after a fallow year.

Organisers confirmed last month that tickets for the weekend were at their highest price ever - Â£408, including a Â£5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of Â£29.50 from the last event in 2025.

Headliners have yet to be announced but organiser Emily Eavis previously said the team was "very excited" and things were "coming together really well".

Glastonbury posted on Instagram shortly after 09:40 to announce that tickets had sold out, and notified those who were in the queue.

"Thank you to everyone who bought one and we're sorry to those of you who missed out on a morning where demand greatly exceeded supply," the post said.

"There will be a resale of any cancelled or returned tickets in Spring 2027."

News.title: Courts backlog will fall despite scrapping of jury trial plan, minister says
News.content:
The courts backlog will still fall despite plans to curb jury trials being scrapped, the justice secretary has told the BBC.

Alex Norris said introducing legislation for judge-only trials "was always going to be the most complicated to implement" and would have slowed down reforms.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's decision abandons proposals introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government to allow judges in England and Wales to make the sole decision on cases that would lead to a sentence of less than three years.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said only complex fraud and financial offences would be judge-only - and it proposes thousands of medium-level crimes should stay with volunteer magistrates, who sit without a jury.

Norris told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the backlog would start falling "in this Parliament", but would not say by how much.

He said it would fall significantly over the next decade "as a result of the changes we're making".

The Conservatives said it was a "major victory" for those who fought to defend trial by jury, while criminal lawyers welcomed the decision but voiced concern about the implications of abolishing a defendant's right to ask for a jury trial.

The Criminal Bar Association (CBA) warned this would keep more middle-ranking cases before magistrates and shift 25,000 cases a year onto magistrates' courts.

Former justice secretary David Lammy first announced the plans to curb jury trials in December following a recommendation in a major review of the court system in England and Wales.

The series of radical reforms, including scaling back jury trials, were presented as the best way of turning around record backlogs which, in turn, were exacerbating the prison population crisis.

The backlog - which has led to record delays for defendants and victims - currently stands at nearly 81,000 cases, having rocketed largely thanks to cuts before the pandemic and court closures during national lockdowns.

News.title: Daughter of MP murdered five years ago tells BBC politicians still at risk
News.content:
Separately, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch confirmed to the BBC the man who pleaded guilty to sending her threatening messages also sent them to her family.

Kieran Kyle, 43, pleaded guilty to two counts of sending communication of an indecent or offensive nature to Badenoch and her family when he appeared in court in September. He will be sentenced on October 29.

"I just think that whether it's Nigel Farage, or even Keir Starmer who had his home fire bombed, that there is a threat to politicians that is increasing and we just need to crack down on this," she told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

Asked how Badenoch coped with threats to her safety, she replied: "it's really tough, but you just have to get on with it".

Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told the BBC he also experienced threats to his safety, told the programme "this was far from where any of us want to be".

"We have to find the middle ground where we're accessible but we're protected and in the overall scheme of things if that requires a bit of extra taxpayers' money, I think hopefully voters would say 'yes'."

Amess said her father "loved meeting people", saying "he was one of the easier members of parliament to take a meeting with because that's what he lived for - to meet people, shake their hands, smile, help them with their problems. My dad wouldn't have wanted constituency surgeries to stop."

She added that he would have wanted to be alerted to someone being reported as a potential threat.

His killer, Ali Harbi Ali had been referred to the government's counter-terror programme Prevent in October 2014 but his case was closed in 2016.

A review published in February 2025 found Ali's Prevent case was closed too early after "problematic" assessments.

News.title: Wales' Elfyn Evans wins his first World Rally Championship
News.content:
Elfyn Evans became Britain's first world rally champion for 25 years after rival Oliver Solberg crashed in a highly dramatic finish to the season in Italy.

Sweden's Solberg was on course to snatch the lead on the final stage of the last round of the World Rally Championship, and thereby deny Evans the title.

But Solberg lost control of his car with less than 100 metres to go of the Rally Italia Sardegna, which meant the glory went to Welshman Evans, a five-time runner-up in the championship.

"It hasn't sunk in," said a shocked Evans.

"I was sure it was over. I feel for Oliver - he had an incredible weekend. I don't know what to say."

The 37-year-old and co-driver Scott Martin had led for much of the 2026 season and took a 21-point advantage into the final round in Sardinia.

But that gap had shrunk to a solitary point by the time the drivers lined up for the last of 17 stages, bringing back painful memories of previous narrow misses for Evans.

Solberg, 25, needed only to beat his Toyota team-mate in the final stage to claim enough bonuses to be champion, but he crashed two corners from the finish.

Evans becomes only the third British man to win the WRC title after Colin McRae in 1995 and Richard Burns in 2001.

News.title: Why Canada is preparing for an unlikely US invasion
News.content:
Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.

He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.

"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.

Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.

So what would it be like if it happened?

The first phase of a war could be quite short.

According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week

Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.

Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.

The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.

The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.

He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.

Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.

An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.

Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.

"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.

"They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."

Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.

But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.

"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.

Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

News.title: Sinn Féin will co-operate with PSNI investigation over Drumcree protest, says McDonald
News.content:
Sinn FÃ©in will co-operate with the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) over any potential investigation into the protest on the Garvaghy Road, the party president has said.

Protesters have remained on the Garvaghy Road since Sunday 27 September as the fallout over the proposed Portadown District Orange Lodge march continues, and rallies on both sides of the dispute were held on Saturday.

Mary Lou McDonald has said that "there's no question with us co-operating with any process that will unfold".

Speaking on Sunday, Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson said police confirmed to them that Saturday's gathering on the Garvaghy Road was "unnotified" and police were "taking evidence".

McDonald and Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill are among those who have attended the protest, which police have described as unnotified and "therefore illegal".

The Portadown District has maintained a presence at Drumcree Church after talks to end the parading dispute ended without agreement on Thursday.

Orangemen attempted to march again on Sunday morning.

News.title: Missing woman found 'safe and well' after appeal
News.content:
A missing woman has been found safe and well after a police appeal to find her.

Leicestershire Police said Charlie Ryan was reported missing on Friday morning.

The force said the 31-year-old was found in the Leicester area on Sunday.

Officers thanked the public for sharing their appeal and contacting them with information.

News.title: Family of teenager killed in crash to sue acquitted driver
News.content:
The family of a teenager killed in a car crash near Stirling two years ago are launching a civil case against the driver who was cleared of causing death by careless driving.

Kyle Marshall, 19, and Jayden McConnell, 17, died when a car driven by Charles Gray spun out of control and into the path of a lorry on the A91 near Bannockburn Interchange in March 2024.

Gray, who had passed his test a month earlier, was acquitted of causing the deaths of his two friends after a five-day trial at Stirling Sheriff Court last November.

According to the Scottish Sun,, external the Marshall family are now suing Gray for a six-figure sum, alleging negligence.

A spokesman for Digby Brown, the law firm representing the Marshall family, confirmed: "A civil action has now been raised in the Court of Session on behalf of the loved ones of Kyle to help them secure answers, support and recognition.

"It would be inappropriate to comment further at this time however we will continue to support the Marshall family during this time."

News.title: Medieval leprosy hospital uncovered in Lincoln
News.content:
The walls of what is thought to be one of medieval England's earliest and largest leprosy hospitals have been uncovered in Lincoln by Time Team archaeologists.

A three-day dig started on Friday on the South Common at the site of the Hospital of the Holy Innocents, which housed up to 20 people with leprosy around the late 11th to early 12th Centuries.

Time Team's Prof Carenza Lewis said they had found traces of square features where it is thought people were housed, which "haven't been excavated before, anywhere".

The dig marks the beginning of a three-year project backed by the National Lottery Heritage Fund.

The remains of the building were found last year during a Local Landscapes and Hidden Histories project.

More than 100 volunteers were involved in excavating test pits which uncovered what were thought to be the medieval boundary walls of the hospital.

News.title: Train station returning to village after more than 100 years
News.content:
Work is beginning on bringing a train station back to the heart of a Greater Manchester village more than a century after its original station closed.

Cheadle in Stockport had a station just off the high street up until 1917.

Funding for a new hub, which would be built next to Alexandra Hospital, was given the green light in 2022, with planning permission granted in 2023 but concerns about its effect on the timetabling of trains elsewhere on the network led to delays.

Stockport Council said the issue had now been resolved and council leader Mark Roberts said it was "a hugely significant moment for Cheadle and for Stockport".

"For years we've fought for this station because we know the difference it will make to residents, businesses and the future prosperity of the area," he added.

Roberts said he was delighted that the initial highways work could now start on site thanks to the persistence and partnership of all involved.

Services are expected to run from Cheadle into Stockport town, Manchester Piccadilly and Chester, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

The project had been held up by an unresolved timetabling issue over concerns the new station could impact trains elsewhere on the network, with a previous proposal made to remove services at Ashley and Plumley.

Stockport Council said the latest assessment by Network Rail and Northern Trains concluded that Cheadle Station could be introduced without removing a significant barrier that had put the project at risk and these plans have now been dropped.

News.title: Porridge makers from opposite sides of globe triumph in world championship
News.content:
The contest rules only allow three ingredients - oats, water and salt.

She only started adding salt to her porridge ahead of the competition, but quickly realised it "really brings out the nuances and different aromas".

She believes her secret weapon may have been the water which she brought with her from her home city.

"It's very soft, and I think the mineral content may have something to do with it. I'm not sure - but it worked last time and this time as well, so maybe it's the water".

In the Speciality Porridge category, Rob, from Sydney, came up with his recipe just a few weeks before competing in the Australian national porridge championships - the Pearly Spurtle - after realising how seriously everyone was taking it.

Tapping into his family heritage - his father is Scottish and his mother is Sicilian - he decided to make a porridge cannoli.

"I then had to engineer it," the 36-year-old told BBC Scotland News.

The cream uses the traditional mix of ricotta, mascarpone and sugar but he blended in porridge, sieved it and added some ground toasted oats.

It provides the filling for shells, made like brandy snaps but using Sicilian Marsala wine instead.

News.title: Man rescued after car crashes into house
News.content:
A man had to be rescued by firefighters from a house that partially collapsed after a car crashed into it.

Police officers, paramedics and firefighters were called to the property on Ninefields, in Waltham Abbey, Essex shortly before 23:00 BST on Friday.

Upon arrival, they found a silver Skoda, which had smoke coming out of it, that had smashed into the corner of a house, leaving it badly damaged.

Essex Police said a man was arrested on suspicion of being unfit through drink or drugs and taken to hospital for treatment.

Another man was safely removed from the rear of the property by fire crew using a ladder, while a woman was also taken to hospital for a "precautionary assessment."

News.title: Debris in engine very likely caused Spitfire crash
News.content:
Debris which had been present in the carburettor of a Spitfire for decades was "very likely" the cause of a crash in which a pilot died, according to a report.

Sqn Ldr Mark Long was killed when the Battle of Britain Memorial Flight (BBMF) plane he was flying crashed in a field in Lincolnshire on 25 May 2024.

A report published by the Ministry of Defence says the debris was responsible for causing fuel starvation, "leading to a loss of thrust required to maintain powered flight".

Just 56 seconds after taking off from RAF Coningsby, witnesses saw the plane turn and plunge to the ground.

Long, who was born in Bury St Edmunds, was flying a Spitfire Mk IX, built in 1944, operated by the RAF's BBMF for commemorative flypasts and displays.

The opening of an inquest heard the provisional cause of his death was head and neck injuries.

The Service Inquiry report, external said chemical analysis revealed evidence that indicated the debris in the carburettor "had been present for decades".

It said: "The presence of multiple, contradictory publications created ambiguity over the correct procedures for carburettor maintenance.

"The panel assessed that this inconsistency likely led to varying interpretations of how extensively the carburettor should have been dismantled, inspected and cleaned, which was very likely to have reduced the reliability of detecting any debris build-up."

The design of the cockpit and restraint were identified as aggravating factors, but the report acknowledged any structural design change would likely require "significant moderations".

"This would not only affect the historic authenticity of the aircraft but would possibly affect overall airworthiness due to a change in aircraft mass and balance," the report said.

Twenty-six safety recommendations were included in the report, including improved maintenance records, reviews of cockpit protection and better training for emergencies.

The report described the recommendations as "robust" and said they "should minimise the likelihood of a recurrence or similar tragedy".

Strictly Come Dancing has eliminated its first contestant from the 2026 series: celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton.

After a week without any public voting, everything changed on Saturday night (3 October) when viewers at home were allowed to pick up their phones and cast their votes for the first time this year.

After the scores were tallied, it was announced that Appleton and his partner Amy Dowden would face Kidulthood actor Jaime Winstone and her partner Carlos Gu in the dreaded dance-off.

Appleton and his partner performed their Cha Cha to “I’ll Be Ready” from Baywatch, while Winstone and Gu repeated their Cha Cha to Roy Orbison’s “Oh, Pretty Woman” from Pretty Woman. The judges ultimately opted to save Winstone and keep him in the competition.

Head judge Shirley Ballas and judges Motsi Mabuse and Anton Du Beke all voted to save Winstone and Gu, meaning Craig Revel Horwood did not need to use his casting vote. However, he said he would have voted the same way when asked by hosts Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe.

Sunday night’s results show also featured a Devil Wears Prada routine from the Strictly professionals – featuring Motsi Mabuse and Craig Revel Horwood – plus a special performance from Matilda The Musical, with the four young performers who play Matilda taking to the stage to sing “Quiet” alongside composer Tim Minchin.

Chris Appleton has become the first celebrity to be eliminated from 'Strictly Come Dancing' ( PA )

The elimination marks the second year that professional Amy Dowden has been in the first couple to leave the dance competition, after her divisive celebrity partner Thomas Skinner was voted off the show in 2025.

Appleton, 43, is used to working behind-the-scenes on the biggest stars’ barnets, with the Brit styling the likes of Britney Spears, Kim Kardashian, Jennifer Lopez, Ariana Grande and others. He recently make the New York Times Best Seller list with his memoir, Your Roots Don’t Define You.

Ahead of his elimination, the hair stylist had said he was “thrilled” to join the Strictly Come Dancing line up. His addition also triggered rumours that Kardashian could be in the audience for his first performance. However, the reality star did not materialise.

Next week, the remaining fourteen couples will take to the dance floor to fight to keep their place in the competition.

Strictly returns at 6:15pm on Saturday, 10 October on BBC One

Aaron Sorkin says “it never occurred” to him that Jesse Eisenberg would not be joining him on The Social Reckoning.

The Oscar-winning screenwriter has previously said that he spent three days trying to convince Eisenberg to reprise his role as Mark Zuckerberg from the 2010 hit The Social Network for its sequel, but that the actor was not persuaded by anything — especially not money.

“I knew what the studio was offering him to do it, but money does not motivate Jesse. It’s infuriating,” Sorkin told Entertainment Weekly in an interview published Saturday. “If anything, money is a disincentive for him. It’s admirable. He’s very concerned about raising his kids with too much money.”

Sorkin, who is stepping in to direct The Social Reckoning after David Fincher helmed the 2010 film, said that he was close to finishing the script for the new movie when he ran into Eisenberg at a party and told him that he planned to send it to him.

Eisenberg “smiled and nodded, and I sent it to him,” Sorkin said. “It never occurred to me that he wouldn’t want to do it.”

open image in gallery Aaron Sorkin said it 'never occurred' to him that Jesse Eisenberg would turn down 'The Social Reckoning' ( Getty Images )

open image in gallery Jeremy Strong is succeeding Jesse Eisenberg in the role of Mark Zuckerberg for 'The Social Reckoning' ( Sony/Columbia Pictures )

Over the next three days, Sorkin said that he planned his arguments to convince the Oscar-nominated actor to change his mind. “This is the only time I’ve written myself an outline. I don’t do it for the movies, but I did it for my conversations with Jesse,” he said.

“It was arguments for why he should do it. They included, ‘We already know you’re going to be great because you were already once.’ You know, ‘Here are the great moments that you’re gonna get to play in the movie.’ And I laid it out for him,” Sorkin recalled.

In the end, Eisenberg still ended up turning down the role. However, Sorkin said that he told him that their conversations made him “come closer to changing my mind than I thought you were going to,” which the screenwriter said was enough for him.

open image in gallery Jesse Eisenberg starred in the 2010 film ‘The Social Network,’ which was written by Aaron Sorkin ( Getty Images )

Jeremy Strong will be taking over for Eisenberg in the role of Zuckerberg for Sorkin’s new movie, which comes out October 9. The movie also stars Mikey Madison and Jeremy Allen White.

When asked about declining the role, the A Real Pain actor also reflected on his conversations with Sorkin, but concluded that he no longer wants “to be associated with that character.”

“It’s an honor to speak to Aaron in any capacity, because he’s so articulate and charming and so bright,” Eisenberg told Variety in June.

“We talked about doing the movie for several days,” he said. “The way Aaron speaks, he speaks so wonderfully, as he writes, that, in a way, if you’re not going to do something with him, it feels almost like you’re letting down America.”

He continued: “I just told him I'm moving in different directions in my life, and you know, what he said sums it up nicely: I don't want to be associated with that character. But all of my reasons for not wanting to do the movie have nothing to do with how wonderful the movie is, and will be, and I’m sure is already.”

A Laotian citizen deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration's immigration crackdown was released from a maximum security prison in the African nation on Sunday after being held there for more than a year, his lawyer said.

Phone Chomsavanh was among five immigrants deported to Eswatini — where he has no ties — in July 2025 in the early days of the Trump administration's secretive and highly contentious third-country deportation program.

Chomsavanh's U.S.-based lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said in a statement announcing his release that he had only been informed that he was being deported to Eswatini shortly before a military cargo plane carrying him and other deportees landed there more than 14 months ago.

Chomsavanh was now being deported to Laos, Nguyen said.

Chomsavanh and the four other immigrants he was deported to Eswatini with were convicted of serious crimes in the U.S., but had served their sentences by the time they were sent to the Matsapha Correctional Complex near Eswatini's administrative capital, Mbabane.

“Years after he finished serving his sentence in the United States, the Trump administration flew him to the small southern African kingdom and handed him over to a maximum-security prison, where he was held for more than a year without ever being charged with a crime,” Nguyen said.

He said in separate messages to The Associated Press that Chomsavanh had left Eswatini and landed in Johannesburg en route to Laos.

An Eswatini government spokesperson didn’t immediately acknowledge Chomsavanh’s release.

Chomsavanh was born in a refugee camp in Thailand after his parents fled Laos, and his family moved to the United States when he was 7, his lawyer said.

Chomsavanh is one of around 500 immigrants who have been deported from the United States to African countries that aren't their home nations since the third-country program began last year, according to rights group Human Rights First, which has been monitoring the deportations.

Around a dozen African countries have accepted third-country deportees from the U.S., some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments. Eswatini, which is Africa's last absolute monarchy and is ruled by a king, was paid $5.1 million by the Trump administration to take deportees, according to the agreement between the countries. Eswatini has received around 30 deportees so far.

The program, which results in immigrants being held in countries they have no ties with and where they haven't been charged with any crime, has been fiercely criticized by rights groups and lawyers. It has been the subject of legal challenges in the U.S. and in some of the countries where immigrants have been sent.

The Trump administration has defended the policy as a way to quickly remove immigrants who have final deportation orders from the U.S. when their home countries might not immediately take them back.

Last month, a U.S. appeals court upheld a judge's ruling to halt the program, because it didn't give immigrants facing removal from the U.S. time to challenge their deportation to a third country because they fear persecution or torture there.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled last week to temporarily allow U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to continue swiftly removing immigrants to third countries, though it will hear arguments in the case in December.

The program has largely been carried out in secrecy, with little transparency over how many immigrants have been deported to third countries, and where and in what conditions they are being held.

The Conservative Party that meets for its conference in Birmingham this week is in better spirits than at any time since they lost the last general election.

That, obviously, is a low bar, given that the debacle represented their poorest electoral performance since the Great Reform Act of 1832, and seemingly consigned them to the wilderness for years, if not decades.

However, the poisoned chalice that was passed to Kemi Badenoch by Rishi Sunak two years ago seems only to have invigorated her and her followers. Threatened with extinction, they have regained at least their composure, if not all their old born-to-rule swagger.

After an uncertain start during which she was patronised by Sir Keir Starmer and subjected to malicious speculation by her own colleagues about her future, the leader of the opposition has made remarkably strong progress with the public.

She now enjoys much improved recognition and rising personal ratings, while the reputations of the other principal opposition party chiefs – Nigel Farage, Ed Davey and Zack Polanski – are becoming tarnished.

She has seen off her more troublesome internal rivals and critics, such as Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman, in what she cheekily calls some “spring cleaning”.

Over the past year she has also dispatched Sir Keir, scored some notable victories (the Mandelson scandal and the Chagos deal), and made the most of the many misfortunes of the Labour government.

She has come to sometimes dominate prime minister’s questions, though she is yet to get the measure of Andy Burnham.

On her right flank, Mr Farage and Reform UK have crumpled in the face of the kind of legitimate media scrutiny that any party with aspirations to govern should expect.

The comfortable polling lead Reform once enjoyed over the Tories has been squeezed; and, for the first time in half a century, the Tories managed to win a parliamentary by-election in Scotland, a small but significant breakthrough for morale well beyond Aberdeen South.

A recent refresh of her shadow ministers has promoted some young talent, and MPs such as Tom Tugendhat are deservedly back on the front line – though the sacking of Mel Stride as shadow chancellor has deprived the team of experience and a leading figure with an appeal to the kind of centre-ground voters they need to attract back from Labour and the Liberal Democrats.

open image in gallery Threatened with extinction, the Conservatives have regained at least their composure, if not all their old born-to-rule swagger ( Getty )

Ms Badenoch is thus clearly in command of her party, and has endowed it with a measure of that most precious of political commodities – momentum.

It is not her fault that their poll ratings remain below where Mr Sunak left them – a whole collection of tawdry past Tory politicians have to take responsibility for that.

The party’s image was so trashed by the time the British people ejected them from office in 2024 that it was always going to take time to repair the damage, as Ms Badenoch has rightly pleaded.

What has happened now is that the moment of maximum danger, of Reform UK totally eclipsing them as the main party on the Right of British politics, has passed. The Conservatives are starting – but only starting – to look more like a viable party of government.

They certainly look preferable when set next to Mr Farage’s band of cryptocurrency-fuelled “fruitcakes, loonies and closet racists”, as David Cameron once derided them.

In the next phase of her leadership Ms Badenoch needs to develop policy, particularly on the economy – and, more problematically for her, on Brexit.

In recent days there have been announcements from the Tories about proposed changes to taxation, childcare and social security as well as on building more prisons.

These have not been entirely convincing – the costings and details remain sketchy – and they give the unfortunate impression that the only people the Conservatives are interested in are pensioners (the triple lock being sacrosanct) and those on six-figure salaries.

Neither can the Tories sustain the pretence that society’s ills can be solved by locking up more criminals, deporting asylum seekers and abolishing the Human Rights Act. The public will not buy that.

There is as yet little sign that the Conservatives are treating the social care and housing crises with the seriousness that the prime minister is, and it is difficult to discern any distinctive messaging on the NHS, schools and boosting productivity and growth beyond tax cuts for business owners and cutting international aid.

Ms Badenoch has always preferred to travel light on policy, but the rumours that she wants a party manifesto ready in case Mr Burnham calls a snap election suggests she knows that she now needs to move much more quickly on developing her plan for government.

This week’s conference will no doubt start to fill in some of the many blanks, but doubts about whether the Tories can be trusted to deliver will remain. Nowhere is the Tories’ credibility more fragile than on Brexit, a decision that is now so regretted and so unpopular with the British people.

This is where Labour has spotted an opportunity and taken the initiative on re-opening the debate – and it places the Tories in the awkward position of defending something that is so disliked but with which they are inextricably linked. They, after all, “got Brexit done” – how can they now disown it?

Whatever was the case in Boris Johnson’s time, being the party of Brexit is no longer an asset, simply because leaving the EU has proved so disastrous.

Ms Badenoch herself was a minor but enthusiastic Leaver during the referendum campaign a decade ago, and seems just as committed to this albatross as ever.

She would be wise to re-evaluate her stance, and not trying to pretend that Britain will be richer and happier if it stays isolated from its major trading, diplomatic and, increasingly, military partners – unwilling even to consider a better, closer relationship with European allies.

The Conservative and Unionist party should at least place great weight on anything that strengthens the position of Scotland and Northern Ireland in the UK, and that necessarily means a closer connection with the EU.

The secret of the Tories’ long historic success lay in their instinct for what’s been called lethal pragmatism – letting nothing get in the way of the pursuit of power.

That is how they recovered from crashing general election defeats before, notably in 1906 and 1945. Failed personalities and once cherished policies were summarily ditched in wholesale acts of renewal.

Ms Badenoch would like to restore her party to office, and she insists it can be done within the span of this parliament.

She cites the example of Labour after 2019, and it is also true that the British electorate is more volatile than in the past – which makes a Lazarus-style recovery more plausible.

Yet the Tories’ ideological attachment to Brexit is an insuperable obstacle on Ms Badenoch’s path to the premiership. Reportedly, she prefers to downplay the issue and not to talk about it. She will not be able to do that for much longer.

Saints veteran defensive end Cameron Jordan's first exposure to the epic displacement caused by Hurricane Katrina occurred when a group of new students from New Orleans arrived at his high school in the Phoenix suburb of Chandler, Arizona.

“Katrinians,” the 37-year-old Jordan said after a recent practice. “That’s what we called them."

Five years later, Jordan arrived in New Orleans as a 2011 first-round draft choice and participated in community service projects at properties still scarred by storm damage.

“I think about the city I came to,” Jordan said, “and how much we’ve grown since then.”

The Saints (1-2) had an extra day this past week to prepare for Monday night's game against the Atlanta Falcons (1-2). They used it to educate players — many of whom were toddlers in 2006 — about the Saints' Week 3 Monday night game against the Falcons 20 years ago.

The “Domecoming,” as it's known in New Orleans, is best remembered for Steve Gleason's block of the game's first punt. Curtis Deloatch recovered the ball in the end zone and reverse-dunked it over the goal post (which was permitted back then) as the crowd unleashed an explosive, cathartic roar — a moment Gleason would say felt like “infinite joy.”

The stadium, used as a shelter of last resort, was damaged by Katrina, contaminated by mold and left in foul-smelling squalor after thousands of evacuees were stuck there — surrounded by flooded streets — for days without power or plumbing. It was closed for 13 months and underwent extensive, fast-tracked repairs before it could welcome back fans, many of whom were still rebuilding their own homes.

Saints coach Kellen Moore gathered the team for a team-produced video about Katrina and the dome's reopening, hoping it would help players appreciate the “unique connection between our city and our football team."

"It’s very much one, very much tied together,” Moore said.

“You see the different videos and recognize streets that we all drive on nowadays and those different things," Moore continued. "They recognize and realize the impact that it had.”

Quarterback Tyler Shough said he teared up while seeing the images of devastation and listening to longtime team employees and former Saints players discuss their memories of Katrina's aftermath.

“It was emotional,” Shough said. “You really feel just how important the Saints are and how important our work is."

Gleason, who has been living ALS for more than a decade, is set to be an honored guest Monday night. So is Hall of Fame quarterback Drew Brees, who'd been acquired by the Saints as an injured free agent less than a year after the storm and was playing his first home game in New Orleans on that Monday night 20 years ago, leading the Saints to a 23-3 triumph.

Gleason's block is immortalized in a bronze statue named “Rebirth” on an exterior Superdome plaza. There also is a larger-than-life poster of Gleason's block on a wall inside the Saints' indoor practice field.

Longtime fans joke that the play might have set a record for simultaneously spilled beverages as fans jumped from their seats, yelled with everything they had, danced, hugged and even cried as the spray of whatever they were drinking rained down on them.

Then-"Monday Night Football" play-by-play announcer Mike Tirico says he's never experienced anything like it.

“It wasn’t just: ’Hey, our team is playing,'” Tirico said in a video posted on the Saints’ website.

Tirico recalled rehearsing how he would call the Saints' first touchdown, intent on exclaiming, “Touchdown, New Orleans,” to emphasize what it would mean to the city.

He did so as Deloatch recovered the blocked punt in the end zone, and then stopped talking while holding up his hands to fellow members of the broadcast team, urging everyone to remain silent and let the sights and sounds of celebrating fans speak for themselves.

“There was nothing any human alive could say that could be better,” Tirico said.

Saints safety Justin Reid was 8 years old and living near Baton Rouge when Katrina hit on Aug. 29, 2005.

While his community did not flood, power was out for about two weeks and evidence of wind damage was everywhere. He took cold showers by candlelight and recalls his father driving around their neighborhood with a trailer, helping neighbors pick up storm debris.

Later, his father took the family to witness storm damage in New Orleans. Reid remembers seeing waterlines left behind on homes after flooding — caused by multiple levee breaks — had receded.

About 80% of New Orleans experienced some flooding. In some neighborhoods, the water level climbed above front doors. Some homes closest to levee breaks had been swept off their foundations and torn apart. Estimates of storm-related deaths range from about 1,400 to 1,800.

For Reid (who does not recall watching the 2006 game live), the Saints' triumph over the Falcons on that Monday night was “poetic,” as was the NFL's decision to schedule another Monday night game with Atlanta at the Superdome within days of its 20th anniversary.

“I grew up in Louisiana, so I know how much football at all levels means to the state,” Reid said. “Football is something that people spend their whole week looking forward to. It’s a beacon of hope for the city. It’s something that brings people together. It’s something that transcends socioeconomic status. It transcends race. And it’s a big deal in the City of New Orleans.”

Ed Sheeran was joined by his first special guest on his beleaguered U.S. tour since all of his support acts withdrew over the Macklemore controversy.

The Fray’s former frontman, Isaac Slade, 45, performed an opening set before Sheeran’s headline performance at Atlanta’s Mercedes-Benz Stadium on Saturday, playing hits like “How to Save a Life” and “You Found Me.”

Sheeran had performed his last three tour dates without any special guests or support acts after musicians – including Finneas and Lukas Graham – all ditched the tour in solidarity with rapper Macklemore, who was removed from the tour last month over his “Free Palestine” remarks onstage in New Jersey.

On Saturday night, Slade, from Colorado, went on to share his own opinions on the war in Gaza, calling on people to “step into that middle place, that common ground.”

“What’s happening over there [in Gaza] is wrong, but if we’re going to get through it, we’re going to need people to step into that middle place, that common ground,” he said, according to videos of the concert.

open image in gallery Ed Sheeran was joined by Isaac Slade as his first special guest on his US tour after all of his support acts withdrew over the Macklemore controversy ( Getty Images )

“That bonfire in the middle of the field that sees both sides, that understands that peace is not a lack of conflict. Peace is not a blank canvas that we need to guard and be polite.”

“[Peace] holds enough beauty, enough tragedy, enough sorrow, enough joy and life if we learn how to integrate it and hold each other in balance. We will find a way through this together,” Slade added.

Slade, who departed The Fray in 2022, had joined Sheeran onstage before the Macklemore fallout, at a concert in Toronto in August.

Sheeran’s apolitical image has been under scrutiny after the British singer insisted in a social media post that he was “not complicit” and that he would not be drawn into a public debate about the Gaza war.

He said it was the “promoter’s decision” to remove Macklemore. Sheeran had personally received a call from Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft, who had said the rapper could no longer perform at his venue due to his pro-Palestine remarks.

open image in gallery Macklemore was dropped from Ed Sheeran’s US tour last month over his calls for a ‘Free Palestine’ onstage ( Getty )

Protesters gathered outside Sheeran’s first concert without Macklemore on September 19.

The controversy has sparked something of a movement in the music industry. On Friday night, country musician Zach Bryan wore a “Free Palestine” shirt during his concert at Kraft’s stadium in Massachusetts.

His guitarist, Noah Le Gros, wore a Palestine soccer jersey onstage alongside Bryan, and later shared a picture of himself in the shirt standing in front of a Kraft Sports and Entertainment sign at the Massachusetts stadium.

Macklemore responded to the situation by announcing a “Free Palestine” tour with unnamed special guests, with proceeds from the shows in Paris, London and Dublin going to organizations supporting Palestinians.

Sheeran said onstage on Sept. 19 that he was “so sorry” for disappointing fans.

He clarified his own stance on the Israel-Palestine conflict, saying, “What happened in Israel, and at the music festival on Oct. 7th, was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate.”
