Sports.title: Tuchel says Alex Scott’s emergence gives England – and Rice – ‘high level’ competition
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel warned that there is competition for Declan Rice’s place in England’s midfield after Alex Scott marked his first international start with an outstanding display during the 7-0 away win against Croatia.

Rice, who struggled with neural pain in his upper hamstring during the World Cup, withdrew from the camp because of load management and the vice-captain’s absence at the start of the side’s Nations League campaign has allowed Tuchel to broaden his options alongside Elliot Anderson in midfield.

England’s head coach has added youth to the squad and enjoyed the competition between Myles Lewis-Skelly and Scott during the past fortnight. Lewis-Skelly did well after starting the 3-2 defeat by Spain and the 2-0 win against Czechia but the Arsenal midfielder was outshone by Scott, who partnered Anderson in Croatia and delivered a performance full of energy, speed and quality on and off the ball.

It was Scott’s second cap – he also impressed after coming on against Czechia in Prague – and the 23-year-old’s excellence was one of many positives on an important night for Tuchel. The manager can feel a new England emerging after the pain of their World Cup defeat by Argentina. The squad has been refreshed and it was interesting that Tuchel used a question about Jordan Pickford’s spot as the No 1 goalkeeper last Friday to suggest, unprompted, that Rice does not necessarily have a guaranteed place in the team.

The bigger picture is that Rice, who has helped England reach two major finals, remains part of Tuchel’s best XI. However, Tuchel delivered another pointed response when asked if the Arsenal midfielder will feel his place is under threat after seeing Scott’s performance in Rijeka.

“Of course, and he does, we need performances like this,” the German said. “This is just the nature of it. We will not survive on two central midfielders. The more the better – and it’s always about the guys who are in camp.

“Declan knows about his importance, and he’s one of the very best midfielders in Europe. Nothing will change that. But it’s exactly what we need. We need more, more, more, more variety. We need more, more, more options. Then it’s always about the guys who are in camp. Alex was in the highest level.”

Anderson and Scott dominated against the experienced pairing of Luka Modric and Mateo Kovacic. The England youngsters built on playing together when Lee Carsley’s under-21 side won the European Championship last year.

“I guess it helps,” Tuchel said. “Not only as players but even in their character. They’re a good mix and match. Alex had a fantastic match, and we need to be strong in the middle of the pitch. I’m very happy with the level that Alex trained at.”

View image in fullscreen Thomas Tuchel said Alex Scott’s commanding performance in Croatia was ‘exactly what England needs’. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

Scott explained his partnership with Anderson. “We work really well together,” he said. “We saw that last year at the Euros and we’ve been speaking about it ever since, playing this midfield together.

“I love playing with Elliot. He makes life so easy for me. He’s one of the best midfielders in the world. We bounce off each other very well. We like getting on the ball, aggressive off the ball, we suit each other. Playing next to him is great and I know he enjoys it as well.”

It is easy to see why Bournemouth were determined not to lose Scott last summer. Arsenal asked about the former Bristol City player’s availability, Manchester United were interested and Chelsea had multiple bids rejected.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Tuchel sees Scott as one of the best midfielders in England. That assessment adds to the sense that not taking him to the World Cup was a mistake. England lacked cover for Anderson and Rice, who made 69 appearances for club and country last season. Tuchel gave no minutes to Kobbie Mainoo and lost Jordan Henderson when the 36-year-old broke a wrist during the celebrations after the last-16 win against Mexico.

But Scott, who may well have ended Henderson’s hopes of a recall, refused to sulk. He used his World Cup disappointment as motivation and has started the season well.

“It gave me more hunger but there’s so many top players for this country,” Scott said. “There was no bad feelings about not going to the World Cup. I went to the prep camp, I wanted to learn as much as I can and it helped me coming into this camp.”

England’s triumph in Croatia keeps them in second place in their Nations League group, three points behind Spain and well placed to reach the quarter-finals in March. They close this extended international break at home against Czechia Harry Kane will expect to equal Peter Shilton’s record of 125 caps and is playing brilliantly with Jude Bellingham.

“They were good in the World Cup,” Tuchel said. “They get better and better. They love playing with each other. They understand each other better.”

Tuchel could rotate against Czechia and has found out more about his squad. The Manchester City full-back Rico Lewis has been added to the senior squad for the Czechia game. “The level, the attitude, from the bench is good. Morgan Gibbs-White had a fantastic training week. Morgan Rogers got a goal. Eberechi Eze is good and is pushing. We need that.”

Sports.title: Shaw seals Manchester City’s thrilling 4-2 win over Arsenal to keep up 100% WSL run
Sports.content:
Manchester City came from behind twice to win an absorbing, six-goal thriller 4-2 and continue their 100% winning start to the Women’s Super League season while heaping further pressure on Arsenal and their head coach Renée Slegers.

The defending champions, helped by Kerstin Casparij scoring a screamer with her very first touch of the ball after coming on as a second-half substitute, stretched their advantage over Arsenal to 10 points after just five rounds of matches, leaving the title hopes of last season’s runners-up hanging by a thread.

Slegers’s team have won just once in the league this term and not since the opening weekend. On Friday, the coach said she retained the full support of Arsenal’s executives.

The match was the first to be played at the Etihad Stadium since the Premier League published the guilty verdict against Manchester City and there was something of a subdued atmosphere outside the stadium in the buildup to kick-off, which quickly changed once the game started, and was wholly different in the second half once the hosts began to take control and their supporters were thoroughly enjoying themselves.

The hosts had frequently insisted their women’s team were treating this as “business as usual”, before their draw with Real Madrid on Thursday. There were very few references to the ongoing saga here on Sunday, aside from some Arsenal fans chanting “same old City, always cheating” during the first half, and one Manchester City fan – – sitting just in front of the media seats – who defiantly shouted about which part of the anatomy people could “stick your 115 charges”, but nobody else joined in. Matters on the pitch were – for 90 minutes, at least – more interesting.

Khadija “Bunny” Shaw thought she had opened the scoring in the first half but her effort – a header from a Carlotta Wamser cross – was correctly ruled out for a foul on the goalkeeper. At the other end, City will have felt aggrieved about the nature of Arsenal’s opener, as replays showed that Lisa Baum appeared to be offside when Lotte Wubben-Moy headed goalwards. Baum was the quickest to get to the rebound after Ayaka Yamashita’s save and poked home, much to the delight of the 2,000 Arsenal fans, just two minutes before half-time.

View image in fullscreen Alessia Russo pounces to make it 2-1 to Arsenal at Manchester City. Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/Reuters

The visitors could not hold on until the break, however, as Lauren Hemp’s deflected strike found its way into the far corner, after good buildup play involving Shaw. To add to Arsenal’s worries at half-time, Mariona Caldentey went down with an injury during City’s move and she looked visibly upset, and in pain, as she was substituted.

Seemingly defying the absence of one of the best players in Europe, Arsenal came out the stronger after half-time, although they nearly conceded when Shaw was played through, one-on-one. Last season’s WSL Golden Boot winner looked certain to score but one slightly heavy touch let her down and Anneke Borbe did well to close her down. Moments later, Arsenal took the lead after another surprising sight – a mistake from Yui Hasegawa. The midfielder lost the ball inside her own area and Alessia Russo pounced, curling a finish into the far corner of the net.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It was her first league goal of the campaign and second in two games after scoring in Wednesday’s 2-2 draw against Paris FC. That will be welcome news for Sarina Wiegman, before England’s World Cup qualifying playoff against Greece. For a sizeable spell after Russo’s goal, Arsenal appeared in control, before a triple substitution from Andrée Jeglertz, including the introduction of Kerstin Casparij, changed the game.

The 26-year-old, playing as an inverted full-back, latched on to a loose ball and curled in a delightful strike to equalise and soon afterwards Hemp tucked a tidy finish through Anneke Borbe’s legs to give the hosts the lead. Suddenly Arsenal’s body language changed and City were on top. They added a clinical fourth when Shaw latched on to Aoba Fujino’s excellent through-ball and her low finish was superb, more than making up for the chance she had squandered earlier.

Sports.title: Jesse Marsch: ‘We Americans have been inundated with propaganda since we were young’
Sports.content:
Peak leaf hasn’t yet arrived in Montreal but the bursts of gold and butterscotch up on the hill that gave this place its name still mushroom out by the hour.

Sitting in a glass-panelled hotel mezzanine at the foot of Mount Royal, Canada men’s coach Jesse Marsch has his mind on another harvest. When this extended autumnal international window ends, he will decamp to Italy, where the olive crops at his Tuscan villa are ready for reaping.

Flight paths between Canada and Europe have been busy lately, and figurative transatlantic distances are closing fast. As Canada’s relations with the noisiest neighbour to the south stretch and fray, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney is forging alliances with the EU so close that the bloc is apparently inventing new membership categories.

As an American residing in Europe who is also a Canadian leader with robust approval ratings, Marsch is watching. To him, it feels right.

“I’ve always thought Canada was a little bit more European than the US anyway. Right?” Marsch tells the Guardian. “But certainly now there’s enough happening politically and economically that you would say, we’re looking much more like that. There’s talk of [Canada becoming an associate EU member] even actually happening. I like that aspect.

“There’s a uniqueness to Canada in terms of how truly multiethnic this country has become. You can see that Canada is not just a North American country any more, you know? That bodes well for our sport and for the makeup of our team, the makeup of our fans.”

Having led Canada’s men to historic highs at this summer’s World Cup, Marsch is feeling his way into his second act in the job. Some of his sideline displays – we’ll get to that meme – may have irked outsiders, especially in his homeland, during the tournament. Yet, having extended for four more years, Marsch is someone an overwhelming majority of Canadians are happy to have at the helm. There are more than a few cross-points between Marsch and Carney.

“My impression is that first of all, he is a really smart guy, but a really normal guy,” Marsch says of Carney, who attended a number of Canada’s World Cup matches. “Sometimes you meet a US president, and you’re overwhelmed, maybe by their presence, the position itself. I’ve met Clinton, George Bush Sr, Obama, Trump, Biden. Oh, and Carter. Six in person. Carney, compared to all of them, the closest would be Obama. A real air of intelligence, but a real air of being a regular guy. I think that that’s perfect for this country and this moment.

“He has shown great support for us. I made a joke with him that ‘I heard you’re an Everton fan?’ and he goes, ‘Yeah’. And I go, ‘I’m sorry about that’. He replies: ‘Why does everybody say that? Everybody has to pick their team and stick by them.’ I said, ‘I appreciate that you don’t switch from Everton to Arsenal or Liverpool, like everybody else’. There’s something so genuine [about] that. Could a president of the US ever be an Everton fan? No chance.”

View image in fullscreen Canada prime minister Mark Carney greeted Marsch’s team in the locker room after the team’s win over Qatar at the 2026 World Cup. Photograph: Jared C Tilton/Fifa/Getty Images

Circumstances, as well as natural impulses, have led Marsch to play statesman during this prolonged cooling of relations between Canada and his home country. He’s been defiant – lashing out at Donald Trump’s “51st state” barbs – then more deft. Sometimes, especially when it comes to the US Soccer Federation he said led him on with a job offer only to renege, he finds it hard to hide his disdain.

This window is the start of turning the page to the next phase of his Canada project. He admits, with a chuckle, that the four years stretching ahead feel long but there are imminent goals – a first trophy in 25 years, cracking and consolidating inside the world’s top 24.

A win over Chile in Toronto and 2-0 win over Peru here on Saturday afternoon in games billed as The Homecoming made for a solid start. New caps have been handed out. Key players arrived thriving in new surroundings, none more than Jonathan David at Atlético Madrid. Extended injury absences and the awkward non-attendance of captain Alphonso Davies (skipping the window to honeymoon) have been overcome.

But Tuesday’s clash with the US in Saint Paul means more American questions are coming. Looking back, the Folarin Balogun affair feels absolutely tailor-made for a Marschian verdict. He, of course, has thoughts.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“Well, this is a deep conversation,” he says, leaning back. “We, as Americans, have been inundated with propaganda since we were young. We’re the No 1 country in the world, we deserve everything, we dominate everything, No 1 in every aspect of life. This is what we’ve been told. So, when things happen and we don’t feel like we’re in control of it … we feel like we deserve to be treated differently because we’re Americans. That is one of the things that infuriates the rest of the world about Americans. And Americans don’t know that if they don’t ever leave the country.

“So what I feel when the Balogun ruling happens is that would never happen in any other country in the world, and this is why everyone around the world hates America. That was proven to be so. The US had had a good World Cup, was doing well. All that switched in one moment. But do I think that that’s about corruption and unfairness? The problem is, football is inundated with this kind of stuff.”

The meme is another World Cup leftover. “I’ve had all kinds of people ask me what it was, was it a meat slicer?” he says of his sideline gyrations during their match against Qatar. The incident spawned a gif which has been used plenty in the Marsch family WhatsApp since. “I don’t know what I’m doing sometimes. As soon as I’ve done it, I’m like: ‘Why did I do that? I’m such an idiot’.”

He doesn’t feel fooled, however, by the sport’s latest, arguably greatest, modern corruption crisis. Defeats to Manchester City in 2022-23 didn’t help the Leeds United side Marsch had managed when they missed safety by five points. That campaign is not one of the “sham” seasons which were part of the damning verdict against City last week. But he’s adamant the unfairness extended to his time in England.

“I think Man City should be punished severely. I think they should have to go down, and by the way, everyone knew about it. Everyone knew,” says Marsch, who also pointed to Everton and Nottingham Forest later being deducted points for issues in the same season when Leeds were relegated below both.

“That summer [2022], us and Man City were the only teams that said we made money. For us, we did make money, because we sold Raphinha, we sold Kalvin Phillips [to City]. We had a lot left over from what we bought. At the time, we weren’t in a position financially to not save. Our ownership didn’t have deep pockets. Whereas when Man City says this, I was literally like, ‘Are you kidding me? Is this some kind of joke?’

“When they said they got Erling Haaland for £52m, it’s like: ‘Yeah, OK, sure!’ So, I knew there were inconsistencies in it, but what can you do? You just put your arms in the air and go, ‘This is football’.”

Sports.title: Let there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honour there | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
At half-time in the 2014 League Cup final, Sunderland led Manchester City 1-0. Yaya Touré equalised with a casually brilliant 30-yard clip 10 minutes after the break, and City went on to win 3-1. City, we now know from the independent commission, were at the time involved in a prolonged and calculated act of cheating, while Touré, the leaks in Der Spiegel suggested, was being paid via a dual contract to disguise exactly how much City were spending. Although precise details were left to the appendices, the commission’s report refers to payments “not recorded in an employment contract … but instead recorded in a consultancy agreement”.

Had Sunderland won, they would not merely have ended a 41-year wait for a trophy but would have qualified for the following season’s Europa League. It’s possible, of course, that the strain the extra games placed on the squad would have led to relegation in 2015, rather than the familiar trope of sacking a manager, in this case Gus Poyet, midway through the season, and surviving thanks to a bump under his successor, Dick Advocaat.

But it’s also possible that the greater exposure brought by European football, the surge of positivity engendered by unfamiliar and unexpected silverware, may have led to Premier League consolidation, stability and semi-regular European qualification.

Should Sunderland feel cheated? Of course they should, just as those who came second behind Lance Armstrong should feel cheated; just as Liverpool and Arsenal should feel cheated over the League Cup finals of 2016 and 2018; just as Stoke should feel cheated over the 2011 FA Cup final; just as Manchester United should feel cheated over the Premier League titles in 2012 and 2018 and Liverpool should in 2014; just as every club who played in the same competitions as City between 2009 and 2018 should feel cheated. But does that mean the 2014 League Cup should be taken from City and awarded to Sunderland?

These are two different questions, and it’s probably best to deal with the latter first – and this, unfortunately, is where subjectivity is unavoidable. I can’t speak for other Sunderland fans but, personally, I wouldn’t want it.

Perhaps this comes from never having seen my club win a major trophy. If it happens, I want it to be pure. I want images that will be remembered down the generations, like the highlights of 1973 – Ian Porterfield’s goal, Jim Montgomery’s save and Bob Stokoe’s celebratory skip across the pitch in mac and trilby.

I want the surge of adrenaline when a goal is scored, the agonised wait of injury time, the rush of the final whistle. I want tears and hugs and community and togetherness, all the things my dad’s generation banged on about. I want to get drunk and sing on a train. I don’t want to find out via an alert on my phone 12 years after the fact as I unpack the dishwasher.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City’s Yaya Touré equalises against Sunderland in the 2014 League Cup final. Photograph: Eddie Keogh/Reuters

Others may feel differently but the arithmetic of trophies won seems far less important than the experience of winning and the memories and sense of comradeship it provokes. Glory denied cannot be rectified a generation later by an independent commission, no matter how august.

Awarding rivals league titles seems even less satisfactory. In the 2017-18 season, for instance, the league was effectively over by the end of January with City 15 points clear.

As City went on to amass 100 points, there was little point in the four sides behind them – Manchester United, Liverpool, Chelsea and Tottenham, who were separated by five points – exerting themselves to try to rein City in.

Their priorities changed. United, Chelsea and Spurs all reached the FA Cup semi-finals. Liverpool got to the Champions League final. In those circumstances, why would any of them have prioritised the league? To award United, who finished second, the title, would seem not just empty but arbitrary.

That, though, does not mean City should not be stripped of those titles. They won them unfairly; why on earth should they be allowed to keep them? (And yes, something similar could be said of Chelsea, but that’s an argument for why Chelsea should also have been stripped of titles, not for why City should not be).

How can those trophies be left in the record books for future generations unquestioningly to see? How can City stand as the fourth-most successful side in league history when so much of that success was achieved by cheating?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The argument will be made that City’s players strived hard for those trophies. But so did players for those other teams, the ones who weren’t cheating. And how much easier to win in a deep squad full of high-grade players, drawn to City by the money they were offering, money whose source, the independent commission concluded, had been disguised in contravention of Premier League regulations.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City with the League Cup in 2014, one of seven major trophies won between 2009 and 2018. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Euphoric memories cannot be expunged, but it is for City fans (and players and coaching staff and directors) to decide what to do with them. If they still want to exult in Sergio Agüero’s 94th-minute winner to claim the 2012 Premier League title, nobody can stop them. But the rest of the world knows what it was based on, that as the rest of the Premier League played to regulations voted in by the clubs themselves, City did not.

That would mean that there was no Premier League champion in 2012, 2014 or 2018, no FA Cup winner in 2011 and no League Cup winner in 2014, 2016 or 2018 (and it does not seem unreasonable to wonder, when all this is done, whether there might be more to be investigated after 2018). If there are blanks on the roll of honour, let them be; there was no honour there.

Let the spaces stand as testimony to what those seasons were. Let them stand as a memorial to the years when a foreign entity tried to subvert English football, when a foreign entity took this country’s greatest cultural mode, and all the passion and all the feeling, all the sorrow and all the joy, all the love it has entailed, and tried to twist it for its own political ends. Let them stand as a warning of the dangers of laissez-faire capitalism, when everything, no matter how beloved, could be sold off to the highest bidder.

And let them stand as a monument to a Premier League that finally – belatedly? – took action, to a process that maintained its independence, to an institution that, at no little risk to its own wellbeing – a risk that has not gone away – in the end preferred justice and fairness and decency over grubby deals with the rich and powerful.

Let the years without a champion stand for ever vacant, both as a rebuke and as a tribute. Sometimes, emptiness can be the most eloquent statement of all.

Sports.title: Alexander’s absence weighs heavy as Bradford try to keep promotion push on track
Sports.content:
It was a bruising start to the week for Bradford City when news filtered through to the players that Graham Alexander had stepped down as manager. They were top of League One and his departure was a sudden and unexpected blow for a side that had started to let imaginations run wild about a return to the second tier for the first time in 23 years.

The coaches Mark Trueman and Colin Doyle took interim charge and called a meeting with the squad last Monday. “Some of the players were a little unsettled, didn’t know what was going on or who was taking the team,” Trueman said. “But the players have just got on with business and that’s the key. It shows the mentality of the team. This could quite easily derail them, but they’ve continued to do the right things.”

If any caretaker can keep Bradford on track, it is Trueman, who has now stepped in temporarily five times since joining the club as an Under-18 coach six years ago. This time, though, is different. Previously, his job was to raise the team during low periods. Now the task is to maintain the upward trajectory that began the moment Alexander arrived in 2023.

Bradford were stuck in the bottom tier of the EFL and sitting in 16th when Alexander took over. They finished ninth in his first season, then third in his second to earn automatic promotion, followed by a stunning fourth-place finish back in League One, losing in the playoff semi-finals last May.

It has been a thrilling ride rarely enjoyed by Bradford fans. They twice reached the EFL Trophy semi-finals in successive seasons. At one stage, they won 10 consecutive home games, breaking a club record set in 1953.Last year they had the best home record of any side in Europe’s top five leagues. Alexander won 79 times in 158 games – the best win rate of any Bradford manager in charge for at least 65 games.

The chief executive, Ryan Sparks, said Alexander and the assistant manager Chris Lucketti, who has followed him to Preston, delivered “some of the most incredible moments in our recent history”.

They looked set to deliver more, with Bradford top of League One when the Preston opportunity came out of the blue. Alexander told the club he had ambitions to manage in the Championship, but you wonder if he might have achieved that with Bradford had he stayed. Perhaps he believed that two promotions in two years would risk them becoming relegation fodder in the Championship, whereas Preston presents a more stable platform. Ultimately, the lure of a club that he once captained – playing 400 games during an eight-year spell from 1999 to 2007 – d in the city where his children were raised proved too strong.

View image in fullscreen Graham Alexander’s sudden departure has left Bradford to rebuild early on in the season. Photograph: Paul Thompson/ProSports/Shutterstock

On forums and social media, fans shared a mixture of sadness, anger and anxiety. Most believe Alexander has left the club stronger, but frustration is shared among a sizeable minority about the timing – less than two months into a season after a summer spent recruiting specifically for his aggressive, direct, high-pressing football. After Jake Beesley headed Bradford into a fourth-minute lead at Reading on Saturday, the 1,118 supporters who made the 400-mile round trip sang about being top of the league, but did not chant for their departed manager once.

Rapid developments in the space of a few weeks leave a huge hole. Bradford now find themselves in unfamiliar territory: it is the first time in 43 years they have lost a manager mid-season, and fans are nervous about the executives’ aptitude for finding a suitable replacement, given the shaky record before landing Alexander.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In the opposition dugout at Reading’s Select Car Leasing Stadium stood one of the favourites to take over. Before the match, Leam Richardson faced questions about whether he was interested. His response – that he would be in the Reading dugout for the match – neatly sidestepped the prospect that he might not be beyond this weekend, though he insisted he had not been contacted.

Nonetheless, Sparks and the head of football, David Sharpe, would have been watching closely from the directors’ box to see whether Reading showed signs of a style of football that would fit the framework Alexander built. Plenty makes Richardson a logical candidate. He previously worked with Sharpe, who was chair at Wigan when Richardson was manager, and he has also coached Callum Connolly, in the Bradford starting XI, and Nick Powell, who came on from the bench.

Others are in the frame, including the Plymouth manager Tom Cleverley, the former Manchester United midfielder – a Premier League winner in 2013 – who at 37 has quietly built his managerial reputation these past two years. Udoka Godwin-Malife’s second-half equaliser meant Plymouth moved above Bradford on goal difference. The next appointment is crucial. Getting Alexander so right makes getting it wrong so much more costly.

Sports.title: Lamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect start
Sports.content:
Lamine Yamal says he feels like Superman or Spider-Man sometimes, and Spain’s fans are starting to wonder if he just might be. There is something comic book hero about what the teenager is doing right now, some unexplained super power swelling inside him. For the third consecutive game he scored inside six minutes, curling in another outrageous goal as Spain completed their World Cup homecoming in Oviedo with a 3-1 win over Czechia that leaves them a single point from the Nations League quarter finals already. Spain’s manager, Luis de la Fuente, put it simply: “Lamine Yamal is on course to become a legend.”

And yet in a game which seemed to have been done at half-time, when Spain led 2-0 after Rodrigo Hernandez had added the second and Lamine Yamal was withdrawn, his show seemingly over, the danger returned. Czechia, vastly improved after the break, pulled one back through Jiri Slama on 69 and then were denied a 79th-minute equaliser when Vassilis Fotias, the referee, who rescued Spain, harshly ruled out a Ryan Naderi goal – apparently for a foul on Robin Le Normand as the free-kick that led to it was swung in.

Reduced to 10 men soon after, still furious, Czechia finally fell with two minutes left when Mikel Merino made Spain safe. The seleccion’s first visit to the Carlos Tartiere in 11 years had ended the way they had hoped. Welcomed back as world and European champions once more, they were applauded off as winners again. A night that had begun with Rodri being presented with the World Cup by Santi Cazorla and Juan Mata, academy products at Real Oviedo and members of the generation to which all others would forever be compared, ended with a jeopardy no one anticipated when it started in a way that has become implausibly, absurdly familiar.

Lamine Yamal had scored after 104 seconds at Wembley and 70 in Seville, as Spain defeated England and Croatia. And the silly thing was that here, his goal might have come even sooner. Fifteen seconds in, the first frisson of excitement went round this place as he chased down the goalkeeper and after just fifty-seven Oviedo almost exploded. But, running on to a Dani Olmo pass, Lamine Yamal calmly guided a shot past the goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky … and past the post.

He would just have to wait until the sixth minute was up instead. Playing a quick one-two with Dani Olmo, Lamine Yamal took possession on the top right corner of the area and curled another outrageous shot into the far corner, the ridiculous becoming routine. They had been playing five minutes 20 seconds, another stadium letting out a roar that spoke of delight but also a kind of disbelief. 320 seconds he had been out there, taking him to 494 seconds to score three.

View image in fullscreen Rodri reacts after scoring Spain’s second in Oviedo Photograph: Petr David Josek/AP

Spain weren’t hurrying but they were controlling, and the chances were accumulating: by half-time they had taken 13 shots to one, and enjoyed 70% of possession. They had also added a second on 32 minutes. Rodri collected near the centre circle and did something he rarely does. The man who sometimes seems to be walking, effortlessly controlling the game with his mind and without fuss, happy enough to drop the ball off to others to do their thing, went off on a run. Advancing through the midfield, he slotted to Pedri whose return, with the help of a defender’s touch, set him up to shoot high into the net.

Next Lamine Yamal slipped in Alex Baena, denied by Kinsky. A little dinked pass from Baena then found Lamine whose shot, slightly scuffed, went wide. At the break Baena, who had drawn “oohs” with one glorious touch, was withdrawn and so too was Lamine Yamal, his work here done, another show over. The game, on the other hand, was not. That at least was Czechia’s intention and it should probably have been their reward too, the visitors taking a decisive step forward and a degree of control. They also reduced the deficit with 20 minutes to go.

The move began deep: as it progressed up the right and through the middle, Jiri Slama was sprinting to catch up. Adam Hlozek saw him coming and played the ball into his path for him to steer it low and true beyond David Raya.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A first error from Spain’s keeper almost gave Czechia an equaliser when Raya stepped out to play and his misplaced pass only found Ondrej Lingr, and a second error really should have done soon after. But if there was relief for Spain when Lingr’s shot drifted wide of an unguarded goal, it was even greater when the referee ruled out Ryan Nadel’s effort.

For Czechia there was disbelief. Michal Sadilek’s long cross had been headed goalwards by Ladislav Krejci, and Raya, reaching by the bar, could not hold on. The ball dropped on the line, where Nadel nudged it in. The referee, though, had blown. For Santi Denia on the touchline it was hard to take and it was equally difficult not to feel sympathy. All the more when Krejci was soon sent off and then Víctor Muñoz was sent clear, dashed into the area where Kinsky blocked and Merino, forever alive, finished off the festivities.

Sports.title: Zigiotti Olme capitalises on Liverpool mistake to keep Manchester United moving up WSL
Sports.content:
Julia Zigiotti Olme’s sixth-minute lob proved enough to earn the Manchester United coach, Eva Olid, a second Women’s Super League victory of the season with a 1-0 home win over Liverpool.

Zigiotti Olme capitalised on a mistake by Liverpool goalkeeper, Khiara Keating, and, despite some late pressure by Gareth Taylor’s side, United held on to make it back-to-back league wins.

After a shaky start under the new head coach, Olid, the Spaniard has now masterminded four consecutive victories in all competitions and United are unbeaten in five matches.

This was United’s 250th match since the team reformed in 2018 and Olid watched her side mark the occasion with the breakthrough after six minutes.

It was a moment to forget for England goalkeeper Keating after her pass out from the back was intercepted by Zigiotti Olme, who composed herself and chipped home in superb fashion.

Liverpool pushed for a leveller and drew a double save from the United goalkeeper, Phallon Tullis-Joyce, midway through the first half. Cornelia Kapocs had a low effort saved by Tullis-Joyce, who got up quickly to deny Beata Olsson on the rebound as well.

United’s Jess Park hit the crossbar before half-time with a left-foot strike from the edge of the box before Keating saved at her near post from Andrea Medina on the rebound. Liverpool’s best chance of an equaliser came 20 minutes from time when Jenna Clark found herself free at a corner but she could not direct her header on target.
