The win moves United level with Liverpool in the WSL, with both teams three points off the European places.

Sports.title: Formula One drivers lash out at farcical Bahrain Grand Prix after 'software' issue caused chaos in Malaysia - as Lewis Hamilton compares bizarre scenes to 'LEGO race'
Sports.content:
Formula One drivers lash out at farcical Bahrain Grand Prix after 'software' issue caused chaos in Malaysia - as Lewis Hamilton compares bizarre scenes to 'LEGO race'

Lewis Hamilton likened Sunday's farcical 'Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia' to a 'Lego race' - a PR stunt he hated at Silverstone in July.

Meanwhile, the governing FIA launched an urgent investigation into the shambles of an event delayed for more than an hour.

This comes after several cars broke down in Kuala Lumpur with software problems on one of Formula One's strangest of days.

Max Verstappen won convincingly but the event will be remembered for the fact that cars could not race in the wet. The software in the half-electric/half-combustion engine power units was exposed to rain for the first significant time and could not cope in such conditions. There was a delay in proceedings lasting 1hr 33min as the technology was rebooted and the race finally went on.

Kimi Antonelli finished second and Hamilton, who drove well after falling back to 18th, finished third, on an afternoon that represented a slap in the face to those who conceived this year's preposterous regulations.

The grand prix, relocated from the Middle East, was pushed back 40 minutes as the rain fell and was delayed for nearly a further hour as gremlins struck on the initial formation lap.

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton were in agreement after the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia

A software issue meant the cars were unable to handle the wet track in Malaysia

Both Verstappen and Hamilton, who denounced the pre-race tour in Lego-built buggies in July ahead of the British race, to a near or total standstill.

'I am pressing the throttle, and nothing is happening,' complained Hamilton, who stopped at the side of the track.

The grand prix was then postponed while the software was rebooted – the most visible sign of the complexity of this year's hybrid engines with their baffling battery components, understood by practically nobody.

Hamilton said: 'It was like the Lego race.'

He added: 'I hope there is a lesson learned.'

The FIA issued a statement within an hour, saying: 'On the formation lap an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit's sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars.

'The FIA Technical Department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain, enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the power unit before the start of the race.'This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and power unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue.'

George Russell, who retired with engine failure while lying third, fell 84 points behind championship-leader Antonelli. There are 183 points to be fought over the concluding seven rounds.

Russell said: 'The whole day felt like a bit of a faff, with the delay, the red flag, and endless laps behind the safety car.

'It didn't feel very F1 today. I would be disappointed if I was in the stands and watching that unfold.'

Verstappen, claiming his first win of the season, has been a consistent critic of this year's regulations.

He said: 'What can you say? That's not what you want for the sport.'

Sports.title: Phil Mickelson is tipped for stunning return to the PGA Tour by LIV Golf's biggest critic in the wake of his 'family trauma' rehab
Sports.content:
Phil Mickelson's biggest critic has tipped him for a shock return to the PGA Tour after it emerged he has been in rehab amid ongoing personal issues.

Mickelson reportedly entered and has already left an addiction center. His representatives told TMZ: 'Phil was seeking treatment for family trauma and addiction.'

The news comes after the 56-year-old, a six-time major champion, stepped away from professional golf this year.

In the meantime, LIV Golf has been torn apart after the withdrawal of Saudi funding, leading to questions over the future of its stars.

Brandel Chamblee, now lead analyst on Golf Channel after his own playing career ended, has been the most outspoken critic of those who turned their backs on the PGA Tour for LIV Golf.

He also has a long history with Mickelson in particular, who told GOLF Magazine in 2018: 'He and I don't see eye to eye on anything.'

Phil Mickelson has been tipped for a PGA Tour return after spending time in a rehab facility

Brandel Chamblee has long been one of Mickelson and LIV Golf's most vocal public critics

But Mickelson has found a surprising olive branch from Chamblee, who believes the legendary leftie would be forgiven and welcomed back if he wanted to be.

Speaking on the We Need a Fourth podcast, Chamblee was asked whether Mickelson has tarnished his legacy for good.

'I don't know about forever,' he said. 'I think we're in a pretty forgiving world. He's obviously got his demons that he fights, and I wouldn't wish them on anybody, but he's not alone in fighting demons.

'I think if he hadn't gone to LIV, he would have been Arnold Palmer reincarnated. He would have been Ryder Cup captain numerous times. He would have been an honorary starter at Augusta. He would have been the lead analyst at CBS. He would have been the pied piper everywhere he went.

'But I think if he came back and said 'look, I've made mistakes, I've tried to deal with them. Sorry for the damage I've caused.

'The game's been so good to me. And for the rest of my life, I'm going to try and be good back to it', I think everyone would put their arms around him and go 'welcome back, sorry you had so much trouble, hope you get your life straightened out'.

'Life's hard, it doesn't matter who you're talking into, running into. Everybody's dealing with something. Everybody's got some battle that they've faced or will face.

'I started doing commentary in 2004, so 2004 until Phil left, I used to say Phil was a gift to the game of golf. His talent, his showmanship, his look at me quality, it was incredible. What a talent, what an amazing talent.'

The golfer and his wife are seen taking in the action on the Sunday of the 2021 Ryder Cup

Mickelson and Amy are pictured with their children, Evan, Sophie and Amanda, after his victory at the 2013 Open Championship

Mickelson stepped away from golf earlier this year and cited an unspecified private family matter involving his wife, Amy, for his absence.

Mickelson has been married to Amy, 54, for almost 30 years after tying the knot back in November 1996. The couple share three children together in Evan, Sophie and Amanda.

He has been candid about his struggles with gambling, previously opening up on his addiction in 2023.

He said at the time that he had 'crossed the line from moderation into addiction which isn't fun at all.'

'The money wasn't ever the issue since our financial security has never been threatened, but I was so distracted I wasn't able to be present with the ones I love and caused a lot of harm,' he said.

He also described how this 'lack of presence' has been 'so hurtful' for his family, saying he's been 'often' told throughout his addiction, 'You're here, but you're not with us.'

'It affected those I care about in ways I wasn't aware or could fully understand,' Mickelson said. 'It's like a hurricane is going on outside and I'm isolated in a shelter oblivious to what was happening.'

'When I came out there was so much damage to clean up that I just wanted to back inside and not deal with it,' he added.

Sports.title: Give me my medal! 'Greedy b*****d' Paul Scholes disagrees with Wayne Rooney after Man United legend said he would NOT accept title if Man City are stripped of trophies
Sports.content:
Paul Scholes has responded to his former Manchester United team-mate Wayne Rooney after the latter said he wouldn't accept the 2012 Premier League title if Manchester City were stripped of it.

Since the bombshell legal verdict that found Man City guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges made against them by the Premier League, there has been much debate over how City's illustrious period from 2009-2018 should be judged.

Rio Ferdinand and David De Gea have publicly called for the 2011-12 prize to be added to their medal collection but Rooney said Man United do not 'deserve' to be awarded it.

Now Scholes has weighed in. The midfielder uploaded a punchy Instagram story in response to Rooney saying: 'Keep hearing ex-team-mates saying they want trophies taking off them but they don't want their medals... f*** that I'm a greedy b*****d I want my medal.'

Rooney took to his YouTube show, Stick to United, to explain that if City were to lose their titles he would not want a Premier League winners' medal for the 2011-12 campaign in which United only missed out on the title on goal difference.

'I have heard Rio has come out saying about getting another Premier League medal... I wouldn't really feel comfortable accepting another Premier League medal, if I'm being honest,' he said.

'I don't think we deserve it, we didn't do enough that season to win the league. I think we were six or seven points clear with four or five games to go and we threw it away.'

Paul Scholes (left) and Wayne Rooney (right) won five Premier League titles together

'I've seen everything that has come out over the past few days and listening to people and I was putting myself in a Man City player's shoes... they're players, they're doing everything they can to try and win the Premier League title and in their mind they have done it, if those players have no understanding of what is going on above them, if that happened to me... I would be absolutely devastated.

'It might happen, they might take them [medals] away, but I wouldn't want it [a medal] because I don't think as a team we deserved it that year because obviously we didn't finish first.

'So when I see team-mates saying "I want a medal", I'm happy with the five I've won. I wouldn't want this one. Should they get it stripped for what the owners have done? Yeah maybe, but I wouldn't feel comfortable accepting it.'

Scholes already has eleven Premier League winners medals in his trophy cabinet with him and Rooney winning five top-flight titles together.

Man City confirmed they have lodged an appeal against the guilty verdict on Friday.

In a statement, they said: 'The club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

'The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

'We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete.'

Manchester City beat rivals Manchester United to the 2011-12 title thanks to Sergio Aguero's dramatic winner against QPR

New Premier League rules state that a hearing must be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing, which can only last five days, concluding.

Daily Mail Sport reported on Thursday that City will attempt to prove their innocence by arguing that the government of Abu Dhabi – rather than the club’s owners – part-funded ‘sham’ sponsorship.

Sports.title: Sepang embarrassment shows F1's new generation of cars are not fit for purpose, writes JONATHAN McEVOY - as Max Verstappen lands first win of 2026 while Kimi Antonelli takes huge step towards drivers' title
Sports.content:
Sepang embarrassment shows F1's new generation of cars are not fit for purpose, writes JONATHAN McEVOY - as Max Verstappen lands first win of 2026 while Kimi Antonelli takes huge step towards drivers' title

Something shocking happened in Sepang today . Formula One revealed itself as a sport that can only be contested in dry conditions, or, to be more accurate, near-dry conditions.

It’s a regrettable case of dodgy engines and shifty rules.

Before we get back to that, the brilliance of Max Verstappen – a champion for every climate – won the ‘Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia’ from Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli in second place, while George Russell, who had run third for so long, retired with an engine problem, his hopes of snatching the title sluiced away again. The Brit shook his head as he leapt out of his car, 84 points back from Antonelli – or a million miles – with seven rounds to go.

Lewis Hamilton took the final podium place for Ferrari, a fine drive by him through the field from more than a minute back after being put on slick tyres rather than the intermediates most of his rivals were wearing at the rain-stained start. That’s Ferrari strategy acumen for you.

But the subject of significant note here was that this generation of cars, with their half-internal combustion engine, half-battery power components, seem incapable of racing when the road is wet.

The software is off-the-dial complicated and the FIA admitted this had not been adequately tested in the wet. They launched a review on Sunday night.

Formula One was plunged into embarrassment at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia

The new generation of cars were incapable of performing in heavy rain

The race was effectively delayed 1hr 33min to allow the track to partially dry, which underlines the point that this was one of the sport’s most embarrassing episodes since Indianapolis in 2005, when six cars started, to hoots of derision, because of concerns over the Michelin tyres at that great track.

This was almost as bad, if not as derided or as obvious. But, still, absurd.

The weather was poor but not awful 30 minutes before lights out, the rain short of biblical. Yes, we stood on the grid with umbrellas, and your shoes got wet.

I have been here in Sepang, an hour or more south of Kuala Lumpur, and seen the ocean fall out of the sky in other years. This was tame by comparison in an area of the world that employs folk to do the easiest job imaginable – weathermen and weatherwomen. ‘Humid today, stormy later.’ Take the rest of the day off.

Some afternoons you can almost drown by the Petronas Twin Towers as the deluge lands.

The half-hearted rain was never a reason not to get on with it.

Yet, that is how it was and no proper explanation was given for the delay at the time. The FIA later explained the software was being reset.

The shenanigans were a shame for the Bahrainis. They staged ‘their’ grand prix here as a result of the war in the Middle East, and in so many ways accomplished it with aplomb. Some 500 marshals and officials travelled from the Gulf kingdom, along with pioneering Crown Prince Salman, who masterminded the confection.

Sunday's race was delayed by over an hour-and-a-half due to strong rain

It was a well-organised home-from-home event in every aspect, down to the last detail, even if the journey by road to the track was slow, the traffic sticky. KL is a big city and that is how it is, no escape. The atmosphere, though, was good and no complaints on that front for such a hastily arranged event.

But the sport itself was a farce.

First, there was a 40-minute delay as the rain fell.

Why?

It is a fair question. Formula One has been held in rain all over the world across many years. Hamilton danced in it at Silverstone, in 2008. It was a defining moment of his career.

After winning seven championships, he does not recall every jot and tittle of his time in two decades, not every race, but he remembers that one. The conditions then in the Midlands of England were far worse than those on Sunday.

You turn back through the pages of history. For example, James Hunt in Japan in 1976, when he took the title and the immortal Niki Lauda pulled out, ceding the championship to ‘Master James’ claiming that to race on would be ‘insanity’.

We add Ayrton Senna at Donington in 1993. It was one of the drives that distinguished his extraordinary gifts.

Verstappen went on to secure his first win of 2026 but questions will cloud the new F1 cars

Michael Schumacher was called the Rain Meister.

Verstappen, victorious on Sunday by two seconds, drove to the best victory I have seen live in my life in a near-monsoon in Sao Paulo, Brazil, two years ago.

Yet here the drivers sat kicking their heels in their garages while they awaited the call to arms. Finally, they were allowed a formation lap.

Several complained they could not accelerate, their cars basically hostage to their hybrid engines (and that damn ‘software’, whatever it is).

Pole-man Verstappen said he could ‘not move’. He later could, randomly picking up pace, but other cars momentarily broke down, including Hamilton’s red car, which for a few seconds sat at the side of the track. He then got going again. Others accelerated and then decelerated. Random stuff.

The race was red-flagged for 53 minutes, as the ‘software’ was rebooted. What does that mean? It seemed as if nothing could move until the track was dry. But, really, it was primarily a technical issue rather than a safety one. A bit of both, maybe.

This was a disastrous look. Fernando Alonso, the double world champion driving for Aston Martin, asked why the hiatus. ‘It’s racing,’ he protested. He was right.

Anthony Davidson, the former F1 driver who still acts as a test driver for Mercedes, tried to explain on Sky the almost inexplicable complexity of these wretched engines.

‘A lot of it comes down to the homework that should have been done before these wet conditions,’ he said. ‘A lot of it can be simulated.

‘What’s happening is if you are off throttle for too long, the turbo spools down and when the drivers put their foot back down it uses all the engine juice.

‘It’s all there to stop teams having traction control. It’s incredibly complicated and you fall into this horrible trap where the engine can’t reaccelerate.’

Do you understand that, folks? (Zero criticism of Davidson’s illumination is implied here.)

As for the race, Verstappen lost his lead but reacquired his advantage he was never to surrender on lap 13 after a poor re-start by Antonelli. All over.

Yet Antonelli, even though the runner-up on the day, commands a title race that has never taken off. Russell looks out of it.

Sports.title: Why Alex Scott can rival Declan Rice and the moment that showed Man City star's mind may have been elsewhere as England strike perfect balance in 7-0 Croatia thrashing, writes JACK GAUGHAN
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel was back to being serenaded by the band of travelling support once Anthony Gordon had put the Nations League tie to bed with England’s third before half time.

Argentina might not be forgotten but the 100 fortunate enough to make this trip to western Croatia were imploring their manager to give them a wave.

He didn’t, they playfully jeered and England continued pouring on the pain for an embarrassed Slaven Bilic.

The most complete performance of Tuchel’s reign answered some post-World Cup questions and provided a blueprint moving forward as they attempt to evolve, writes Daily Mail Sport's JACK GAUGHAN from Rujevica Stadium.

A perfect cocktail

Tuchel has talked over the past few days of using that second half against Croatia in Dallas as a ‘memory’ to build on. When England, in his words, were ‘free’ and ‘took the risks that were worth taking’ during the group stage victory.

That is not necessarily just releasing the shackles without thought but picking their moments and there was enough of that for England to truly mix things up. Goals deriving from counter attack positions and goals from more patient build-up, Jude Bellingham’s a product of a 27-pass move.

That particular passage of play suddenly quickened and devastated an ageing Croatia, just as Harry Kane’s did minutes after the break, coming from a slow approach involving Alex Scott and then Elliot Anderson breaking lines.

It was a blend of English qualities: players capable of mastering the ball but players who happily lean into their physicality as well.

Tuchel talked over the past few days of using that second half against Croatia in Dallas during the World Cup as a ‘memory’ to build on

Jude Bellingham’s goal against Croatia, England's second, was a product of a 27-pass move

Dovetailing

Clearly Tuchel wants more genuine competition for places and aside from the goalkeeping situation has even referenced Declan Rice as somebody who might be mindful of those coming up behind him in midfield.

One is Bournemouth’s Scott, paired with Anderson in behind Bellingham. The 23-year-old’s performances in training across camp have caught the eye and his cameo in Prague did too.

'His first start and what a start,' Tuchel said here at full time. 'He is so smooth on the ball, his decision making. He plays with so much confidence. He is so active. The work rate off the ball makes him the complete package. We had a lot of variety in the centre of the pitch.'

The way in which Anderson and Scott were so at ease with each other – be it mopping up or instinctively knowing who goes and who stays – was built in the Under 21s last year, when lifting the European Championship trophy.

They are close, immediately gelling off the pitch and part of a coffee club during that tournament in Slovenia. Incidentally, one of the first occasions Scott met Tuchel was the night England won that competition, the England boss accidentally tapping his broken jaw during celebrations in the dressing room.

If that might have been painful, Scott’s presence in Rijeka saw Anderson look as comfortable as he ever has in an England shirt, albeit against wounded opposition.

Minds elsewhere?

Anderson appeared serene for the vast majority of it, running midfield, although there was one mistake that had seemingly allowed Manchester City team-mate Mateo Kovacic to nick one back for the hosts.

Anderson dallied in his own box, his pocket picked, but Kovacic inexplicably smashed wide when presented with effectively an open goal from eight yards. The 6,000 schoolkids collectively gasped.

These sort of incidents have been commonplace for City stars over the international break, which is understandable given the bombshell verdict of financial impropriety at the club and the uncertainty around that.

The way in which Anderson and Scott were so at ease with each other – be it mopping up or instinctively knowing who goes and who stays – was built in the Under 21s last yea

Crafty Kane

Croatia broke in a brief moment of excitement for the home crowd, Martin Baturina ahead of anybody in an England shirt. The vuvuzelas began to screech. And then, from nowhere, the last man came to the rescue, expertly reading the game and cutting out the counter. Kane, that was.

Kane was further back than anybody and generally this could have been the deepest he has ever operated for England.

Time and again he dropped off the front, basically operating as a No8, to engineer chances for others, most notably punching through the lines when finding Jarell Quansah in the build up to Gordon’s header.

He might be bearing down on the likes of Robert Lewandowski in the list of all-time international goalscorers but Kane continues to offer so much more for Tuchel.

Sports.title: Anthony Gordon is playing with swagger and belief - and his telepathic connection with Lewis Hall could mean Thomas Tuchel FINALLY solves a problem area in his team
Sports.content:
Anthony Gordon is playing with swagger and belief - and his telepathic connection with Lewis Hall could mean Thomas Tuchel FINALLY solves a problem area in his team

It’s a goal and an assist once an hour for Anthony Gordon in an England shirt at the moment. Eight of those vital contributions in his last six games since clambering off the bench for the rescue act against DR Congo, another two added to the growing collection during Saturday’s demolition job in Croatia.

Count winning a penalty in the Azteca as the assist it was and the statistics are even more favourable: a goal contribution every 53 minutes.

Whatever the numbers, something has clicked inside somebody who has felt somewhat underappreciated by the English public and actively wanted to leave the Premier League to alter perceptions of his abilities.

Barcelona suits him, the £68million man whose performances in Catalonia are delighting Culers in much the same way as his use of Spanish at the summer unveiling.

Thomas Tuchel has noticed an extra air of confidence to him through this international camp (three goals and an assist), a sense of greater understanding around new-found seniority and a belief that he is now one of England’s main pillars.

Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and Bukayo Saka are locks in three of the attacking positions. It’s impossible to argue against Gordon’s inclusion as the fourth after the past few months.

Anthony Gordon (centre) and Lewis Hall (right) have a flourishing understanding

‘Anthony plays with a lot more edge,’ Tuchel said. ‘He’s for sure found another level, another gear, and is very decisive.’ The very best grow the higher they climb.

Gordon believes that Congo, changing the game in Atlanta’s indoor arena when the air was rapidly leaving England’s World Cup balloon, positively shifted his international arc.

By his own admission, it takes him a while to settle within a group – although that hasn’t seemed a problem at Barca – and now approaching 30 caps, it has become time to take ownership of the left wing. Particularly as Marcus Rashford nudged himself back into the frame last season and provided stiff competition in America.

Gordon’s goal in Rijeka on Saturday evening, England’s third of the night, was a flying header to follow up another smart header in Prague days earlier. To highlight just how things are landing for him right now, the former Newcastle United forward has not scored a single header across 248 career club appearances.

There is a swagger, noticeable in how he toyed with markers at the weekend. Josip Stanisic of Bayern Munich will have endured nightmares. The way Gordon stopped an attack dead, stood Stanisic up and then strutted past provided embarrassment for a full back who started both legs of the Champions League semi-final under Vincent Kompany last season. Croatia might as well have picked one of the kids in the stands.

Poor Stanisic was only provided mercy by Slaven Bilic once Gordon had earned his rest, which in itself felt unfair. Yet there might be some relief that the 25-year-old didn’t make the experience even more chastening, missing three big chances across his 70 minutes. It really could, and should, have been 10.

One of those arrived seconds after Kane’s early opener and engineered by Lewis Hall, his former team-mate at St James’ Park. Hall’s had a strong week himself after Nico O’Reilly’s injury and the connection between the two is obvious, a telepathy that Tuchel must want to tap into more.

Quieter and more reserved, Hall is offering evidence that an incisiveness from the middle third – the pass for that Gordon chance had precision and perfect weight – is being matched by defensive doggedness. Possessing both is a rare find in modern full backs.

Gordon's form for Barcelona and England has taken him to a different level this season

To illustrate that, during a brief moment of England panic – Croatia breaking and the visitors defensively misshapen – Hall held up the galloping Franjo Ivanovic to allow others a return to their normal positions and the danger was adequately snuffed. Later on, and with England already five goals up, it was Hall’s relentless pressing inside the Croatia box that prompted a gift for Saka to smash into the net’s roof.

Hall had to deal with the setback of missing out on the World Cup squad and felt he was worthy of a spot, the response being an encouraging start to this campaign and carrying on where he left off for Newcastle. Hall, 23, has spoken openly about having to ‘play catch up’ with Tuchel’s general messaging during the camp, with the majority of the players familiar after seven weeks together Stateside.

Individually things are going well and as a pairing, they look a proper package. Tuchel loves his combinations – Bellingham and Kane, Guehi and Konsa, Quansah and Saka when Reece James isn’t fit. He wants them all over the pitch and the left-hand side has felt like a forever problem for England.

Gordon has unequivocally done more than anybody else to nail down the attacking spot, with Hall now in a straight battle with O’Reilly for the supporting role. Even before this week, the left has appeared in ruder health than for some time.

In the knockout stages of 2021, 2022 and 2024 tournaments, Luke Shaw had the place sorted for himself but there was uncertainty about what lay ahead of him. Phil Foden’s versatility meant he was shunted wide in 2022 and two years later, in a bid to play the Manchester City star inside, Shaw operated as a wing back as Gareth Southgate went to a back three to the detriment of any real flair.

The combinations weren’t quite there and Tuchel has had some questions answered across his tenure, with some crystallised during the first camp of the season.

‘I don’t want to write Nico O’Reilly off because he played for us in the first match,’ Tuchel said. ‘Lewis had two good matches now. He loves to play in the offensive full back position, he’s very good on the ball. He loves ball possession. He is very clinical, loves these little movements.

‘He played very well with Anthony. You can see that they’ve played many seasons together in the coordination of their movements. He helped Anthony a lot.’

Gordon has now taken ownership of the left wing position under Thomas Tuchel

Saturday was their 58th start together for club and country; as Tuchel alluded to, it showed. There is a little more power and physicality than advertised in them, Gordon leaning into his wiry frame and hustling in recovery runs to back up his mate, with Hall’s engine providing a different dimension going the other way.

‘I’m nowhere near the player I can be,’ Gordon told ITV last week when dissecting the move to Barca and his increased international standing. He regularly journals private targets and starring in La Liga appears to have been one. ‘Maybe delusionally I’ve [envisioned] it from a young age. Why would I have so much confidence from a young age? It makes no sense. I can’t explain why.

‘I’ve become a different player in a lot of people’s eyes. I always felt in England that people respected me because I was fast and I pressed but they never actually respected the quality and IQ that I play with. Only the players I play with seem to notice that. Now that I’m at Barcelona and playing a different style, those qualities are highlighted much more and people are starting to take notice that I’m not just quick.’

He spoke at length with Kane about the prospect of Barca, the side effects of leaving familiarities, and given the captain’s explosion at Bayern – in the running for this year’s Ballon d’Or – the feedback was to go for it wholeheartedly.

Gordon has never been shy, Everton fans will tell you that with the way he moved to Newcastle, and is still surprised at coming off against Argentina as England retreated. In being honest with himself in the quest for constant improvement and proving he deserves a place on this stage, he vows to become more selfish around the box.

Five assists in his first four Barca matches suggests that might need a bit of work. Not a lot else does and it is inarguable that Gordon looks even slicker with his mate behind him.

Sports.title: Imperious Jude Bellingham cements his status as the future of Thomas Tuchel's team: Real Madrid star a class above as England humiliate old foes Croatia in seven-goal thrashing, writes IAN LADYMAN
Sports.content:
The Croatians here by the Adriatic did their best to make this rivalry feel the way it used to. They filled this tiny little stadium with thousands of schoolkids to get round the fact this was supposed to be a behind closed doors game.

In the crowd on the far side some of the children even held up a banner.

‘It’s not coming home,’ it read, in reference to a familiar Croat poke at perceived English arrogance.

They even had a familiar face on the touchline. After an absence of 14 years, Slaven Bilic – architect of his country’s most famous victory over England at Wembley in 2007 – was back in charge of Croatia.

But out there on the grass, out where it mattered, Thomas Tuchel’s brilliantly enterprising and energetic England humiliated, embarrassed and shamed their opponents on a quite remarkable night for both nations.

They outplayed them, out thought them, out ran them and frankly ruined them. They won by seven when it could have been a dozen.

Children in the stands. Men against boys on the field. What a night for Tuchel’s team.

So, yes, this seems to be a rivalry that’s now over. Dismantled 4-2 by England at the World Cup in June, Croatia fielded eight of that line up here, including 41-year-old Luka Modric. But this is a Croatia team on the wane. England, despite last weekend’s defeat to world and European champions Spain, are suddenly trending spectacularly in the right direction.

Bellingham was head and shoulders above the rest and has cemented his position as the player around whom the future of this England team will now surely be built

England were magnificent, with this probably their best football under Tuchel

The presence of more than 6,000 children – along with endless parents and coaches – seemed a little bit like a V-sign to UEFA. It’s in the regulations but even so. This game was supposed to be played in an empty stadium because of alleged far-Right behaviour by Croat supporters.

This in no way felt like a punishment and all that can be hoped is that the Croatian youngsters enjoyed their evening out watching the likes of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane and Anthony Gordon.

England were, it must be said, absolutely fabulous. Magnificent, even. This was probably their best football under Tuchel and for some long while prior to that. Yes, Croatia were woeful with a back line so square Kane could have parted his hair with it.

But they are the 14th ranked team in the world so still England had to play their football and they did so with a hunger and a tempo that made a mockery of the fact this four-game international period was supposed to be a test of their physical and emotional capacity.

Bellingham was once again head and shoulders above the rest and over the course of games against Spain, Czech Republic and now Croatia, the 23-year-old has cemented his position as the player around whom the future of this England team will now surely be built.

There were outstanding performances from Kane, Anthony Gordon, Bukayo Saka and, on his first start, Bournemouth’s Alex Scott. But it was Bellingham who ran this game, easing his way through the Croatian midfield imperiously as though he owned it.

His first contribution of note was to free Gordon down the inside left channel in only the third minute.

That was to become a pattern and though Gordon was denied by goalkeeper Dominik Livakovic on that occasion, he was given no chance five minutes later when Bellingham released Kane down the other side and the England captain drove his 88th international goal high into the roof of the net with his right foot.

Livakovic had conceded four against Spain earlier in the week and here the story of the night was set astonishingly early.

Croatia were no match for England in central areas – in terms of appetite as much as anything – while their back four was pierced monotonously by England’s deep runners.

The Croatians filled this tiny little stadium with thousands of schoolkids to get round the fact this was supposed to be behind closed doors game

MATCH FACTS Croatia (4-2-3-1): Livakovic 7; Stanisic 5 (Kramaric 75mins 6), Vuskovic 6, Gvardiol 6, Perisic 5; Modric 5 (Jakic 57mins 6), Kovacic 5; Ivanovic 5, Sucic 5 (Pasalic 45mins 5), Baturina 5 (Vlasic 45mins 5); Musa 5 (Matanovic 45mins 6) Booked: Kovacic Manager: Slaven Bilic 3 England (4-2-3-1): Pickford 6; Quansah 7, Konsa 6, Guehi 6, Hall 7 (Lewis-Skelly 79mins) 6; Scott 7.5 (Garner 70mins 6), Anderson 7.5 (Gibbs-White 70mins 6); Saka 8, Bellingham 9, Gordon 8 (Eze 70mins 6); Kane 8 (Rogers 70mins 6) Goals: Kane 8 & 53, Bellingham 21, Gordon 39, Saka 45 & 68, Rogers 88 Manager: Thomas Tuchel 8 Referee: Sven Joblanski (Ger)

Gordon was denied twice more in the ninth and 25th minutes – the second from point blank range – but in the middle of that he played his part in setting up England’s second. A Saka cross to the far post was slightly overhit but when Gordon pulled it down, he was criminally given all the time in the world to ease it square to Bellingham to tap it in.

Already there was a sense of inevitability about the game and indeed the result. Croatia showed no sign of a response. There were other near misses – one from Kane and a shot over from Elliot Anderson – before Jarell Quansah and Bellingham laid on simple finishes for Gordon – at last – Saka as half-time neared.

Around this time there was also a moment of vague comedy at the other end. Having finally mustered some impetus of their own, Croatia seemed set to at least score a goal but when Manchester City’s Mateo Kovacic rounded Jordan Pickford eight yards out, he somehow sliced the ball wide.

With the game over by half-time, England could enjoy themselves. This was probably the first time Tuchel’s team had played without pressure since before the World Cup. Tuchel resisted the temptation to make changes at half-time while Bilic, perhaps understandably, did not. He made three.

His team were helpless, though. Helpless and hopeless. What was particularly embarrassing was that the goals kept coming the same way. Only eight minutes had gone in the second half when Anderson crossed low from the right and Kane slid the ball in at the far post. It seemed that the only ones here who couldn’t see the repeat patterns were the players in the red and white squares.

The sixth goal arrived with 22 minutes left as the Croatian defence presented the ball to Kane who presented it to Saka who slammed it in. On the touchline, Bilic was nowhere to be seen by now. He had taken refuge on the bench, seeking in vain some kind of shelter from the worst night of his life.

By the time he reappeared with three minutes to go, it was to see England substitute Morgan Rogers roll in number seven. That made this Croatia’s record ever defeat and by now many of the children in the stands had disappeared.

Homework must have felt preferable.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel says Jude Bellingham has 'gone up a level' since the World Cup as he lavishes praise on star man after England's 7-0 rout of Croatia
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel hailed Jude Bellingham after another scintillating night in an England shirt, believing that the Real Madrid superstar has gone up another level in recent months.

Bellingham scored one and recorded a hat-trick of assists during the demolition of Croatia, with team-mates queuing up to lavish praise on the vice-captain.

The 23-year-old became the first midfielder to record four goal involvements in an England match for since David Platt scored four against San Marino in 1993.

Roy Keane claimed that Bellingham 'can go on to become one of the greatest players of all time' and Tuchel has seen more improvement.

'At the moment it seems like [he has gone up a level] and you always need to,' Tuchel said. 'The level you showed last week is never enough, it's just the nature of football.

'It's like you can never stand still, it's like walking against an electric escalator. You have to develop and push for the next level. That is always necessary.'

Jude Bellingham impresses again as he continues to break records in an England shirt

Bellingham created an astonishing eight chances and laid on for Bukayo Saka's first goal seconds before half time.

'He was amazing tonight,' Saka said. 'He deserved [England] player of the year and he probably deserves man of the match tonight as well. He was special. I'm happy to play with him and happy to have him in the England team.'

Tuchel admitted that the atmosphere in a stadium populated by 6,000 schoolchildren and 100 away fans was 'strange' but couldn't hide his excitement at the way in which England dismantled Croatia.

And he believes nights like this are a way of erasing the pain of July's World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina.

'The speed and technical quality, the hunger off the ball, was the very highest level,' the German said. 'I'm very happy about the attitude. We were never arrogant, always humble. It was a complete 90-minute performance.

'If you feel pain you have to play with the pain. The same with disappointment. It was not easy at the beginning of the camp. We'll always have a scar, feel pain, but this is the way to move forward. We've played in the same manner all three matches.'

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
