World.title: 10 African countries with the longest coastlines
World.content:
African countries are surrounded by the Atlantic and Indian oceans, as well as the Mediterranean Sea and Red Sea, giving dozens of countries access to major maritime routes.

Some African countries, however, have significantly longer coastlines than others. Island nations such as Madagascar benefit from their extensive maritime boundaries, while several mainland countries also have coastlines stretching thousands of kilometres.

Based on coastline data attributed to the CIA World Factbook, here are the 10 African countries with the longest coastlines:

1. Madagascar — 4,828 km

Madagascar has the longest coastline in Africa, stretching approximately 4,828 kilometres.

The island nation lies off the southeastern coast of mainland Africa in the Indian Ocean. Its large size and extensive shoreline make it the continent’s leading country by coastline length.

2. Somalia — 3,025 km

Somalia has Africa’s second-longest coastline at approximately 3,025 kilometres.

Its coastline extends along the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, giving the country one of the most extensive maritime frontiers on the African mainland.

3. Morocco — 2,945 km

Morocco ranks third with approximately 2,945 kilometres of coastline in the CIA-derived dataset.

The country’s coastline faces both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. This makes Morocco one of Africa’s most strategically positioned coastal countries.

4. South Africa — 2,798 km

South Africa has approximately 2,798 kilometres of coastline.

Its coastline stretches from the Atlantic Ocean in the west to the Indian Ocean in the east, giving the country access to two major ocean systems.

5. Mozambique — 2,470 km

Mozambique has a coastline of approximately 2,470 kilometres, making it the fifth-longest in Africa.

The country’s eastern coastline runs along the Indian Ocean, with numerous bays and islands contributing to its extensive maritime geography.

6. Egypt — 2,450 km

Egypt has approximately 2,450 kilometres of coastline.

The country has coastlines along both the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea, giving it an important position between Europe, Africa and Asia.

7. Eritrea — 2,234 km

Eritrea’s coastline stretches for approximately 2,234 kilometres.

The country occupies a strategic position along the Red Sea, opposite the Arabian Peninsula, and its coastline includes numerous islands.

8. Libya — 1,770 km

Libya has approximately 1,770 kilometres of Mediterranean coastline.

Its coastline makes Libya one of the countries with the longest Mediterranean shores in Africa.

9. Angola — 1,600 km

Angola has approximately 1,600 kilometres of coastline along the Atlantic Ocean.

Its coastal position has historically made the country an important part of Atlantic maritime trade in southern Africa.

10. Namibia — 1,572 km

Namibia rounds out the top 10 with approximately 1,572 kilometres of coastline.

Its Atlantic coast is dominated by the Namib Desert, creating the distinctive landscape for which the country’s shoreline is known.

World.title: 2027: ADC accuses APC of threatening voters with AK-47
World.content:
By Luminous Jannamike

ABUJA – The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council, ADC PCC, has accused the All Progressives Congress, APC, of threatening Nigerians with violence ahead of the 2027 presidential election over an alleged AK-47 threat by the party’s Edo State chairman, Jarrett Tenebe.

The council said the alleged threat, coupled with a reported attack on ADC members and destruction of their vehicles in Gegu, Koton Karfi Local Government Area of Kogi State, showed the need for urgent action to prevent intimidation and violence ahead of the election.

In a statement by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, on Sunday, the ADC PCC demanded that the police, Department of State Services, DSS, and Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, investigate Tenebe over the alleged threat.

Ologbondiyan said the council had waited for the APC leadership and President Bola Tinubu to condemn or demand a retraction of the alleged statement but received no such response.

“We are shocked that a state chairman of a ruling party, Mr. Jarrett Tenebe, can stand before the public and threaten Nigerians with AK-47 rifles if they refuse to vote for his party, the APC,” he said.

He urged the Inspector-General of Police, the DSS Director-General and INEC to invite Tenebe for questioning, arguing that the alleged threat violated the Electoral Act and the Constitution.

Ologbondiyan also challenged the APC’s claim of securing 2.5 million votes in Edo State for Tinubu in 2027, saying such a figure could not be achieved through a free, fair and credible election.

He attributed the alleged threat to growing political desperation within the ruling party, citing what he described as increasing hardship, insecurity and dissatisfaction among Edo voters.

According to him, the alleged statement had reinforced concerns that the APC might resort to violence and intimidation in its bid to retain power in 2027.

The ADC PCC also appealed to the United Nations, European Union, African Union, ECOWAS, United States and other democratic countries to monitor developments ahead of the election and prevail on the Federal Government and APC to ensure a peaceful and credible electoral process.

Ologbondiyan said the 2027 election would be ‘a referendum’ on the performance of the APC-led administration, insisting that intimidation would not stop Nigerians from exercising their constitutional right to vote.

The council also called for investigation into the reported attack on ADC members and destruction of vehicles belonging to supporters in Gegu, Koton Karfi.

“We call on the members of our Kogi State chapter, particularly in Koton Karfi Local Government, to name everyone they identified in the course of the needless attack,” he said.

Ologbondiyan urged security agencies to thoroughly investigate the incident and prosecute anyone found culpable.

World.title: 2027: Kano APC chieftain urges unity, dialogue
World.content:
…Appeals to Tinubu, Yari to reconcile party leaders

By Henry Umoru

ABUJA — Ahead of the 2027 general elections, a chieftain of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Kano State, Aminu Shehu Uba Sharada, has appealed to President Bola Tinubu and the Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council (PCC), Senator Abdulaziz Yari, to urgently intervene in what he described as disagreements among party leaders and stakeholders in the state.

Sharada, who is Personal Assistant to Senator Orji Uzor Kalu, made the appeal in a statement on Sunday, saying the differences within the Kano APC needed to be addressed to prevent possible consequences for the party in the 2027 elections.

He urged the national leadership to initiate consultations, reconciliation and genuine political engagement with relevant stakeholders in the state.

Sharada said, “Let me be frank: anyone giving the impression that everything is fine within the Kano APC is not giving the President the full picture.

“There are disagreements and visible concerns among party leaders and stakeholders, and if they are not addressed early, they could have wider consequences for the party.”

According to him, there was no justification for the continued disagreements and confrontations within the party, arguing that the challenges ahead were bigger than individual interests.

“At this point, I believe there is no justification for the continued disagreements, confrontations and arguments within our party in Kano State. The challenges before us are bigger than individual interests, and the only way forward is for our leaders and stakeholders to come together and resolve their differences in the interest of the party,” he said.

Sharada said the APC’s immediate responsibility should be to build a united party capable of securing electoral victories at the presidential, governorship, senatorial, House of Representatives and State House of Assembly levels.

He therefore appealed to Tinubu and Yari to pay particular attention to the situation in the Kano chapter and facilitate what he described as a timely intervention.

“This is not the time to take sides or deepen existing divisions. It is time for consultation, reconciliation and genuine political engagement.

“Every leader and stakeholder has a role to play in bringing the various interests together and rebuilding confidence within the party,” he said.

Sharada said the APC had a broad base of committed members and stakeholders in Kano, adding that what was needed was leadership capable of bringing the various interests together, listening to their concerns and establishing a common direction.

He urged the national and state leadership of the party to act swiftly and place the interests of the APC above personal disagreements.

“There is still time to resolve our differences. What is required now is the political will, sincerity and leadership to do so,” he said.

World.title: Free Zones: Preserving Nigeria’s Industrial Advantage
World.content:
Nigeria’s free-zone regime is approaching a critical policy test. As the Federal Government moves to tighten tax and customs administration, it must also guard against weakening one of the country’s few established mechanisms for attracting large-scale, export-oriented investment, writes James Emejo

Nigeria’s ambition to build a $1 trillion economy will ultimately be measured in factories, exports, jobs and the volume of long-term capital committed to production—not in the number of policy documents it produces.

That places the country’s free-zone regime at an important crossroads.

The emerging debate over proposed changes to the fiscal and customs treatment of free-zone enterprises is ostensibly about revenue, tax compliance and closing loopholes. But beneath the technical provisions lies a much bigger economic question: can Nigeria tighten oversight without weakening the incentives that make its special economic zones attractive to investors in the first place?

That question assumes greater significance against the backdrop of the federal government’s $1 trillion economic ambition, which depends heavily on expanding productive capacity, attracting foreign direct investment, increasing exports and deepening manufacturing.

The draft Nigeria Export Processing Zones (Domestic Sales, Fiscal Alignment and Customs Treatment) Regulations, 2026, obtained for this report, offers an insight into the proposed framework.

Issued under the Nigeria Export Processing Zones Act and the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, the draft says its objectives include improving investor confidence, protecting government revenue and enhancing the global competitiveness of the zones.

Under the existing free-zone architecture, approved enterprises enjoy exemptions from certain taxes, levies, duties and foreign-exchange restrictions, alongside other incentives designed to attract investment and support export-oriented production.

The proposed regulations retain several of those incentives but introduce new conditions around domestic sales.

Under the draft, an enterprise would qualify for tax exemption on profits where at least 75 per cent of its annual turnover comes from exports and not more than 25 per cent from sales into the Nigerian Customs Territory.

More significantly, from January 1, 2028, profits arising from sales into the Nigerian Customs Territory would become fully taxable, irrespective of the proportion of domestic sales.

For investors making long-term commitments, that is not a minor administrative adjustment.

A refinery, petrochemical complex, automobile plant, pharmaceutical facility or export-processing operation can take a decade or more to recover its capital. Investment decisions are therefore based not only on today’s tax rate but on the credibility and durability of the rules under which capital is committed.

This is where the government faces a delicate balancing act.

There is a legitimate case for preventing abuse of free-zone incentives. Companies that divert duty-free goods into the domestic market outside approved arrangements should not be permitted to use the zone regime as a mechanism for avoiding legitimate duties and taxes.

The draft itself provides for consequences for unauthorised movement of duty-free goods, including customs duties, import VAT and other applicable charges, administrative penalties, seizure and possible prosecution.

The issue, therefore, is not whether government should enforce compliance. It should.

The more consequential question is whether enforcement can be strengthened without progressively eroding the economic proposition that distinguishes a free zone from an ordinary industrial location.

That distinction matters because incentives are not supposed to be an end in themselves. Their economic justification is that they help Nigeria attract productive capital that might otherwise go elsewhere.

The Dangote lesson

Nigeria already has a powerful domestic example of what such an investment proposition can produce.

The Dangote Refinery and Petrochemical complex is located within the Dangote Industries Free Zone in Lekki, Lagos. The project illustrates the scale of industrial investment that can emerge where infrastructure, fiscal incentives, customs arrangements and regulatory support converge.

The facility’s economic significance extends beyond its physical size. A project of that scale has implications for domestic refining capacity, petrochemicals, foreign-exchange demand, industrial supply chains, employment and the country’s ability to retain more value from its energy resources.

That experience raises a fundamental investment question for policymakers: if the fiscal and regulatory advantages of free zones are substantially reduced, what would persuade the next investor considering a $500 million, $1 billion or $5 billion project to locate inside one?

Nigeria is competing for capital with jurisdictions that deliberately construct specialised investment environments around taxation, customs, infrastructure and regulation.

The country therefore needs to measure the free-zone regime not only by revenue forgone but also by the investment, employment, exports, technology transfer and industrial capacity generated in return.

Reform without policy rupture

The proposed changes also bring the question of policy consistency into sharper focus.

An investor entering Nigeria today is making a decision based partly on the rules currently in force. If those rules change substantially after capital has been committed, the economic effect extends beyond the immediate tax liability.

Investor confidence is particularly sensitive to policy predictability because industrial capital is relatively immobile.

A government can amend a tax regulation quickly. A company cannot relocate a refinery, factory or processing plant with the same speed.

The draft recognises this problem to an extent. It provides that enterprises enjoying incentives validly granted before the commencement of the new Act may continue to enjoy them for the unexpired portion of their statutory approval period, subject to applicable law and the terms of their original approval.

That transitional principle is important.

Government can distinguish between incentives granted to existing investors under established legal arrangements, new incentives for future investors and benefits that should be withdrawn from enterprises that breach their obligations.

Such differentiation would allow fiscal reform without creating unnecessary uncertainty around investments already made in reliance on government-approved arrangements.

Who regulates the zones?

Another critical issue is institutional coordination.

The draft provides that the Nigeria Export Processing Zones Authority (NEPZA) shall remain the exclusive regulator for licensing, operational oversight, supervision and non-tax administration within the zones.

The Nigeria Revenue Service would have responsibility for tax administration, while the Nigeria Customs Service would retain responsibility for customs control and enforcement.

On paper, the division is logical.

The problem arises when separate mandates become competing centres of authority.

A free zone requires a regulator capable of coordinating the commercial and operational realities of the zone while allowing tax and customs agencies to perform their statutory responsibilities.

That makes the institutional strength and clarity of NEPZA particularly important.

The Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment has maintained that the reform is intended to improve fiscal accountability while preserving the competitiveness of free zones. Minister Jumoke Oduwole has also said the reform process involved NEPZA and the Oil and Gas Free Zone Authority and that the agencies would retain licensing and operational responsibilities.

The next step should therefore be greater transparency around how the proposed framework was developed, including the inputs received from NEPZA, operators, workers and other stakeholders and how those submissions influenced the final provisions.

The concerns raised by workers and unions also deserve consideration, particularly where they relate to employment, investment flows and the operational sustainability of the zones.

But those concerns should be tested against evidence.

The government should publish the economic assumptions behind the reform: how much additional revenue is expected, what investment impact is anticipated, how many jobs could be affected and what happens to exports and new capital under the proposed regime.

That would move the debate from competing assertions to measurable outcomes.

The bigger problem: an outdated law

There is an even more fundamental issue that should not be lost in the tax debate—the age of the legislation governing NEPZA.

The NEPZA Act, enacted in 1992, predates the current structure of global supply chains, digital commerce, modern special economic zones, contemporary investment financing and many of the regulatory standards now used to compete for international capital.

Its limitations have increasingly become part of the investment challenge.

Modern investors require legal frameworks capable of dealing with complex ownership structures, infrastructure financing, public-private partnerships, dispute resolution, cross-border transactions, technology partnerships and evolving international trade arrangements.

An outdated statutory framework can create uncertainty even where the underlying commercial opportunity is attractive.

That suggests that the immediate debate over tax treatment should ultimately lead to a broader legislative reform.

Rather than repeatedly modifying an old framework through administrative and fiscal interventions, the government could pursue an executive bill to replace the existing NEPZA Act with a modern Special Economic Zones law designed around contemporary investment realities.

Such legislation could establish clearer rules for licensing, governance, incentives, customs treatment, infrastructure development, investment protection and regulatory coordination.

A national economic strategy

There is also a case for stronger coordination of the country’s special economic zones.

Free zones cut across taxation, customs, trade, ports, infrastructure, investment promotion, manufacturing and foreign exchange. Their success therefore cannot depend entirely on the priorities of one ministry or agency.

A coordinated national framework involving NEPZA, OGFZA, the finance and industry ministries, the Nigeria Revenue Service, Customs, the Central Bank, port and infrastructure agencies and private-sector operators could provide a more coherent strategy.

The objective should not be to create another layer of bureaucracy, but to prevent conflicting policy objectives from undermining one another.

Nigeria’s economic challenge is ultimately larger than the question of how much tax a free-zone company should pay.

The more important question is what kind of productive economy the country wants to build.

Factories create jobs. Export industries generate foreign exchange. Petrochemical plants create downstream industries. Industrial parks create supply chains. Large-scale investments expand the tax base over time.

That is why the fiscal value of free zones should be assessed alongside their wider economic returns.

Government has a legitimate interest in revenue mobilisation. It also has a legitimate interest in preventing abuse of tax and customs incentives.

Those objectives do not necessarily conflict with maintaining a competitive investment regime.

The policy challenge is to design a system that is tough on abuse, rigorous on compliance and predictable for legitimate investors.

For Nigeria, the test of the proposed reform should therefore extend beyond the tax ledger.

If the new framework produces greater revenue while attracting more factories, exports and capital, it will have strengthened the economic case for free zones.

If it increases the immediate tax take but makes long-term investors more hesitant to commit capital, the country may simply be transferring revenue from tomorrow’s productive economy to today’s fiscal accounts.

That is a calculation worth making before the rules are finalised.

Nigeria’s $1 trillion ambition requires productive capacity at a scale the conventional economy has struggled to generate. Free zones can form part of that strategy—but only if the incentives, regulation and institutions surrounding them are credible enough to support long-term investment.

The answer, therefore, may not be to weaken NEPZA because its framework requires reform, but to modernise the law, clarify institutional responsibilities, strengthen enforcement and make the investment proposition more predictable.

The country needs a free-zone system that protects public revenue without taxing away the very industrial ambition it was created to attract.

World.title: NOSC Selects Dear Ajayi as Nigeria’s Official Submission for 99th Oscars
World.content:
Vanessa Obioha

‘Dear Ajayi’, a 2026 film directed by Damilola Orimogunje, has been selected as Nigeria’s official submission for the Best International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards.

The Nigerian Official Selection Committee (NOSC) announced the selection in a statement, saying the film emerged after a review of eligible entries and will be submitted to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences for consideration.

“We congratulate the filmmakers behind ‘Dear Ajayi’ on their selection,” said Stephanie Linus, Chairperson of the NOSC. “We look forward to presenting the film for the Academy’s consideration and wish the team every success in the next stage of the process.”

Set in 1990s Nigeria, the film follows two estranged sisters forced to live together while caring for their paralysed mother. It had its world premiere at the 23rd edition of Giornate degli Autori (Directors/Authors’ Days), an independent sidebar of the Venice Film Festival.

The Nigerian-German co-production was produced by Nigeria’s 2o9ine Films with Depth and Optics Productions, and Germany’s Mayana Films.

Bimbo Akintola and Tosin Adeyemi star as the two sisters.

The 99th Academy Awards ceremony is scheduled to take place on March 14, 2027, at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood, Los Angeles.

World.title: Nora Awolowo Named Canon Ambassador
World.content:
Iyke Bede

Nigerian filmmaker and cinematographer Nora Awolowo has been named a brand ambassador for Canon, following her involvement in the Guinness World Record-setting screening of ‘Black Market’ in Lagos.

Awolowo produced the film through Rixel Studios. Its September 26 screening at Tafawa Balewa Square attracted 51,258 people, earning recognition from Guinness World Records for the largest audience at a film screening. The previous record of 43,624 was set in 2015 by the Filipino film ‘Felix Manalo’.

Directed by Fatimah Binta Gimsay, ‘Black Market’ follows five market women involved in a cross-border smuggling operation.

Awolowo, who founded Rixel Studios, has worked across cinematography, documentary filmmaking and film production. Her credits include the historical drama ‘Lisabi: The Uprising’.

Speaking on her appointment, Awolowo said, “I’m incredibly grateful for the journey, for every person who has believed in me, every story that has trusted me with its images, and every lesson that brought me here. From my first Canon to this moment. What a journey.”

As Canon ambassador, Awolowo will collaborate with the company on visual storytelling and mentorship initiatives for emerging creators.

World.title: Corporal Punishment Ban: Stakeholders Seek Clearer Discipline Framework, More Counsellors
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare

Stakeholders in the education sector weekend called for a comprehensive review of school discipline frameworks, stronger parental involvement and increased deployment of guidance counsellors to help schools manage student misconduct following the ban on corporal punishment.

They made the call at the Lagos State school discipline policy roundtable organised by the Ajoke Ayisat Afolabi Foundation (AAAF), with support from SIFAX Group, in Lagos.

The roundtable, themed, ‘Assessing the Impact of Banning Corporal Punishment on Discipline in Schools: Exploring Alternative Strategies for Managing Student Misconduct’, brought together policymakers, educators, students, civil society organisations and other stakeholders.

The event also formed part of activities marking International Teachers’ Day and featured the recognition of outstanding teachers in Lagos State following AAAF’s statewide nomination exercise.

They include Mrs. Modupe Odumade of Ijaye Ojokoro Senior High School, who emerged as the highest-ranked teacher, followed by Mrs. ThankGod Priscilla, Mrs Ramota Balogun, Mr. Akinola Oluwatobi and James Mary Omolade.

The stakeholders called for increased recruitment of guidance counsellors, specialised teacher training and stronger collaboration among parents, schools and government agencies.

They agreed that sustainable reform of school discipline in Lagos required shared responsibility among government, schools, parents, civil society organisations and students.

According to them, “There is a need for clearer disciplinary procedures, stronger safeguarding mechanisms and sustained stakeholder engagement to ensure that school discipline promotes accountability while protecting the dignity and rights of learners.”

Participants agreed that although the ban on corporal punishment was consistent with child protection principles, schools needed clearer operational guidelines, stronger institutional support and effective alternatives for addressing behavioural challenges.

A statewide policy review conducted by AAAF across the five divisions of Lagos State provided a major focus of the discussions.

The study involved 451 students, 42 school leaders and teachers, while 150 students participated in focus group discussions across 15 schools.

Presenting the findings, the researchers said that while most students surveyed considered discipline in their schools to be relatively good, many educators expressed concerns about inadequate guidance on disciplinary alternatives following the ban on corporal punishment.

The report identified gaps in policy implementation, teacher capacity, institutional support and stakeholder engagement.

It recommended greater clarity in disciplinary policies, continuous teacher training, the development of school-level disciplinary frameworks, stronger parental participation and periodic reviews of discipline policies to reflect emerging realities.

The study also proposed structured escalation procedures for dealing with offences, with disciplinary measures made proportionate to the nature and severity of misconduct.

In his remarks, Chairman of SIFAX Group and Chairman, Board of Trustees of AAAF, Dr. Taiwo Afolabi, who was represented by the Deputy Director, Strategy and Operations of the organisation, Oliver Omajuwa, said discipline remained fundamental to educational success and national development.

Declaring the roundtable opened, he stated that the discussion was not merely about policy but about safeguarding children’s future, strengthening teachers’ confidence and building a society anchored on responsibility and character.

He said schools should be environments where children could learn in safety and teachers could teach with dignity, adding that discipline should promote character, responsibility and growth rather than fear and resentment.

He urged stakeholders to approach the issue with open minds and develop practical solutions that would place the best interests of children at the centre of educational reforms.

Lagos State Commissioner for Basic and Secondary Education, Jamiu Tolani Ali-Balogun, said discipline begins at home, arguing that many behavioural challenges confronting schools reflected wider societal problems.

He stated that while government policies were important, their effective implementation depended largely on cooperation among parents, schools and communities.

He expressed concern over what he described as a growing disconnect between parents and schools, noting that some parents failed to respond when invited to discuss behavioural concerns involving their children.

“We must create society first. It is not just about policy. Parents are critical to discipline,” he said, urging families to take greater responsibility for the moral upbringing of their children.

Also speaking, Executive Secretary of the Lagos State Domestic and Sexual Violence Agency, Lola Vivour-Adeniyi, explained that corporal punishment often failed to produce lasting behavioural change.

She advocated disciplinary approaches based on communication, guidance and accountability, describing physical punishment as a lazy approach that could create fear without necessarily developing character.

Participants also identified emerging challenges requiring new approaches to school discipline, including social media influence, changing family structures, peer pressure, mental health concerns and neurodiversity.

They stressed the need to equip teachers with the knowledge and skills required to understand and respond appropriately to these realities.

Students who participated in AAAF’s essay competition on school discipline also contributed to the debate, challenging stakeholders to move away from traditional punitive approaches towards strategies that develop character, responsibility and self-control.

The winner of the competition, Olachiwa Sharon Iwala, said true discipline should enable children to make responsible choices even when no authority figure was present.

She advocated guidance and counselling, restorative justice measures and clear disciplinary codes as alternatives to physical punishment.

Another student speaker, Anuoluwa Mudahiru, urged policymakers to move beyond the debate over whether teachers should flog students, arguing that greater attention should be given to building a school system capable of producing disciplined, responsible and self-motivated young people.

World.title: Sacrifices of Our Fallen Heroes ‘ll Not Be in Vain, Says Naval Spokesperson
World.content:
*As widows of fallen personnel appeal to corporate organisations for support for families

Linus Aleke in Abuja

The Director of Naval Information, Navy Captain Abiodun Folorunsho, has said that the Armed Forces of Nigeria (AFN) is working hard to ensure that those left behind by troops who died in active service are not neglected, assuring them that: “We will not allow the sacrifices of our fallen heroes to be in vain.”

This comes as the widows of fallen heroes appealed to corporate organisations and foundations to support the families of fallen military personnel, particularly widows and children who continue to face financial and social challenges following the loss of their breadwinners.

The widows made the appeal during the Military Widows Outreach Programme, organised by the Military Widow Support Initiative (MWSI) at the Naval Base Abuja Parade Ground on Saturday.

Speaking at the outreach programme, the Naval spokesperson, Captain Folorunsho, said the initiative was established to complement the support already provided by the Armed Forces of Nigeria.

He said there was no way the Armed Forces, as an institution, could bridge the huge gap alone.

According to him, “We thought it wise to pull funds from our sponsors to see how we can also add to what the military is already doing for them. A number of these people are the true warriors; they are the true heroes because it is they who are really paying the sacrifice.

“It is because of them that we can do what we are doing. Their spouses and children have had to pay the ultimate price so that Nigeria can be won.

“So, yes, we started this three years ago, just pulling funds, personal funds from us and from some of our friends, to assist these widows to adequately cater for their families.

“We will not allow the sacrifices of our fallen heroes to be in vain.”

Speaking during the empowerment programme, Mrs Olubunmi Oni, whose husband, the late Major S. Oni, who died in active service in Niger State in 2023, said widows of fallen heroes continued to face significant challenges.

She said: “We would really appreciate it if a lot of organisations, NGOs and foundations could continue to reach out to fallen heroes’ wives and children, help them with their academics through scholarships, and help the wives get jobs and empowerment for their businesses.

“So, this would also make us happy and help us know that we are not alone in this and that our husbands did not die for nothing.”

Lamenting the difficulties some widows face in accessing the benefits of their deceased husbands from the relevant authorities, Mrs Oni said such issues should also be addressed.

“These are things that should also be looked into so that course mates and friends of the late officer or soldier can also assist these women in accessing their benefits,” she said.

Another widow, Mrs Ibrahim Adeze, appealed to the government and corporate organisations to create employment opportunities for young widows of fallen heroes to enable them to provide for their families.

“I would appreciate it if they could give them jobs to do, enlighten them about available schemes or train them so that they can become economically independent.

“Another thing they can do to help the widows is to ensure that they are not misled by bad elements by making sure that, after the training, they are properly mentored. This will help ensure that the skills and training they receive enable them to stabilise their homes,” she said.

The programme brought together 500 widows of military personnel who paid the supreme price in service to the nation, with interventions focused on welfare support, empowerment and strengthening the economic resilience of beneficiaries.

The widows called for sustained support in areas such as education, healthcare, skills acquisition, housing and other forms of assistance that could improve the welfare and livelihoods of affected families.

They also urged well-meaning individuals, corporate organisations, foundations and other stakeholders to partner with relevant government agencies and associations to provide sustainable interventions for the families of fallen heroes.

World.title: NAFDAC DG Seeks Foreign Partners’ Support For Local Vaccine Production
World.content:
Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja

The Director General of the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC), Prof. Mojisola Adeyeye, has solicited the support of international partners to establish vaccine manufacturing facilities in Nigeriia.

She said that opening vaccine manufacturing companies will hasten the push by the agency to attain World Health Organisation (WHO) Maturity Level 4 for vaccine lot release.

Adeyeye made the call at the 8th Nigeria Pharma Manufacturers’ Expo in Lagos, jointly organised by the Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Group of Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (PMG-MAN) and PGE Expo Pvt Ltd.

A statement signed by NAFDAC’s Resident Media Consultant Sanyo Akintola said that the DG acknowledged the continued support of international partners in NAFDAC’s attainment of Maturity Level 3, and challenged them to contribute to fill-and-finish modular vaccine manufacturing.

According to Adeyeye, NAFDAC has nine functions to meet for full benchmarking for medicines and vaccines, but has only been benchmarked in eight, with lot release for vaccines outstanding.

“We want to call on our international partners that have been of tremendous help. Without them we wouldn’t have been here. I want to challenge them to contribute to fill and finish modular vaccine manufacturing so that we can get our vaccine lot release,” she said.

Adeyeye said Nigeria has what it takes to attain the level except local vaccine manufacturing, adding that the cost has been estimated and will not be too high. “We cannot afford to go back to where we used to be,” she said.

Recalling that Nigeria used to manufacture vaccines, Adeyeye said it is time to return to local production.

She commended President Bola Tinubu for the Executive Order 2024, describing it as game-changing and bringing life to NAFDAC’s clamour for incentives for local manufacturers operating under harsh conditions.

“I was championing incentives for the manufacturers until President Tinubu came on board with the Executive Order of 2024,” she said, noting that both the Coordinating Minister of Health and Minister of State bought into the rationale leading to unlocking the healthcare value chain.

She said NAFDAC’s Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) Roadmap audit of over 165 companies, funded by USAID and executed by United States Pharmacopeia, led to improved quality and 70 per cent decrease in import of products under the ‘5 plus 5’ and Ceiling Initiatives between 2021 and 2025.

She also said that NAFDAC became a member of International Medical Device Forum in 2023 while, its Yaba laboratory became WHO pre-qualified in September 2023, and it became the first agency in sub-Saharan Africa to be successfully re-benchmarked for Maturity Level 3.

In his remarks, Chairman of PMG-MAN, Mr. Oluwatosin Jolayemi, described the expo as only complete pharma manufacturing platform in Central and West Africa and commended Adeyeye for driving international best practices.

He called for the extension of the presidential executive order by two years at expiration in March 2027, saying medicine security requires policy consistency.

No fewer than 132 companies from US, China, Argentina, Egypt, India, Rwanda, Austria, UAE, France, Germany, Indonesia and Nigeria participated in the two-day expo.

World.title: Shettima Arrives Katsina to Inaugurate 11.2km Roads, Launch 230 Mass Transit Vehicles
World.content:
Francis Sardauna in Katsina

Vice-President Kashim Shettima has arrived in Katsina State for a one-day official visit during which he is expected to inaugurate 11.2 kilometres of road projects and launch 230 mass transit vehicles.

The vice-president, who was received by Governor Dikko Umaru Radda on arrival at the Umaru Musa Yar’Adua Airport, Katsina, also inspected a quarter guard mounted by the personnel of the Nigerian Air Force.

During the visit, Shettima is scheduled to inaugurate three major road projects executed by Governor Radda’s administration.

The projects include the dualised 4.80-kilometre Kofar Sauri–Central Mosque Roundabout Road; the dualised 2.40-kilometre Central Police Station Junction–Kofar Kaura Underpass Road; and the newly constructed 4.00-kilometre Filin Polo–Ring Road.

The vice-president will also launch 30 CNG hybrid buses and 200 Phase I electric tricycles at the Old Ministry of Works as part of efforts to strengthen mass transportation in the state.

Shettima is further expected to receive new defectors into the All Progressives Congress (APC) at a political gathering at the Peoples Square, Government House, Katsina.

At the time of filing this report, the vice-president was at the Muhammadu Dikko Stadium, Katsina, where he was flagging off the Community Investment Fund under the Nigeria for Women Programme Scale-Up (NFWP-SU).

The World Bank-supported initiative focused on supporting women’s economic empowerment and financial inclusion in the state.

Among those who joined Governor Radda to receive the vice-president were the Emir of Katsina, Alhaji Abdulmumini Kabir Usman, members of the State Executive Council and other top government officials

World.title: Ndume Lauds Tinubu For Increase In Military Personnel Salary
World.content:
Folalumi Alaran in Abuja

A member of the National Assembly, Senator Ali Ndume, has hailed President Bola Tinubu for making good his pledge to increase the salary of Armed Forces personnel.

The former Senate Leader thumbed up the president in a release issued at the weekend.

Reacting to the increase in the salary of both officers and men of the three services which took effect from September 2026, the ranking senator praised Tinubu for walking his talks and urged him to continue to do everything necessary to boost the morale of personnel of the Nigerian military.

He however tasked military personnel to redouble their efforts in combating insurgency, kidnapping and banditry.

The former Chairman of the Senate Committee on Army maintained that in the last three years, the present government has shown commitment to curbing insecurity by taking proactive initiatives in terms of financing to procure adequate arms and ammunition and doing everything necessary to boost the morale of the Armed Forces personnel.

His words: “Making a pronouncement is one thing, redeeming your pledge is a different ball game entirely.

“President Tinubu has shown times without number that he keeps to his words. It is heartwarming to note that the salary increment he promised the Nigerian Army has been redeemed.

“I want to urge our officers to redouble their efforts to curtail insecurity since the present administration is doing everything to boost their morale. They should do more now that they also have more troops on the ground with the recent recruitment.

“The activation of the Army Aviation would also go a long way in complementing the efforts of the Air Force now that we also have attack helicopters in the six geo-political zones.”

Ndume reiterated his appeal for better, coordinated synergy between the infantry and the Air Force in the war against insurgency and banditry.

The Presidency had last month issued an official statement with a commitment to commence implementation of new salary package for certain categories of Armed Forces personnel.

According to a statement attributed to presidential spokesperson, Bayo Onanuga,

officers above the rank of colonel, including brigadier generals, major generals, lieutenant generals and generals, would receive a 30 percent salary increase.

He also added that personnel from lieutenant colonel down to warrant officer would get a 50 per cent increase, while those from private to staff sergeant would receive an 80 per cent increase.

The presidential aide, who said the new package would raise the annual salary bill for armed forces personnel from N660 billion to N924 billion, declared that over 250,000 personnel of the Nigerian Armed Forces would be beneficiaries..

World.title: Cape Town areas to experience 11-hour water shutdown
World.content:
The City of Cape Town has confirmed that some areas will experience a 10-hour water shutdown on Wednesday,

The Water and Sanitation Directorate said the planned maintenance forms part of ongoing efforts to upgrade critical infrastructure and improve water supply across the city.

CAPE TOWN AREAS SET TO EXPERIENCE WATER SUPPLY DISRUPTION

The City of Cape Town said planned maintenance work, including pipe and valve installations, repairs, and replacements, will result in water supply disruption to these areas:



Part of Grassy Park – The water supply to Dieman Road, Iris Road and possibly surrounding streets in Grassy Park will be shut off temporarily on Wednesday, 7 October 2026, from 08:00 until 19:00. This will allow the maintenance teams to safely connect the newly installed pipelines to the existing water supply infrastructure in the area.

“These streets and possibly surrounding streets will experience no water during this period,” the municipality said.

Parts of Woodstock – The City of Cape Town will start with the pipe replacement project that will affect the water supply intermittently to parts of Woodstock from Monday, 5 October 2026 until Friday, 30 April 2027.



The metro municipality said this will result in the water being shut off in Ravenscraig Road, Woodlands Road, Pine Road, Queens Road, Beyers Road, Warwick Street, Salmon Street, Coventry Road, Duke Road, Park Road, High Street, and possibly surrounding streets in Woodstock temporarily from 08:00 until 17:00 daily.

“This will allow the maintenance team to safely carry out the pipe and valve replacement in the area using trenchless technology, which is less of an inconvenience to residents and motorists. These streets and possibly surrounding streets will experience no water during this period and will be notified in advance when they will be affected,” the municipality said.

Parts of Strand – Similarly, the City of Cape Town will shut off the water supply to parts of Broadlands Road, from the vicinity of the Strandfoam Group (Pty) Ltd to the N2, Lwandle Helderberg Industrial and possibly surrounding streets in Strand temporarily on Wednesday, 7 October 2026, from 09:00 until 18:00. This will allow the maintenance team to safely carry out a new connection to the 300mm-diameter water main in the area. These areas and possibly surrounding streets will experience no water during this period.



ZERO-PRESSURE TESTS

Additionally, the City of Cape Town said it will conduct zero-pressure tests (ZPT) and conditional assessments on the water supply network, resulting in water supply disruptions in the following areas:

Wednesday, 7 October 2026, 09:00 to 16:00: Martinville – Bizweni.

Martinville – Bizweni. Thursday, 8 October 2026, 09:00 to 16:00: Helderzicht, Lourensia Park, Paardevlei, Victoria Park, Silvertas, Garden Village and Carey Park.

Helderzicht, Lourensia Park, Paardevlei, Victoria Park, Silvertas, Garden Village and Carey Park. Thursday, 8 October 2026, 09:00 to 16:00: Da Gama Park, Welcome Glen and Scala Road.

Residents have been advised to store water in advance as a precautionary measure in clean, sealed containers for domestic use during this period.

World.title: ‘Heist of the century’: Fans react to Orlando Pirates’ R20.2m court bid
World.content:
Orlando Pirates supporters have reacted after the club launched an urgent court application to freeze R20.2 million allegedly diverted from its accounts.

The matter was filed in the Johannesburg High Court, with the funds reportedly linked to hundreds of unauthorised transactions allegedly involving former finance manager Darryl Joselowsky.

According to reports by Sowetan, Pirates is seeking to freeze four bank accounts allegedly linked to Joselowsky, which have a combined balance of R20.2 million.



The club is also seeking further information from Standard Bank to establish where the money went and who ultimately benefited from the transactions.

Orlando Pirates, however, stressed that the court application does not constitute a finding of wrongdoing.

“The application is not a finding of wrongdoing and should not be interpreted as one. The individual concerned is cooperating, and the Club is committed to a fair process for everyone involved,” the club said in a statement.

The allegations have sparked plenty of reaction among football supporters on social media, with some questioning how a club of Pirates’ stature could allegedly lose such a substantial amount of money through unauthorised transactions.

Fans react to Orlando Pirates ‘losing millions’

@SpholaM6 wrote: “For such a big institution to have these weak internal controls when it comes to its banking process is shocking…”

@Deeflowwd4 added: “They were busy swearing at Pitso and Modiba while a heist of the century was in place.”



Meanwhile, @SundownsOGs joked: “Darryl Joselowsky won’t see heaven. So the whole Betway Premiership prize money is gone.”

“He is very brave. Pickpocketing the Iron Duke?” tweeted @S_Gwiliza.

Orlando Pirates are in action this coming weekend against Mamelodi Sundowns in the MTN8 final.

What’s your take?

World.title: IFP leader calls for no bail and life sentences for convicted rapists
World.content:
Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) leader Velenkosini Hlabisa says people accused of rape should not be granted bail and those found guilty should receive life sentences without parole.

Hlabisa made the remarks while addressing party members at the Greyville Racecourse in Durban on Sunday, 4 October, where the party launched its eThekwini manifesto.

IFP CALLS FOR TOUGHER ACTION AGAINST RAPE

During his address, Hlabisa urged men to join the fight against gender-based violence (GBV) and femicide, emphasising their responsibility to protect women and children.



“Once you are arrested on a case of rape, the person must not be given bail until the case is finalised. When found guilty, the person must be given a life sentence without parole because rapists and murderers are monsters in our society who must be removed once and for all,” said Hlabisa.

Hlabisa’s comments come amid continued concerns about GBV and femicide in South Africa, with political parties calling for stronger action against perpetrators.

SIBIYA FACES RAPE AND OTHER CHARGES

IFP leader Velenkosini Hlabisa’s remarks also come as suspended Deputy National Police Commissioner Lieutenant-General Shadrack Sibiya faces six charges, including rape, sexual grooming of a minor, human trafficking and negligent handling of a firearm.

Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman and sexually grooming a 16-year-old girl. He has denied the allegations, telling the Randburg Magistrates’ Court that his sexual encounter with the 18-year-old was consensual.

His bail application is ongoing, with the state opposing his release. The matter was postponed to 7 October.
