World.title: Sudan: WFP Strongly Condemns Attack on Trucks in South Kordofan, Killing One Driver
World.content:
Abyei and Southern Kordofan are key areas in the dispute between north and south Sudan.

Khartoum — The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) strongly condemns an aerial attack that hit two contracted trucks carrying WFP food commodities in South Kordofan in the early hours of Saturday, 3 October 2026.

One driver was killed in the air strike. We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends and colleagues.

The contracted trucks were en route from Dilling to Kadugli and clearly marked as humanitarian vehicles. Additional details regarding the circumstances of the incident, including the extent of the damage to the food cargo, are still being collected.

WFP calls for a prompt and impartial investigation into this incident and for those responsible for any violations to be held accountable.



This latest attack comes only one day after a WFP truck struck an explosive device in Dilling, South Kordofan, after delivering lifesaving food assistance.

WFP urges all those involved in the hostilities to respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, and ensure the safe and unimpeded movement of humanitarian personnel and cargo.

These incidents underscore the increasingly challenging security environment in Sudan and the risks that aid workers face when delivering life-saving assistance to communities in need. WFP remains committed to safely delivering life-saving assistance to millions of women, men, and children who depend on humanitarian support across Sudan.

# # #

The United Nations World Food Programme is the world’s largest humanitarian organization saving lives in emergencies and using food assistance to build a pathway to peace, stability and prosperity for people recovering from conflict, disasters and the impact of weather extremes.

World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia Captures Tigray Capital As Its Regional Rivals Meet in Egypt
World.content:
Ethiopian federal forces have regained control of the Tigray rebels' regional capital, local sources said on Sunday, while Ethiopia's regional rivals gathered in Egypt to discuss the risk of a wider war.

The capture of Mekelle, capital of Tigray, deals a major blow to the opposition alliance that rules the northern region.

The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which leads the alliance, said in a statement posted on Facebook it had retreated from the capital and that the regional government would be "temporarily moved out of Mekelle and operate from somewhere else".

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The TPLF launched a fresh offensive against the federal government last month, drawing counterattacks and sparking fears of a return to the devastating civil war of 2020-2022.

As concerns grow that the violence could spread beyond Ethiopia's borders, the presidents of Egypt, Somalia, Sudan and Eritrea were set to meet in the Egyptian city of Alamein on Sunday to discuss the conflict.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of directly backing the Tigray rebels, with the support of Sudan and Egypt, which all three countries deny.

Rebels flee

A source close to a pro-government militia, the Tigray Peace Forces, told Reuters its fighters entered the centre of Mekelle on Saturday afternoon, followed by the Ethiopian military.

Federal troops were patrolling Mekelle and manning key institutions on Sunday, a local journalist told French news agency AFP, as communications were restored for the first time in more than a week.

"We have taken control of Mekelle and we are marching forward," a commander with a pro-government militia said.

Businesses and shops remained closed, with owners moving stock to safer locations ahead of time, fearing looting and vandalism.

"There are no police. Last night, we had to organise ourselves and take care of security," one resident told AFP.

A local business owner, Filmon Equar Hailu, told the Associated Press civilians looted government offices and hauled away equipment from police headquarters as rebel fighters withdrew.

He said he heard celebratory gunfire overnight into Sunday morning as small groups of pro-government fighters entered the city.

Renewed fighting in Tigray raises risk of a wider regional war

Egypt talks

The TPLF has long been the dominant force in Tigray, ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year. It was also the dominant group in a coalition that ruled Ethiopia between 1991 and 2018.

Since it launched its campaign against the federal government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on 23 September, a counteroffensive has seen Ethiopian forces push deep into rebel-held territory.

Analysts say the fighting threatens to escalate into a wider regional conflict.

Sunday's mini-summit in Alamein - taking place on the sidelines of an African Business Forum - was set to bring together Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somalian President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Sudanese Armed Forces head Abdel Fattah al-Burhan.

Before the talks, Sisi urged "dialogue, not confrontation".

Ethiopia's new rebel war redraws alliances across the Horn of Africa

Eritrea, which shares a long border with the Tigray region, is most directly involved in the conflict.

It accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to its coastline. Analysts say it has backed the rebels in Ethiopia in a bid to keep the conflict away from its border.

Close 

The African Union has urged restraint, warning that renewed tensions threaten the 2022 peace agreement that ended the previous hostilities in Tigray.

The TPLF's war with the federal government killed some 600,000 people between 2020 and 2022, according to AU estimates.

The TPLF also pulled out of Mekelle during that conflict, apparently to spare the city from destruction.

The rebels' leader Debretsion Gebremichael implied this week that the group would continue guerrilla-style attacks, as they did last time Mekelle fell. "We operate under a strategy to strike the enemy wherever we choose," he said.

(with newswires)

World.title: Nigeria: Nigerian Drugmaker Fidson Selected to Manufacture Generic Influenza Antiviral Under Global Licence
World.content:
The selected manufacturers are from Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Nigeria, Uganda, Ukraine and Vietnam.

A Nigerian pharmaceutical company, Fidson Healthcare Plc, has been selected to develop and manufacture a generic version of baloxavir marboxil, an antiviral medicine used to treat influenza.

The selection makes Fidson one of 11 manufacturers across nine countries chosen under a voluntary licensing agreement between the Medicines Patent Pool (MPP) and Swiss pharmaceutical company Roche.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The company disclosed this in a press release signed by its media contact, Tope Akindele. The MPP, a United Nations-backed public health organisation, also announced the sublicence agreements on 25 September.

The selected manufacturers are from Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Nigeria, Uganda, Ukraine and Vietnam. The MPP said the arrangement is intended to "diversify supply pathways for influenza treatment, support regional production, and strengthen preparedness for future outbreaks and pandemics."

What it means for Fidson, Nigeria

The selection makes Fidson one of the manufacturers that would develop, manufacture and supply generic versions of baloxavir in 129 countries covered by the licence, subject to regulatory authorisation.

The agreement also gives selected manufacturers access to technical data, reference products for bioequivalence studies and other support to facilitate product development and regulatory approval.

The MPP said it selected the manufacturers following an open Expression of Interest process and an assessment of their technical and regulatory capacities and commitment to producing quality-assured baloxavir products.

The organisation said having manufacturers in different regions would help build production capacity closer to the populations the medicines are intended to serve and strengthen the resilience of global supply.

For Nigeria, the selection places a local pharmaceutical manufacturer in a global effort to expand production of an influenza antiviral while strengthening domestic and regional pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity.

Selection strengthens Africa's role

Fidson's Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Biola Adebayo, described the selection as a validation of the company's commitment to quality-assured pharmaceutical manufacturing and innovation.

"Being selected by the Medicines Patent Pool as a sublicensee under the Roche-MPP voluntary licensing programme for baloxavir marboxil is both an honour and a validation of Fidson's longstanding commitment to quality-assured pharmaceutical manufacturing, innovation, and improving healthcare outcomes," Mr Adebayo said.

Close 

He said the partnership would allow the company to contribute to efforts to strengthen regional health security and preparedness for future health emergencies.

"As an African healthcare company, we are proud to contribute to global efforts aimed at strengthening regional health security, enhancing preparedness for future health emergencies, and ensuring that life-saving medicines reach the patients who need them most," he said.

Mr Adebayo said the partnership also demonstrated the growing role of African manufacturers in the global health ecosystem.

He said Fidson would work with Roche, the MPP and other stakeholders to support broader access to baloxavir across eligible markets.

Part of pandemic preparedness

The announcement came as global leaders gathered in New York for the United Nations General Assembly to discuss pandemic prevention, preparedness and response.

The MPP said the licensing arrangement is designed to build manufacturing capacity before, rather than during, a health emergency.

Charles Gore, Executive Director of the MPP, said the organisation would work with the selected manufacturers on product development and regulatory approval, aiming to make quality-assured generic baloxavir available as quickly as possible.

"By combining global manufacturing capacity with regionally focused production, we are helping build a more geographically diverse and resilient supply base for the future," Mr Gore said.

World.title: Nigeria: How Tinubu Ran Nigeria During Four-Week Trip Abroad - Shettima
World.content:
Mr Shettima the economic difficulties facing Nigerians and said the government is working on measures to reduce the impact of the hardship.

Nigeria's Vice President Kashim Shettima has said President Bola Tinubu remained in regular contact with his administration and received updates on developments in the country during his four-week stay abroad.

Mr Shettima disclosed this on Saturday after meeting Mr Tinubu at the president's residence in Lagos, four days after the President returned to Nigeria from his extended working vacation.



The vice president said, while speaking to journalists after his meeting with Mr Tinubu, that he and Mr Tinubu spoke "almost every other day" throughout the president's stay abroad, with regular updates on developments in the country.

"We have been in regular contact throughout his sojourn abroad," Mr Shettima said. "We speak almost every other day, and we are updating him. We are updating him on developments in the nation, and we are happy he's back on the beat."

The comments provide an insight into how the administration operated while Mr Tinubu was outside the country for about four weeks, during which the president's absence generated public discussion amid his failure to hand over to the Vice-President.

The presidency had earlier said Mr Tinubu continued to keep in touch with officials at home and directed the affairs of the country while abroad.

It cited, among other decisions, the president's directive for an independent panel to investigate the deaths of 37 illegal miners in Minna.

Mr Shettima's account adds that the president was receiving frequent briefings from his administration throughout his absence.

We appreciate pains Nigerians are going through -- Shettima

The vice president also used his meeting with Mr Tinubu to defend the administration's economic policies, particularly the removal of petrol subsidy and the unification of the country's multiple exchange rates.

He said the decisions were taken when the economy was "teetering on the verge of collapse", arguing that Mr Tinubu had the courage to implement what he described as far-reaching reforms.

"When we assume the mantle of leadership, our foreign reserves was a staggeringly low $3.9 billion that was not enough to import oil for one month," Mr Shettima said.

"He saved the economy. I want Nigerians to understand this fundamental truism. We are on the road to Caracas. He saved our economy. He saved the nation from falling to pieces."

Mr Shettima, however, acknowledged the economic difficulties facing Nigerians and said the government is working on measures to reduce the impact of the hardship.

"We appreciate the pains Nigerians are going through, but tough times do not last forever. Tough people do," he said.

He announced that the federal government would, in the coming weeks, introduce new transport and logistics initiatives in the North-east, including 10,600 electric tricycles and 300 buses and electric taxis.

He said the initiatives were designed to reduce the burden on Nigerians and "ameliorate the sufferings" of people in the region.

Mr Shettima also described the Nigeria Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) as a major intervention for students from poor backgrounds, saying the scheme would help students with limited financial means gain access to higher education.

He said the government would continue to introduce programmes aimed at easing the hardship experienced by Nigerians.

"Politics is in the air, but we will combine politics and governance," Mr Shettima said.

Close 

Mr Tinubu left Nigeria on 30 August for London for a working vacation where he spent a week before travelling to Paris, France where he met French President Emmanuel Macron, businessman Vincent Bolloré and other business leaders during his stay.

He also witnessed the signing of an agreement between the Ogun State Government and DP World for a proposed deep seaport and economic zone in Ogun Waterside.

The president returned to Nigeria on 29 September, arriving at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport in Lagos ahead of Nigeria's 66th independence celebration.

The president dismissed the concerns about his health as political rumour, and said he is healthy and ready to resume duties.

"Rumor will always be emanating from politics, but the facts remain, I'm here. Healthy, sound, and ready to go," he said. "I am ready to kick, ready to work. There's nothing wrong."

World.title: Uganda: Uganda's UN-Supported Wildlife Forensics Lab Turns Ivory Seizures Into Convictions
World.content:
A lab technician carries out a test at the Uganda Wildlife Forensics and Timber Laboratory in Entebbe.

The package originated in Entebbe, Uganda, bound for Cairo, containing 10 kilograms of thumb-sized pieces that could have been either bone or elephant ivory.

When detectives from the Uganda Police Force and investigators from the Uganda Wildlife Authority intercepted the package in January 2025, they needed more than suspicion to investigate the person who sent the package.

The police sent a sample to the Uganda Wildlife Forensics and Timber Laboratory in Entebbe, a facility that has been supported since 2019 by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Scientists found a distinctive cross-hatched pattern associated with elephant ivory. DNA testing later confirmed that the material came from an elephant, lab manager Patrick Chiyo told UN News.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

© European Union A lab technician carries out a test at the Uganda Wildlife Forensics and Timber Laboratory in Entebbe. Two months later, police arrested the man who sent the package. At his residence, investigators found additional elephant ivory, along with warthog ivory. He was charged with attempted trafficking and illegal possession and sentenced to 15 years in prison or a fine equivalent to 140 million Ugandan shillings - or more than $35,000 USD.

For Mr. Chiyo, the case illustrates why forensic evidence matters in the fight against wildlife crime: it can establish what an animal product is when traffickers have cut it into small pieces or removed the physical characteristics that would make it easy to identify.

"Poachers are removing identification features from wildlife carcasses to evade detection," Mr. Chiyo said.

He added that DNA reports are increasingly being required by Uganda's wildlife court and that suspects are pleading guilty more often thanks to the lab.

From seizure to science

Evidence from the UN's 2024 World Wildlife Report shows that Uganda is as a significant hub of organised wildlife trafficking networks - especially of elephant ivory but also pangolin, a scaly anteater.

In April, the Uganda Wildlife Forensics and Timber Laboratory opened with support from Denmark, the European Union and UNODC to help address the ivory issue.

It builds on a national training and technical support centre established in 2019 as a pilot wildlife forensics facility through a partnership involving UNODC, the TRACE Wildlife Forensics Network and the Ugandan Government. The earlier facility has assisted hundreds of investigations and prosecutions connected to illegal wildlife trade.

The lab's work often begins far from Entebbe. Officers may seize sacks containing ivory pieces, pangolin scales or smoked bushmeat. Because these seizures can be bulky, scientists collect samples at police stations, documenting each step along the way.

Evidence is photographed before it is opened, and again after sampling. The original exhibit is returned to police custody, while sealed samples are transported to the lab for analysis.

The process can take a significant amount of time, Mr. Chiyo said, but it can be decisive, especially when animal remains are incomplete, altered or difficult to identify.

In one case in 2023, Mr. Chiyo travelled about four hours north of Kampala after a suspect was arrested with six skins, six heads, two sacks of meat, 24 hoofed legs and a fetus believed to be from wildlife. The skins appeared to come from antelope, but their exact identity could not be confirmed from appearance alone.

Mr. Chiyo and his team collected samples from the skins and fetus, then used DNA analysis to determine that they came from bushbucks. Mr. Chiyo later testified in court, and the suspect was sentenced to three years in prison.

Targeting wildlife crime

The lab most commonly receives evidence involving elephant ivory, bushmeat and pangolin scales, Mr. Chiyo said.

Bashir Hangi, from the Uganda Wildlife Authority, told UN News that elephants, pangolins, primates and some bird species are among the animals most threatened by illegal poaching and trade in Uganda.

Some people hunt animals for household consumption, while others kill wildlife for commercial gain, Mr. Chiyo said. Commercial trade is the larger threat for wildlife conservation, he added.

Although Mr. Chiyo said Uganda does not have a domestic market for ivory and pangolin scales, there is a thriving market for poached bushmeat. Authorities have encountered cases involving nearly a tonne of meat, he said.

Mr. Hangi said wildlife crime is driven both by organised criminal networks and by local communities facing economic hardship.

The impacts can also fall heavily on communities living near protected areas, where wildlife-related conflict and crop raiding have caused significant problems.

Mr. Chiyo said enforcement must reach the person who kills or captures an animal and those higher up in criminal networks who also profit. Prosecuting higher-ups requires more investment in interagency networks, he added.

© European Union A sample is tested at Uganda's Wildlife Forensics and Timber Laboratory. At the same time, he said, criminal justice is not enough. Alternative livelihoods are important, although they may not eliminate poaching linked to cultural values. He suggested a combined approach of livelihood support, preventive patrols and legal deterrence.

"A living wildlife is worth more benefits for many more people than a dead one," Mr. Chiyo said.

New focus on timber

The Entebbe lab expanded into timber forensics in April, adding a new capability as Uganda confronts the environmental consequences of illegal logging and timber trafficking.

According to Ugandan authorities, Uganda's forest cover has fallen from 24 per cent in 1990 to roughly 13 per cent in 2025, in large part due to timber trafficking. The new forensic capacity is intended to strengthen efforts to investigate illegal logging.

© Adobe/Pawel A safari vehicle passes through Bwindi Impenetrable Forest in Uganda. Timber cases are more complicated than wildlife cases, Mr. Chiyo said, because harvesting is also permitted and regulated in many circumstances. Determining whether a piece of wood was obtained illegally can require additional steps and presents different challenges from identifying animal products.

Close 

The lab is only beginning to handle timber cases and has not yet seen evidence that illegal timber is moving through the same networks or routes as wildlife products, he said.

Critical for conservation

Still, the lab's expansion reflects an increased recognition of the role of cracking down on wildlife and timber trafficking on protecting the environment.

Gladys Kamasanyu, the chief magistrate of the Uganda Wildlife Court, told UNODC in April that criminal justice and law enforcement can play a key role in these efforts.

"The forensic laboratory is critical to the criminal justice system, significantly enhancing the court's ability to hold offenders accountable by providing objective, scientifically validated evidence to protect Uganda's natural heritage for future generations," Ms. Kamasanyu said.

Recognising the same relationship between law enforcement and conservation, Mr. Chiyo said his benchmark for success in the next few years would be "a sustainable and fully government supported wildlife and timber forensic laboratory in Uganda."

At the current lab, however, each confirmed DNA sequence and seizure can help close the gap between a suspicion of trafficking and a prosecutable crime.

"Enhancing criminal justice through wildlife and timber forensics is an important pillar in environment protection," Mr. Chiyo said. "Environmental justice will usually benefit the very vulnerable in society."

World.title: Ethiopia: Tigray Rebels Reportedly Abandon Capital As Ethiopian Government Forces Advance
World.content:
Tigray rebels are abandoning their regional capital in northern Ethiopia, local residents said on Saturday, as pro-government forces advanced on the city. The region is in the grip of the worst fighting since the civil war of 2020-2022.

Fighting erupted on 23 September as the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched attacks into neighbouring states, raising fears of a return to all-out conflict.

But federal forces and pro-government militias have pushed them back and are heading north towards the regional capital, Mekelle, witnesses told French news agency AFP.

"TPLF militants and leaders are leaving Mekelle," a local journalist said. Federal forces had not yet been seen inside the city, an opposition stronghold.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Government offices and police stations were left without security personnel, residents said.

"I am concerned that government and public property could be exposed to looting because there are no security forces in the city," one told AFP.

Another said: "I am worried that lawlessness could spread in the city, and I am also afraid for my life. I want us to quickly return to law and order."

Ethiopia accuses Sudan, Eritrea of backing Tigray forces as fighting escalates

Government counteroffensive

The taking of Mekelle by pro-government forces would be a major setback for an opposition alliance formed last month by TPLF and six other armed movements to fight Ethiopia's federal government.

After launching their offensive last month, the rebels initially made advances in Afar and Amhara states - which border Tigray - with the help of local militias.

But they were pushed back this week, and Ethiopian federal forces and allied fighters have launched a counteroffensive pushing into Tigrayan territory.

On Friday, a pro-government militia said it had recaptured Mekelle's main airport.

"We have taken full control of Mekelle Alula Aba Nega Airport. We are currently clearing the city of Mekelle," the Tigray Peace Forces militia posted on X late on Friday.

The claims could not be independently verified, with media prevented from travelling to affected areas and significant communications disruptions.

Close 

Meanwhile a humanitarian source told AFP on condition of anonymity that the TPLF had been pushed entirely out of Afar.

Ethiopia's new rebel war redraws alliances across the Horn of Africa

The conflict has triggered a breakdown in Ethiopia's relations with Eritrea and Egypt, who it accuses of supporting the rebels.

Addis Ababa expelled Eritrean and Egyptian diplomats on Thursday, prompting tit-for-tat expulsions in return.

The African Union, which is based in Ethiopia, said it was "following with concern the heightened tensions between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt", urging "maximum restraint".

The TPLF's civil war with the federal government killed some 600,000 people between 2020 and 2022, according to AU estimates.

(with newswires)

World.title: East Africa: What Washington Agreed to Last Month - Somaliland
World.content:
Berbera sits on the Gulf of Aden, about 150 miles south of Yemen. Its deep-water berth and the Emirati investment behind it are what Somaliland has been offering Washington.

analysis

Somaliland's president spent two weeks in Washington this month offering almost everything he has. Access to the port at Berbera. Access to the territory's minerals. Military access, which he called a matter for negotiation and declined to rule out. He only asked for one thing in return. Recognition. He went home without it. The same month, the United States secured expanded security rights in Greenland and agreed in writing that sovereignty stays with Denmark.

What Somaliland Offered

Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, known as Irro, arrived on September 5 for his first visit to the United States since winning Somaliland's presidency in November 2024. On the 14th, he gave the keynote address at the Hudson Institute, at an event titled Somaliland as a Strategic Partner in the Horn of Africa.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

His pitch was the seaport. Irro described Berbera as a modern deep water facility that United States Africa Command had already assessed and in which the Emirati operator DP World has invested $442 million. More than twelve percent of global maritime trade passes through the Bab el-Mandeb strait every day. He argued that Somaliland has protected its coastline from militants and pirates for three decades without any recognition at all.

Two days later he went further. In an interview with Semafor he said Somaliland was not giving anything away for free. He offered American investors the port and the minerals. On military access he said it was a matter for negotiation, and he would not rule out a future base agreement. Ten days later he added more. In an interview with the Council on Foreign Relations he suggested renaming Berbera International Airport after President Trump, having earlier floated a Trump Tower in Hargeisa.

What They Got

Nothing, so far. Irro himself said there is no American promise on recognition. A source told Politico there is no change in American policy towards Somaliland.

On September 16, China warned Irro that crossing its line on Taiwan would bring serious consequences, and publicly affirmed that Somaliland remains part of Somalia. That handed Mogadishu an endorsement from a permanent member of the Security Council in the middle of a rival's tour.

The Hudson appearance also drew criticism at home. Clips circulated of Irro hesitating on questions about minerals and regional security. The event's moderator, Joshua Meservey of the Hudson Institute, said afterwards that Irro had made the right argument, while also observing that Somaliland has not consistently made the case for the reason recognition is necessary.

What Happened For Greenland

On the evening of September 18, President Trump announced an agreement with Denmark and Greenland giving the United States permanent control over security in Greenland. He described it as an agreement with no end, at no cost. The three governments signed it in New York on September 22, and the White House released the text the same day.

Copenhagen and Nuuk described something narrower. Greenland's prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, said the agreement recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of Greenlanders to self-determination. A State Department official told CBS News it gives permanent access and overflight rights, allows more bases and bars non-NATO members from building their own.

None of this is new ground. American forces have been in Greenland since 1941, and a 1951 defence agreement gave the United States the right to operate bases there, with Danish sovereignty expressly preserved. Reading the text signed this month, ABC News reported that it does not appear to add materially to that access. What Washington secured was a broader scope and a bar on rival powers. The access itself it already had.

Set the two outcomes beside each other. In Greenland, Washington obtained security control, overflight rights and the option of more bases, and conceded in writing that sovereignty is unchanged. In Somaliland, Washington was offered a deep-water port, a mineral concession and a negotiable military base, and conceded nothing.

Two Governments, One Port

The Greenland agreement works because everyone with a claim signed it. Denmark holds sovereignty. Greenland holds self-government. The United States holds the access. Three parties, one signature page.

That page does not exist for Berbera. Two governments have now offered Washington the same port. In a letter dated March 16, 2025, Somalia's president offered the United States exclusive operational control of the port and air base at Berbera. Somalia's foreign ministry confirmed the letter to the Associated Press as an authentic draft, and Semafor reported that the offer was made to head off any American recognition of Somaliland, and that Mogadishu does not control the sites it was offering.

This month Hargeisa offered the same port. So the government with the recognition does not control Berbera, and the government that controls Berbera does not have the recognition. Each has offered the port to Washington. The Greenland model needs both names on one page, and these two will not sign the same page.

What the Continent Has Not Done

Somaliland declared the restoration of its independence in 1991, three decades after joining the former Italian-administered south to form Somalia. No state recognised it until Israel did in December 2025. The African Union has been asked directly. In 2005 it sent a fact-finding mission to Hargeisa, which reported that the 1960 union had never been ratified and called Somaliland's search for recognition historically unique in African political history. It recommended that the Union find a special method of handling the case, and never adopted the report.

The reason is Article 4(b) of the AU Constitutive Act, which carries forward the 1964 decision of the Organisation of African Unity that the borders states held at independence are to be respected. The chairperson of the AU Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, said in December 2025 that recognising Somaliland would set a dangerous precedent for Somalia's unity and territorial integrity. The closest any neighbour has come was Ethiopia's memorandum with Hargeisa in January 2024, which traded access to the sea for the prospect of recognition. Mogadishu treated it as an act of aggression, and the two governments buried it in Ankara that December.

A Hidden Cost

The argument for recognition, as it is being made in Washington, is about maritime security and great power competition. It has a hole in it, and it is the counterterrorism side.

Close 

Israel recognised Somaliland in December 2025. Within days the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, warned that any Israeli assets in Somaliland would be legitimate military targets. The Wall Street Journal reported in August that a four-member Houthi delegation crossed from Yemen in June to Jilib, al-Shabaab's stronghold in southern Somalia, to discuss countering Israeli activity around Berbera.

The cost is not hypothetical. Maersk suspended new cargo bookings to and from Berbera in April, citing scheduling changes. It came days after the Houthi authorities in Sanaa warned about expanding Israeli engagement in the Horn. One country's recognition of Somaliland has already cost the port Irro is selling one of the world's largest shipping lines.

The larger cost is in the south. The United States fights al-Shabaab through the federal government in Mogadishu, which offered Washington Berbera for the express purpose of preventing recognition of Somaliland. A deal with Hargeisa over the same port is a deal made against the government the southern fight depends on.

What to Watch

Whether any American official says anything on the record about Somaliland. Whether the African Union revisits the findings of its own 2005 mission. Whether the Berbera offer appears in a written instrument rather than an interview. And whether Maersk or any other line resumes bookings at Berbera, which would be the first real signal that the Red Sea risk calculation has changed.

Somaliland is selling something Washington has stopped buying.

Jim Loucks is a former U.S. counterterrorism advisor and career law enforcement professional. He is based on the Kenyan coast. He writes on counterterrorism and national security issues.

World.title: Nigeria: Boko Haram Fighters Gun Down Farmers in Borno
World.content:
Suspected Boko Haram insurgents have ambushed and killed 15 farmers, while abducting three others in Marte Local Government Area of Borno State.

According to local sources, the tragic incident took place across the Ala, Gumna, and Musune wards near the headquarters of the area council, on Wednesday.

While initial reports of the attack reached the community on Wednesday evening, the task of recovering the bodies could not be completed until Thursday morning.

Recounting the borrowing aftermath of the assault, an anonymous source said, "Five bodies were initially recovered from the field, while others were found later. Three persons are still missing, and sources indicate they were abducted by the insurgents."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Public Relations Officer, Borno State Police Command, DSP Kenneth Nahum Daso, confirmed that 15 people lost their lives and confirmed that authorities were actively investigating the situation.

"We are making efforts to determine the whereabouts of the three people still missing," Daso said.

A grieving relative, whose cousin was among the victims, shared details of the execution-style killings.

She explained that the victims had gone to their farms to harvest crops when they were ambushed.

"They were forced to lie down and were shot in the head at close range. It was a gory sight," she said.

According to the relative, local community members bravely mobilized to scour the fields, retrieve the bodies, and ensure they were buried according to Islamic rites.

The massacre has drawn widespread outrage, with the human rights organization Amnesty International strongly condemning the violence as a horrific violation of international humanitarian law.

In a statement released on Friday, the organization expressed deep concern over the escalating violence against vulnerable populations in Northeast Nigeria.

"Amnesty International strongly condemns the horrific killing of at least 15 people in Marte Local Government Area of Borno State," the statement read. "The victims, who were local residents venturing into the surrounding areas to earn a living or harvest their crops, were ambushed and targeted by a suspected Boko Haram group."

The rights group emphasized that the deliberate targeting of civilians by non-state armed groups constitutes a war crime.

"Amnesty International calls on the Nigerian authorities to take immediate, transparent, and human-rights-compliant measures to protect vulnerable communities living in the region," the statement concluded.

Despite ongoing military operations in Nigeria's Northeast, farming communities continue to face severe security threats as insurgents frequently target agricultural workers in remote areas

World.title: Former Chicago mayor Rahm Emanuel declares America is ready for a Jewish president
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, who is weighing a 2028 Democratic presidential bid, said Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press" that America is ready to elect its first Jewish president, arguing that voters should be more concerned about Americans losing faith in the country than his own religious beliefs.

When moderator Kristen Welker asked whether the country was ready for a Jewish president, Emanuel answered yes before turning the question toward what he described as a broader loss of confidence in America.

"My faith is not your problem," he said. "The fact that Americans have lost faith in America, that's our problem. And we should work on that because I've seen a generation of people with an emptiness who've lost faith in America because they think America lost faith with them. That's our problem. It's not my faith."

JEWISH HOUSE DEMOCRAT RECALLS COLLEAGUE SAYING THERE IS NO ANTISEMITISM BECAUSE 'ALL THE JEWS ARE RICH'

Elizabeth Barcohana, chair of the California Republican Party’s Subcommittee for Jewish Engagement, dismissed Emanuel’s remarks in a Sunday statement to Fox News Digital.

"He sounds pathetic," she said.

Emanuel, who served as Chicago mayor, a Democratic congressman, White House chief of staff under former President Barack Obama and U.S. ambassador to Japan under former President Joe Biden, has increasingly fueled speculation that he could seek the Democratic nomination in 2028.

During Sunday’s interview, he said he would not alter his religious identity for political support and pointed to his record in government as evidence of how his faith influenced him.

ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS

"If my faith is a problem for you, don't vote for me," he said.

"I'm not changing my faith," Emanuel said. "My faith led me to struggle and fight the insurance companies that were denying kids healthcare. My faith led me to take on a failed education system where we were known as the worst city, and I walked out, and we were the best city on education."



"My faith guided me to make sure that the American people and their families had what it took as a government fighting powerful forces, whether it's pharmaceutical companies, insurance companies, or in fact, educational failed bureaucracy," he added.

Emanuel directly connected that message to a possible campaign, saying restoring Americans’ confidence in the country would become part of his mission should he enter the race.

"If I decide to run, that is our collective mission, is to restore that faith," he said.

RAHM EMANUEL WARNS NEW GENERATION OF DEM SOCIALISTS DON'T LIKE AMERICA

The remarks came just over a week after Emanuel discussed his presidential ambitions directly with Fox News Digital at the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin. When asked what separated him from a potentially crowded Democratic field, Emanuel pointed to three attributes.

"Candor, authenticity and strength," he said.

Emanuel said that his experience across different levels of government meant he would know what to do immediately upon taking office, saying he "knows what to do on day one."

At the time, Emanuel had been openly considering a White House run as other Democrats also positioned themselves ahead of 2028.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Emanuel, however, told Welker on Sunday that he believed Americans would ultimately judge a candidate beyond religion and reiterated that his own faith was not negotiable.



"I believe in the goodness and the grace of the American people – but my, I will not change my faith," he said.

World.title: Mac malware can hide commands in your iCloud calendar
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

You probably use your calendar to keep track of appointments, birthdays and the occasional reminder you immediately snooze. Hackers apparently see another possibility. Security researchers have uncovered a new version of MacSync malware that can use a public iCloud calendar event as part of its infection chain. Hidden inside the calendar data are commands that help download more malware onto a Mac.

The calendar itself does not suddenly infect your computer because someone sent you an invitation. The attack starts earlier, usually after someone downloads and runs a malicious app. Still, the iCloud trick shows how attackers can hide parts of an attack behind familiar services many of us trust. Once MacSync gets inside, it can go after a lot more than your calendar. Here's how MacSync works, what it can steal and the steps you can take to protect your Mac.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare with AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed.

Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist.

Watch the free replays and get your checklists at CyberGuyLive.com

THOUSANDS OF HACKED SITES TRICK YOU INTO INSTALLING MALWARE

What is MacSync malware?

MacSync is an information-stealing malware family targeting macOS. Earlier versions shared similarities with the Atomic macOS Stealer, better known as AMOS. Researchers say MacSync has since developed additional capabilities of its own. Kaspersky says the malware first appeared on the dark web in 2025 under the name Mac.c. Its creators later renamed it MacSync. Researchers first spotted this newest version in the wild in September 2026.

MacSync operates under a malware-as-a-service model. That means different criminals can use the malware while choosing their own methods for getting it onto someone's Mac. Attackers have previously spread MacSync through social engineering and ClickFix-style attacks, where a bogus message tells someone to copy and run a command. Criminals have also disguised it as free software, cracked applications and unfamiliar new apps. We've seen similar tricks before. In one Mac campaign, fake CAPTCHA instructions convinced users to paste commands into Terminal, which then installed information-stealing malware.

How hackers can abuse iCloud calendars

Here's where this latest version gets particularly sneaky. Kaspersky found one MacSync infection chain where a downloader connected to a public iCloud calendar. Instead of using the calendar to schedule anything, the attackers placed malicious commands inside the event description. The malware then feeds that calendar information into the Mac's zsh command-line shell.

FAKE CHROME UPDATE SCAM COULD INFECT YOUR COMPUTER

Most of the calendar text produces errors because the Mac does not recognize normal calendar information as commands. However, when it reaches the malicious instructions placed after the event's description field, those commands can run. They ultimately download a compressed archive from iCloud containing another malicious app. That app then starts another stage of the infection.

Think of the calendar as a hiding place for instructions. The attacker still needs to get malicious software running on the Mac first. However, using Apple's infrastructure during the infection chain can make the activity look less suspicious. Importantly, Kaspersky says at least one sample pointed to a public iCloud calendar. Other samples used attacker-controlled servers instead.

A fake crypto wallet helped spread MacSync

Researchers also found attackers disguising MacSync as a fake cryptocurrency wallet called Toria. The criminals went beyond creating a download page. Kaspersky says they built a dedicated website for the nonexistent wallet and promoted it on X and Telegram.

That is a good reminder that a polished website or active social media account tells you very little about whether software deserves your trust. Crypto owners appear to be an especially attractive target because stealing wallet data or browser extension information can quickly lead to stolen funds. However, you do not need to own cryptocurrency to have something MacSync wants.

What MacSync can steal from your Mac

Once installed, the information-stealing portion of MacSync searches through a wide range of sensitive data. Researchers say it can target browser history, cookies, saved logins and passwords. It also searches for crypto wallet extension data, cryptocurrency wallet applications and Telegram information.

MacSync can collect the Mac user's login information and Keychain file. It also gathers system details including installed apps, running processes, hardware information and the device model. Developers and more advanced users face additional exposure because the malware searches configuration files for SSH, ZSH, AWS, Kubernetes and Git. It can also collect ZSH and Bash command histories. For the average Mac owner, the takeaway is simpler. If malware gets access to saved passwords or browser data, an attacker may gain another route into your online accounts.

The new MacSync backdoor raises the stakes

Kaspersky also discovered a separate backdoor component written in Objective-C. It disguises itself as Finder, the file-management app built into macOS. The malware tries several methods to stay on the Mac after a restart. These include a LaunchAgent, changes to the .zshrc configuration file and modifications to global Git hooks. It can also terminate several macOS notification processes. Kaspersky says this prevents the system from notifying the user about the new LaunchAgent. From there, attackers can send instructions to the infected machine.

Researchers found commands designed to deploy a browser extension, replace an installed Ledger wallet app and collect additional system information or files. Most of those commands ultimately execute AppleScript supplied by the attacker's command-and-control server. Kaspersky inferred what the individual commands do from their names and the status messages they send because researchers did not have the AppleScript payloads themselves. That limitation is important. Researchers can see what the backdoor appears designed to accomplish, but they did not observe every possible server-delivered script.

One MacSync command remains a mystery

Researchers also found a command called live_browser. That command downloads and executes a component called sn_relay. Kaspersky says its exact contents and purpose remain unknown. Based on the command's name and messages sent back to the server, researchers suspect attackers may use it for some form of man-in-the-middle attack against browser traffic. Kaspersky has not confirmed exactly how that function works. That unanswered question shows why malware research often changes as investigators obtain more samples.

Why Mac users keep getting tricked

Macs include built-in security protections, but many recent attacks focus on persuading the person sitting in front of the screen to bypass those protections. ClickFix attacks are a perfect example. A website may tell you something went wrong and provide a command that supposedly fixes the problem. In reality, you may end up launching malware yourself. We've previously reported on Shamos malware, another Mac threat that used bogus troubleshooting instructions to trick people into running commands in Terminal. The same basic lesson applies here. Be suspicious whenever a website asks you to open Terminal, paste a command or enter your Mac administrator password to install an unfamiliar program.

Mac malware increasingly targets familiar tools

MacSync fits a pattern we've been tracking for a while. Attackers often disguise malicious software as something useful or familiar, whether that means a fake app, a bogus utility or software promoted through social media. In this case, researchers found one infection chain that used Apple's iCloud infrastructure to help deliver additional malware. That does not mean opening iCloud Calendar puts your Mac at risk. The bigger warning comes earlier in the attack. Be cautious when an unfamiliar app asks for your administrator password or a website tells you to open Terminal and run a command.

Apple says macOS has built-in protections against these attacks

According to Apple, macOS includes several layers designed to help prevent malicious software from running, including Gatekeeper, XProtect and Apple's notarization system for software downloaded outside the Mac App Store. Apple recommends the Mac App Store as the safest place to get Mac software. For apps downloaded elsewhere, Apple says macOS uses protections such as notarization and XProtect to detect known malware and block it from running.

On macOS 26.4 and later, Apple added protections aimed more directly at attacks that try to trick people into pasting commands into Terminal. Terminal paste protection can show a warning when text is pasted into Terminal from common attack sources such as web browsers, messaging apps and other communication software. Apple says XProtect can also inspect activity that starts from pasted commands, including in third-party terminal apps. It can check related network activity against Apple's Safe Browsing Service and block behavior associated with known malware techniques.

Apple also says macOS 26.4 and later can scan AppleScript and JavaScript for Automation scripts using XProtect. If a script matches a known malicious signature, macOS can block it and alert the user. Safari adds another layer of protection. According to Apple, Fraudulent Website Warning can alert users when a website is suspected of phishing or distributing malware, while Apple Safe Browsing is designed to block malicious domains associated with attacks.

Apple also stresses that social engineering remains a major part of attacks like these. Scammers may try to persuade people to download software or paste malicious commands themselves. Apple recommends downloading software only from sources you trust and keeping your Mac updated with the latest available software and security fixes.

8 ways to protect your Mac from MacSync malware

MacSync relies heavily on getting someone to run a malicious app at the beginning of the attack. That gives you several opportunities to stop it.

1) Avoid copying Terminal commands from websites

A legitimate website rarely needs you to copy an unfamiliar command into Terminal to prove you're human, repair a browser problem or complete a download. Apple says macOS 26.4 and later can warn some users when commands copied from places such as websites, messages or email are pasted into Terminal. XProtect can also block activity associated with known malicious commands and techniques.

2) Download apps from trusted sources

Whenever possible, get software through the Mac App Store or directly from a developer's official website. Apple recommends the Mac App Store as the safest place to get Mac software. For apps downloaded elsewhere, macOS uses protections including Gatekeeper, notarization and XProtect to help identify and block malicious software. Be especially cautious with cracked software, free copies of paid apps and unfamiliar programs promoted through social media.

3) Treat administrator password requests seriously

MacSync's infostealer asks the user for an administrator password and adapts its prompt to match the app it is impersonating. If an unfamiliar app unexpectedly asks for your password, stop and verify why before entering anything.

4) Use strong antivirus protection

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious downloads and known malware before they compromise your Mac. It can also give you another layer of protection when a convincing scam gets past your first line of defense. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

5) Keep macOS updated

Install macOS updates when Apple releases them. Updates can patch security weaknesses and improve built-in protections that malware developers continually try to evade.

6) Check your browser extensions

Remove extensions you no longer use and investigate anything you do not recognize. MacSync's backdoor includes a command designed to deploy a browser extension supplied by the attacker's server.

Safari: Open Safari > click Safari in the menu bar > Settings > Extensions . Review the extensions listed on the left. Uncheck an extension to disable it. If you want to remove one that came with an app, uninstall the associated app from your Mac.

Google Chrome: Open Chrome > click the three dots in the upper-right corner > Extensions > Manage extensions . Review the list , turn off anything suspicious or click Remove to uninstall it. You can also click Details to review what websites an extension can access.

Microsoft Edge: Open Edge > click Extensions to the right of the address bar > Manage extensions . Turn off anything you do not recognize or select Remove from Microsoft Edge to uninstall it.

7) Protect important accounts with 2FA

Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) wherever it is available. If malware steals a password, that extra verification step can make unauthorized account access harder.

8) Change passwords if you suspect an infection

Start with your email, financial accounts and other sensitive services. Use a separate trusted device if possible. Create strong, unique passwords with a password manager, then check active sessions so you can sign out devices you do not recognize.

Kurt's key takeaways

MacSync is a good example of how attackers can turn familiar parts of your Mac into camouflage. An iCloud calendar, Finder and a familiar-looking password prompt can all make something dangerous seem routine. This attack still needs you to run malicious software before it can really get to work, which means your choices can stop it early. If a website tells you to paste something into Terminal or an unfamiliar app suddenly asks for your administrator password, stop and ask yourself why. Those few seconds of skepticism could save you from handing over passwords, private files and access to your accounts.

Would seeing an iCloud address or another familiar Apple service make you more likely to trust what you're downloading, or are you suspicious anytime a website asks you to run commands on your Mac? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

World.title: Terror cells inside foreign airlines 'certainly a possibility,' retired pilot warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The man who once carried the nuclear football for former President Bill Clinton is sounding an alarm on potential terror cells inside foreign airlines after a FlyDubai copilot allegedly attacked the captain of an Israel-bound flight and sent the plane into a death-defying, aeronautics-defying dive.

"It’s possible that terror cells can exist inside airline companies – overseas, probably a lot easier than here, but it's certainly a possibility," retired Air Force Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson, a former 16-year Delta Air Lines pilot, told Fox News Digital on Thursday. "And I think it is something that DOJ needs to take a...really good look at."

The warning came after a FlyDubai flight from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after the copilot attacked the captain mid-flight, reportedly with the crash ax. The flight was carrying 174 passengers and eight crew, and investigators are still probing the motive, including possible terrorism or mental health factors – both of which leave Patterson concerned for public safety, if not national security.

FORMER ISRAELI PM HAILS ‘HEROISM’ AFTER PASSENGERS HELP THWART ALLEGED COCKPIT ATTACK

"If you’ve got somebody that’s, you know, radicalized and if he doesn’t tell his company or his buddies, you’re never gonna know," Patterson said, noting most protocols rely on "self-reporting your activities." "So that's part of the problem, I think, that we're going to start seeing pop up in airline profiles and pilot profiles is we have a lot of people out there that probably shouldn't be flying airplanes."

The warning comes amid the revelations that a crash ax found behind the copilot chair in the Boeing 737 was used to bludgeon in the pilot in an effort to commandeer the aircraft.

"Every 737, and that's what I flew my entire life of all the different models, has a crash ax in the cockpit right behind the copilot so that we can, if we have to, either crack into the door or crack into into the windows in the event of an emergency, we can do it," Patterson said. "If the copilot used the crash ax, that is savage because that thing will hurt you."

FLYDUBAI PILOT SHOWED WORLD 'THE HIGHEST FORM OF COURAGE,' INDIA'S PM SAYS

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told "FOX & Friends" on Thursday morning that the copilot appeared to have undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination," but said officials would need days to determine whether he had ties to Iran. President Donald Trump since came out with the belief there were ties to Iran.

WATCH: PATTERSON CALLS COCKPIT AX ATTACK 'SAVAGE':

"International carriers and a few domestic carriers cast a very wide net looking for applicants to be aircrew members and pilots," Patterson said, noting he has emailed Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy of his concerns. "And sometimes that net is a little too wide for who they attract to their airlines."

Patterson said U.S. and foreign airlines typically focus heavily on background checks, medical history and aviation violations, but warned that personality changes or radicalization can be difficult to detect once a pilot is hired.

Patterson also warned that pilots often fly with colleagues they barely know – much less a deep understanding of their mental health.

"You never know what you're gonna bring to the table, what you gonna find in the cockpit next to you when you first get to the cockpit, because we don't fly with the same guys multiple times – we fly with different people almost every single time," he continued. "So every single time we get in a cockpit, we're meeting somebody for the first time, nine times out of 10.

"So we never know who we're getting either. And that's why the initial conversation in the cockpit's important. What's your background? What's mine? How's your family life? What's going on in your world? That kind of stuff will flesh out some of that stuff, but you can't flesh it all out. There's just no way. And you don't know."

There remains a potential security loophole that needs to be closed with that 737 crash ax in the cockpit, regardless of whether U.S. commercial crews are only randomly screened at airports, according to Patterson.

"It's right there," Patterson said Thursday before official reports noted the crash ax as the weapon used by the suspected terrorist. "You know, I can easily see the co-pilot saying he needed to stretch. He pulls out of the seat because we do this in the 737. It's a very tight cockpit.

"Occasionally one pilot will get up, stand in the back of the cockpit and just stretch, you know, get the blood pumping. And it would be very easy for the copilot just to reach down while standing up and grab that ax. I mean, I can see it happening, and God forbid if it did because that's brutal."

AMERICA BUILT A FORTRESS AFTER 9/11. THEN THE THREAT STARTED HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT

The terrorist scheme puts a great emphasis on the fact the U.S. should scrutinize not only domestic airline hiring, but also foreign crews entering American airspace, he warned.

"I think the United States needs to take a close look at not only who we are allowing to operate heavy machinery in this country, and by heavy machinery, I mean aviation, airplanes," Patterson said. "Who we are hiring and putting into those positions of authority, and then more importantly, who are we allowing from the other carriers to fly into our airspace?"

Netanyahu noted to Fox News that the FlyDubai co-pilot attack was an Omani national who made it through a "loophole" of an Israeli restriction against pilots from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel.

While "9/11 changed everything in terms of aviation for everybody," clearly there is far more work to be done to ensure airline safety, he concluded.

"You never know what you're carrying on the back of of the airplane," he said. "Sometimes the guy you're flying with is a wild card and sometimes the guys in the back the airplane are a wildcard. And I think that just some companies do the job, the security job, and they do the vetting screening better than other companies do."

World.title: Kelsey Mitchell’s Caitlin Clark comments deserve context, including the benefits of all that attention
World.content:
Indiana Fever guard Kelsey Mitchell spent part of her season-ending press conference explaining what it’s like to play alongside Caitlin Clark. She talked about nasty online messages, the attention that follows the Fever and how difficult some days have become.

"I don’t think people really understand how much we endure, man," Mitchell said Saturday. Later, she asked people to give the players "grace."

Some coverage quickly turned that into Mitchell taking a shot at the Fever fanbase. I don’t think that’s an accurate reading of what she said.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Mitchell has publicly praised Clark in the past and acknowledged the opportunities she helped create. She’s also allowed to explain what’s difficult about being her teammate. Neither makes her an enemy of the woman playing beside her.

WNBA FIGHT OVER MALES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS EXPOSES HOW THE LEFT KEEPS ANSWERING A QUESTION NOBODY ASKED

But the benefits of all that attention still belong in this discussion. Mitchell’s salary went from under $60,000 in 2020 to $206,000 in the season before Clark arrived in the WNBA to $1.4 million in 2026.

That’s a pretty substantial part of the Caitlin Clark experience, too.

Mitchell didn’t single out Fever fans

Mitchell discussed getting "a lot of flak" for "being on her team," referring to Clark. She also referenced people throughout the basketball world and spoke positively about the Fever organization, praising it as "unbelievable."

I read that as a broader description of the scrutiny that comes with playing alongside Clark. Her answer didn’t establish whether the criticism came from Fever fans, Clark’s detractors or some combination of the two. Those people exist, obviously, and being associated with the league’s biggest star makes Mitchell a target for their criticism, too.

That’s different from declaring that Indiana’s own fans are the problem. Mitchell didn’t identify everyone sending her messages, and we shouldn’t fill in those blanks just because one interpretation makes for a more inflammatory headline.

For example, The New York Times-owned Athletic ran the headline: "Kelsey Mitchell counters Fever GM’s defense of fans, vows to ‘be selfish’ in free agency." There’s one problem: None of Mitchell’s quotes in the story identifies Fever fans as the people she’s criticizing.

Mitchell played six WNBA seasons before Clark arrived; her professional career didn’t begin when the rest of the country started watching the Fever.

She’s experienced a version of this franchise that most of its current audience never saw. So, yes, I’m interested in hearing her describe what changed. That’s a worthwhile subject for reporters to explore.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

And Mitchell has described the positive changes.

In a recent SLAM interview, she credited Clark and Angel Reese with creating opportunities for players throughout the league.

"When Angel Reese and CC came in, it opened up so many doors for us: resources, financial, all of it," Mitchell said.

ANGEL REESE’S LATEST WNBA CONTROVERSY SHOWS HOW VICTIMHOOD BECAME CENTRAL TO HER BRAND

Mitchell explicitly recognized the financial benefits, and portraying her as someone who refuses to acknowledge them would be wrong.

Mitchell’s experience is worth covering

Jason Whitlock raised a worthwhile point on X while discussing Mitchell and teammate Aliyah Boston.

"Their complaint is the media only covers one aspect of the Caitlin Clark experience," Whitlock wrote. He also argued the two Fever players "have every right to explain their experience playing in the shadow of Caitlin Clark."

Mitchell’s perspective belongs in the coverage, and reporters should be interested in what she says, particularly given how long she’s been in Indiana.

Where I’d push back is the idea that discussing the benefits amounts to telling her to shut up. Asking players to keep the upside in perspective doesn’t prevent them from explaining the downside. And explaining the downside doesn’t mean the rest of us have to agree with every conclusion they draw from it.

For example, Mitchell described the difficulty of competing for fans who might not like her. But having fans dislike you is a fairly standard part of the athlete experience. They don’t have to appreciate your effort or acknowledge that you’re doing your best because they want you to fail.

My main complaint with many WNBA players is that they often act like the unpleasant parts of being a public figure are something uniquely unfair to them. They aren't. I'm not a professional athlete, nor am I a very recognizable figure. But even I've received plenty of online hate for doing my job.

It comes with the territory, and the same attention that helps drive bigger paychecks also brings more criticism.

That's the tradeoff and most people happily make that deal.

The bigger paycheck is part of the story

Spotrac lists Kelsey Mitchell's WNBA cash earnings from 2018 through 2025 at $1,122,442. Her $1.4 million salary this season exceeded what she earned over those first eight seasons combined, and she's in position for another seven-figure contract in free agency this offseason.

Mitchell’s performance earned her a maximum contract. The new collective bargaining agreement made that maximum much more valuable, raising it to $1.4 million as part of an enormous increase in player compensation. The previous maximum was around $250,000 per year.

Clark’s ability to attract viewers is central to the league’s growing business. ESPN and ABC aired five WNBA regular-season games that averaged more than 2 million viewers this year, and all five featured Indiana.

CBS, NBC, ION and Prime Video also drew their biggest regular-season WNBA audiences for Fever games.

PRIME VIDEO WNBA BROADCAST CREW EMBARRASSES ITSELF WITH COVERAGE OF A'JA WILSON FAN INCIDENT

Then Thursday’s season-ending game against Las Vegas averaged 2.25 million viewers across USA Network and CNBC, making it the second-most-watched WNBA first-round playoff game ever. Can you guess who played in the most-watched first-round game ever? Yeah, it was Clark and the Fever against the Connecticut Sun in 2024.

The point is simple: Clark's massive audience has value, and the players are benefiting from it.

And that’s where I still have a problem with the way this subject gets discussed around the league. The negative attention regularly becomes the main story, while the benefits get left out. I think that’s often because those benefits point to a story many WNBA players and media members don’t want to tell: a White girl from Iowa is driving the league’s popularity spike.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Getting obnoxious DMs from online trolls is part of the experience. But so is earning more in one season than you earned in the previous eight. Letting the first part dominate how you describe the whole thing gives the trolls an awful lot of influence.

Mitchell isn’t nearly the worst example of that attitude. But Saturday’s answer still fit a familiar pattern of emphasizing what players have to endure without spending much time on what they’ve gained.

Courtney Williams offered some useful advice last year

Last year, Minnesota Lynx guard Courtney Williams gave what I thought was perfect advice for dealing with online hate.

"Press the block button, bro. Press the block button and then move on," Williams said.

Then came her most important comment: "We wanted more eyes on the game... So let’s embrace it."

Credit to Williams for having the guts to say it. It's unfortunate that many of her colleagues didn't seem to heed her advice.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Mitchell has acknowledged the good that came with Clark’s arrival, and she deserves credit for that. But Saturday, she spent a lot of time explaining what she has to endure as Clark’s teammate. If we’re going to tell the full story of Mitchell’s experience, what she’s gained from all that attention belongs in it, too.

That includes the $1.4 million paycheck.

With ibogaine unavailable for medical use in the United States, some Americans are traveling to Mexico to seek treatment.

While Mexico has emerged as one of the leading destinations for ibogaine treatment, psychedelic retreats have also expanded elsewhere in Latin America, including Costa Rica, where travelers seek alternative wellness and recovery experiences, according to reports.

Ibogaine drew renewed public attention following the death of Presley Gerber, the 27-year-old son of Cindy Crawford.
