BRETT MCGURK: No U.S. intelligence of a warning or indicator. I can't speak to whether the Israelis – the Israelis still have, to this day, not had a commission of inquiry. We had the 9/11 Commission that made a number of reforms that have helped keep our country safe since 9/11. The Israelis still have not done that. I think they have – they should do that.

But from what I, in dealing with all of these guys in Israel, security echelon, political echelon, I think they had an assumption that was deeply engrained that Hamas was deterred, assuaged, and was not about to do something massive on any scale like this. I think that was a false assumption in their system, failure of imagination, and it was tragic.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Let me ask you about the Israeli prime minister. In February of 2024, you talk about a meeting you had with him. You were very focused on these hostages and trying to get them out. You said, "for more than 30 minutes, he never mentioned the hostages. Netanyahu was animated in discussing the military campaign and far less so when discussing the hostages, when he chose to discuss them at all."

BRETT MCGURK: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Why? Why do you think that is?

BRETT MCGURK: Netanyahu was focused far more on the military campaign and assuring Hamas can never retain power in Gaza. Believing the military campaign and the pressure on Hamas would lead to a deal that released all the hostages, whereas we were trying to focus on a phased deal that at least let's – get some of the hostages out first. And Netanyahu always believed that more military pressure will actually deliver a better deal, whereas Sinwar believed more time would put more pressure on the U.S. and others to deliver him a better deal. That's what makes this almost an impossible situation to deal with.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You felt the U.S. was putting more value on those lives than the Israeli government did?

BRETT MCGURK: The U.S. role in this, in all dimensions, we were trying to stop a war and get the hostages home. And the two were – the two were completely linked. And to reduce human suffering as much as possible in Gaza.

You know, Netanyahu, I describe him as, obviously, very confident in his assumptions. And he has a brother who was killed in the Entebbe raid, very confident in terms of his belief and how to deal with these groups. And yet I believe a lot of times there were miscalculations.

MARGARET BRENNAN: National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan has publicly suggested that the U.S. focus was so much on the hostages that it was almost a trap, as he put it, in thinking that we can get to a ceasefire and a hostage deal, and other things were sublimated to that objective. I mean, in hindsight, do you share that feeling?

BRETT MCGURK: The war would not have stopped without the hostages. I don't – I don't believe that.

About a month into the war we had – we had a deal with Hamas. Not easy. I describe what it was like to get, for all women and children, it's very clear, all women and children hostages are going to come out. And in exchange for a number of Palestinian prisoners. And we had a ceasefire for eight days. And about 100 hostages came out. Three of those women that did not come out, because on the eighth day Hamas said, we're not going to release the younger women, actually. We released the young toddlers, like Abigail, the young American girl. We released the 80-year-old grandmothers. We're going to hold on to the younger ones. They said, we can't find them, which was completely untrue. So –

MARGARET BRENNAN: Wasn't part of the excuse that they were military age too?

BRETT MCGURK: No. Well, they said some – they claimed that.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

BRETT MCGURK: But they said, let's keep a ceasefire and talk about the older men. And in the book I go through this night, midnight here in Washington, December 1st, and it's a moral quandary. And this is what a hostage taker does. Hamas is as good as Iran is. They're masters at this. They put the moral onus on the other side. Do you skip the younger women, start talking about older men, keep the ceasefire, or say, no, you broke the deal?

(END VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We'll have more from Brett McGurk when we come back.

(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We pick up our conversation with Brett McGurk about the negotiations with Hamas in 2024 to release the hostages and end the Gaza war.

(BEGIN VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: All of what you were trying to do was happening at the same time as the American political cycle here, a presidential election. And there appeared to be unquestioning U.S. support for Israel and providing military support to Israel. And this became a political issue, particularly among Democrats. Then, the Republican candidates, including now President Donald Trump, were criticizing that you weren't strong enough in support of Israel. How aware were you of the politics of the moment, as you're making decisions like this?

BRETT MCGURK: I'm very independent. So, I've worked with Republican presidents, Democratic presidents. I was a law clerk for two judges appointed by Republicans, one by a Democrat. And – but let me bring you into the Oval Office and kind of, in a scene in which I think encapsulates this very issue.

April 4, 2024. President Biden, it's his re-election. He's on the campaign trail. Obviously frustrated about the situation. Unable to articulate, because the hostage talks have now collapsed. They recently collapsed for a number of reasons I go through in the book.

He's frustrated by being unable to point to how are we actually going to try to bring this to a close. We had a horrific air strike from the Israelis that killed nine aid workers with World Central Kitchen, Jose Andreas –

MARGARET BRENNAN: An Israeli drone hit the clearly marked convoy.

BRETT MCGURK: And – which – which was so tragic – so horrific. And so, we have a call with – between Biden and Netanyahu. And Biden is just like, you know, completely fed up. And at the same time, however, Iran is planning to launch – we have intel – intelligence that Iran is about to launch a massive ballistic missile drone attack directly against Israel, which is totally unprecedented. And – which if those missiles get through, you're talking about thousands of casualties.

So, this is how kind of everything converges. And I think at that moment, if not for that impending missile attack, which we then had to deploy military forces. We built an unprecedented coalition with air partners, European partners and, of course, the U.S. military and General Kurilla (ph), who was kind of putting this together. If not for that, I think on that – in that moment, I think we would have taken some pretty draconian measures against Israel.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Really?

BRETT MCGURK: Yes. I do not –

MARGARET BRENNAN: Draconian how? What do you mean?

BRETT MCGURK: Well, I think we would have – you just mentioned cutting off weapons and other things. That was very much on the table. But also at that time in April, Congress bipartisan – a massive bipartisan majority approved a $26 million aid package for Israel, right in April, right in that moment. But the – the focus very quickly shifts to, how do we defend Israel from this – from this missile attack. It ended up being 120 ballistic missiles, 170 drones, 30 cruise missiles, all launched to land at the same time.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But on the World Central Kitchen event, the – people remember that. There was outrage around that. You wrote that, "President Biden told Bibi Netanyahu," the prime minister, "that he could, in theory, cut Israel from military aid at a finger snap –

BRETT MCGURK: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Leaving Israel on its own. You think I'm Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal?"

BRETT MCGURK: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But he didn't. He didn't cut.

BRETT MCGURK: Well, I mean, we –

MARGARET BRENNAN: Did he actually mean that as a threat?

BRETT MCGURK: We selectively – we talked about it in that – in the Oval Office around that time. We selectively, after that call, the president stopped all sales and deliveries of heavy payload munitions, 2,000-pound bombs. We stopped –

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, he delayed them, ultimately.

BRETT MCGURK: We didn't deliver them and we didn't approve any other sales. President Trump reversed that immediately after coming into office.

MARGARET BRENNAN: It was such a public debate at the time about America's role in the world, the standards America is held to, and whether America is complicit in how our weapons are used. And under the Leahy Law, as you know, you know, countries that receive U.S. weapons have to avoid committing human rights violations or risk losing the weapons supply.

Blinken said –

ANTONY BLINKEN (Former Secretary of State): It was reasonable to access that in certain instances Israel acted in ways that are not consistent with international humanitarian law.

MARGARET BRENNAN: And that "Israeli civilian harm mitigation efforts were inconsistent, ineffective, and inadequate."

Do you agree with that State Department memo?

BRETT MCGURK: No aid to any country is unconditional, including – including to Israel. And – but security assistance is a – is a complex, multi-institutional, multi-branch endeavor. And again, these – most of these appropriations were appropriated by massive, bipartisan majorities in Congress at the time. But – and the – and the State Department has a role and the Pentagon has an important role.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right. He was saying hit the brakes on deliveries. Or reexamine (ph).

BRETT MCGURK: Again, we hit the brakes on some – on some deliveries, again, selectively. But to have a broad-based stoppage of support, again, for Israel, at a time – I don't know what the timeframe was for that statement, but I can –

MARGARET BRENNAN: It was in May, in 2024.

BRETT MCGURK: So, in May – yes, so in May, we just had the largest ballistic missile and drone attack ever in history. We helped the Israelis defeat it.

We say to Netanyahu, Biden's quote in that meeting is, "I just saved your ass." We're getting back to the hostage deal, OK?

We spent the month of May putting together a detailed, four-page, three- phase agreement, single space, every detail there. We go to the Israelis and to Netanyahu and say, we need you to sign up. And it went very far in the direction of Hamas. Frankly, it was a better deal for Hamas than what they have right now.

And Netanyahu, on May 27th, signed onto that deal. On May 31st, because what were we doing in May? On May 31st, President Biden laid out that deal to the world in a speech. And he said, Israel has accepted this deal. Hamas, say, yes, let's end this war. The U.N. Security Council endorses that deal. It's May 31st.

What happens? In early June, after this is on the table, we can stop the war right now if Hamas says yes. Khamenei, supreme leader of Iran, gives a defiant speech praising October 7th, and basically Iran is telling Hamas to not – to not compromise in any of – of the terms. Hezbollah launches its largest attack of the war, 250 rockets into northern Israel. This is – when we have a ceasefire deal on the table.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

BRETT MCGURK: We don't get an answer from Hamas until July 2nd, almost five weeks later. And they put all sorts of things in it that set the talks back.

So, I say this because we were working to end this crisis and end this war. And if you want – in May, June, and we had the deal on the table to do it.

My approach would have – is, this deal is on the table to stop the war. All pressure, everything, public, everything else, has to come down on Hamas and their enablers to say yes to end this deal – or to end this war.

But Hamas did not say "yes." and they kept stringing this out. And they would put an issue on the table, then Israel would take a hard position. But that's what was happening in May. And if you go to that – you know, Biden goes to the world and says, this is the deal. He had a phone call with I think 18 heads of state because these hostages are from countries all around the world. They all said – they called on Hamas to take the deal, and Hamas did not take the deal. I mean we were working at that time to end the war through a deal. And I think, again, all vectors of pressure should have been on Sinwar to say yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're not saying –

BRETT MCGURK: And the war would have stopped.

MARGARET BRENNAN: You're not saying that the Democratic Party pressure and calling out compliance with U.S. law was enabling Hamas? That's not what you're saying?

BRETT MCGURK: No, no, no. I – but I'm not – and also not –

MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're saying it's almost like naive?

BRETT MCGURK: And I'm also not getting into internal party debates. I've never been a part of that. I'll let – I'll let political parties have their debates. Not my role at all. I come back to the question, how do you end this crisis?

MARGARET BRENNAN: Uh-huh.

BRETT MCGURK: And I think the record shows, if you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going end to the crisis. It's going to make it worse.

(END VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: Our full conversation's on our website, facethenation.com, and our YouTube page.

We'll be right back.

(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: That's it for us today. Thank you all for watching. Until next week. For "FACE THE NATION," I'm Margaret Brennan.

(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

World.title: Transcript: Zach Lahn, Iowa GOP nominee for governor, on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 4, 2026
World.content:
The following is the transcript of the interview with Zach Lahn, Iowa GOP nominee for governor, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 4, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Welcome back to Face the Nation. We turn now to the Republican running for governor of Iowa, Zach Lahn. He joins us from Belle Plaine. Good morning.

IOWA REPUBLICAN GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE ZACH LAHN: Good morning, Margaret.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We look at diesel prices. They're north of six bucks. President Trump's trade war with Canada and China have made things expensive for farmers. You know that well in Iowa. Are the president's policies a headwind for your party?

ZACH LAHN: I think when you talk about what's going on with affordability for farmers, and by the way, this is something we launched our campaign on in the beginning. You have to take a step back and really understand what's been going on for decades in the agriculture industry, where we've seen consolidation after consolidation of businesses taking choice and competition away from farmers, we've reached monopoly stages there. And now what we're seeing with some of the increased prices on diesel is kind of just another one of these pieces that's adding up to that. And we've been focused, you know, in the state on how do we cut the gas tax and other priorities to help farmers have more affordable fuel when they go into harvest. So this has been a part of our campaign since the very beginning, and I really think farmers understand that for a long time they have been treated as price takers, and really the deck has been stacked against them. And now when you add in the higher cost of diesel, we really have a problem.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well - you just mentioned there big AG. You are campaigning with a promise to break up big AG monopolies. You said you're going to tax the heck out of Wall Street hedge funds that own farmland. Those sound more typically like progressive policies than conservative ones. How do you convince Iowa Republicans?

ZACH LAHN: Well, I just say that, you know, breaking up monopolies was first done by Republicans. The Sherman Antitrust Law is a Republican. Teddy Roosevelt broke up two of the biggest companies in existence. A monopoly is a failure of the free market. I think we forgot that in large part, and now we're paying the consequence for it. So my priority is to increase the funding to the Attorney General's office to take on these anti-competitive lawsuits because farmers across the country are waiting for someone to take the first step here and really give them a fair deal, and so I think that these are ideals of the Republican Party. But really, they're just the right ideas, the right thing to do.

MARGARET BRENNAN: It's - it's an interesting position, though, given that the party has typically been very close to the agriculture industry. I know you have focused in your campaign on the cancer rate in Iowa. It has the second highest cancer incidence in this country. You say it's nitrates and pesticides, including glyphosate, that cause it. President Trump signed an executive order to boost production of glyphosate based herbicides. How do you reconcile those presidential decisions from the policy you have?

ZACH LAHN: Well, I would just say first that I was one of the first people to come out and say that this was the wrong move to sign that executive order. I think that if we could give the president the advice on that, that he would understand that better. But what we have focused on a campaign that's focused on Iowa issues specifically, and this is something that Iowans are facing. We have the fastest rate of new cancer anywhere in the country, number one. And if you move out of the state of Iowa to say a state like Nevada, your chance of getting cancer any given year goes down by 40 percent. These are very specific Iowa based issues, and we've been focused on them. High nitrate load in water is one of the top causes of colon cancer, bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, and we've got some of the highest levels in the country, if not the highest levels. So, we are focused on providing incentives to farmers, real incentives, to adopt different types of practices to allow them the ability to really change what they're doing to stop these products from getting into the streams in the first place, clean up our water at the source, and help farmers make sure that they're not losing money by doing it by providing real incentives that help them actually make money by adopting these practices. Because it really goes back to farmers are operating on razor-thin margins right now, and the idea to experiment with something new is not very appealing when you could be the first in a line of five generations that loses your family farm.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right and that's one of the arguments - for continuing to use this herbicide that has arguably ties to - cancer. Is that it's just frankly cheap - Your position --

ZACH LAHN: Okay --

MARGARET BRENNAN: -- You just said if the president had more information, maybe make a different decision. Just for the record, RFK Jr., the HHS secretary, says he opposed it. Told the president he opposed it, and the president did it on national security grounds. But he has been out there, the HHS secretary. He's been campaigning for you. Many of your platform issues are very popular with the MAHA movement. Should America view your race as a test of Kennedy's popularity?

ZACH LAHN: Well, I think that Kennedy is very popular, and Iowa is very popular across the country. But it's more so the principles that he represents, which are similar principles to what I represent. Look, we all want healthy kids. We want clean water. We want to make sure we have less medications for our kids. We want to solve these issues that have been causing a rise in, you know, chronic illness, in autoimmune conditions, not just amongst kids but amongst adults, and we believe that food is medicine. That it's the first line that you need to be looking at is, what food are we putting into our body, and this is one of the reasons that a top priority of mine, my moonshot for the state of Iowa is to see a day in which 80 percent of the food served in our public schools is grown in the state of Iowa and we can do that. It will take time, but this might be, you know, the only nutritious meal a kid has all day and Iowa has the best farmland in the world, the best farmers in the world. We can do this and lead the country on it. And this is one of the first steps that we can take to really make sure that we're cleaning up our food supply, we're getting kids healthy food.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, we will continue to watch your race - and see if Iowa, as you say, is -is an outlier here and maybe starting something new. Thank you, Zach Lahn, for your time today. We'll be right back.

World.title: Transcript: Sen. Mark Kelly on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 4, 2026
World.content:
The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Mark Kelly, Democrat of Arizona, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 4, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to Arizona Senator Mark Kelly. He joins us from Charleston, South Carolina, where he is campaigning for his fellow Democrats. Good morning to you, Senator.

SEN. MARK KELLY: Good morning.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Our CBS polling shows that Democrats have reason to be optimistic about taking the House, but how much harder will it be in the Senate?

SEN. KELLY: Well, Margaret, there is a lot of energy in the states I've been to recently. Whether it's Ohio or Iowa, Kansas, Georgia, now here in South Carolina, I think we have real opportunities in a lot of places. But also, I mean, this could be, you know, close elections in many of these states. But I'll tell you this: people are frustrated and they're fed up with Washington D.C. right now, and they know that this president is not addressing, you know, any of the needs that affect them and their families. I mean, the cost of living is way too high. The price of everything just keeps going up, and people can't afford their lives.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, President Trump announced Friday he's going to send $90 payments to 20 million older Americans this month, Medicare Part B enrollees. That's in addition to sending $500 in terms of checks to ACA refunds to a million people. Also said if Republicans win, then he'll send everyone $5000 bucks. Do you support any of that? And what exactly is the Democratic message on lowering costs for Americans?

SEN. KELLY: Well, certainly trying to help some working class people and seniors on a fixed income. But you got to remember, this is a guy that gave a big tax cut to the wealthiest Americans, to billionaires and millionaires, and then to partially pay for it, he's kicking people off of their health care, off of Medicaid. He's taking food benefits away from people that are having a hard time affording food, even children, in order to to help out his family and his friends, so I think people should see this for what it is, especially this $5,000 payment, if Republicans maintain control of the House and the Senate. I mean, this is just a- a payoff, and he's trying to buy votes. I mean, are you surprised with this president, who, in my view, is the most corrupt occupant of the Oval Office ever? I'm not surprised, but it's not right.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But what is the affirmative Democratic message here, other than we're not him?

SEN. KELLY: Well, we're going to lower costs for the American people.

MARGARET BRENNAN: How?

SEN. KELLY: We've got to win the House and, or the Senate. Well- well, how will we do this? I have legislation with- with Chris Van Hollen. We've got to get Republicans on board. It raises taxes for people who make over a million dollars a year in income, and it provides tax cuts for people, individuals, and even couples up to- who make up to about $160,000 a year- that's some relief. Ending this war in Iran that he started without a- any kind of a strategic goal or a plan, has jacked up prices for the American people- ending that would help. Getting this tariff policy reversed, these ridiculous tariffs that have also jacked up prices. The American people pay this. For some reason the president thinks that foreign countries are paying for these tariffs, that is not true. So there are things, a lot of things, we can and will do once we win back the House and, or the Senate.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, Republicans have pulled funding, as I understand it, from North Carolina's Senate race, they've redirected it out to Kansas. Not typically a place a Republican would have to spend money to- to keep an advantage, but what seats specifically are you optimistic you can turn blue?

SEN. KELLY: Well, there are a lot of them. I spent some time in Kansas with Adam Hamilton. He's a pastor. He's- he's a great guy. He is the right person for Kansas. He understands what Kansans are dealing with. Josh Turek in Iowa, similar kind of situation where that's a very winnable race. Mary Peltola in Alaska, Troy Jackson in Maine, Sherrod Brown in Ohio. I'm gonna do an event, you know, here today with Annie Andrews in South Carolina. Yeah, I understand it's South Carolina, but she is a pediatrician, she's working incredibly hard, she's raising the resources to be successful. And then there are the House races. Admiral Nancy Lacore, I did an event with her yesterday here in South Carolina- can be critical to Democrats winning back the House of Representatives. She's a- she's a three-star admiral, a naval aviator like myself, who was fired by Pete Hegseth early in this administration.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, a number of Senate Republicans have expressed some concern about Secretary Hegseth's firing. He also announced this past week he's going to cut by 20% the number of generals and admirals. He says in order to try to change the culture and what the media calls a purge, he says is simply a matter of accountability. Do you have any insight into who he will be targeting in these cuts, and if Democrats take some control, do you have any ability to stop it?

SEN. KELLY: Well, he often fires people because of the color of their skin or because they're women. He also seems to be looking for--

MARGARET BRENNAN: He would deny that.

SEN. MARK KELLY: --loyal- of course, he would deny that. I think anybody would deny that. But it's pretty obvious when you have a list of seven people who don't promote from one-star to two-star, and five of them are either black or women. It's pretty obvious. Also, right off the bat, firing CQ Brown without giving any reason, without any particular reason why one of the most qualified professional aviators, but a four-star general, chief of staff of the Air Force, fired. Lisa Francetti--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. KELLY: --the chief of naval operations, fired. The commandant of the Coast Guard, also a woman, was fired. The- the list goes on, Margaret. This is a pattern with this Secretary of Defense, and it's damaging our readiness. And when you hurt readiness, it means that all of us, everybody watching the show, you and your family, are less safe because we have the most unqualified Secretary of Defense we've ever had in this country's history.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, he gave a big speech this past week. The secretary said that every military branch has hit its recruiting targets ahead of the end of the year. He also argues military sexual assaults are on the decline. I know they have been on the decline for a few years now, but what is your response to his argument that he's doing something right?

SEN. KELLY: Well, he's doing very little right. Remember, Margaret, this is a guy that gets on a stage in front of the senior leadership of the U.S. military and runs around talking about killing people and lethality, and that the rules of engagement- I'm going to paraphrase, but he talks about how he wants to eliminate or reduce the rules of engagement, and you see the consequences of that in Iran. And he- his plan is what we went into Iran with, and he has bombed or attacked over 15,000 targets, depleting our munition supply. This thing has been a disaster because the Secretary of Defense has no idea what he's doing--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. MARK KELLY: --and to some extent, he's also a yes- a yes-man for the president. Nobody seems to want to push back against this president, who--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. MARK KELLY: --who I- I think is checked out from even trying to do this job.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.

SEN. MARK KELLY: Got us into another war with- without- without a plan and without explaining- explaining to the American people what are we going to get out of this.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Senator, I'm sorry to cut you off, but I'm out of time, I have to leave it there. Thank you. We'll be right back.

World.title: Transcript: Energy Secretary Chris Wright on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 4, 2026
World.content:
The following is the transcript of the interview with Energy Secretary Chris Wright that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 4, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation. We begin with one of the Trump administration officials tasked with working to lower those high gas and oil prices, Energy Secretary Chris Wright. Good morning to you.

SECRETARY OF ENERGY CHRIS WRIGHT: Good morning, Margaret.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, it's good to have you here. You said this past week that Americans can expect lower gasoline prices and diesel prices by election day. The Wall Street Journal editorial board has a piece outlining that the campaign to squeeze around financially is working, but they can still knock out significant Gulf energy infrastructure. They could be planning an October surprise before the U.S. midterms. We are still seeing Iranian attacks on ships now. I mean, how can you be so confident prices are headed down?

SEC. WRIGHT: Well, because we've got increasing supplies coming out of the Strait of Hormuz and they've continued to rise over the last months, over the last recent weeks. We've got U.S. gasoline production today at record high. We have demand for gasoline, as we come out of the summer driving scene, starting to go down. Similar stories with diesel. Diesel's mostly been infected by the Russia-Ukraine war and also by China's decision not to export diesel or gasoline into the marketplace. And of course, we're living with two refineries that were recently closed, large refineries in California that Gavin Newsom forced the closure of. And frankly, 15 years of Democrat policies that have been energy subtraction, trying to close coal plants, close refineries, and shrink our capacity. Which means when you get in crisis, we're just less resilient than we should be.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But you still think that in the next four weeks prices are going to go down?

SEC. WRIGHT: Absolutely. Diesel prices have been going down. Gasoline prices have been going down. I expect that to continue.

MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to talk about diesel in a minute, but I- I was reading that the U.S. was sending more defensive equipment to the Gulf countries to protect their oil infrastructure. I see there was a gathering of national security advisers at Camp David on Friday to talk about Iran and the conflict in Yemen. Can you share any outcome from that? I mean, is- is the U.S. about to escalate? We did just see a third carrier strike group get sent to the region.

SEC. WRIGHT: Look, the president has- has taken a strong stand that Iran, the world's greatest terrorist regime- regime, cannot and will not have nuclear weapons. So, of course, we're looking at every avenue to achieve that goal economically, to be prepared for what comes militarily. But we cannot pass to the next administration an Iran armed with nuclear weapons. Not only is that a threat to peace and stability--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.

SEC. WRIGHT: --that's a massive long-term threat to energy prices.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Right, but he's also said that they're not seeking a nuclear weapon. He said that just the other day that they might have actually already stopped. But in the immediate sense of threats to our neighbors who have refinery and production capacity, how do you guarantee that there is no October surprise that sends those prices going the opposite direction?

SEC. WRIGHT: Hey, well, there's no guarantees. There's no guarantees in conflict. There's no guarantees in life. But everything we're doing is to grow the supply of diesel, to grow the supply of gasoline, and frankly, again, to reverse years of policies that have been directed exactly the opposite, to shrink our ability to produce, refine, and deliver hydrocarbons.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Can you say whether the president has decided he will escalate post-election day? That's when that third carrier strike group will be arriving, mid-November.

SEC. WRIGHT: Oh, I'm definitely not going to get in front of presidents' plans or policies. But remember--

MARGARET BRENNAN: He'd thrown that out there himself.

SEC. WRIGHT: He's- he's always planning for contingencies and he's always negotiating. How you communicate, what you- what you lean in on, it sends a message to the other side. He's been a master, a master at doing that.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So he's got both tracks still going, diplomatic and military pressure?

SEC. WRIGHT: Of course, of course. At all times.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, you talked about diesel. The world's wealthiest countries, the G7, this past week agreed to release 100 million barrels of fuel over four months. They're going to front load it with a lot of diesel in the next 20 days. I know you asked our friends and allies to consider doing this. How significant a price impact and for how long?

SEC. WRIGHT: It's a big deal. It's a big deal. Europe has very large diesel stores. They, you know, they don't refine enough diesel to supply their own economies, so naturally they store a lot of diesel. They're very keen to see American diesel continue to flow to Europe. They've got a lot of diesel in stores. Why not release some of that? This is what you store diesel for. When all the Russian exports of diesel are shut down, when the Chinese have said we're not going to deliver any more diesel, and you still have a reduction of diesel flows coming out of the Gulf, but we're restoring those, but that takes time. This is just common sense. This lowers diesel prices, not just in the United States, but it lowers them in Europe and around the world. But it will drive diesel prices down as those releases come. It'll drive diesel down through the winter in the United States and around the world. And- and by then we'll be in another place. We'll have more refining capacity online. I- I suspect we'll continue to see diesel decline as we go into next spring as well.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So below six bucks? Which is where it is.

SEC. WRIGHT: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. By post-midterms?

[CROSSTALK]

SEC. WRIGHT: It's- it's down a little over 20 cents so far.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEC. WRIGHT: I think you'll see it continue to go down. Yeah, you should see it below $6 before too long. But exactly when, I certainly don't know that.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So the allies did this after President Trump said he was considering a diesel export ban. You had so many quotes where you were telling people, "This was not a good idea." "Let's not do a diesel export ban." But the president kept saying it was a consideration. Has he completely ruled out an export ban at this point?

SEC. WRIGHT: Look, every day he's throwing out ideas. He's engaging with discussions with me, others in the administration--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Even when you're saying it's not a good idea?

SEC. WRIGHT: Absolutely. No, he- he- he's--

MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're the expert.

SEC. WRIGHT: --he says well- well, but there's different ways to slice this cat. There's different ways to look at it. He's always looking, "How do I lower energy prices? How do I lower heating prices, electricity prices, gasoline prices, diesel prices?" In fact, I would say his constant communication of that may have been quite helpful in achieving- in achieving the deal we just struck.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because people thought he might actually not listen to you and go ahead and do it?

SEC. WRIGHT: I--

MARGARET BRENNAN: That was the- the ploy, essentially?

SEC. WRIGHT: It wasn't a ploy. It's just a constant dialog about the many levers we have. How can we drive down diesel prices and drive down gasoline and other prices along with it?

MARGARET BRENNAN: So we checked, and it looks like because of this Lindsey Graham bill that gives the president more, sort of, powers to punish the buyers of Russian fuel, he has to make a decision by October the 18th as to whether he's going to put tariffs on the biggest buyers. That would be China, and that would be India. Is he going to do that?

SEC. WRIGHT: Look, he- he leaves every decision till the end. He'll evaluate the trade-offs. He has worked ceaselessly to try to end this war. Not only would end- would ending this war end the killing of- of tens and of thousands of people every month, it would dramatically lower energy prices. He's wanted to end that conflict, yes, since before he was president. So, and- and there is constant, constant dialogs with both sides in that to try to bring that war to an end.

MARGARET BRENNAN: But at this point, like, what's the direction here? You just had this big state visit. Are we actually in a position where the U.S. might put tariffs on China for buying Russian oil? Are we actually going to see that, and what impact would that have?

SEC. WRIGHT: Again, I won't get in front of the president on that. We're trying to have the best relations we can--

MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm sure you've looked at the projections on what it would do for pricing.

SEC. WRIGHT: Of course, we're trying to have great relations with China and move that ball forward. I think things are going reasonably well there. But then the flip side is you've got to look at every leverage you've got to bring a murderous conflict to an end.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So he may and you would encourage him to?

SEC. WRIGHT: I'm not going to say- I'm not going to say on--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.

SEC. WRIGHT: --either one of those. He's- he's looking to how to end that conflict and how to lower prices for Americans every day.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah. Well, the date just stood out, you know, weeks before the midterms, doing something that could arguably push prices back up. And so, if it's a national security decision versus a political one. Be interested to know your point of view.

[CROSSTALK]

SEC. WRIGHT: If his decisions were political he would have just kicked the can down the road and delivered a nuclear-armed Iran to the next president. You've got to respect that. That's an incredible move to lean in and say I'm not going to let them become nuclear-armed. He knew it was going to elevate energy prices in the short run. He said, "I'm going to take a hit there, but I got to do the right thing."

MARGARET BRENNAN: You did tell him that? That there would be a huge energy price spike when he made the decision.

SEC. WRIGHT: He- he was well aware of- of the risk to energy flows that were coming out of the Persian Gulf region. He said, "I simply cannot. The world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran, and I'm not going to do it."

MARGARET BRENNAN: Secretary Wright, thank you for your time today.

SEC. WRIGHT: Thank you, Margaret.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Face Nation will be back in a minute. Stay with us.

World.title: Energy Secretary: Trump was "aware of the risks to energy flows" before Iran war
World.content:
Washington — Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday that President Trump was "well aware of the risks to energy flows" before launching the war in Iran earlier this year, but argued "the world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran."

"He knew it was going to elevate energy prices in the short run, he said, 'I'm going to take a hit there, but I got to do the right thing,'" Wright said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Americans have been feeling the financial squeeze of soaring gas and diesel prices in recent months. But the Trump administration has pointed to the potential threat a nuclear-armed Iran could pose, and how it could represent a long-term threat to energy prices. Wright defended the president on Sunday, arguing that Mr. Trump has taken a "strong stand that Iran, the world's greatest terrorist regime, cannot and will not have nuclear weapons."

Wright expressed confidence that prices will fall, pointing to increasing supplies coming out of the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. gasoline production, the summer driving season slowing, among other factors. Asked whether he expects prices to go down over the next four weeks — as Republicans eye a tough environment in the lead up to the midterm elections — Wright said, "absolutely."

"Diesel prices have been going down, gasoline prices have been going down," Wright said. "I expect that to continue."

Diesel prices soared of above $6.50 a gallon in recent weeks, squeezing farmers, who rely on diesel to run agricultural machinery, along with industries from construction firms to food banks, which rely on diesel to fuel their vehicles and delivery trucks. Wright noted that diesel prices are down a little over 20 cents so far in recent days, adding that he expects the prices to continue to go down.

"You should see it below $6 before too long," he said. "But exactly when, I certainly don't know that."

Wright said "everything we're doing is to grow the supply of diesel, to grow the supply of gasoline, and frankly, again, to reverse years of policies that have been directed exactly the opposite-to shrink our ability to produce, refine, and deliver hydrocarbons."

Wright wouldn't weigh in on the president's plans and whether things would escalate militarily after the midterm elections. But he said Mr. Trump is "always planning for contingencies and he's always negotiating," and both diplomatic and military tracks remain open.

The energy secretary said securing the agreement from the Group of Seven countries last week to release 100 million barrels of fuel over four months is a "big deal." He called it "common sense" and said it will drive diesel prices down in the U.S. and around the world through the winter.

"Europe has very large diesel stores. They don't refine enough diesel to supply their own economies, so naturally they store a lot of diesel. They're very keen to see American diesel continue to flow to Europe. They've got a lot of diesel in stores. Why not release some of that?" Wright said. "This is what you store diesel for when all the Russian exports of diesel are shut down, when the Chinese have said we're not going to deliver any more diesel, and you still have a reduction of diesel flows coming out of the Gulf. But we're restoring those, but that takes time."

Asked whether the president has ruled out an export ban on diesel, which Wright has opposed, Wright said "every day" Mr. Trump has been "throwing out ideas," and the president remains engaged in discussions.

"There's different ways to look at it. He's always looking, 'How do I lower energy prices? How do I lower heating prices, electricity prices, gasoline prices, diesel prices?' In fact, I would say his constant communication of that may have been quite helpful in achieving the deal we just got," he said.

Wright added, "It's just a constant dialogue about the many levers we have, how can we drive down diesel prices and drive down gasoline and other prices along with it?"

World.title: Samuel Alito says that political attacks aimed at Supreme Court can be "quite damaging"
World.content: Rare interview with Alito As the Supreme Court is set to start its new term, Supreme Court justice Samuel Alito sat down with CBS News' Jan Crawford in a rare interview ahead of the release of his new book, saying that political attacks aimed at the high court -- most recently by President Trump on his social media platform -- "can be quite damaging."

World.title: Trump names national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new AI czar
World.content:
Trump names national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new AI czar

toggle caption i Mariam Zuhaib/AP

Director of national intelligence Jay Clayton is the new White House AI czar, President Trump said on Sunday.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that Clayton will lead the White House's new "Super Intelligence Force," a group that will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence."

Trump prefers the term "super intelligence" to "artificial intelligence." He said his "Super Intelligence Force" will "coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies."

Before being confirmed earlier this year to lead national intelligence, Clayton was United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, and chairman of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

Trump's announcement follows various statements of alarm from tech leaders over risks in the rapid development of AI, including that it could go rogue. Trump has largely brushed aside the warnings and attempted to reframe concerns around AI.

Sponsor Message

On Tuesday, Trump met with AI executives at the White House, and said afterwards that leaders of several artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews of their work.

Meanwhile, the White House also launched a revamped government website this week, America.gov , which says it is sourced via artificial intelligence from "official government sources."

In his social media post, Trump also named other members of his "Super Intelligence Force". He said it will include: Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, and Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael.

It is unclear what Clayton's appointment as AI czar means for the AI industry, as current artificial intelligence regulation by the U.S. government is limited. Congress has not passed federal law broadly regulating the use or development of AI. Some states, including California, have enacted measures about AI, including requiring entities to be transparent when it is used .

During an interview with CNBC last month, Clayton called super intelligence a "national security issue." He also pushed back against calls for a "pause" in developing the technology, pointing out that other countries around the world are continuing to develop AI. "I don't think any American should think that that's a good strategy," he said.

Sponsor Message

In December 2024, president-elect Trump announced he would appoint David Sacks, a Silicon Valley investor, as an AI and crypto czar , with a brief to advise the administration on policies surrounding AI.

Earlier this year, Sacks stepped down from his role and became co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. He has backed AI leaders Sam Altman and Dario Amodei's warnings about the technology, and the idea of a "slow down" in AI development. Last month, Sacks wrote on social media that the tech leaders should "stop pretending you need anyone else's permission" to make such moves.

World.title: Cornell president calls gang rape allegations 'deeply disturbing'
World.content:
Cornell president calls gang rape allegations 'deeply disturbing'

toggle caption i Matt Rourke/AP

Cornell University's president has said the institution "must do better" following a civil lawsuit filed in recent weeks alleging a gang rape at a fraternity house in 2024.

In an eight-minute video statement released by Cornell on Saturday, president Michael I. Kotlikoff acknowledged questions over the university's handling of the female student's sexual assault allegations, which were reported to Cornell University Police and school officials a few weeks after she said the attack happened.

"I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say. We don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves," Kotlikoff said in the statement. "We must do everything we can to prevent what happened to Jane Doe and everyone before her and anyone after her from ever happening again."

Last month, a former Cornell student, identified as "Jane Doe," sued the seven alleged rapists and the university, saying she was drugged and repeatedly raped in October 2024. Attorneys for some of the men have denied the accusations.

Sponsor Message

Kotlikoff called recent days one of the most difficult weeks in Cornell's history.

"What happened to Jane Doe in 2024 is deeply disturbing and will weigh heavily on our community for years to come. My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," he said. "It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use. It also raises questions around the investigations conducted after the allegations were reported."

Jane Doe first reported her claims to Cornell University police and university Title IX investigators shortly after the alleged incident, which happened when she was 20 years old, at the Chi Phi fraternity house. She also reported the sexual assault to the campus health clinic.

According to the lawsuit filed against Cornell, Chi Phi fraternity, seven fraternity members and other defendants in September, Jane Doe said she consented initially to sexual contact with two men she knew at the fraternity house while intoxicated. She alleges, as the night went on, she was then drugged and raped by multiple men, and could not give consent.

The Tompkins County district attorney declined to file charges. He has said recently he didn't receive full transcripts from Jane Doe's interview with Cornell Police, in which she clearly stated she had been raped.

Sponsor Message

"As a community, we must foster a culture in which sexual assault is inexcusable and ensure our community is empowered and understands informed consent, body autonomy and prevention. We all have a role to play in keeping each other safe," said Kotlikoff in his video message.

Last week, Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed New York State Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the case and condemned the handling of the investigations. Kotlikoff said he welcomes the governor's decision, and that the university's board of trustees will soon announce plans for an independent review by an outside law firm into "all aspects of Cornell's handling" of the case.

"We will also lend our full support to legislative efforts to change New York's sexual assault laws. You have my commitment that this will not be a moment that passes," he said.

Kotlikoff added the university would take immediate actions to be more transparent, strengthen sexual assault prevention and education efforts and substance use resources. He said the university will also take a serious look at the role of sororities and fraternities in campus life.

World.title: U.S. Marine arrested for alleged murder of a woman in Okinawa, Japan
World.content:
U.S. Marine arrested for alleged murder of a woman in Okinawa, Japan

toggle caption i Hiro Komae/AP

TOKYO — Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine in the alleged robbery and murder of a woman on Okinawa, officials said Sunday, the latest criminal case on the southern island where the heavy American troop presence has remained a sensitive issue.

The Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested a 20-year-old Marine stationed at the Futenma Air Station on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old local woman at a hotel in Naha, Okinawa's capital city, and taking her wallet and backpack in the early hours of Saturday.

Kyodo News agency, citing the police, reported the woman's body was found in her hotel room and she appeared to have been strangled to death.

Sponsor Message

Police said security camera footage showed the man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the victim and coming out alone. An officer arrested the suspect after spotting him walking alone on a street in Naha's entertainment district late Saturday, Kyodo said.

"The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases," newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters. "It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged."

"I must say, discipline and troop education are not working at all," said Koja, referring to the U.S. military's measures taken in response to past criminal cases.

Some 50,000 U.S. troops are deployed in Japan under a bilateral security pact, about half of them on Okinawa, whose strategic role is seen as increasingly important for the Japan-U.S. military alliance amid growing tensions with China. Japan's southwestern shift in its military focus centers heavily on Okinawa and its nearby islands.

Okinawans have long complained about noise, pollution and crime related to U.S. bases, with crimes involving U.S. service members on Okinawa complicating ties between Japan's central government and the Okinawa administration. The latest case comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's cabinet pushes to further fortify its Japanese military presence on Okinawa and work more closely with the U.S. military.

Sponsor Message

"The occurrence of the heinous crime is extremely regrettable," Takaichi said in her message on X. She said her government has strongly protested to the U.S. side and demanded maximum cooperation with the Japanese authorities in the investigation, as well as tougher discipline for U.S. service members and preventive measures.

Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass to his office and conveyed "outrage," the ministry said in a statement.

Glass, on X, expressed condolences to the victim's family, adding that the United States is cooperating with the Japanese national and local governments.

The U.S. Marine Corps said in a statement the suspect is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force on Okinawa and that it is fully cooperating with Japanese authorities. "The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior."

Futenma base, located in a densely populated area in central Okinawa, has been a sore spot for many Okinawans for decades, who demanded its relocation. Despite protests, the central government greenlit construction to relocate the base to Henoko on Okinawa's eastern coast, though the project has faced massive delays.

A high-profile 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. service members sparked massive protests against the heavy U.S. troop presence on Okinawa. The number of arrests related to U.S. service members and their families exceeded 100 last year, according to prefectural police. Repeated occurrence of sexual crimes and some of their delayed disclosures have also sparked outrage on Okinawa in recent years.

World.title: How the Cornell case is affecting women who have experienced sexual assault
World.content:
How the Cornell case is affecting women who have experienced sexual assault

toggle caption i Olivia Petter

When Olivia Petter first saw the news about the sexual assault allegations at Cornell University, she was shocked by how familiar parts of the story felt for her.

"The more I found out, the more triggered I became," she said. "I think for me, the worst thing was seeing the group messages that these boys were allegedly sending to each other on the night of the alleged rape."

Reading those exchanges brought the London-based author back to boarding school in England, where she says older boys targeted her and her friends from the age of 13.

"They would walk past us and whisper 'Fresh meat,'" Petter said. "They would rate us out of ten and shout numbers at us when we walked down to the dining hall." Petter says she recalls boys pulling down girls' trousers while they held their lunch trays, humiliating them in the school cafeteria.

Sponsor Message

After a party, when she was 17, she remembers a boy putting a "hand down my pants" when she was trying to go to sleep. "No preamble. We hadn't been kissing... and I was kind of wriggling, trying to get him to stop."

"The thing that people need to understand is when something like that happens to you, it's really hard to just say, no, get off me, because your body goes into this panic mode," she said. "You freeze and it takes a while for you to understand what's happening."

"There were just so many instances of sexual assault and we didn't really recognize it at the time because we didn't have the language," she said, adding that the culture continued into her time at university.

Petter, now 32, is among those sharing their own experiences online in response to the recent rape allegations that have emerged at a Cornell University fraternity house.

A former Cornell student, identified as Jane Doe, sued the university and the seven alleged rapists last month, saying she was drugged and repeatedly raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, when she was 20 years old. Attorneys for some of the men have denied the accusations.

Sponsor Message

The case has led to a wider reckoning over attitudes to sexual violence. On social media, many women have been using the hashtag #IamJaneDoe to discuss their own experiences of sexual assault and rape.

toggle caption i Heather Ainsworth/AP

Other universities have acknowledged the issue, too. As the case has become a national news story, the editorial board of The Daily Pennsylvanian — a student newspaper at the University of Pennsylvania — published a recent piece titled "Penn has a Cornell problem, too."

For some survivors, following the coverage can feel like reliving an earlier assault, says Hannah Braunstein, a Washington D.C. based psychotherapist and trauma specialist. She says stories like these can bring back more than just memories for people who've been sexually assaulted.

"Suddenly, they're inundated with all of this news and then their own experience through memories or body sensation is beginning to unfold for them. It can be absolutely horrifying," Braunstein said. "And it can immediately transport them back in time."

For Erin Smith that reaction was immediate. The yoga instructor and mindfulness coach, who lives in Winchester, Ky., first saw the news about Cornell on social media and immediately searched for more details.

"I was so enraged, I set my phone down and just paced around my kitchen like a caged tiger," Smith recalled. She says the story brought back the physical distress she remembered from being assaulted as a child.

"I had that feeling in my stomach that happened during my experience [when] I was 12," said Smith, who is now 53.

toggle caption i Katherine Dooros/Katherine Dooros Photography

Braunstein says repeated exposure to stories like these can intensify emotions. Yet, people may feel compelled to keep reading, hoping more information will help them feel better.

"We keep searching for more information because we think if we understand every detail, then finally we'll feel better internally," she said. "But, often it does the opposite, and keeps people activated internally."

Sponsor Message

Braunstein recommends using a timer to keep news or social media checks to five minutes a day. When someone feels overwhelmed, she suggests turning their attention to their immediate surroundings.

"One thing I talk about with clients in my office is using first sight, looking around the room and calling out what you see, noticing what you hear," she said. "Feeling your feet on the floor. That's a grounding technique that works."

Smith said she eventually recognized that she needed a break from the comments on social media. Spending time outside, being with her dog and playing guitar has helped her feel calmer. But, she said the anger remains, so she has started to write about it.

Petter also turned to writing. As she continues following the case, she wants to use her anger to start a dialogue around sexual assault.

"I want to hold on to the rage because I think rage is powerful and will enable me to have these conversations with the people in our lives," she said. "And when I say people, I mean men."

Petter says she wants men to have those conversations among themselves, too, and challenge derogatory comments about women within their own friend groups, including online.

For Smith, the Cornell case feels personal because it brings so many survivors of sexual assault back to their own experiences.

"I think that's why so many women are triggered right now, because Jane Doe is all of us." she said. "We all have some sort of story."

World.title: She died covering war for Fox News. Her parents blame the network — and a star reporter
World.content:
She died covering war for Fox News. Her parents blame the network — and a star reporter

AFP via Getty Images, Paula Bronstein for NPR and family photos/Collage by Mark Harris for NPR

🎧Prefer to listen to this story? Hear it in the NPR app.

NPR Ukraine producers Polina Lytvynova and Hanna Palamarenko contributed to this story.

When the Fox News Channel hosted hundreds of advertisers and industry executives at the ornate Hammerstein Ballroom in Manhattan two years ago, the network centered attention on a tragic yet heroic figure: the war correspondent Benjamin Hall.

"From Ukraine to the Middle East, and here at home, the dedicated journalists of Fox News are trying to inform Americans, even in the most perilous of circumstances," Hall proclaimed.

Hall knows peril all too well. In the first weeks of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a strike by Russian forces hit the car in which Hall's team had been traveling outside Kyiv.

Sponsor Message

Hall had nearly died. He lost his right leg below the knee, most of his left foot and part of an eye.

Two years after the attack, Hall stood center stage on prostheses, in a suit that ended just above his knees. He entered to a standing ovation.

toggle caption i Seth Wenig/AP

"These stories, they need eyes on the ground," Hall said. "They need a human perspective. They need us to bear witness."

But at what cost?

Though gravely injured, Hall was the lucky one. The strike killed all four people who traveled with Hall that day:

The two Ukrainian soldiers who served as guides. Pierre Zakrzewski, a beloved Fox war videographer. And Oleksandra Kuvshynova, known as Sasha. The 24-year-old Ukrainian had just joined the team as a producer and interpreter.

Fox has described the deaths as tragic and honored the fallen. Yet two multimillion-dollar lawsuits against the network blame it for what happened.

One of those lawsuits has been filed by Kuvshynova's parents, who also squarely blame Hall. In their first joint interview about the tragedy, they tell NPR they are speaking out to honor their daughter's life and document what they contend is the injustice of her death.

toggle caption i Paula Bronstein for NPR

Two high-risk security advisers who worked for Fox News in Ukraine bolster the family's claims. In separate interviews with NPR about what happened, they say Fox News and its star correspondent ignored repeated and urgent warnings to stay away from the danger zone outside the city limits of Kyiv.

Sponsor Message

"If you took Benji out of the equation, this never would have happened," Aaron King, one of those security advisers, said. The other adviser, Shane Thomson, has joined the Kuvshynovs' lawsuit, alleging Fox scapegoated him for the tragedy.

This story is based on 15 interviews and a review of hundreds of pages of legal documents, as well as Fox's own broadcasts. Fox News, citing the ongoing litigation, declined NPR's repeated and detailed requests for interviews with Fox officials, news executives and lawyers. The network also did not make Hall available for interviews for this story. It additionally declined to respond to specific questions raised for this story.

toggle caption i Sam McQueen for NPR

Yet one of the most revealing witnesses to Hall's character is Hall himself. He wrote a memoir, published a year after the attack, in which he acknowledged increasingly embracing risk as his career and ambitions progressed. The same year, he also presented his story in a Fox documentary.

Fox and its founder, Rupert Murdoch, have faced controversies, scandals and litigation before. Often, accusations center on the network's right-wing ideology, Murdoch's own political agenda or their relentless pursuit of profits.

This is different.

Two words define the underlying allegations in the Kuvshynovs' wrongful death lawsuit against Fox and Hall: ambition and negligence.

Fox calls the deaths tragic but rejects responsibility

Covering any armed conflict by definition involves peril. Hazards are often ambiguous; the boundaries of battle zones are fluid. Combat journalists for many news organizations, including NPR, have been killed.

But the Kuvshynovs and their legal team say what happened to their daughter was preventable — and foreseen. "This was a very avoidable danger that they were specifically warned about, as to [the] exact time and place that they could not go," charges Stephen Humphreys, a lawyer for the Kuvshynovs and Thomson.

toggle caption i Paula Bronstein for NPR

In court statements in the Kuvshynovs' suit, Fox acknowledges the tragedy of the deaths of Kuvshynova and Zakrzewski. But the network counters the plaintiffs' claims on technical and legal grounds.

Sponsor Message

In declining comment for this story, Fox pointed NPR to a statement released in March 2024, when the lawsuit was filed.

"While we understand the grief and continue to mourn the loss of both Pierre Zakrzewski and Sasha Kuvshynova, we will respectfully defend against the inaccurate claims within this lawsuit," Fox said.

"The safety of our journalists has always been our number one priority and we are immensely grateful to the Fox News journalists who have covered the war in Ukraine and we remain committed to reporting from the region," the statement continues.

Hall: "I learned that I could control my fear"

AFP via Getty Images and family photos/Collage by Mark Harris for NPR

It wasn't clear that Hall would get to Kyiv in early 2022.

A dual British-U.S. citizen, Hall was inspired by his globe-trotting family's past. He wrote in his memoir that at the outset of World War II, his dad's family was in the Philippines. Japanese forces took Hall's grandfather prisoner and executed his grandmother and other relatives. U.S. troops rescued Hall's father, then just a boy.

In chronicling combat, Hall wrote, "I saw a lot of death, had guns pressed against my head, dreamed horrific dreams — all of it an echo of what my father endured in Manila."

In his 20s, Hall pinged from one hot spot to another, freelancing for outlets like Vice and Esquire, and Fox.

The first time Hall saw a man die was in Misrata, Libya, in 2011. He had a choice, he recounted in the memoir, titled Saved: He could turn away or, perhaps, "invade the dignity of those moments in order to 'get the story.'"

"I did not have the time to consider all the moral angles. I could either keep filming, or stop filming, and I chose to keep filming," Hall wrote. He added that he had just escaped being killed too.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Paul Morigi/Getty Images

Back in London, Hall registered that he had undergone a profound transformation. "I learned that I could control my fear, even bury it, and keep moving forward into danger," Hall wrote. "I learned that the hellishness of Misrata was not enough to stop me from going to combat zones.

"And I learned that my normal civilized life would never be the same again. No — this was who I was now."

Years later, his colleague Trey Yingst would call Hall "the gold standard" for war zone reporting for the network.

But there was at least one early red flag. In a sworn affidavit for the Kuvshynovs' lawsuit, former Fox News international producer Phil Ittner said he had previously lodged a formal internal complaint that Hall's behavior in Syria had placed colleagues in danger.

"Ben Hall was addicted to the adrenaline rush of taking risks," Ittner wrote in the affidavit. "I worried that he put his career promotion ahead of the safety of the crew working with him." He called for Hall to be pulled from the field. Instead, Ittner wrote in the affidavit, Fox never responded. No known consequences ensued. (In its legal filings, Fox responded that Ittner has no knowledge of events in Ukraine as he had been forced out of the network three years earlier.)

In 2015, Hall promised his girlfriend, Alicia Meller, that he would find a safer path as they started a family. They soon married. He also took a full-time job in Fox's London bureau, which still entailed covering conflict and strife. But in 2021, Hall moved to Washington, D.C., to cover the U.S. State Department.

toggle caption i Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images

"I made that final decision to pull back from the front lines," Hall wrote. "It was much harder than I imagined it would be to make this professional change in my life; the pull of distant wars never weakened or went away. But I understood new paths were opening for me."

That new path lasted roughly four months.

On Feb. 24, 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the invasion of Ukraine. Hall got a call from a Fox News executive: Would he go overseas and cover the war? As he wrote, "I understood my obligations to Alicia and my family, and I knew I had to stop putting myself in dangerous situations."
