World.title: I moved to Mexico City in my 20s. Here’s what I learned
World.content:
If you move to Mexico City in your 20s, I hope it becomes a home and not just a destination.

I came to Mexico at 25 thinking I was moving abroad one more time. I had already lived outside Spain, so I knew what it meant to arrive somewhere new, figure out a city, make friends and eventually find my way around. I thought Mexico City would be another chapter in that story.

A year later, I realized something else happened. I didn’t just move to Mexico; I started building a life here.

When you’re in your 20s, it’s easy to romanticize starting over somewhere else. How many of us, after a mental breakdown, have thought about leaving everything behind? Maybe moving to Paris like Blair, or finding the messy, exciting life Carrie Bradshaw had in New York City in her 30s.

I’m not saying New York or Paris won’t give you what you need to find. They might. But I found something in Mexico City that I wasn’t necessarily looking for: a place where I could become a slightly different version of myself.

Asking better questions in a new city

For me, my 20s have become less about figuring everything out and more about asking better questions. Do I want to become a mother? Will I get married? What do I want my career to look like? What kind of woman do I want to become? What do I want my future family to look like? I don’t have the answers yet. But living abroad has made me more conscious of the questions.

When I told my friends in Europe that I was moving to Mexico, some of them were worried. I wasn’t particularly afraid. My biggest concern was more mundane: I love walking, and I simply wondered whether I would be able to walk as much as I did back home. I quickly found out I could. I walk from our apartment in San Miguel de Chapultepec to Condesa to see friends, or go to a class. I walk through Chapultepec Park almost every day, and sometimes all the way to Polanco, which can take close to an hour.

One of the first things Mexico City taught me was how easily we can misunderstand places we’ve never experienced ourselves.

Before coming to Mexico, I only knew two Mexicans. They had been exchange students in Finland when I was studying there in 2020 and 2021. We weren’t friends. I just remember them being very good at beer pong and drinking rum or gin with water.

Then I arrived. And I started meeting people.

Finding kindness in the unlikeliest moments

Before Mexico, the country that completely changed my understanding of human connection was Cuba. I would need to write another article about everything that island gave me, but I truly thought nothing could surprise me in the same way again. Until Mexico did.

On my third day living in Mexico City, I was waiting in line to pay for a haircut. The woman behind me noticed what I was doing and immediately told me there was a cheaper hairdresser in the shop across the street. This act of kindness was the first one that people have shown me here. They aren’t normally dramatic moments, but they happen very often. Sometimes it is smiling in the street, starting a conversation or simply making an effort when they have no reason to.

At home, you move through your busy day surrounded by people and routines that are familiar. Abroad, you become more aware of your interactions, and they end up becoming part of what makes a place feel like yours.

There was another adjustment I was not expecting. As a European — very active and not particularly patient — I was struck by how slowly life seemed to move here. I learned that “ahorita” doesn’t necessarily mean right now. It can mean soon. It can mean later. Most of the time it’s just a polite way of saying something will happen when it happens. And you’ll get your coffee when you’re meant to get it. If you’re in a hurry, I recommend you insist a couple of times.

How different neighborhoods shape who you are

One of the things that continues to amaze me about Mexico City is how different each neighborhood feels. Polanco and Santa Fe have their own rhythm: business, luxury, restaurants, offices, polished cars and people dressed for work.

Then you go to Condesa or Roma, and suddenly you’re surrounded by leafy streets, cafes, parks and lots of dogs. I spend a lot of time in Parque México with a good friend of mine who has lived here since 2024, and we still find ourselves surprised by what we see: people dancing, doing karate, playing pickleball, learning to skate, practicing hula-hoop, someone selling poems, couples sitting on benches, foreigners taking photographs of a scene that locals barely notice because, to them, it’s simply Tuesday. That is Mexico City.

The Historic Center still leaves me speechless: the old buildings, the ruins, the Zócalo, Alameda Central, Palacio de Bellas Artes, Museo Nacional de Arte (MUNAL), the markets and the streets where centuries of history exist on top of each other.

And then there is Coyoacán, Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera, colorful markets, museums, and streets that feel completely different from the rest of the city.

The most interesting part is not just that these neighborhoods look different. They also make you feel different. You become a different version of yourself depending on where you are in the city. And in your 20s, that gives you something I have learned to appreciate: perspective.

Experiencing Mexican art and architecture

I’ve visited many museums since arriving — some of the famous ones and others that are less known. I don’t want to pretend I can explain Mexican art after a year here. But I can say that I have never experienced history through public art in quite the same way. The murals of Diego Rivera are not simply beautiful paintings. They tell stories about Mexico, its people and its history. Artists like Frida Kahlo transformed personal pain into art and became part of a cultural identity recognized around the world. I was also so impressed by Luis Barragán. Have you seen his house in San Miguel de Chapultepec? It was designed in the late 1940s, and I swear if you discover it today, you’ll want to move in there. Mexico City reminds me that contemporary doesn’t always mean new.

The joys of Mexican food

The same happened with food. Unpopular opinion: I’m not a foodie. I enjoy a latte and a cookie as much as avocado toast or a good meal at a cool restaurant every once in a while. Just give me some food when I’m hungry, and I’ll be happy. But even I have been fascinated by Mexican food. Mexican cuisine was recognized as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2010, and one of the things I’ve learned is that there is no single thing called “Mexican food.” Ingredients, dishes and traditions change so much from state to state.

Even as a vegetarian, I have found myself trying things I never expected to eat: nopal, huitlacoche and many other ingredients I did not know of before arriving.

And Mexico City is not only Mexican food. You can eat Thai, Italian, Spanish, Chinese … you name it, you’ll find it. I even discovered one of my favorite Lebanese places here in the Historic Center.

Lessons in community through Día de los Muertos

I moved to Mexico City about a year ago, just as the rainy season was ending and Independence Day celebrations were beginning. I was warned before arriving that people knew how to celebrate. “But isn’t that true everywhere?” I thought. Especially coming from Spain, where we’re always down to party. But I understood quickly that celebration here can mean something bigger than drinking late into the night. There is a sense of community, belonging and gathering together.

To this day, experiencing Día de los Muertos in Mexico has been one of the best experiences of my life. We went to the village of Malinalco, less than two hours from Mexico City, to visit family altars. We entered house after house, each one belonging to families that had lost someone that year. Every house was different. Some had large patios and modern buildings; others were old. In all of them, they replicated the profession of the person who had died through objects, decorations and food: a baker, a secretary, a police officer, a chef. The altars were filled with bright orange cempasúchil flowers and candles.

In some of them, we lit our own candles as a sign of respect. Every family gave us something to eat and drink — from tamales and tacos to mezcal, tequila or warm spiced wine. In some of them, you could really feel the presence of the person being remembered. How generous of those families, after losing their loved ones, to celebrate their lives with us, strangers to them. It was so magical. I left with tears in my eyes from the lesson in humanity I had just experienced.

Building a life together while making it your own

I’m not single, and my boyfriend and I moved here together. Some people might think moving with your partner in your 20s means you miss out on the experience. That hasn’t been our case. If anything, moving here has made us more intentional about building a life, both individually and as a couple.

Marta Delgado is a Spanish writer and marketing professional from Galicia, Spain, currently based in Mexico City. She writes about culture, lifestyle, and what it means to build a life abroad, drawing from her own time living in different countries.

ANALYSIS · LATIN AMERICA · CLIMATE AND MARKETS

Key Facts — The region Latin America borders the Pacific where El Niño forms, and in several of its countries dams supply over 70 percent of electricity.

— Why it matters The event dries out Colombia, the Amazon and Central America, and drenches coastal Peru, Ecuador and the southern farm belt.

— Why now The central Pacific ran 3.1°C above normal in late September on NOAA’s traditional measure, beating the weekly record set in 2015.

— What happened CEPAL, the UN’s economic commission for the region, says an extreme event could cost at least 2 percent of regional GDP over three years.

— The split Peru, Ecuador, Colombia and Central America lose most, while Argentina, Uruguay and Chile gain water and harvests.

— What it means for you Expect dearer food and power in the Andes and Central America, bigger farm exports from Argentina and a tighter Panama Canal.

— Still open On NOAA’s official relative index the event is not yet a record, and the peak is due between November and January.

El Niño has returned with unusual force, and by one widely used measure it has already set a record. For Latin America this is less a weather story than an economic one.

The warming of the tropical Pacific moves rain away from some countries and dumps it on others. That splits the region into clear losers and quiet winners, with consequences for food prices, power bills, currencies and trade.

How a Warm Pacific Moves Rain Around the Americas

In a normal year, trade winds push warm surface water west across the Pacific towards Asia. Cold, nutrient-rich water then rises along the coasts of Peru and Ecuador and feeds one of the world’s richest fisheries.

When the winds weaken, the warm water drifts back east and the rain belt follows it. Weather patterns across the Americas shift with it.

Coastal Peru and Ecuador get warm seas and heavy rain. Colombia, Venezuela, Central America and the northern Amazon tend to dry out.

Further south the effect reverses. Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and southern Brazil usually get extra rain, and central Chile often has a wetter winter.

El Niño also strengthens high winds over the Caribbean that tear storms apart. By 21 September the Atlantic had not produced a single hurricane, a first since 1914.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why This Event Stands Out

Scientists track El Niño through sea temperatures in a patch of the central Pacific known as Niño 3.4. In the week centred on 23 September, that patch ran 3.1°C above normal.

That beat the weekly record of 3.0°C from November 2015 in data from NOAA, the US weather and oceans agency. Off Peru and Ecuador the anomaly that week was larger still, at about 4.7°C.

There is a catch: NOAA’s official index strips out the general warming of the tropical oceans. On that measure this El Niño is not yet a record.

That may change soon. NOAA puts the chance of a very strong event this winter above 90 percent.

It also gives 75 percent odds that by December this will be the strongest El Niño since at least 1950.

The World Meteorological Organization says the odds of the event lasting through February are close to 100 percent. UN Secretary-General António Guterres put it bluntly: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes.”

Berkeley Earth, a climate research group, expects the central Pacific to peak just over 4°C above normal between November and January. A Science study of Galápagos corals, published in August, found El Niño swings about 37 percent larger than before industrialisation.

The heat reaches the atmosphere with a delay of several months. Britain’s Met Office says 2027 is very likely to become the warmest year on record.

A Bill of at Least 2 Percent of Regional GDP

CEPAL, the UN’s economic commission for the region, published its estimate on 21 September. An extreme El Niño could cut regional output by at least 2 percent over three years, it said.

Half of that loss would come in the first year. The commission also warned that poverty could rise by up to 4.8 million people by the end of the decade.

UNICEF counts 25.8 million children in Latin America and the Caribbean exposed to the droughts and floods.

Two weak points explain the size of the hit. In several countries dams supply more than 70 percent of electricity, and much of the region’s food comes from rain-fed farms.

History shows how long the damage can last. A 2023 study in Science put global income losses from the 1997-98 El Niño at US$5.7 trillion over the following years.

Help is arriving, but on a modest scale. On 2 October CAF, the Latin American development bank, offered a credit line of up to US$1 billion to affected countries.

Peru and Ecuador: Flooded Coasts and an Empty Sea

Peru sits closest to the warm water, and its central bank has already cut its forecasts. It now expects growth of 3.2 percent in 2026 and 3.0 percent in 2027, with El Niño behind most of the downgrade.

The bank sees fishing output falling 30.7 percent this year. The first anchovy season landed only 24.6 percent of a quota that was already the smallest in a decade.

That matters far beyond Peru, which supplies about a fifth of the world’s fishmeal. Prices for the fish feed hit a record of about US$2,500 a tonne in May.

Dearer feed squeezes salmon farmers in Chile and shrimp farmers in Ecuador. A weak second anchovy season would keep that pressure on into 2027.

ENFEN, Peru’s El Niño forecasting committee, expects an “extraordinary” coastal event through January, its highest category. It sees heavy rain on the northern coast, a farm-export hub, from October, becoming more frequent in November.

The government declared a 60-day emergency in districts of 23 regions on 1 September. The consultancy Preciso estimates farm-export losses of about US$1.5 billion over 2026 and 2027, with the 2027 mango crop roughly halved.

Prices are already moving. Lima’s annual inflation reached 4.55 percent in September, above the 1 to 3 percent target, and tomato prices jumped 29 percent.

Ecuador faces floods and drought at once. By 30 September heavy rain had killed 35 people since January, officials said, and on 2 October it flooded parts of Guayaquil.

Yet the Amazon and southern basins that feed most of its hydropower are drying out. By late September the Coca river, which drives the country’s largest power plant, had dropped below the flow the plant needs.

That raises the risk of power cuts in November and December, two years after blackouts of up to 14 hours a day. Because Ecuador uses the US dollar, it cannot cushion the blow through its currency.

The coast also hosts its export engines. About 87 percent of shrimp farms sit in flood-prone areas, and rice prices have jumped 39 percent.

Colombia and Central America: Running Short of Water

Colombia relies on rain for roughly 70 percent of its electricity. Inflows to its reservoirs were 66 percent of the historical average in late September, according to XM, the grid operator.

XM warns of a shortfall in guaranteed supply equal to 8.3 percent of demand. In a bad case, reservoirs could drop to 15.7 percent by mid-2027, against a 2024 low of about 27 percent.

On 18 September wholesale power peaked at COP 1,513 per kilowatt-hour (about US$0.46 at 3,273 pesos to the US dollar). Imported gas, needed for backup plants, already covered 23 percent of gas supply in the first quarter.

On 30 September the central bank raised its key rate to 12.25 percent, naming El Niño as a risk to food prices. Bogotá’s water, rationed in 2024, looks safer this time, with its main reservoir 95 percent full.

In Central America the damage is human rather than financial. In parts of the Dry Corridor, a farm belt from Guatemala to Nicaragua, drought wiped out most of the first maize crop.

Guatemala counts about 227,000 hectares hit by drought, the most in a decade, and about 3.1 million people facing crisis-level hunger. In July, white maize in Honduras cost 24 percent more than a year earlier.

The World Food Programme says about 4.2 million people in the region could face food insecurity. In the communities they surveyed, aid groups recorded more than 6,000 migration movements between May and July.

The Panama Canal: Tighter, Not Yet Broken

The canal runs on rainwater stored in lakes that refill each wet season. Rain in its watershed has been 34 percent below average this hydrological year, the Panama Canal Authority said in August.

Panama declared a national emergency on 25 August, and daily transit slots fell from 36 to 32. One gas shipper, SK Gas of South Korea, paid a record US$5.3 million at auction to jump the queue.

September rains brought relief. On 28 September the authority raised the limit to 33 transits a day and allowed deeper drafts of 49 feet.

That is well above the 22 daily transits of the 2023-24 drought. But the canal’s new budget assumes 29.5 large-ship transits a day and drafts near 44 feet in the driest months.

The authority still budgets revenue of about US$5.56 billion for the fiscal year that began on 1 October. A new reservoir on the Río Indio, meant to secure the canal’s water, will not be ready before 2031.

Brazil: One Country, Two Climates

Brazil shows both faces of El Niño at once. Government forecasters expect a hotter, drier North and Northeast, and more rain and flood risk in the South.

The Rio Negro at Manaus fell 5.21 metres in September, to 18.88 metres. In early September the Geological Survey of Brazil forecast a low of between 12.31 and 16.50 metres by the end of October.

The bottom of that range would approach the record low of 12.11 metres, set in October 2024. Low rivers slow the barges that supply the Manaus free-trade zone and carry grain to northern ports.

In the South, by contrast, October inflows to hydropower dams are forecast at almost twice their usual level. That revives memories of the 2024 floods in Rio Grande do Sul, which killed more than 180 people.

For now, power bills are easing. The regulator dropped its electricity surcharge for October after five months, because more rain in the South and Southeast steadied reservoir levels.

CONAB, the national supply agency, sees record crops of 148 million tonnes of corn and 181.6 million tonnes of soybeans. It expects slightly lower soy yields, partly because of the weather risk.

Rain has slowed the cane harvest and mills are favouring ethanol, so Centre-South sugar output is down 14.4 percent this season. Arabica coffee trees flowered about a month early, which raises the risk of an uneven 2027 crop.

In a June central bank survey, economists saw El Niño adding 0.3 points to inflation this year and 0.4 points in 2027. The government has set aside R$1.335 billion (US$256 million, at 5.22 reais to the US dollar) for food stocks, health and fire-fighting.

Brazilians vote for president on Sunday 4 October. Whoever wins inherits a drought in the North and flood risk in the South.

The Southern Cone Collects a Rain Dividend

For Argentina, El Niño is mostly good news. Its weather service expects above-normal rain from October to December across the Litoral and much of the farm belt.

The Rosario Board of Trade projects record farm-sector exports of US$42.2 billion for the 2026-27 season, even assuming normal yields. It expects about US$40 billion of hard currency to flow in during 2027.

Better yields could add more. IERAL, an Argentine think-tank, says extra rain could add about 11 million tonnes of corn and soy, worth up to US$4 billion.

In the strong El Niño of 2015-16, Argentine soy yields averaged 3.02 tonnes a hectare against a seven-year norm of 2.71. Those dollars matter for the central bank, which held US$48.65 billion in gross reserves on 2 October.

The risk is too much water. The Salado basin, home to about a quarter of Argentina’s grain, flooded in 2025 at a cost of about US$2 billion.

Uruguay’s forecasters see a 60 percent chance of above-normal spring rain in the north, good for pastures, corn and hydropower. Paraguay is a mixed case, with the Paraná river running high.

The Paraguay River is another matter. At Asunción it stood at just 0.46 metres on 3 October, about two metres below normal, which keeps barge traffic constrained.

Chile is a quiet winner. A mostly wet winter left its reservoirs 22.6 percent fuller than a year earlier, with snowpack about 75 percent above normal.

What It Means for Markets

The clearest price signal is rice, driven mainly by India’s weak monsoon. Chicago rough rice futures closed at US$16.36 per hundredweight on 2 October, 47 percent above a year earlier.

That helps rice exporters in Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina but hurts importers.

Raw sugar rose about 10 percent in September as weather hurt crops in Thailand and India and rain slowed Brazil’s harvest. In Ecuador, rain has already halted the sugar harvest, forcing imports.

Palm oil, by contrast, has fallen 7.5 percent over the past month. Drought damage to palm trees in Indonesia and Malaysia shows up in harvests only months later.

That later squeeze could favour palm growers in Colombia, Ecuador and Central America in 2027.

Energy is a separate story. Brent crude near US$102 a barrel reflects the crisis around the Strait of Hormuz, not the weather.

Expensive oil still adds to the strain on importers already paying more for food. Asian LNG prices have also more than doubled in a year, which matters for Colombia as its dams run low.

Monetary policy is already reacting. Colombia is raising rates and Peru has little room to cut, while Brazilian economists expect inflation near 5 percent this year.

What Comes Next

The next markers are close. NOAA publishes its next El Niño update on 8 October, and Peru’s ENFEN follows on 15 October.

The event should peak between November and January, with the heaviest rain on Peru’s north coast in the southern summer. The tests for the Panama Canal and Colombia’s dams come later, in the dry months of early 2027.

Argentina’s payoff arrives with the harvest between April and June 2027. NOAA sees a 55 percent chance that the Pacific returns to neutral in that same window.

None of this is fixed. Forecasts shift, and a warm Pacific loads the dice rather than deciding outcomes.

It also does not mean the whole region loses. Argentina, Uruguay and Chile stand to gain, the canal is well above its 2023 lows, and Colombia has not ordered power rationing.

For investors, the weather has become a regional macro variable. In 2027 it sits beside interest rates and elections as a driver of Latin American markets.

What is El Niño in simple terms?

El Niño is a periodic warming of the tropical Pacific that weakens the trade winds and shifts rainfall around the world. It returns every two to seven years and usually lasts about a year.

Which Latin American countries are most exposed?

Peru and Ecuador face coastal floods and losses at sea. Colombia and Central America face drought, with strain on power and food. Argentina, Uruguay and Chile are likely to benefit from extra rain.

Will El Niño affect travel in the region?

Possibly, in specific places. Floods have already hit coastal Ecuador, heavy rain is forecast for Peru’s north coast, and Ecuador may face power cuts. Bogotá’s water supply looks secure this time.

How long will this El Niño last?

The WMO puts the chance of it lasting through February 2027 close to 100 percent. NOAA sees a 55 percent chance of neutral conditions by April to June 2027, though price effects can last longer.

World.title: Jão’s tour lands in Brasília on 12 December
World.content:
Downtown São Paulo, Brazil (Photo: Fulviusbsas / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0).

BRAZIL · MUSIC

Key Facts — What Jão performs his Memórias Póstumas tour, a theatrical arena show of contemporary Brazilian pop.

— When Saturday, 12 December 2026.

— Where Ginásio Nilson Nelson, Brasília–DF.

— Tickets Face values range from R$130 (about US$25) to R$990 (about US$190), before booking fees. General sale opened on 1 October 2026 via Eventim.

— Good to know Children aged 5 to 15 may attend only with a parent or legal guardian; those aged 16 and 17 may attend without one.

Jão brings his Memórias Póstumas tour to Ginásio Nilson Nelson in Brasília on Saturday, 12 December 2026.

Brazilian pop artist Jão plays Brasília on 12 December 2026 at Ginásio Nilson Nelson, the fourth Brazilian stop of his Memórias Póstumas tour. Tickets are sold through Eventim, with face values from R$130 (about US$25) to R$990 (about US$190) before booking fees. The show is presented by Itaú Live with Budweiser as the official beer sponsor.

Who is Jão?

Jão is one of Brazil’s biggest pop artists of the past decade. He built a large following with confessional songwriting and a theatrical live show, moving from smaller venues to headline arena tours. For a foreigner in Brazil, he is a useful introduction to contemporary Brazilian pop that mixes MPB sensibility with international production.

The tour takes its name from his album Memórias Póstumas, a record that anchors the setlist and visual concept. The production is handled by 30e in partnership with U.F.O Produções, with Itaú Live presenting and Budweiser as the official beer sponsor. That level of corporate backing signals a high-profile national tour rather than a modest club run.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why the Brasília date matters

Brasília is the fourth Brazilian stop on the tour, after Rio de Janeiro on 31 October, Belo Horizonte on 21 November and Recife on 28 November. The capital date gives the tour access to the Federal District’s large student, professional and diplomatic population, plus visitors from Goiás and the wider central-west region.

The Nilson Nelson arena sits in the central SRPN sports and events district, close to Brasília’s main hotel and transport corridors. That makes the show a regional event rather than a small local concert. The tour later continues in Lisbon on 19 March 2027 and São Paulo on 27 March 2027.

Tickets and prices

General sale opened on 1 October 2026 at 10 a.m. online through Eventim and at 11 a.m. at official box offices. Itaú Private Bank and Itaú Personnalité customers had an earlier presale from 29 September, followed by a broader Itaú presale on 30 September. Itaú cardholders were offered a 30% discount during the presale and could pay in up to three interest-free instalments.

Eventim’s listed Brasília prices include half-price, social and full-price tiers, with the VIP Super Fã Itaú package reaching R$990 (about US$190). The listing says prices include taxes, while any booking fee is calculated during checkout.

Foreign residents should understand a few local terms. Meia-entrada is the legally discounted half-price admission for eligible groups such as students, seniors and people with disabilities; proof may be required at entry. Entrada social is a reduced-price category generally linked to a charitable or donation requirement. Check Eventim’s conditions before paying for any discounted ticket.

Venue and practical tips

O Ginásio Nilson Nelson fica em Brasília–DF. The venue is a long-standing indoor arena used for concerts and sporting events. Its central location means most hotels in the Plano Piloto hotel sector are a short taxi or ride-share trip away.

The age rating allows children and teenagers aged 5 to 15 only with a parent or legal guardian. Those aged 16 and 17 may attend without one. Bring a valid photo ID, especially if you bought a half-price or social ticket. For foreigners, a passport or Brazilian foreign resident ID should work, but confirm accepted identification directly in Eventim’s checkout.

Brasília in December is warm and usually dry, with occasional late-afternoon rain. The arena is covered, but queues form outside, so carry water and sun protection if you arrive early. Use official taxi ranks or ride-share apps after the show rather than accepting unsolicited rides.

World.title: Sorriso Maroto brings pagode to Brasília on 5 Dec
World.content:
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva at the Palácio da Alvorada, Brasília, 9 July 2026. (Photo: Ricardo Stuckert / Lula Oficial, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Key Facts — Who it is for Foreign residents and travellers wanting an introduction to Brazilian pagode music and romantic samba culture.

— What you need A ticket bought from the official Ingresse listing, plus a light rain jacket for possible December showers.

— What it costs Official prices are not confirmed; an event guide lists R$80 to R$385, about US$15 to US$73.

— How long it takes The tour suggests a longer set than a typical festival appearance, with gates opening around 3 p.m.

— Where to apply Buy tickets through Ingresse, the Brazilian platform handling sales for the Brasília date.

— Biggest trap Buying from unofficial vendors risks resale markups or invalid tickets; always use the official vendor.

Who is Sorriso Maroto?

Sorriso Maroto is a Brazilian pagode group formed in Rio de Janeiro. The band built a career on romantic lyrics, melodic cavaquinho and a polished stage presence that appeals well beyond the traditional samba audience. For a foreigner new to Brazilian music, pagode is a lighter, more pop-friendly offshoot of samba, often built around love songs and crowd singalongs.

The group’s catalogue includes hits such as “Assim Você Mata o Papai,” “Sinais” and “Eu Vacilei, Mas Eu Te Amo.” These songs are staples at Brazilian parties and have kept the band relevant for nearly three decades. The current tour, “Sorriso Eu Gosto no Pagode,” is a roda de samba project that revisits that repertoire in a more intimate, circle-based format.

The band’s official website describes the 2026 tour as a national series of more than 10 events. Brasília is one of the key dates on that run, bringing the group to the federal capital’s lakefront entertainment district.

Downtown São Paulo (Photo: Fulviusbsas / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0).

The Brasília date and what to expect

The show on Saturday 5 December 2026 is at an open-air entertainment complex in Brasília’s South Sports Club Sector. The venue sits near Lake Paranoá, in the Asa Sul area, and is known for hosting large concerts with a relaxed, outdoor atmosphere.

This is common for evening shows at Na Praia, where alcohol is served and security checks are standard. The format of the “Sorriso Eu Gosto no Pagode” tour suggests a longer set than a typical festival appearance, with the group moving through its romantic-pagode hits and newer material.

For foreign residents and travellers, the show is a good introduction to a musical style that dominates Brazilian social life. Expect a crowd that sings along to nearly every song, and a relaxed dress code suited to Brasília’s warm December evenings.

Tickets and prices

Ticket sales are handled by Ingresse, a Brazilian platform widely used for concerts and festivals. The Eventim page supplied as a reference does not state a final price or clearly identify the sales platform, so buyers should look for the official Ingresse listing for the Brasília date.

Official prices are not confirmed in the available primary listings. A Brazilian event guide reports a range from R$80 to R$385 (about US$15 to US$73), depending on ticket batch, sector and platform fees. Treat that range as indicative rather than a confirmed official price. Prices in Brazil often rise as cheaper batches sell out, so buying early is usually cheaper.

When buying, check whether the ticket is for the pista (general standing area) or a front-stage sector. Some Na Praia events also sell tables or premium areas, but no details for this specific show have been confirmed. Always buy from the official vendor to avoid resale markups or invalid tickets.

Venue, getting there and safety tips

The complex is near Brasília’s lakefront leisure district, a short drive from the city’s hotel sector and the main government buildings. Public transport in Brasília can be limited late at night, so ride-hailing services or private cars are the most practical options after the show.

If you drive, confirm event-day parking instructions with the organiser before leaving. Traffic around the venue can be heavy when gates open and again when the show ends. Arriving early, around the 3 p.m. gate opening, helps avoid the worst congestion and gives you time to find your sector.

For foreign visitors, standard Brazilian event advice applies: keep your phone and wallet in a front pocket, avoid displaying large amounts of cash, and use official ride-hailing apps rather than street taxis late at night. The venue has security and medical staff on site, but it is still wise to keep an eye on your belongings in crowded areas.

What else to do in Brasília that week

Brasília is a planned city known for its modernist architecture by Oscar Niemeyer and urban design by Lúcio Costa. If you are in town for the show, the Cathedral of Brasília, the National Congress and the JK Memorial are all within a short drive of the Asa Sul area. The city’s lakefront, near the venue, has restaurants and bars that stay busy on weekends.

Brasília’s rainy season generally begins in October, while December falls within the rainy season, so afternoon showers are possible. The venue is open-air, so check the forecast and bring a light rain jacket if needed. Evenings are usually warm, so most people dress casually.

For food, the Asa Sul neighbourhood has a strong selection of Brazilian and international restaurants. Many visitors combine a show at Na Praia with dinner nearby before gates open. Reservations are recommended on weekends, especially for larger groups.

Where can I buy tickets for Sorriso Maroto in Brasília?

Tickets are sold through Ingresse. Look for the official listing for the Brasília date on the Ingresse platform.

What time does the Sorriso Maroto show start?

The event listing gives the time as “Em breve”; a separate event guide lists 3 p.m.

How much do tickets cost?

Official prices are not confirmed. An event guide lists a range from R$80 to R$385 (about US$15 to US$73), depending on sector and batch.

What is the Sorriso Maroto Brasília concert date?

The show is on Saturday 5 December 2026 at an open-air entertainment complex in Brasília’s South Sports Club Sector, near Lake Paranoá. Gates are listed as opening around 3 p.m.

World.title: Guyana Passport Holders Get Saudi Visa on Arrival
World.content:
Irfaan Ali (centre left) and senior Guyanese officials at talks with a Brazilian delegation in Georgetown on 6 May 2022 (Photo: Alan Santos/Palácio do Planalto, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

GUYANA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — The country Guyana is a small South American nation on the Caribbean coast, bordering Brazil, Venezuela and Suriname.

— What happened Guyana’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation announced on 3 October 2026 that Guyanese passport holders may obtain a Saudi visa on arrival or e-visa without holding a US, UK or Schengen visa.

— Who is who The announcement came from Guyana’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, which said the change followed intensified bilateral discussions with Saudi Arabia.

— Why now The ministry said the move is intended to expand trade, investment, tourism and people-to-people links between the two countries.

— What it means for you Guyanese travellers can apply directly for an e-visa or request a visa on arrival, but a visa is still required and admission remains subject to Saudi immigration rules.

— Still open The ministry did not publish the fee amount, visa validity, permitted stay, health-insurance requirements, eligible entry points or processing times, and no Saudi government circular confirming the change was located.

Guyana has opened a new travel route to Saudi Arabia. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation announced on 3 October 2026 that Guyanese passport holders may now obtain a Saudi visa on arrival or an electronic visa without holding a valid US, UK or Schengen visa.

INews Guyana reported the ministry’s statement, which described Guyana as the only South American country whose passport holders have this facility without a third-country visa. The change removes a condition that previously shaped access for many Guyanese travellers.

What the announcement says

Eligible travellers may apply directly for an e-visa or request a visa on arrival using a Guyanese passport and paying the applicable visa fee. The ministry said the facility covers Umrah, tourism, visiting family or friends and other visits.

The release did not say that the route covers employment, study, residence or Hajj travel. A visa remains required. This is not visa-free entry, and admission remains subject to Saudi immigration rules at the border.

The ministry did not state the fee amount, visa validity, permitted stay, health-insurance requirements, eligible entry points or processing times. It also did not publish a Saudi government circular or a bilateral agreement confirming the change.

File photo: Guyana.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why the change matters

The ministry said the decision followed intensified bilateral discussions with Saudi Arabia. It framed the move as a way to expand trade, investment, tourism and people-to-people links between Georgetown and Riyadh.

For a small country with a growing international profile, easier travel access can support business missions, religious travel and family visits.

The ministry was explicit that no other South American passport holder enjoys the same facility without a third-country visa.

What travellers should check

Before the announcement, Guyanese travellers generally needed a visa in advance. A limited Saudi visa-on-arrival or e-visa route reportedly applied where the traveller held a valid US, UK or Schengen visa.

Third-party guidance still reflected that older position at the time of the announcement, creating a possible implementation discrepancy. Travellers should verify eligibility, fees, insurance, passport validity and arrival procedures through Saudi Arabia’s official visa platform or a Saudi diplomatic mission before booking.

No published Saudi primary-source confirmation was located in the available results. That leaves room for caution until Riyadh issues its own circular or updates its official visa portal.

What comes next

The practical test will be how Saudi immigration officers and airline check-in desks apply the new rule. Until Saudi Arabia publishes matching guidance, travellers may face questions at departure or on arrival.

The ministry’s announcement is a diplomatic signal as much as a travel update. It suggests Guyana and Saudi Arabia are moving closer on mobility, trade and investment.

For now, Guyanese passport holders have a new option to pursue. The details that matter most, such as cost and length of stay, remain to be confirmed through official Saudi channels.

Can Guyanese citizens enter Saudi Arabia without a visa?

No. Guyanese passport holders still need a visa, but they may now apply for a visa on arrival or an e-visa without holding a US, UK or Schengen visa.

What travel purposes does the new Saudi visa route cover?

The ministry listed Umrah, tourism, visiting family or friends and other visits. It did not say the facility covers employment, study, residence or Hajj travel.

How much does the Saudi visa on arrival cost for Guyanese travellers?

The ministry did not state the fee amount. Travellers should check Saudi Arabia’s official visa platform or a Saudi diplomatic mission for current fees and requirements.

Has Saudi Arabia confirmed the new visa rule for Guyana?

No Saudi government circular or bilateral agreement confirming the change was located in the available results. Travellers should verify the rule through official Saudi channels before booking.

World.title: Colombian Report Says FBI May Arrive, OFAC Weighs More
World.content:
Medellín seen from El Poblado, where many foreign residents settle (Photo: CONOCER (Wikivoyage), Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

COLOMBIA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — The country Colombia is Latin America’s third-most populous nation and a longstanding US ally in the fight against cocaine trafficking.

— What happened The US Treasury’s OFAC sanctioned then-President Gustavo Petro, his wife Verónica Alcocer, his son Nicolás Petro, and then Interior Minister Armando Benedetti on 24 October 2025.

— Who is who Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the designations under Executive Order 14059, which targets the international illicit-drug trade.

— Why now A Colombian outlet reported on 3 October 2026 that the FBI could arrive in October and that OFAC is weighing more sanctions; the 2025 designations remain the only confirmed US action.

— What it means for you US persons are generally barred from transactions with the four sanctioned individuals, and entities they own 50% or more may also be blocked.

— Still open A Colombian outlet reported the FBI could arrive in October and that OFAC is evaluating more sanctions, but no US agency has confirmed that account.

Washington sanctioned Colombia’s then-president and three close associates in October 2025, and a Colombian news report published on 3 October 2026 says the FBI could arrive in the country in October and that the US Treasury is weighing further measures.

The sanctions were announced on 24 October 2025 by the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, known as OFAC. The Colombian outlet El Diario reported on 3 October 2026, citing El Tiempo, the possibility of an FBI arrival and additional sanctions review, but no US agency has confirmed that account.

What the US Treasury announced

OFAC designated then-President Gustavo Francisco Petro Urrego, his wife Verónica del Socorro Alcocer García, his son Nicolás Fernando Petro Burgos, and then Interior Minister Armando Benedetti under Executive Order 14059. That order targets people involved in the international illicit-drug trade.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the action was based on allegations that Petro’s government had allowed drug cartels to flourish. The Treasury release does not establish those allegations as judicial findings.

Under standard OFAC rules, the designations block property and interests in property under US jurisdiction. They also generally prohibit US persons from conducting transactions involving the four individuals, absent authorisation or an exemption.

File photo: La Candelaria district, Bogotá, Colombia.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The State Department’s parallel move

On the same day, the State Department said Secretary of State Marco Rubio would not certify Colombia’s counternarcotics performance for certain FY2025 foreign assistance. Principal Deputy Spokesperson Thomas Pigott cited the statutory framework in Section 7045(c)(3)(A) of the FY2024 appropriations law, continued through FY2025 appropriations.

That decision was an executive-branch funding-certification matter, not a court ruling. It signals a sharp deterioration in a relationship that has long been central to US drug policy in the hemisphere.

Colombia has received billions of dollars in US security and development aid over decades. The certification decision could affect some of that assistance, though the State Department release did not specify exact amounts.

What the local report claims

El Diario reported that the FBI would arrive in Colombia in October and that OFAC was evaluating additional sanctions. The report should be treated as an attributed account, not confirmation of an announced US operation.

The primary releases available do not confirm an FBI deployment, specify an October arrival date, identify an FBI mission, or announce further sanctions beyond the 24 October designations. Any subsequent action would require a new official announcement from the FBI, Treasury, State Department, or another competent authority.

No US agency had confirmed the report by 4 October 2026.

What it means for investors and travellers

For US persons, the sanctions create immediate compliance obligations. Banks, companies, and individuals must screen transactions involving the four designated people and any entity they own 50% or more.

The broader diplomatic chill could affect trade, investment, and travel sentiment. Colombia remains a major US trading partner, but the October 2025 sanctions targeted a sitting head of state, and Petro left office when his term ended on 7 August 2026.

Foreign investors will watch whether the certification decision leads to reduced US assistance or new conditions on cooperation. The situation remains fluid, and official channels have not confirmed the FBI arrival reported by El Diario.

Who did the US sanction in Colombia?

The US Treasury sanctioned then-President Gustavo Petro, his wife Verónica Alcocer, his son Nicolás Petro, and then Interior Minister Armando Benedetti on 24 October 2025.

Has the FBI confirmed it is going to Colombia?

No. A Colombian outlet reported the FBI could arrive in October, but no US agency has confirmed that account.

What do the OFAC sanctions mean for US persons?

US persons are generally barred from transactions involving the four sanctioned individuals, and entities they own 50% or more may also be blocked.

Why did the State Department act?

Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to certify Colombia’s counternarcotics performance for certain FY2025 foreign assistance, citing a statutory framework in US appropriations law.

World.title: Colombia Orders University of Córdoba Inspection
World.content:
File photo: Bogotá, Colombia.

COLOMBIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Colombia is South America’s second-most populous nation, with a presidential system and a long tradition of public universities that operate with legal autonomy.

— What happened President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered an Education Ministry inspection of the University of Córdoba for 5 October 2026.

— Who is who Jairo Torres Oviedo is the rector, serving a third consecutive term for 2026–2031.

— Why now The president accused Torres of changing university rules to remain in office and of improperly influencing electoral procedures, including the alumni representative election.

— What it means for you The dispute tests how far Colombia’s executive can press oversight powers against a public university whose rector has a favourable court ruling.

— Still open The inspection will examine the rectorate, electoral procedures and statutory compliance; any disciplinary or criminal consequences require action by competent bodies.

Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella has ordered an inspection of the University of Córdoba for 5 October 2026, directing Education Minister Ilva Myriam Hoyos Castañeda to review the rector’s office, recent elections and compliance with university statutes. The move escalates a public confrontation between the national government and the university’s rector, Jairo Torres Oviedo, who is serving a third consecutive term.

El Universal reported that the president’s announcement followed accusations that Torres had changed university rules to remain in office and had improperly influenced electoral procedures, including the election of the alumni representative to the Superior University Council. The president said the university should be led by an academic and alleged “corruption and politicking” in the rectorate.

What the inspection will examine

The Education Ministry’s inspection is expected to focus on three areas: the rectorate, electoral procedures and statutory compliance. De la Espriella asked the ministry to exercise its statutory inspection and oversight powers, a mechanism available to the executive branch for supervising public universities.

The president also asked the Procuraduría General de la Nación, Colombia’s public oversight body, to prioritise a disciplinary case whose closure was reportedly revoked on 30 July 2026. He separately requested that the Fiscalía General de la Nación, the attorney general’s office, prioritise criminal complaints involving Torres and his associates.

These requests do not by themselves change Torres’s legal status. Any disciplinary, criminal or administrative consequences would require action by the competent bodies, and the president’s statements alone do not overturn existing court rulings.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Education Ministry (Colombia) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The legal backdrop

The Fifth Section of Colombia’s Council of State, the country’s highest administrative court, declared Torres’s election legal. That ruling did not remove or suspend him, and the university continued to recognise him as rector for the 2026–2031 period.

The Council of State’s decision is the principal contrary legal development in the story. The president’s accusations, as reported by local outlets, are allegations and do not establish criminal liability.

The dispute therefore pits the executive branch’s oversight powers against a court ruling that validated the rector’s election. How the Education Ministry’s inspection interacts with that ruling will be closely watched by university administrators across Colombia.

Who gains and who loses

For the government, the inspection is a show of executive authority over a public institution and a signal that de la Espriella is willing to confront university leadership he considers illegitimate. For Torres, the inspection creates administrative pressure even as he holds a favourable court ruling.

Students and faculty at the University of Córdoba face uncertainty about institutional stability. The university is a major public higher-education institution in Colombia’s Caribbean region, and prolonged conflict between its rectorate and the national government could affect governance and funding discussions.

The broader higher-education sector is watching too. A precedent in which the executive branch uses inspection powers aggressively against a university with a court-validated rector could reshape the balance between university autonomy and government oversight.

What comes next

The inspection scheduled for 5 October 2026 will produce findings that the Education Ministry can use to recommend administrative measures. The Procuraduría and Fiscalía will separately decide whether to advance the disciplinary and criminal matters the president asked them to prioritise.

Torres has not been removed or suspended by any of these actions. The Council of State ruling remains in force unless a competent body issues a new decision.

For now, the University of Córdoba continues to operate under its current rector while the inspection proceeds. The outcome will clarify whether the president’s public campaign translates into formal administrative or legal consequences.

Why did Colombia’s president order an inspection of the University of Córdoba?

President Abelardo de la Espriella accused Rector Jairo Torres Oviedo of changing university rules to remain in office and of improperly influencing electoral procedures, including the alumni representative election.

Has the rector of the University of Córdoba been removed?

No. The Fifth Section of Colombia’s Council of State declared Torres’s election legal, and the university continues to recognise him as rector for 2026–2031.

What will the Education Ministry inspection examine?

The inspection will review the rectorate, electoral procedures and compliance with university statutes, according to the president’s order.

What other bodies has the president asked to act?

De la Espriella asked the Procuraduría General de la Nación to prioritise a disciplinary case and the Fiscalía General de la Nación to prioritise criminal complaints involving Torres and associates.

World.title: Lula Warns of a “Gang Leader” on Eve of Brazil’s Vote
World.content:
BRAZIL · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Brazil, Latin America’s largest democracy, holds a presidential first round on 4 October 2026 with 12 approved tickets.

— What happened President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said on 3 October 2026 that his camp faced a “gang leader” and organised crime, without naming Flávio Bolsonaro.

— Who is who Lula is running with Geraldo Alckmin; Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, is running with Alfredo Gaspar for the PL.

— Why now The remarks came during Lula’s final campaign march in São Paulo, the day before voting.

— What it means for you The rhetoric sharpened an already polarised contest, but no candidate was legally designated as an organised-crime leader in the reports.

— Still open A runoff, if no candidate wins outright, is scheduled for 25 October 2026.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said on Saturday, 3 October 2026, that his political camp was confronting a “gang leader” and organised crime during his final campaign event before Sunday’s presidential first round. He did not name his principal challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro of the PL.

Correio Braziliense reported that Lula framed the vote as a choice between “democracy and sovereignty” and “barbarism and corruption,” and urged supporters to seek votes through election day. The remarks came during a campaign march in São Paulo, which marked the end of Lula’s official first-round campaign.

What Lula said at the final rally

Lula did not specify whom he meant by “gang leader.” G1 reported that he associated his adversary with organised crime without naming Flávio Bolsonaro directly.

The president also claimed that his allies had helped arrest what he called a “Social Security gang” created under former President Jair Bolsonaro. He referred to the imprisonment of banker Daniel Vorcaro, linked in the speech to the Banco Master case.

The allegation was political rhetoric, not an identified criminal charge against a named presidential candidate. The reports do not establish that Flávio Bolsonaro or another candidate had been legally designated as an organised-crime leader.

File photo: A Brazilian electronic voting machine.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The challenger’s closing message

Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, held a separate final campaign event in São Paulo. He predicted victory in the first round, according to G1.

The Superior Electoral Court, known as the TSE, listed 12 presidential tickets for the election. They included Lula–Geraldo Alckmin and Flávio Bolsonaro–Alfredo Gaspar.

Voting takes place on 4 October 2026, from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Brasília time. A runoff, if required, is scheduled for 25 October 2026.

Why the rhetoric matters

Lula’s language signalled how sharply the campaign had narrowed into a contest over legitimacy and public safety. By invoking organised crime without naming a candidate, he left room for interpretation while energising his base.

For international investors and professionals watching Brazil, the tone matters because it frames the political risk around the vote. A polarised first round can delay policy clarity, even when the electoral calendar itself is fixed.

The TSE’s published calendar kept the process predictable. That institutional continuity is what markets tend to watch most closely in Brazil’s elections.

What comes next

Brazilians vote on 4 October 2026. If no candidate secures enough support to win outright, the top two face a runoff on 25 October 2026.

The final campaign events in São Paulo closed a first round that both major camps framed as existential. The next phase will test whether that rhetoric translates into turnout or legal challenges.

For now, the electoral authorities have set the rules and the dates. The contest itself remains open.

Did Lula name Flávio Bolsonaro as a gang leader?

No. Lula used the term “gang leader” on 3 October 2026 but did not name Flávio Bolsonaro or any other candidate.

When is Brazil’s presidential first round?

Voting takes place on 4 October 2026, from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Brasília time.

How many presidential tickets were registered?

The Superior Electoral Court listed 12 presidential tickets for the 2026 election.

When is a runoff, if needed?

A runoff, if required, is scheduled for 25 October 2026.

World.title: Lula Campaign Asks TSE to Probe US Consulate Closures
World.content:
File photo: Campaign posters of Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro in Brazil.

BRAZIL · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Brazil, Latin America’s most populous democracy, votes in the first round of its presidential election on 4 October 2026.

— What happened President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election campaign asked the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) on 2 October 2026 to include the United States’ suspension of in-person consular services in an existing investigation into alleged foreign interference.

— Who is who The petition was submitted to Sebastião Reis Júnior, the TSE inspector general for electoral justice. The campaign cited Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and Eduardo Bolsonaro in its allegations.

— Why now The US Embassy announced on 1 October that in-person services in Brasília, São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Porto Alegre and Recife would be suspended from 2 October, citing security concerns without public details.

— What it means for you The dispute adds diplomatic tension to an already polarised election and could affect consular access for foreign residents and travellers in Brazil.

— Still open TSE officials must decide whether to incorporate the shutdown and related documents into the pending investigation. No public US reopening timetable was reported.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election campaign asked Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) on 2 October 2026 to include the United States’ suspension of in-person consular services in an existing investigation into alleged foreign interference in the election. The request came one day after the US Embassy announced the shutdown and two days before the 4 October first round.

The campaign’s lawyers submitted the petition to Sebastião Reis Júnior, the TSE inspector general for electoral justice, according to G1 and Opera Mundi. They described the shutdown as an “anomalous diplomatic gesture” that could destabilise the election and argued that it should be considered alongside the campaign’s allegations of US interference allegedly involving Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and Eduardo Bolsonaro.

What the US Embassy announced

The US Embassy said on 1 October that in-person services at the embassy in Brasília and consulates in São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Porto Alegre and Recife would be suspended from 2 October because of “security concerns.” It gave no public details about the threat or a reopening date.

The available reports do not establish whether visa and passport processing continued during the suspension. The embassy’s announcement came amid heightened political tension in Brazil, with the presidential election only days away.

Lula’s campaign argued that the timing of the suspension, so close to the vote, made it relevant to the TSE’s existing investigation. The filing requested inclusion of the new facts and documents without changing the original scope of the case.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on TSE (Brazil) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The campaign’s allegations

The campaign also cited a 28 September 2026 letter from US Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Tim Kaine and Peter Welch to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, warning against US interference in Brazil’s election. The letter, according to the campaign, added weight to concerns about external involvement.

Those allegations remain claims by Lula’s campaign. The cited reports provide no finding by the TSE that the United States, Rubio or the Bolsonaro brothers coordinated the consular suspension.

The Bolsonaro brothers have not been shown by the TSE to have any role in the embassy’s decision. The campaign’s petition asks the court to examine the facts, not to presume a conclusion.

Federal Police operations on the same day

Separately, Brazil’s Federal Police carried out two search-and-seizure operations on 2 October, in São Paulo and the area around the Federal District, investigating an alleged plan targeting US diplomatic facilities. Phones and computers were seized.

The Federal Police said it had not yet found evidence confirming the initially reported risks. The investigation remained confidential.

The parallel operations added another layer of complexity to an already tense relationship between Brasília and Washington in the final days of the campaign.

What happens next

TSE officials must decide whether to incorporate the shutdown, the senators’ letter and related documents into the pending investigation. The court has not set a public deadline for that decision.

The Federal Police will analyse the seized devices and may take further measures. No public US reopening timetable was reported.

For foreign residents, investors and travellers in Brazil, the suspension raises practical questions about consular access. For the election, it adds a diplomatic dispute to a contest already marked by sharp polarisation.

Why did Lula’s campaign ask the TSE to investigate the US consular suspension?

The campaign argued that the suspension, announced two days before Brazil’s 4 October 2026 first-round election, was an “anomalous diplomatic gesture” that could destabilise the vote and should be examined alongside existing allegations of foreign interference.

Which US consular services were suspended in Brazil?

The US Embassy suspended in-person services at the embassy in Brasília and consulates in São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Porto Alegre and Recife from 2 October 2026, citing security concerns without public details.

Has the TSE found evidence of US interference in Brazil’s election?

No. The allegations remain claims by Lula’s campaign, and the cited reports provide no finding by the TSE that the United States or the Bolsonaro brothers coordinated the consular suspension.

What did Brazil’s Federal Police do on 2 October 2026?

The Federal Police carried out two search-and-seizure operations in São Paulo and the area around the Federal District, investigating an alleged plan targeting US diplomatic facilities, but said it had not yet found evidence confirming the initially reported risks.
