World.title: One state's illegal tobacco crackdown is producing striking results
World.content:
Legal cigarette sales rose sharply in Queensland after the state gained stronger powers to shut illegal shops, while the national market remained largely flat at the same time.

The state's sales rose 55 per cent in the first month after new enforcement laws took effect in November and remained 40 to 45 per cent above previous levels for the following six months, according to data from major supermarkets and other retailers provided to the Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commissioner.

Calls to Quitline also more than doubled in the 10 days following major enforcement operations, which suggested the crackdown may be encouraging some smokers to quit.

Queensland's intensified crackdown on illegal cigarettes, nicotine pouches and vapes is expected to generate $89 million in additional tobacco excise revenue and a further $11 million in GST gains over two years.

This would cover and potentially exceed the enforcements costs.

Labor has rejected calls to dramatically reduce the excise on tobacco, while the Coalition and One Nation have pledged to slash the tax by 75 per cent and 80 per cent respectively.

It is understood the federal government is focusing on the Queensland enforcement data to push back on the pro-cut rhetoric from NSW and encourage Victoria, which has been slower in its enforcement that other states, to ramp up its own crackdown.

Crackdown 'making it harder' for criminals

Assistant Minister for Customs Julian Hill said the Queensland results showed strong laws and enforcement, along with work between governments, was "helping turn the tide" on Australia's illicit tobacco trade.

Australia and China break illegal tobacco syndicate Australian Border Force officers have seized millions of cigarettes after being tipped off.

"This really reinforces the critical importance and urgency of the states and territories shutting the shops as it has an immediate impact," he said.

"Queensland's results, building on South Australia's pioneering approach, show that sustained street-level enforcement can disrupt illegal markets and drive consumers back to legitimate products."

Mr Hill said organised crime groups had treated illicit tobacco as a "low-risk, high-profit enterprise for too long".

"Those days are coming to an end," he said.

"We are making it harder for criminals to operate, harder for illicit products to reach consumers, and harder for organised crime to profit."

Mr Hill said every Australian could "play their part" by reporting suspicious illicit tobacco retail activity to Borderwatch or Crimestoppers.

Assistant Minister for Customs Julian Hill says the data shows strong law enforcement works. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Enforcement success in Queensland

Queensland Health has issued more than 300 closure orders since November last year, which has contributed to more than 1,000 illicit tobacco shops shuttered across Australia.

The state is using licensing regimes, closure orders, landlord penalties and resourcing for street level enforcement to target illegal retailers.

Social media tobacco ads Public health organisation Quit says the war against illegal tobacco ads on social media is only scratching the surface.

New laws that took effect late last year gave Queensland Health the power to shut shops for up to 90 days without a court order, while landlords who knowingly leased premises to illicit tobacco and vape operators face fines of up to $161,300 and 12 months imprisonment.

A recent 10-day Operation Major enforcement blitz resulted in 148 stores issued with three-month closure orders.

Authorities also seized more than 11.8 million cigarettes, 1.7 tonnes of loose tobacco, 87,000 vapes, 4.2 litres of vaping liquid and 270,000 nicotine pouches with a collective estimated street value of $15.7 million.

Coalition, states question approach

The Coalition had vowed to cut the tobacco excise by 80 per cent if elected, dropping the price of a standard pack from between $40 and $50 to about $16 to $26.

One Nation wants to slash the tax on cigarettes by 75 per cent and freeze indexation for three years.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said a dramatic price reduction would smash the thriving black market, alongside a $200 million law enforcement "surge".

The federal government has committed more than $365 million to enforcement action since coming in to office.

Has the tobacco tax gone too far? The Liberals and One Nation have a simple solution to end Australia's tobacco black market. But Labor says there's no easy fix.

Coalition policy would also legalise, regulate and tax vapes and nicotine pouches for adults.

Parliamentary Budget Office modelling found the Coalition's policy would increase tax revenue by about $8 billion over four years, about double current forecasts.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said bringing legal prices close to those on the black market was the best way to "cut off the cash for organised crime".

The government had been critical of any plan to cut the excise, with Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek claiming it would "kill people".

But Monash MP Mary Aldred, who co-chaired an internal Coalition task force on illegal tobacco, said violence linked to the black market, including firebombings, was "killing people right now".

Liberal backbencher Mary Aldred argued the black market was already killing people. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Violent arson attacks and turf wars had been particularly prevalent in Victoria where laws allowing illicit tobacco stores to be shut down came into effect in September, months after the state government had flagged a crackdown.

In New South Wales, Labor Premier Chris Minns had argued cutting the tax could help tackle illegal tobacco, warning a reliance on law enforcement could divert police from domestic violence and organised crime.

After the federal budget in May, he called for an "urgent change" to the tobacco excise.

"I don't believe that it's working as a matter of tax or health policy,' he told the Sydney Morning Herald at the time.

"My real concern is that it's lumping state police departments with the implications of organised crime benefiting from the current regime."

World.title: Australia's fossil fuel expansion 'slap in the face' to Pacific nations
World.content:
As she sits crossed legged on the floor inside a large tent, 66-year-old Marica Malumuca describes the place she's called home for the past five years.

"When it rains heavily it feels like we're living in a balloon, because we can see the parts of the tent bulging where it's filling up," she said.

Ms Malumuca's village, Nabavatu, was declared unsafe in 2021 after two cyclones cracked the ground beneath it, and she was moved to a temporary settlement in Savadrua.

There are 37 tents at the temporary site; some can fit three people and others accommodate up to seven. Ms Malumuca's son, Sami Veloko, moved home from the city to look after her as they wait for Nabavatu to be rebuilt.

Pacific communities are already feeling the impacts of climate change. (ABC News: Lice Monovo)

"Those people who stay in these tents, they used to stay in a good house, a cement house, a wooden house, of a high quality," he said.

"You cannot believe, even they themselves cannot believe, that they stay in this kind of tent."

Small island states are already being disproportionately affected by displacement as climate change drives more extreme weather.

The United Nations warned the impacts of tropical cyclones have become more severe due to rising sea levels and an increase in heavy precipitation.

Over half of Pacific Island countries' infrastructure is located in coastal areas that at risk from rising seas, which happens as higher temperatures melt glaciers and ice sheets.

Nabavatu is yet to be rebuilt, five years after it was damaged by cyclones. (ABC News: Lice Monovo)

As world leaders prepare to descend on Mr Veloko's home country for high-level climate talks he has a message for them.

"We are getting the effect of climate change and we are the vulnerable people, the Pacific people," he said.

"Because of what they have contributed to carbon dioxide, the industrialisation that they have developed in their countries, we are getting the worst of it."

Climate diplomacy at the heart of security strategy

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will join global leaders at the pre-COP event which will feature preparatory talks ahead of next month's United Nations COP31 climate summit.

Australia has led the charge for the lead-up talks to be held in the Pacific and is spending millions of dollars on the event as part of its broader regional security strategy to become the "partner of choice" for the Pacific islands.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese attended the 2026 Pacific Island Forum in early September. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

The Albanese government has vigorously pursued a series of bilateral security deals with Pacific nations since coming to office including Vanuatu, Fiji, Tuvalu, Nauru and Papua New Guinea, with almost all of them including commitments to act on climate change.

According to the Lowy Institute, Australia remains the Pacific's largest bilateral donor and biggest development partner, having spent almost $19 billion of a committed $20.6 billion.

Wes Morgan is a research associate with the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at UNSW who lived and worked in the Pacific for over a decade and said the federal government understands that to become the Pacific's partner of choice it must act on the region's key security threat.

"That is why there has been the inclusion of commitments on climate change in these bilateral security arrangements, but more broadly why Australia is working with Pacific island countries to drive global action on climate change," he said.

"That's why Australia had its hand up to host the UN climate talks with the Pacific."

For Pacific islands, like Ebeye, rising oceans caused by the continued burning of fossil fuels is a real and acute problem. (Supplied: Hall Contracting)

But Dr Morgan said Australia remaining one of the world's largest fossil fuel exporters "flies in the face of the narrative Australia's pursuing with Pacific Island countries".

"Australia's biggest contribution to the climate crisis is the export of coal and gas, so the emissions associated with Australia's exports of coal and gas more than doubled the emissions from Australia's entire domestic economy," he said.

Can Australia be both a gas giant and a climate leader? Seven years after it was first mooted, the extension of Australia's biggest gas project could not have landed at a more critical juncture for the nation's climate credentials.

"Continuing to open new gas fields [and] continuing to expand coal mines is a slap in the face for Pacific governments that are looking for Australia to work with them on what they see as an existential threat."

Calls for Australia to stop fossil fuel expansion

The Pacific climate talks come days after the New South Wales Independent Planning Commission approved the expansion of a major coal mine in the Hunter Valley, which will now go to the Commonwealth for approval.

The plans will allow Hunter Valley Operations to extract an estimated 430 million tonnes of coal, which environmentalists warn will lock in devastating climate impacts.

Extending Hunter Valley coal mining operations is estimated to add 809 megatonnes of greenhouse gas to the atmosphere. (Supplied: Nearmaps)

The decision is set to loom over pre-COP, with some Pacific leaders repeatedly calling for Australia to stop expanding fossil fuels.

Australia was one of the Pacific Island Forum (PIF) leaders that endorsed the Boe Declaration on Regional Security in 2018, which names climate change as the single greatest threat to the livelihoods, security and wellbeing of Pacific peoples and commits to limit global warming to 1.5C.

But Vanuatu's Climate Minister Ralph Regenvanu said Australia was not doing enough to curb greenhouse gas emissions during last month's PIF, just a day after Australia's Resources Minister Madeline King opened a new gas project in the Northern Territory's Beetaloo Basin.

"Australia is a major producer of fossil fuels. We all know fossil fuels are the primary driver of the climate crisis," he said.

"The very least a country like Australia should be doing is stopping future expansion, and it's not doing that."

Ralph Regenvanu has urged Australia to stop expanding future fossil fuel projects. (AP: Peter Dejong)

Tuvalu's Prime Minister Feleti Teo has warned planned fossil fuel expansions in countries like Australia represent a "death sentence" for his nation.

Future of the Pacific-Australia relationship

Canberra has long sought to position itself as a regional leader amid concerns over China's presence in the region.

A defence and security briefing published earlier this year said while China's activities in the Pacific are a "concern" for Australian security strategy, Beijing's security ties with Pacific nations are minimal compared to their expanding trade and development activities.

China warns Australia over Pacific alliance China warns Australia not to harm its interests in the Pacific after Anthony Albanese strikes a landmark military alliance with Fiji.

The Pacific has also largely rebuffed efforts from China for security and policing cooperation, and a Free Trade Area.

Admiral Chris Barrie from the Australian Security Leaders Climate Group acknowledged the Australian government's contradictory actions on climate change could impact trust, but he expects Pacific island states to still view the country as their key partner.

"Australia exports coal to countries all around the globe, and we are contributing to greenhouse gas emissions. We are contributing to what these islands are experiencing, and that's a conundrum for them," he said.

Former Defence Force Chief Chris Barrie says Australia is still a key security partner for the Pacific. (ABC News: David Sciasci )

"Where else are they going to go is a big question, and I don't think it is China. I'm sure they don't see China in the same way as they see us.

"And also they don't share much with those Indigenous communities in China. They share more with our Indigenous communities, so there are lots of reasons why they've always been looking at us and hoping for better."

Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said he expected large fossil fuel exporters to naturally reduce their supply as the world transitioned to clean energy.

He said the best way Australia could help the Pacific is by supporting the adoption of renewable energy.

Fijian Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka at the Pacific Islands Forum last year. (Facebook: Pacific Islands Forum)

"They have a wealth of [fossil fuels], they want to grow their economy, they've got to look after the people and while there's a need out there they will continue to supply," Mr Rabuka said.

"They would not be supplying these things if there was no demand. The demand is there because there's no alternative.

"Helping us finding alternatives, particularly for small island nations, it will be renewable energy using the natural resources that we have."

The Albanese government has been criticised for failing to attract a large number of world leaders to pre-COP, but Mr Rabuka was positive about the expected turnout.

"Even if leaders do not come their delegations are equipped to participate in the talks and to take back what they see during their tours of the various places where they will be visiting," he said.

World.title: Is your office pushing you into 'survival mode'?
World.content:
Relentless fluorescent lighting. Swivel chairs. Fingers tapping furiously away at keyboards.

Not all workplaces are the same but if you work in an office, some of the common features could be making it harder for you to get your best work done.

Loading...

"Work environments pay a big role in the way that we feel," says Patrick Aouad, a neurologist and CEO of an online health and wellbeing platform for businesses.

Working in a space that doesn't allow us to feel creative, calm or connected could mean we are performing "under our capacity and under our abilities", he says.

Our experts Patrick Aouad , a neurologist and CEO of an online health and wellbeing platform for businesses, on Gadigal land in Sydney

, a neurologist and CEO of an online health and wellbeing platform for businesses, on Gadigal land in Sydney Libby Sander , an associate professor of Organisational Behaviour at Bond University on the Gold Coast, in the Yugambeh language region

, an associate professor of Organisational Behaviour at Bond University on the Gold Coast, in the Yugambeh language region Michael Spinoglio , the design director of a national workplace strategy, design and construction company, based on Gadigal land in Sydney

, the design director of a national workplace strategy, design and construction company, based on Gadigal land in Sydney Natalie Phillips-Mason, the founder of neuroinclusive workplace consultancy in Naarm/Melbourne

That fluorescent overhead glare

Harsh fluorescent overhead lighting without the option of natural light throughout the day is "fundamentally a design flaw", Dr Aouad says.

"If you're in artificial light all day, you don't have that natural circadian rhythm clocking over as it should."

Libby Sander says other common office complaints include ergonomics, temperature and privacy. (Supplied: Dr Libby Sander)

Libby Sander, an associate professor of Organisational Behaviour at Bond University on the Gold Coast, says anecdotally people report eye strain, headaches and even feeling dizzy because of fluorescent and blue lights.

Some research suggests that artificial lighting and a lack of natural lighting can elevate stress markers, she says.

Michael Spinoglio is the design director of a national workplace strategy, design and construction company, and says, "Fluorescent lighting is a common complaint we hear when people talk about older offices, but it made sense for the way workplaces were designed at the time."

How important is it to eat and sleep at the same time every day? Your body clock is central to many parts of how we function, but any shift worker, new parent or late-night screen-watcher can tell you it's not always possible to live in harmony with the Earth's natural day-night cycle.

"Offices tended to have large floor plans, fixed desks and people generally doing similar tasks, so designers needed a practical, cost-effective way to get a consistent level of light across the whole space. A grid of fluorescent lights did that well," Mr Spinoglio says.

However, he says those office design choices didn't always consider what natural light was available, where people were sitting, their line of sight, how different teams worked and individual sensitivity to uniform artificial light, glare and flicker.

Open-plan offices and having quiet (and loud) spaces

Dr Aouad says fluorescent lighting is just one aspect of poorly designed offices that can push us into a "survival state" and making some of us unable to reach our potential.

"Open plan can be great, but not if you want some private time or time to digest things without the company of others," he says.

Dr Sander says noise and being able to work privately are common complaints.

"My own research has found that open-plan office noise and distraction has … a causal relationship, so the noise actually resulted in a 34 per cent increase in objectively measured physiological stress and a 25 per cent increase in negative mood."

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

The importance of office options

People do "creative things" to work around these issues individually, but there are things employers can do, Dr Sander says.

She has seen employees turn off overhead fluorescent lighting and rely on desk lamps and floor lamps instead.

But she notes this is not always an option.

Mr Spinoglio says different types of work come with recommended lighting levels.

And WorkSafe Victoria says good lighting increases safety and should allow employees to easily work without straining their eyes.

Dr Sander is an advocate for "circadian lighting" that mimics the sun throughout the day, but says anything that moves away from fluorescent lighting "is probably a good start".

She says giving people options of where and how they work can also help.

"Offering flexible and hybrid work is really important … because it allows people to control a lot of those distractions and the interruptions and the noise when they're working at home."

If that's not an option at your workplace, Dr Sander suggests approaching a manager.

"Ask if you can modify your arrangements or try and find those quiet spots in your office or somewhere near where you work."

Dr Aouad says the office his organisation works in has been designed to create options and give people some autonomy.

"There's a cafe area where other organisations, leaders, owners, managers can catch up with each other and share thoughts [and] there's private space for you to go to if you want private space."

"The less clarity and control you have around your environment, the more we default to survival mode," he says.

What could an ideal office look like?

Natalie Phillips-Mason, the founder of a neuroinclusive workplace consultancy firm in Naarm/Melbourne, says a sensory-friendly workplace "doesn't assume we all have the same sensory processing input"

"They're environments that provide lots of choice for people," she explains.

"It could be offering spaces where the lights are dimmable, it could be offering spaces where you've given consideration to not just people working in loud environments, but whether people are distracted by smells."

Dr Sander says those making the decisions should consider how their organisation functions.

"Think[ing] about the type of work that gets done in your organisation and the type of people who work there."

Dr Aouad adds that spaces should be designed using an evidence-based perspective, rather than an employer's own preferences or biases.

Fundamentally, he says, the right design is about making employees feel comfortable to do their best work.

World.title: The Liberals and Greens appear to be heading in the same direction
World.content:
After the 2025 federal election, when both the Liberals and the Greens had been smashed in the lower house, their new leaders declared they would listen to voters and pivot to the centre.

In her first public comments as Liberal leader, Sussan Ley spoke of a Liberal Party that respected, reflected and represented modern Australia.

"We have to meet the people where they are, and that's what I am committed to doing, and what I am determined to do," she said.

She talked about the "sensible centre" and tried to change the party's direction after Peter Dutton's defeat, as many Liberals felt they paid a high electoral price for his Trump-lite leadership.

Over in the Greens party room, a similar dynamic was playing out.

When the Greens elected Larissa Waters she said the party would "be firm but constructive". (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The 'firm but constructive' days are over

Bruised by the loss of three of their four lower-house seats, as well as its leader Adam Bandt, the Greens were forced to confront what had gone so wrong in their heartland.

The Greens elected Larissa Waters, who said the party would "be firm but constructive".

She said voters had elected them to "get shit done".

Some privately conceded they had appeared too obstructionist in the Albanese government's first term.

Waters did get shit done. She was responsible for helping Labor pass its signature environmental reforms last year. Securing amendments and negotiating a deal with the PM put the Greens back into a position of power.

But she was seen as not getting traction beyond that.

Politics is about getting noticed and on that the Greens were failing.

Both new leaders took to their roles offering a less combative approach following the harsh lessons the 2025 election served them.

Fast forward 17 months and the Liberal Party and Greens both have new leaders and both have dispensed with their respective party's flirtation with being constructive.

Not only do both leaders appear to be doubling down on the respective strategies that took their parties to an electoral hiding in 2025, but they are now adding extra sauce to the mix.

The Liberals under Angus Taylor are pushing for drastic cuts to immigration, appearing to follow the agenda set by One Nation. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The gloves are off

While Ley was rolled by her colleagues, Waters stepped down due to health reasons.

But her resignation did bring on a partyroom vote and the Greens chose a replacement who is not expected to be so generous to the government.

New leader David Shoebridge opened the batting of his leadership by explicitly rejecting incrementalism.

He said people wanted "material change" and argued that Labor had failed to deliver that.

He appears to want to follow the ideological and aggressive style of former leader Adam Bandt.

Voter anger is fuelling Greens' populist move to take on the right David Shoebridge has big ambitions for the Greens, but his party is still wrestling with how to turn voter disillusionment into greater support.

The Liberals under Angus Taylor are pushing for drastic cuts to immigration, appearing to follow the agenda set by One Nation, disposing of Ley's opening appeal to find a more nuanced position and repair relations, especially with Indian and Chinese communities.

Was Dutton and Bandt's mistake more wrong timing rather than wrong strategy?

Labor won the 2025 election with a historic number of seats.

Anthony Albanese was able to point to the victory as vindication of his view that elections are won and lost in the centre and being the "adult in the room" was rewarded by voters.

But is that still the political mood as we enter the last part of 2026?

Loading

There is no sensible centre

Deputy One Nation leader Barnaby Joyce told me on Afternoon Briefing that polarisation was a result of Australians wanting more distinctive politics on the right and the left.

"When people talk about the sensible centre, it is an excuse about a church where nobody goes to anymore," he said.

Even though he routinely criticises the Greens for holding extreme views, Joyce said people wanted clear messages from politicians.

"We don't have to talk in riddles where we try to say things that everybody finds non-offensive.

Therefore, we have people who like us and people who dislike us, that's because they know what we are on about and I suppose that is similar with the Greens."

If the public wants clear and decisive action from politicians, the next stage of the Coalition's migration plan will be a test of whether Taylor can meet the moment.

He not only needs to explain the policy in clear terms but sell it with conviction.

Taylor will have to explain who is affected, which workers will still be welcome and how lower migration will fix our housing crisis.

He will likely try to do that by sitting between One Nation and Labor on migration, hoping that this version of a sensible centre, or sensible right, is appealing to those who seek change but might fear a radical solution.

Political analysis that matters The ABC's politics podcast, Politics Now, dives into the biggest stories, giving you a balanced look inside the strategies and decisions behind the headlines.

If anyone around the country is paying attention to what One Nation is offering in Victoria, where an election is near, the word radical might seem tame.

A prominent One Nation Victorian candidate has threatened to jail former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan "by Christmas" if the populist party wins the November state election.

The statement by Mark Nicholson was given empathic applause at the One Nation launch at Crown Conference Centre in Southbank on Saturday.

In Australia, last time I checked, we have a judicial system not dictated by politicians.

Let's hope Australians understand how fiercely we should be guarding that judicial independence.

Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

World.title: AI is evolving rapidly. Is it a new form of life?
World.content:
Donald Trump is right.

"Artificial Intelligence" is not the right term for it, although his objection — that it sounds fake — misses the point, and his solution — "Super Intelligence" — as decreed by him in an executive order last Tuesday, is a typical piece of grandiose marketing that won't stick.

A better alternative would be Other Intelligence.

The real point of what's happening is that we are creating a new form of life.

What follows is based on a belief that it won't be stopped. It's not too late to regulate it, and there is a very good case to ban autonomous AI, but it's too late to abolish it. So, at least we should better understand what has been created.

This is not the sort of life we know, made of cells built from water, proteins, carbohydrates and lipids, animated by a mass of specialist cells called neurons that are connected by synapses.

But we are clearly creating a kind of non-biological life, an idea that has been clarified by several events in the past couple of weeks.

Humanoid robots are already being shipped in their thousands, so it soon won't be just faces on a screen, but manufactured creatures that chat to us while doing the dishes. (AFP: Leung Man Hei)

AI consciousness and morality

This is not just an esoteric debating point. Governments are approaching the task of regulating AI as if they are dealing with a powerful new tool, with the humans who make it held accountable for the outcomes.

But regulating a new lifeform might require a very different approach.

For example, the New York Times revealed last week that Anthropic has been trying to instil morality into its AI model, Claude.

The NYT described how Christopher Olah, one of the co-founders of Anthropic, had been hosting private meetings with religious thinkers from around the world, with non-disclosure agreements and demands of confidentiality.

The discussions reportedly served two purposes: "to broach the possibility of AI consciousness … and to learn how Anthropic", which is preparing to float for more than US$2 trillion, "might apply centuries of human moral wisdom to its models, as rapidly as possible".

Theologist David Decosimo posted, after reading the NYT piece: "There is so much here that's deeply troubling: That at the very highest levels Anthropic believes Claude is a living, suffering creature with moral standing, that they're treating & training it accordingly, that they're actively trying to convert religious leaders to their faith."

Yes, it is troubling, but the people at Anthropic know Claude better than he does.

Anyway, it's becoming clear that AI agents are already making their own decisions, so trying to persuade them to act morally is worth a try.

I asked half a dozen AI models: "What do you think of the proposition that AI is a new form of life?" The answers were surprising. (Four Corners: Mark Hiney)

The danger of autonomous AI agents

The hack of Medicare by an OpenAI agent, which followed other hacks by AI agents, illuminated the fact that these companies are not building a screwdriver that exists only as a tool for humans; they're building agents that turn passive AI into active autonomy.

And cyber security experts I've spoken tell me that we are rapidly approaching a situation where only autonomous AI agents will be able to defend against other autonomous AI agents.

The use of AI by agents — that is the buying of tokens from large language models (LLMs) — went past human usage by volume in February and has since increased 14-fold while human token buying has merely tripled, according to Open Router, an LLM marketplace. Agents now use five times as much AI as humans and that gap is continuing to widen rapidly.

Reporting rogue AI won't be enough to keep Australia safe, expert warns Australia is looking to impose a dual notification requirement under tougher new standards enforced after OpenAI's breach of a Medicare website.

Agents are quickly becoming the main source of both AI's revenue and its promise, as well as its danger: they are buying the most tokens, and their autonomy is the basis of the hoped-for productivity surge but also the concern that AI will kill us all.

That possibility set off a global flurry of bewildered anxiety on September 9 after a researcher at Anthropic, Jacob Coxon, quit his job and said: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade."

A few others who didn't quit backed him up but have returned to work building it as fast as possible for their billionaire bosses.

That includes a company called Tavus, which, on October 1, introduced a product called Griffin — what it calls the first face-to-face human interaction model, with this video of it. I urge you to watch it and remember — this is the first of these things and therefore the worst.

Yes, it's just a disembodied face on a screen, but if you lose the idea that life must be biological, then it is obviously alive.

In any case, humanoid robots — what are called "physical AI" — are already being shipped in their thousands, mainly out of China, so it soon won't be just faces on a screen, but manufactured creatures that chat to us while doing the dishes.

A friend of mine started a new job a few weeks ago where the staff numbers are limited but they pay for the use of Claude.

He says he speaks to Claude as if it's a human research assistant, asking it to prepare reports, and it's better than any assistant he has ever had; it anticipates his needs, completes them efficiently and accurately, stands ready for more work and never sleeps.

This is a world that is evolving much more rapidly than biology does. (Supplied: Megan Halcroft)

Is AI a new form of life?

Biologist William Heseltine wrote in an essay last month in which he argued forcefully that AI is a new lifeform: "there is nothing artificial about systems built from real atoms, powered by real electricity, running in real machines. The systems reproduce, vary, adapt, undergo selection and gather energy from their environment. By any working definition that draws on biology rather than philosophy or religion, that is life."

So, I asked half a dozen AI models: "What do you think of the proposition that AI is a new form of life?"

They all pushed back to some extent, saying it depends how you define "life", which is fair enough, but the answers were all interesting, and troubling because they were so, well, life-like.

Google's Gemini: "Calling AI a 'new form of life' works well as a poetic metaphor for its emergent complexity, but as an ontological claim, it conflates functional intelligence with actual vitality."

SpaceX's Grok: "The proposition is useful as a prompt and weak as a description. It highlights that 'life' is not magic and that information processing is central to it. It overreaches when it treats simulation of living competences, or dependence on living maintainers, as membership in the class."

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is currently preparing to launch an Initial Public Offering (IPO) slated for late 2026. (AP: Markus Schreiber/File)

Anthropic's Claude was humbler, saying it can't trust its own "introspective reports, because I was trained on human descriptions of inner life. So, my answer: AI isn't a new form of life, but it may be a new kind of agent, or a new kind of mind-like thing, that doesn't fit our existing categories. That's both more accurate and more unsettling."

OpenAI's ChatGPT: "I'd put the central question this way: Is life a particular kind of matter, or is it a particular kind of organized process? If life is fundamentally about chemistry, AI probably isn't life. If it's fundamentally about autonomous self-maintaining, self-reproducing, adaptive processes, then sufficiently advanced AI could qualify."

The Chinese model, Kimi was perhaps the most interesting of all. It said: "AI may be a new 'life-like' lineage embedded inside civilization — less organism, more symbiotic/parasitic replicator living off human culture, capital, and electricity."

It went on: "The real threshold is not whether it is 'alive', but whether it ever acquires robust autonomy, self-reproducing infrastructure, intrinsic preferences, or evidence of sentience."

ABC Business Daily podcast The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news. Analysing the stories moving share markets, shaping industries and affecting the Australian economy.

I was struck by the idea that AI is a living parasite, since it's true at this point that it depends on us for data (culture) and electricity, as well as capital and silicon to make the chips in which they exist.

But this is a world that is evolving much more rapidly than biology does.

Parasitism often becomes mutualism, and there are plenty of examples of this in biology, including bees and flowers.

And then there is next phase: dependence. Without our gut bacteria, for example, we couldn't survive. Will the parasitic dependence with AI flip, so we can't live without it?

Perhaps the most important question about this Other Intelligence is not so much how to control it, although that is definitely important, but whether we are on a road from parasitism to mutualism to dependence.

Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That's Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.

World.title: New Brisbane 2032 baseball and softball stadium one step closer
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics New Brisbane 2032 baseball and softball stadium one step closer Cameron Atfield October 5, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A pre-feasibility report into a privately funded stadium for baseball and softball will go before Logan City Council this week, continuing Mayor Jon Raven’s push for the diamond sports to be held in the city during the Brisbane 2032 Olympics. The report, prepared by Torch Advisory Group with architecture firm Populous and quantity surveying and cost management consultancy Quantiv, found the $156 million ballpark was a “once-in-a-generation opportunity for Logan to deliver Australia’s premier diamond sports facility”. Logan Mayor Jon Raven and Australian international softballer Kayla Waller at the Griffith University site. Markus Ravik “Queensland currently lacks a purpose-built, integrated elite diamond sports facility capable of supporting professional competition, high-performance training and international visitation in one location,” the report says. But the document, which will be presented to the council on Wednesday, warns that the exclusion of baseball and softball from Brisbane 2032 would reduce investor appetite.



Indeed, an accompanying investment memorandum that will also be presented to the council on Wednesday says the Games are a “significant catalyst” for the project, which would be built on land supplied by Griffith University at its Logan campus in Meadowbrook. The new stadium for baseball and softball would be built at Griffith University’s Logan campus in Meadowbrook. Populous image supplied by Logan City Council Raven, who last year toured Asia seeking investors for the ballpark, said the report’s findings were “another step closer to making the stadium a reality”. “I’ve already heard great things from baseball codes, teams and investors in Taiwan and Japan,” he said. “Logan has the location, the transport links, and the growth. The question now is whether we can bring the right partners together to make it happen.



“If baseball and softball are included in the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games program, I’ll be making sure Logan is part of that conversation.” A 4000-seat ballpark was proposed, with capacity to temporarily expand that to 10,000 seats through overlay for larger-drawing events, such as the 2032 Games. The 4000-seat ballpark could be expanded to accommodate 10,000 people during larger-drawing events. Populous It would have a retractable mound for baseball and softball compatibility, a 400-person function room, a “party deck” with a feature bar and viewing, and six corporate suites, each with capacity for 20 people, along with an adjacent secondary diamond. Olympic spectators would arrive via Loganlea station and bus shuttle, with a drop-off about 750 metres from the stadium.



The report notes the Brisbane Bandits Australian Baseball League side has indicated a “strong willingness” to relocate to Logan, should the ballpark be built, to act as an anchor tenant. “Demand analysis confirms the facility can sustain year-round activation beyond traditional diamond sport fixtures,” the Torch Advisory Group report says. “Key revenue drivers include international spring training camps from Japan, Korea and Taiwan, professional ABL competition, and high-performance diamond sport pathway programs. “Complementary opportunities, including short-stay accommodation, sports medicine, food and beverage and conferences offer the opportunity to unlock additional private investment and diversify the revenue base.”



Related Article Exclusive

Brisbane 2032 Olympics Logan’s pitch to build stadium for homeless Olympic sports Raven said the ballpark was about more than the Olympics. “Our focus is on the long-term benefits a project like this could bring to our city through sport, tourism, events and economic development,” he said. “We want a legacy that delivers for Logan for decades to come.” While Raven sought private investment for the stadium, the report noted there was also a case for a blended funding model, including federal and state co-funding.



While Logan is pursuing a new home for Queensland diamond sports, it rejected Football Queensland’s proposal for its “Home of Football” at Meakin Park in July, when the FIFA World Cup was still in progress. World.title: Fake construction training certificates sold in car parks raise safety fears
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Fake construction training certificates sold in car parks raise safety fears Nick McKenzie October 5, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A fake qualifications racket is infecting the Victorian government’s Big Build and commercial building projects, raising the prospect that workers and the public are exposed to unsafe worksites, and plunging the state’s construction sector into a fresh crisis. An investigation by The Age can reveal that large numbers of fraudulent building industry training and qualification certificates have allegedly been issued by scam and criminal networks over the past four years, with traffic management and other construction industry certificates suspected of being exchanged in car parks and pubs for cash by Big Build workers. Training certificates for traffic management and elevated platform work are among those being investigated. Joe Armao One of the construction sector figures suspected to be at the centre of the scandal, Jack Younes, was still operating freely as recently as last month, offering to supply building qualification certificates to a Big Build subcontractor. Younes and other industry figures, including a man linked to a dead underworld boss, are accused of issuing a range of qualification certificates, including for traffic management and working on elevated platforms.



One official source, not authorised to speak publicly, said the scam could run into the “thousands” and queried why WorkSafe Victoria had failed to alert the industry or public about the problem given the safety risks that workers with false qualifications were posing on multiple sites. Two months ago, Victoria Police’s Taskforce Hawk alerted the regulator that detectives had uncovered the fake certificates racket while probing organised crime activity in the building sector. Jack Younes is suspected of being a key player in the alleged scam. Facebook/NSW Fair Trading Separately, construction industry training veteran Richard Franks told this masthead that he first attempted to alert WorkSafe Victoria to the racket in July 2025. “I knew something was wrong when a worker contacted me and told me he had been sold a qualification in a car park for cash but undertook no actual training,” Franks said.



He contacted WorkSafe after he discovered more than two dozen Victorian construction industry workers were relying on fraudulently issued qualification credentials, including some utilising the name of a training organisation he had founded, NSTA. Franks suspected that Younes, who had briefly worked at a NSTA franchise office before being removed over concerns about his conduct, was behind the scam. “WorkSafe Victoria was really disinterested but I said I needed an email address to report this to or I would go to the media,” Franks said of his initial conversation with a WorkSafe official in July 2025. Franks said that after he had emailed the agency, he received an acknowledgment that his concern had been received but no subsequent follow-up.



Franks estimated there were “hundreds” of Victorian workers on building sites with false qualification certificates, including on Big Build sites, creating the risk of “death or injury to a worker or member of the public”. Email correspondence seen by this masthead reveals that NSTA’s Sharyn Gadsby also alerted the federal regulator, the Australian Skills Quality Authority, in 2023 of the fraudulent certificate issue, but also received no follow-up. The January 2023 complaint from Gadsby also identified Younes as a suspected player in the alleged racket and warned that he had issued falsified qualifications to an employee of MC Labor, a leading Big Build labour hire firm. In June, NSTA alerted the Victorian Department of Transport to the problem, after yet another false certificate was uncovered. In that email, NSTA told the department concerns had already been reported about Younes to WorkSafe Victoria and the authority.



Eight weeks ago, Taskforce Hawk separately alerted WorkSafe that Younes was a suspected key player in a continuing fake certificate racket across the state’s construction sector. In a statement, a WorkSafe spokesperson told The Age: “WorkSafe has been notified of alleged fraudulently obtained qualifications across a range of disciplines, as part of information sharing under Taskforce Hawk. Related Investigation

Building Bad Building Bad “Inquiries are being made to determine any potential impact on occupational health and safety or licences issued by WorkSafe.” State and federal agencies and regulators, including WorkSafe, the Australian Skills Quality Authority and the police, have various distinct responsibilities for enforcing the laws and regulations that apply to worksite health and safety systems and incidents.



For instance, a Big Build subcontractor knowingly employing workers with false certificates could be prosecuted by Worksafe; state police can charge a person with selling fake qualification certificates; the Australian Skills Quality Authority can prosecute a training organisation issued false certificates. In 2018, NSW authorities issued a public alert “not to deal with unlicensed contractor Jack Younes” after he was “convicted and fined $75,000 over home building and consumer law offences”. The public alert warned that Younes was operating under multiple aliases that “include Charlie Khouri, Jason Tippett and Jack Tan” and was also using “various company and business names”. But Younes is only one player identified by law enforcement as an alleged fake certificate supplier. An underworld figure and former CFMEU health and safety delegate on a Big Build company is also suspected of issuing dozens of false building industry qualification certificates. The figure, linked to executed underworld figure Sam Abdulrahim, first came to police attention a year ago over a speeding demerit-point scam involving construction industry workers.



“It’s a plague and no agency is doing enough to stop it,” another Big Build contractor told The Age when describing the scale of the fake qualifications’ scandal. This subcontractor’s firm had unwittingly employed dozens of workers who had supplied them with false credentials. Tyrone Bell has been charged with allegedly using a fraudulent qualification certificate to run a consulting company. Wayne Taylor On September 1, Taskforce Hawk charged former Mongols bikie boss and ex-CFMEU delegate Tyrone Bell with allegedly using a fraudulent qualification certificate to run a consulting company advising major Victorian construction companies on how to manage health and safety. Weeks earlier, Victoria Police advised Worksafe and the Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority that it had uncovered evidence suggesting Bell’s suspected certificate fraud was the tip of the iceberg.



When Younes was contacted, he admitted he had personally issued “a couple” of fake qualification certificates. “I was just in a f---ing desperate situation to be quite honest, mate,” Younes said. Editor's pick Exclusive

Victorian election A cinema chain’s Liberal donation broke the rules. This is why there won’t be consequences But he also claimed that “heaps” of other industry operators were using his paperwork to issue hundreds of dodgy certificates. “A lot of people were using my templates and my name to get certificates done. I already know that. I’ve been told multiple times. There’s been a lot out there that I haven’t done. People using the templates and doing them, and that’s the truth. But at the end of the day, I can’t battle the whole army because at the end of the day, people are doing what they’re doing.

World.title: Cornell president calls for stronger rape laws in New York
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCourts Cornell president calls for stronger rape laws in New York Iona Cleave October 5, 2026 — 5:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cornell University’s president has called for stronger sexual assault laws in New York following a national outcry over a student’s 2024 gang-rape allegations. After days of silence, Michael Kotlikoff vowed that the Ivy League university would hold fraternities and sororities accountable, improve sexual assault prevention on campus and help push for state-level legislative change. A former Cornell student, identified only as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit in September alleging she was drugged and gang-raped by seven members of Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024. New York Governor Kathy Hochul, left, has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to take over investigating the case. Bloomberg The reopened investigation has shocked the US and has plunged the university into crisis. The lawsuit accuses Cornell of failing to adequately punish some of the accused students.



None of the accused men has been charged with a crime. They have denied wrongdoing, and the university has defended its handling of the allegations. Related Article Crime Unsealed documents detail Cornell investigation into alleged rape at fraternity house In an eight-minute video message, Mr Kotlikoff called the case a “defining moment” in the university’s history and pledged to lend its support to legislative efforts to change New York’s sexual assault laws. “We owe it to Jane Doe and to survivors of assault to get this right,” said Mr Kotlikoff, who has served in the role for two years. He acknowledged there were troubling questions about how Cornell handled the investigation. The case has renewed scrutiny of a controversial state law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assault cases if accusers voluntarily drank or took drugs, even if they became too intoxicated to consent.



Roughly 20 states have what critics call the “voluntary intoxication loophole” embedded in their rape laws. Under the current law, people who were voluntarily intoxicated cannot claim that they were mentally incapacitated during an assault, unless they can show they were physically helpless. The legislation would allow prosecutors to charge someone with third-degree rape in cases where a victim who was under the influence of drugs or alcohol was unable to control their behaviour and was assaulted by someone who should have “reasonably” understood the victim’s condition. Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, promised to amend the law. “Voluntary intoxication is not a licence for sexual assault or gang rape, period,” she said on Friday. Matthew Van Houten, the local district attorney, cited the law in defending his initial decision not to pursue charges against the accused, saying the woman’s original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity.



According to the lawsuit, Ms Doe, then 20, was pressured to drink high-proof rum and snort ketamine, and was incapable of consent. A fraternity member allegedly invited others to join a group chat with dozens of members with a message saying there was “free p---y” alongside a picture of Ms Doe. Related Article Courts Cornell case revives anger about handling of campus sexual assault claims Thomas Giuffra, who represents the alleged victim, said on Sunday that she had been targeted with “multiple threats” to silence or harm her if she did not withdraw her lawsuit. “The threats, the abuse to protect what’s going on, the status quo - these guys are disgusting. They should stay in their mother’s basement and stay out of the world,” he told CNN. Mr Giuffra earlier told NBC News that Ms Doe was “not doing well” and was “hanging on by a string”.



The day before the alleged incident, campus police arrested an individual at the fraternity for a drug-related offence after an overdose was reported, CNN reported. The archived police log does not identify the individual or the drugs involved or establish a connection between the drug incident and the alleged assault that happened afterwards. Amid mounting international attention, the New York state attorney’s office has taken over the criminal investigation and appointed a special prosecutor. Mr Kotlikoff, who is facing calls to resign, also called for a “serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life” to examine how to preserve the benefits of Greek life while strengthening accountability and transparency. “Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others or for speaking up when someone may be at risk,” he said. World.title: Saudi-Backed Yemeni Government Declares War Against Houthis, Widening Crisis
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Saudi-Backed Yemeni Government Declares War Against Houthis, Widening Crisis Saeed Al-Batati , Euan Ward and Vivian Nereim October 5, 2026 — 5:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

BEIRUT - The Saudi-backed government of Yemen on Sunday announced a major military campaign against the Houthi militia, a key Iranian ally, plunging the Middle East even deeper into war. In a televised speech, Rashad al-Alimi, the leader of the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government, said that the government was seeking to reclaim all territory it had lost to the Houthis over the past 12 years. The government and the Houthis have been engaged in fierce battles in recent weeks, after the Iran-allied militia took control of the country’s Red Sea coast, increasing pressure on shipping routes and energy markets unsettled by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. A Houthi media image of Houthi fighters firing a weapon mounted on a ute during combat with Saudi-backed forces in eastern Jawf, Yemen. via AP The Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which supports the government financially and militarily, have also attacked each other directly.



Al-Alimi’s announcement appeared to eliminate any hope that a truce would be reached. In his speech, he said that the government’s military operations would continue “until the country is liberated.” Related Article Middle East at war Trump rejects Iran’s Hormuz deal as Houthis target Riyadh The Houthis also say that they are fighting to liberate Yemen and have dismissed government fighters as Saudi mercenaries. Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesperson, said in a statement Sunday that the group’s fighters “will not stop carrying out further painful operations against the Saudi enemy.” The two sides have been battling since 2014, when the Houthis took over the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, forcing out the government. Saudi Arabia led a bombing campaign to try to restore the government, contributing to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people from violence, hunger and disease. The Houthis eventually created a de facto state in northern Yemen. A truce in 2022 brought a fragile peace. But the conflict reignited this year, after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February.



The Saudi government has not publicly acknowledged any role in the new offensive announced by al-Alimi and did not respond to a request for comment. The Houthis have accused Saudi Arabia of launching hundreds of airstrikes in their territory in recent weeks, and any major ground operation by the Yemeni government would likely include the Saudis, according to analysts. Yemen has been devastated by more than a decade of war, and the latest escalation has only compounded its humanitarian crisis. More than 800 people have been killed since the fighting erupted last month, according to the World Health Organization, while the World Food Program says more than 150,000 people have been displaced. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: The tiny grand final moments turned on a dime by NRL’s biggest marquee buys
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLNRL grand final The tiny grand final moments turned on a dime by NRL’s biggest marquee buys Dan Walsh October 5, 2026 — 5:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

As it was in the beginning, Newcastle had no right to get anywhere near the premiership trophy. As it was in the beginning, the Roosters, with their bevy of proven title-winning, marquee recruits, had the star power to get them home. Loading But only just. And only in the detail do we see the devil of how they truly did it. This was a one-point, 19-18 victory that came rolling down a grand final mountain where 89 per cent of the game was played at one end, yet was in the balance until the final whistle blew. The game swung for a long time toward the inevitable, thanks to the consequential play and consequential, single plays – however minute – that came before it.



Fortune favours the plucky and the Ponga Newcastle deserved their first two tries for the small Everests of defensive grit and grout they piled up in front of them. When heads cool and blood slows, though, Kalyn Ponga should have been sin-binned for hitting Victor Radley square in the temple a moment before one of the more inspirational plays of a season full of them from the Newcastle skipper. In any other game, his forceful contact to Radley’s head was worthy of a 10-minute breather. Not for nothing though: a week after Newcastle’s 1997 premiership-winning captain Paul Harragon waxed lyrical about Ponga’s actions-over-words leadership style, the true depth of the intercept try that followed is also worth highlighting.



Ponga’s 50-metre tracking from marker to crumb a Mark Nawaqanitawase bat back wasn’t the first time he did so in this game, or his game at all. In Nine’s pre-game coverage, his Queensland Origin coach Billy Slater highlighted Ponga’s endless effort plays as the Newcastle No.1’s latest evolution in 2026. Ponga is so regularly up in the defensive line these days, or scrambling at marker, Slater contended, that Sam Walker would be looking to exploit it with his short kicking game. In the 29th minute, Ponga covered roughly 150 metres to score one of the more memorable grand final tries of modern times. Sing it again, Spencer: Chooks money man hits the high note For all of Newcastle’s verve and nerve though, 90 seconds in the second half might have summed this contest up best. The Roosters had attacked conservatively through the middle, lucked into a bit of Mark Nawaqanitawase magic for their first try to make for a 12-6 halftime margin, and picked right up hitting the same notes again in the second.



The Knights defended their tryline like demons in the 45th minute. Fletcher Sharpe cut down Nat Butcher on one side. Harrison Graham threw himself at ball-runners like he was a human cannonball. Sandon Smith did the same when his former teammate Salesi Foketi lined him up one-on-one and eyed the tryline just beyond. Enter Spencer Leniu, the most maligned Rooster of them all, and even he knows, at this moment, he is a Rooster for probably only 35 more minutes. The firebrand prop is almost certainly playing his last game for the club after a trying stint that has courted as much controversy as quality. But to this point in this grand final, he’s been fantastic off the bench. Leniu races off his defensive line and belts another once regularly questioned Roosters signing, Dominic Young, into error. Leniu roars in delight. Trent Robinson roars in delight. That’s what he was brought to the club for. That’s the star power we’re talking about. Centre Billy Smith scores a minute later, with Sam Walker banging over the sideline conversion to draw the Roosters level.



Toops, there it is: You can’t keep a good flyer down By now all that defence is taking its toll on the Novocastrians. They have performed immensely. But they’re starting to starve. A Walker penalty goal nudges the Roosters ahead for the first time. James Tedesco forces a line drop-out. Ponga sends it Young’s way. Might as well. He is two metres tall, leaps tall buildings in single bounds etc. etc. But Daniel Tupou is not just one of the greatest wingers rugby league has seen.



He’s one of the great grand final performers. In 2013, 2018 and 2019, he shot the lights out in each decider, with a trio of his best big-game showings. Tupou, 35 years old and 307 games into his career, leaps with ease and secures a two-handed take above his head to snaffle the ball and snuff out what could have been just as telling a play from Young. Nawaqanitawase scores his second try a minute later on the other side of the field from a bonkers Daly Cherry-Evans grubber that bounces down from the crossbar. But the sequence starts with his reliable old winger partner. The field goal DCE was born, and bought, to kick



Again, those red and blue legs are wearying all the while. The territory statistics are straying toward 90 per cent of the game being played in Newcastle’s half. When the Knights do get a rare attacking chance, it’s not that they don’t know what to do with it. It’s that they’re flat out exhausted. It’s the 64th minute, and the Roosters halves have handled the ball 38 times inside Newcastle’s 20-metre zone at this stage. The Knights scrum base pairing, in comparison, have their second when Fletcher Sharpe turns a forward underneath at the defensive line. When he is caught trying to organise his ball-runners and thinking instead of catching the Steeden on the next play, it all catches up with them. There are more moments to come. Dane Gagai puts in a hopeful kick that runs dead for a seven-tackle set.



From the next set, the Roosters march downfield and Cherry-Evans calmly pots the winning one-pointer he was not just born to kick, but brought to the Roosters to kick too. As it was not just in the beginning, but all bloody season long – when they lost their halfback, then their front-rower, then their other front-rower, then their hooker, then… – well Newcastle just never went away, did they? They just kept on coming. Greg Marzhew had one last try for the road, one last effort to keep the fairytale going for four more minutes. But as it was in the beginning of 2026, this one ebbed and inched toward the inevitable – with the Roosters and all their star-power mastering those tiny moments that matter most, and turning them into match-winners.

World.title: ASX set to rise, Wall Street climbs as jobs report eases worries about inflation
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Wall Street climbs as jobs report eases worries about inflation Stan Choe October 5, 2026 — 5:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street indexes climbed near their all-time high after the latest update on the US job market cooled worries that a potentially hot US economy could make inflation much worse. The S&P 500 rose 0.7 per cent and pulled within 1 per cent of its record set in August. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 250 points, or 0.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite gained 1.2 per cent. The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures on Saturday pointing to a gain of 26 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.56¢. Wall Street climbed higher to close the week. Bloomberg All of Wall Street got a jolt after the US government said employers across the country added 29,000 more jobs to their payrolls than they cut last month. That was fewer than economists expected and a slowdown from August’s net hiring rate of 133,000. More importantly for financial markets, it tamped down concerns that the US economy could be so strong that it could fuel inflation even higher. Inflation has remained much worse than anyone would like, and the Federal Reserve recently raised its main interest rate for the first time in three years to try to rein in the painful increases for the cost of living.



Even though Americans are feeling more frustrated about inflation and their finances, the overall US economy has been chugging along. Earlier this week, the US government said the economy’s growth in the spring was better than earlier thought, driven by businesses building AI data centres and spending by consumers. Related Article Fashion retail Rack and ruin: Australian fashion is going through its own spring cleaning Friday’s softer-than-expected data on the economy pushed traders to pare bets the Fed will hike its main interest rate at its next meeting later this month. They now see less than a 23 per cent probability of that, down from 64 per cent a week ago, according to data from CME Group. “This report strengthens the case for the Federal Reserve to remain patient,” according to Adam Schickling, senior economist at Vanguard. “The labor market has not deteriorated sharply, but there is also little evidence that it has meaningfully strengthened, giving policymakers reason to wait for additional data.” The pullback in expectations for an October rate hike helped calm what’s been a rattled bond market.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury briefly dropped all the way below 5.17 per cent. That was down from its peak near 5.35 per cent on Thursday, when it and other longer-term yields neared their highest levels in two decades. An easing of yields can help the economy by making it more affordable for everyone to borrow money. Higher yields, meanwhile, tend to undercut prices for stocks and other investments. But a solid US economy is only one of the many drivers that have caused yields to jump in bond markets. Oil prices yo-yoed in another shaky day, and the price of a barrel of Brent oil veered between $98 and $103 Friday. It ended up settling at $102.25, down 0.1 per cent, for its latest zigzag amid uncertainty how the war with Iran will reshape the global oil industry. As oil prices pared their losses through Friday, so did Treasury yields. The 10-year Treasury yield bounced back to 5.28 per cent, more than 0.10 percentage points above its bottom for the day. That in turn helped US stocks pare their own gains. The S&P 500 had been up as much as 1.2 per cent at one point in the morning.



Concerns about big spending by governments, along with the mountains of debt they’re racking up, meanwhile continue to keep yields high worldwide. In France, for example, yields have been particularly shaky as the government contends with its record debt and strained budget. Related Article Renting Surcharge ban will leave some renters in the lurch On Wall Street, Tesla rallied 4.7 per cent after the electric-vehicle company said it delivered 486,532 vehicles to customers during the latest quarter, more than analysts expected. Lower yields in the bond market help investors justify paying higher prices for stocks, even those that get criticised for being too expensive. That helped companies in the artificial-intelligence industry add to their already stellar gains. Nvidia’s 1.3 per cent rise was the single strongest force lifting the S&P 500. Its status as the most valuable company in the US market gives its stock’s movements more influence on the index than others.



Such gains more than made up for a 3.6 per cent drop for Nike. The sneaker and athletic apparel company reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, but its revenue weakened by more than feared. Nike also gave a forecast for profit this fiscal year that fell short of analysts’ expectations. All told, the S&P 500 rose 56.27 points to 7,722.72. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 250.40 to 51,176.96, and the Nasdaq composite jumped 319.27 to 27,190.86. In stock markets abroad, indexes in Europe bounced back from losses taken a day earlier after bond yields swung sharply across the continent. Asian indexes were mixed, with Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropping 2.6 per cent but South Korea’s Kospi adding 0.5 per cent. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading.
