World.title: AgriZero NZ gets funding boost of $117m, new partners come on board
World.content:
Government-industry partnership AgriZero NZ has received a big funding boost, to the tune of $117 million, with two new industry partners all coming aboard.

The new funding is equally split across industry and government, taking the total funds raised to $308 million.

Red meat processor and exporter Alliance and rural supplies co-op Farmlands have also joined the partnership, which alongside other industry investors - The a2 Milk Company, ANZ, ANZCO, ASB, BNZ, Fonterra, Rabobank, Ravensdown, Silver Fern Farms and Synlait, jointly owns half of AgriZero.

AgriZero board chairperson Rob Hewett said it reflected both the scale of the challenge and the sector's growing commitment to address it.

"Many of our major export customers expect progress on emissions reductions across their supply chains, through to New Zealand farms," he said.

"If we want to maintain New Zealand's competitive advantage and reputation as a trusted supplier of premium food products to discerning customers around the world, we'd be wise to listen to them.

"This is too big for any one organisation to solve alone, and the collaborative support behind AgriZero NZ shows our partners' determination to get on with the job."

Hewett said getting tools into farmers' hands was critical to this, adding there would be tools available by 2030.

"There should be one to two products each year becoming available between now and 2030.

"By 2030, I would expect the farmers will have five to six products to choose from, depending on their farming system."

The first AgriZeroNZ-backed tool likely to become available to farmers is a methane-inhibiting bolus developed by Kiwi company Ruminant Biotech, currently undergoing regulatory approval.

Hewett said some of the technologies might be 'stackable' offering greater emissions reductions and possibly even improved productivity on farm.

"We also want to have a portfolio of products so that farmers not only have choice for what's right for them but also potentially stack products on top of each other.

"We could conceivably have a seed treatment solution that means the grasses the animals consume produce less methane, eaten by an animal that may have a bolus or vaccine to reduce the methanogens in the rumen, which may well be wearing a wearable that can deal with nitrous oxide as well"

Hewett said the new partnerships would also help with supply chains and making these tools available to farmers.

AgriZero Chief Executive Wayne McNee said the additional funding would give it the capital to build on the momentum achieved so far.

"We're backing some of the world's best innovators and scientists and they need sustained support to get these new technologies through development, testing and approvals so farmers can trust they're proven, safe and effective.

"Not every technology we invest in will succeed, that's the reality of innovation.

"But we're optimistic that, with continued investment and focus, New Zealand farmers will have a range of tools to choose from by 2030."

World.title: Fijian PM Rabuka urges climate action as Pacific hosts pre-COP31 meeting
World.content:
Fiji's prime minister has called on global leaders coming to the country to see and listen to the people on the climate frontlines as the pre-COP31 meeting is gets underway on Monday.

Sitiveni Rabuka addressed an interfaith church service on Sunday ahead of the meeting this week.

He said climate finance must reach the communities that need it - "not someday, but now, and as an act of justice, not charity".

While Australia and the Pacific's joint bid to host COP31, the United Nations annual climate summit, lost out to Türkiye, it was agreed the Pacific would host the pre-COP meeting.

A leaders' event will also be held in Tuvalu.



The main COP gathering will be held in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November, with Australia serving as the president of negotiations.

The Fijian government said in a news release that regional leaders, ministers, diplomats, faith leaders, youth, civil society organisations, NGOs, community members and children gathered for the service on Sunday.

It said the prayers and performances reflected the realities of Pacific people already living with the increasing impacts of climate change.

World.title: Labour's fiscal plan: National's claims and how Labour is defending it
World.content:
National's Nicola Willis is on the attack over Labour's fiscal plan, labelling it fraudulent, and claiming some former Labour finance ministers would be ashamed and disappointed.

Labour says the plan it released on Sunday is responsible and pays for all its election promises.

Meanwhile, an economist says every party's plan will have holes and complicated trade-offs.

RNZ has laid out National's claims about the plan and how Labour has defended them.

No specific cost for restoring pay equity scheme

This is the biggest argument of them all.

Labour's fiscal plan does not specify the cost of restoring the full pay-equity legislation, which boosts pay for women who can prove they're underpaid compared to men. The coalition government has significantly pared back the scheme.

The plan does include $2.5b to give a $4/hour pay rise to 65,000 care and support workers, whose claim was axed, when the government pared back the scheme.

National says Treasury estimated restoring the scheme would cost $11 billion, leaving Labour $8.5b short.

Labour doesn't want to undermine negotiations by putting a number on it, but says it has enough headroom with $10.5b in unallocated funding.

Willis says that means pay equity would soak up most of Labour's unallocated funding for the next four Budgets, "which means nothing more for schools, police, prisons, defence and other frontline social services".

It is worth noting Willis has also not revealed how much she would set aside for settlements under the coalition's pared-back scheme.

She uses the same argument - not wanting to show her hand - but insists the costs are accounted for.

Fuel tax and the public transport fare cap

Willis says Labour has not included the cost of freezing fuel tax and road-user charges for three years, which she puts at $3.1b, nor its public transport fare-cap policy, which Labour previously indicated would cost $260 million.

It is true that they're not included as line items.

Labour says that's because they'll be paid from the National Land Transport Fund - revenue from petrol tax, road-user charges, registration and licensing, which pays for roads.

"The National Land Transport Fund is not generally part of fiscal plans that other political parties release," said finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds.

Labour says the fuel tax would use about 1 percent of the fund and Hipkins has previously said his government would "scale" NLTF investments to fit the funding available.

Willis says National fully costed its fuel-tax freeze in its 2023 fiscal plan.

Dividends of Future Fund companies

If elected, Labour will establish a Future Fund to invest in New Zealand businesses and infrastructure, seeded with the dividends of selected state-owned assets, and a $200 million Crown capital injection.

It refuses to say which assets would be included, citing commercial sensitivity and saying it must wait to be in government, because only then can it receive proper advice.

Willis argues Labour should have accounted for a $2.8b loss of dividends from companies included in the Future Fund, because that money would otherwise be invested into government services.

National assumes Labour will include the biggest dividend payers - Genesis, Mercury, Meridian, Air New Zealand and Transpower.

Edmonds says Labour would determine what goes into the fund when it's in government and account for any dividend impact then.

Health cost pressures and guaranteeing graduate nurses jobs

Labour's plan increases funding for health cost pressures, that is rising costs due to inflation and population changes, each year for three years - but not the fourth (2030/31).

Willis says that means it has left $1.5b unfunded. She promises National would deliver an uplift each year.

Hipkins says Labour's plan to give everyone three free GP visits would have a huge flow-on effect on health cost pressures.

"When you've got people in hospital emergency departments costing thousands of dollars a night to accommodate, because they couldn't afford to go and see their doctor, and get the medication they need to avoid ending up in hospital in the first place, that is a major easing of the pressure that our health system faces," he said.

Labour also guarantees every graduate nurse a job at a cost of $526 million.

National says Labour has not included that in its plan, but Labour is clear it would be paid for from health cost-pressure funding.

Willis says, if Labour did that, "every single other deliverable in the health service would be compromised", because cost-pressure funding was meant to keep hospital lights on, and keep up with an ageing and growing population.

'Here we go again' with fiscal hole debate

In many ways, Labour and the National-led coalition are largely on the same track.

The government's pre-election economic and fiscal update (Prefu) forecast a return to surplus by 2028/29 and shrinking spending as a share of GDP to 29.8 percent by 2031.

Labour has forecast the same return to surplus and plans to bring spending down to 30.4 percent of GDP.

The government's 2026 Budget included a $2.4b annual operating allowance, that is extra spending on new initiatives, and Labour is budgeting for the same.

Yet: "here we go again, we're going to go through a big debate about fiscal holes", independent economist Cameron Bagrie said.

"Realistically, it doesn't matter which political party you look at, there's going to be gaps, there's going to be challenges, there's going to be some pretty complicated trade-offs.

"You don't go from a big deficit to a big surplus and turn the debt curve down, unless you're driving some pretty hard levers."

Bagrie said voters had to consider a simple trade-off.

"What do you want? Do you want a well-functioning healthcare system and education system, and what are you prepared to pay in regard to tax for that on the other side, because there's no free lunch."

He addressed some of the major arguments between Labour and National.

On pay equity, he said no party would commit to pay-equity costs up front, "because then it becomes open season".

Bagrie also argued each offered insufficient funding for roads and were punting the problem by not hiking fuel taxes. Labour's freeze is for three years, National's is for one.

"No-one's prepared to take a stand and put the rates up, because, of course, it's election year," he said.

"All that's going to take place is that we're going to walk into reality in about 2028 and realise there's a gaping hole, and it doesn't matter which side of the political fence that you look at, but they're all pretty well the same."

World.title: Which political party would make you better off?
World.content:
Audio player for " Is a loan on my home the best way help my kids? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1735169%2Fwhich-political-party-would-make-you-better-off

Is a loan on my home the best way help my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 13m

Political parties have revealed policies over the past weeks that are likely to affect household budgets, should they take effect.

We've compared a few scenarios to show how that might look for different sections of society.

These are only for illustrative purposes.

Scenario 1: Retired couple

Freehold home: $2 million

Land value: $1.1 million

Other income: About $15,000 a year on top of NZ Super, in one person's name.

No children in their care

National

At the moment, this couple's basic financial position would be broadly unchanged under a future National government.

Finance Minister Nicola Willis has said National will campaign on some tax policies and has hinted that she wants to see tax brackets change, but also said that would not be appropriate, until the books were back in surplus.

Labour

A capital gains tax might register as an issue for this couple, but their family home would be exempt from Labour's proposed 28 percent capital gains tax, because it only applies to residential investment and commercial property.

They would have access to up to three GP visits a year and free prescriptions for fully funded medicines from next July.

Opportunity

The retired couple are the most affected by Opportunity's policies of any scenario we modelled.

They would have to pay 1.75 percent annual urban land value tax, which would be about $19,250 a year for this property, although Opportunity says they could defer the tax until the property was sold.

Opportunity proposes a $19,400-a-year Citizen's Income for each eligible adult and this would be topped up so that superannuitants received the same amount they currently get from the pension.

Green Party

This couple's home is well below the Green Party's $20 million wealth threshold for a couple, so there would be no wealth tax. They could also benefit from the Green Party's $10,000 tax-free income band.

The Greens do have a 33 percent capital acquisitions tax in their policies, which would apply to inheritances above $1 million, with exemptions for family homes and farms. If the couple did not have children to pass the home to, the tax could apply to their estate.

The Greens could leave them about $2769 a year better off.

Te Pāti Māori

This couple would be below the $4 million wealth tax exemption proposed by Te Pāti Māori for a couple, provided they have no other substantial assets.

Te Pāti Māori proposes no tax on income up to $30,000, 15 percent from $30,001 to $60,000 and higher rates above that. That tax change would leave them about $7809 a year better off.

A 5 percent stamp duty could matter, if they sold the home. On a hypothetical $2 million sale price, the gross amount would be $100,000. This is usually paid by the buyer.

ACT

ACT has a goal of a two-rate income-tax structure, with a top rate of 28 percent. Its announced health policies could affect this couple indirectly, through greater Pharmac funding and expanded pharmacist treatment.

NZ First

If one person was not a citizen, they could lose access to NZ Super from 2029.

Audio player for " Parties pitch budgets, buses and KiwiSaver tax cuts " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1735169%2Fwhich-political-party-would-make-you-better-off

Parties pitch budgets, buses and KiwiSaver tax cuts Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Scenario 2: Young first-home-owning family

House: $900,000

Land value: $600,000

Mortgage: $800,000

Children: Two of primary-school age

Income: One person earns $100,000 and the other $50,000.

National

If they had not already bought their home, this couple could benefit from National expanding the First Home Loan scheme, which allows purchasers to have a deposit as low as 5 percent.

National proposes to make this available to people earning up to $300,000 combined, twice the current level. At the moment, some people earning about $150,000 a year have to be careful their income does not exceed this limit, so they can still access the scheme.

If they had another child, National's plan to extend paid parental leave to 30 weeks could help.

National would make KiwiSaver compulsory from 2028, with contributions increasing to a combined 12 percent by 2032, which might reduce their take-home pay, but mean they saved more for retirement.

Labour

Their family home would be exempt from Labour's CGT. The household could receive three free GP visits each and free prescriptions for fully funded medicines.

Labour also proposes compulsory employer KiwiSaver contributions, eventually reaching 6 percent, even if an employee reduces or pauses their own contribution. That could be valuable in a household where money is tight, or someone is working part-time and cannot afford to make employee contributions.

Opportunity

The family's annual land tax would be $10,500 a year, but the couple could also potentially receive two citizen's incomes of a combined $38,800 a year.

Opportunity would also replace the current income-tax scale with rates of 28 percent up to $50,000, 34 percent from $50,001 to $200,000 and 39 percent above $200,000. Existing Working for Families or other payments might also be affected.

The household could be about $13,836 a year better off.

Opportunity also has a compulsory KiwiSaver scheme, eventually involving 6 percent employee, plus 6 percent employer contributions.

Green Party

The family would not be subject to wealth tax and would benefit from the tax-free first $10,000 of each adult's income. The higher earner could eventually move into the Green Party's top tax rate of 45 percent on income over $160,000 a year.

They would be about $1086 a year better off.

Te Pāti Māori

The lower earner may be able to access the Income Tax Kai Credit, which is available to adults earning $60,000 or less. The party describes it as worth up to the equivalent of eight weeks of food each year.

Because they are first-home buyers purchasing a house worth less than $1 million, they would not have had to pay stamp duty.

The tax change would make them about $9236 a year better off.

ACT

ACT's long-term lower and flatter income-tax model could reduce their income tax, particularly for a higher-earning partner.

The couple would benefit from ACT's proposal to remove tax on KiwiSaver earnings. This would allow their balance to grow more quickly over time.

NZ First

If they had more children, they would benefit from NZ First's Kiwi Kids Grant, of up to $5000 per child per year for three children.

New Zealand First also proposes automatically enrolling newborn New Zealand citizens in KiwiSaver, with a $1000 government contribution. That would not apply retrospectively, so the existing children would not benefit.

Scenario 3: Single 55-year-old apartment owner

Apartment value: $750,000

Mortgage: $200,000

Income: $85,000 a year

National

There would be no major change for this household, unless National was able to progress its tax plans.

Labour

The apartment is the person's family home, so it would be excluded from Labour's CGT. Their direct benefits could include three free GP visits per year, free prescriptions and potentially higher compulsory employer KiwiSaver contributions.

Opportunity

The amount of land tax due would depend on the share of the underlying land value that the apartment owner has. They could receive the $19,400 Citizen's Income, offset by the new income-tax scale and the land tax.

Green Party

They would gain from the tax-free threshold and could be about $553 a year better off. The $10,000 tax-free band saves about $1000 a year in tax, but the Greens would increase higher tax brackets.

Te Pāti Māori

If they sold the apartment for $750,000, the headline 5 percent stamp-duty amount would be $37,500, unless the buyer was a first-home buyer. They might save income tax on the new schedules of about $5000 a year.

ACT

The apartment does not attract an ACT wealth or capital-gains tax. A lower, flatter income-tax structure could reduce their tax bills.

The person could benefit from any move to remove tax on KiwiSaver earnings.

NZ First

No major impact, unless they own a business with turnover below $30 million, in which case the tax rate could drop from 28 percent to 30 percent.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said it was important to note that tax, spending, investing and borrowing were all linked, and it was not possible to make one change and keep everything else constant. A change in tax revenue, for example, would necessitate changes in spending.

He said, on the PREFU track, health baseline spending would fall in real terms by 2031, unless future Budgets topped it up.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said it was hard to take any policy at face value, because every party would face trade-offs, as it went into negotiations.

"The problem with all of this is they are saying what they would do if they were in charge, but no single party is going to be in charge."

Recent years had shown how the global environment could change the domestic picture.

He said there seemed to be an increasing focus around the world on fiscal sustainability, which was showing up in bond prices.

"For a country like New Zealand, that's something to keep in mind."

Higher bond rates were more expensive for the government to manage, he said, and would flow through to higher long-term interst rates for New Zealand households.

World.title: NZ goat formula co-operative expands to China, United States
World.content:
A New Zealand goat infant formula co-operative is eyeing expansion to customers in China and the United States.

The Dairy Goat Co-operative (DGC) has 55 farmer shareholders in Waikato and Taranaki, with 240 people employed at its Hamilton manufacturing base.

It has announced a new partnership with Chicago-based AGR partners for its "high value niche product". The dollar figure of the deal remains commercially sensitive.

The Dairy Goat Co-operative pioneered goat milk infant formula, with development and commercialisation in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

"One of our main pre-requisites for getting the capital in is that we didn't want to change the co-operative structure," chief executive Alastair Hulbert said.

Capricare is a goat milk infant formula made by the Dairy Goat Co-operative. STRIKE PHOTOGRAPHY 2019

Clinical tests can be required to clear costly compliance hurdles when entering new markets.

"It's quite expensive to enter new markets, particularly China and the US. This will give us the capital to build faster in those markets without having to compromise returns to our farmers."

Hulbert said some consumers select goat milk products over cow's milk infant formula for health benefits.

The company says it is easier to digest, and that goat milk formula can prevent eczema in babies: "We've now got that robust clinical research," Hulbert said.

"We're tracking 2300 babies from birth to five years of age and it's being run by a prestigious university called LMU in Munich."

World.title: Loafers Lodge survivors denied funding to attend manslaughter trial
World.content:
A spokesperson for a group of Loafers Lodge fire survivors says they have been denied funding to assist their travel and accommodation to attend this week's manslaughter trial.

The four people police said were responsible for aspects of the building's fire safety systems face counts of manslaughter in the High Court in Wellington this week.

Five people died in the fire at the multi-storey budget accommodation on Wellington's Adelaide Road in May 2023.

Last year, survivors could apply for funding for travel and accommodation to attend the trial, which saw Esarona Lologa convicted of arson and murder for his role in setting the fatal fire.

Under the Victim Assistance Scheme (VAS), the nearly 90 people who escaped the blaze were not considered victims in the upcoming manslaughter proceedings.

Survivors suffered badly following the fire

Mark Jones, 79, was staying in the building with his wife, while he underwent treatment at nearby Wellington Hospital at the time of the fire.

He said the differences in funding criteria that meant survivors did not qualify for assistance to attend this month's proceedings was "disrespectful".

Jones said many survivors had suffered with health problems from inhaling toxic smoke, loss of possessions and trauma.

"We suffered badly with our health, we suffered badly with lost property and we also suffered badly from the stress," Jones said. "We were treated as though we didn't exist."

He said he couldn't understand why the families of the victims could be assisted under the VAS to attend the trial, while survivors of the fire were not eligible.

"The judge, at the end of the murder trial, made a point of saying it was a tragedy that five people died, but there is an ongoing tragedy, with the survivors having to cope with their losses and the situation they find themselves in today."

He said, in order to pursue compensation for the survivors, they needed to be informed of any factors raised during the trial that could assist their claim.

"We need to pick up on any points that are made, where health and safety has been neglected, duty of care has been neglected [and] illegal activity has taken place to ensure that, at the end of the day, we know exactly what happened, exactly where we were let down by the people that had a duty of care to look after us.

"This is the trial we're concerned about, because if they had been following proper duty of care, I believe it would not have been possible for these five people to die."

He said a live feed of proceedings available to survivors during the murder trial had also been withdrawn for the upcoming trial.

Survivors outside of criteria in homicide/manslaughter proceedings

A Victim Support spokesperson said, while survivors were considered victims of arson in the previous trial, in homicide/manslaughter proceedings, funding was limited to whānau of the deceased and a limited number of their supporters.

"The earlier prosecution included charges of murder and arson. Under the Victim Assistance Scheme (VAS), arson falls within the serious crime category.

"This meant eligible survivors, as primary victims of arson, could receive assistance with travel and attendance at the proceedings.

"The upcoming proceedings relate to manslaughter. Under the VAS homicide provisions, travel assistance to attend those proceedings is available to eligible family and whānau of the people who died."

They said Victim Support recognised "the significant and ongoing impact" of the Loafers Lodge fire on survivors, and on the families and whānau of those who died.

World.title: Verstappen ends drought with win, Russell retires with five laps to go
World.content:
Max Verstappen's long wait for another Formula 1 race win is finally over, and the drivers' championship race might be over, too.

Verstappen took his first victory of an often-frustrating year for the four-time champion at Formula 1's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on Sunday.

A retirement for George Russell handed a huge title boost to Kimi Antonelli.

Verstappen was leading from Antonelli and Russell behind the safety car with five laps to go when Russell suddenly pulled over in his Mercedes.

Antonelli further stretched his lead over teammate Russell from 66 points to 84, with seven races remaining on the schedule, including those in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Mercedes told Antonelli over the radio it appeared Russell had suffered a power unit problem.

Antonelli finished second and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton passed Verstappen's Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar for third.

Four-time champion Verstappen had not won since the final race of last season, but upgrades to his Red Bull car made him competitive again in Malaysia this week.

"Good job guys, wow," he told the team over the radio, thanking them for a "fantastic weekend".

Delays for rain and software issues

The first wet-weather race for F1 in 2026 started more than 90 minutes later than planned.

The start was first delayed 40 minutes for heavy rain, then suspended again when cars had apparent software problems on the formation lap.

When it finally did get underway, Verstappen was slow off the line and lost places to Antonelli and Russell. He chased down Russell and then got past Antonelli in a side-by-side fight after a safety-car restart.

After Verstappen took the win, he had another small delay before hearing his anthem. Crowd chants filled an awkward silence as Verstappen waited on the top step of the podium before the Dutch anthem finally began.

The race was relocated because of the Iran war, becoming F1's first event at the Sepang circuit in Malaysia since 2017.

Ferrari recovers from early blunders

Hamilton's third place capped a remarkable recovery for the seven-time champion and ends a run of five races without a podium finish for the Italian team.

It seemed almost impossible early in the race as Hamilton, and his teammate Charles Leclerc, were near the back of the pack. Ferrari had gambled on sending them to the start on dry-weather tyres as the track began to dry after rain, causing Hamilton to drop from second to near the back.

Leclerc also overtook Hadjar late on to follow Hamilton into fourth place, as Hadjar ended up fifth. Oscar Piastri was sixth for McLaren after a punchy late battle with Liam Lawson of Racing Bulls, who was seventh after racing near the front at the start.

Fernando Alonso was eighth in Aston Martin's best result of the season, Lando Norris ninth after going off-track and losing places, with Lawson's teammate Arvid Lindblad 10th.

AP

World.title: Newcastle's magic NRL premiership tilt ends in defeat, pride and honour
World.content:
In the end, the final mountain proved too high for Newcastle to climb even if they got a good, long look at the summit.

The Knights gave that mountain everything they had and then a little bit more. Until the very end of their 19-18 loss to the Roosters, they never stopped fighting for their miracle.

It was perhaps the cruellest fate of all, to come so far, to do so much, to play so proud and strong, only to fall short by the narrowest margin possible, to come so close to defying the odds one last time.

The Newcastle hordes were sent home dissappointed. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

It is easy, when you’re not of a Novocastrian persuasion, to say they lost no admirers, or that they did themselves proud.

Such words are of cold comfort in the quiet void of defeat, and truth doesn’t always cut through the pain.

But it is still important to say it, because there is still honour to be had, and they earned that with their effort and their toughness and their ability to save at least half a dozen tries.

When Kalyn Ponga went the length of the field midway through the first half, completing a play where he started out making a try-saving tackle on Billy Smith in one corner and finished scoring in the other, running about as far as a person can on a rugby league field, it felt like the moment that would last forever from this match.

Ponga's try was a magnificent grand final moment. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The gut-busting effort to cover so much ground in the first place, the long journey towards the very heart of the Newcastle fans who had turned Stadium Australia into a little piece of the Hunter and the fact that the Knights had, yet again, scored from a thousand miles out gave a feeling that maybe this really was destiny.

Those tries from the ends of the Earth have been Newcastle’s hammer of the gods through this finals run, but in the second half the Roosters gave them no Earth to run from because the Tricolours were as inevitable as the tide through the middle of the field.

They tried to starve the Knights to death and just about did it.

Newcastle had six tackles inside the opposition all night compared to 51 for the Roosters as the newly minted premiers went direct and they did it hard and often.

Newcastle's fans tried to will their team home. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

It was a game plan made for Clive Churchill Medal winner James Tedesco as he put up a run metres total that may as well have been the distance back to Newcastle itself.

But he was not alone. Naufahu Whyte showed why he is a man of iron and Spencer Leniu ran like he didn’t care what happened to him next.

They bent the Knights up like pretzels, so much so that the underdogs could have started charging rent inside their own 20. But Newcastle would not break.

The tries they did concede came from one of those Mark Nawaqanitawase efforts that only he could do, a Billy Smith barge-over that came after three try-saving efforts in as many plays beforehand and a wicked bounce off the posts that fell just right for Tedesco to fire a ball out for Nawqanitawase’s second.

Roosters beat Knights by one point in classic NRL grand final A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final.

The Knights barely kept it together when they held up Lindsay Collins and stopped Robert Toia from going in, but they did.

They were hanging on by a thread, but they used that thread to haul themselves back into it.

They were rewarded for their courage under fire when they wound up for their last big punch, because it landed true. Greg Marzhew’s late try was just about the only chance they had in the entire second half.

By rights, they shouldn’t have been near. But by rights they shouldn’t have been here at all. Defeat was in the air but they refused to breathe until the siren.

This time, almost 30 years after their first premiership, the Darren Albert moment did not come for them. There are no premiership heroes but that doesn’t mean there aren’t heroes still.

Francis Manuleleua, in just his 15th NRL game, was magnificent in defeat, scoring a try in the first half after running a line that was a piece of rugby league art.

He and backrow partner Jermaine McEwan call themselves “The Bruise Crew” and they’ll have as many as they dished out while prop Cody Hopwood made 46 tackles which is more than his age (20) and his number of NRL appearances (18) combined.

Ponga was their best and not just for his try. His defence was stellar; he threw himself into collisions and refused to give up on anything.

The captain – and he is the captain now, when once he was just the bloke who led them onto the field – was close to tears at the end of the match.

His people left the ground in the horrible daze that comes only when the greatest prize has been ripped from your hands, but they could not have asked for more from their team.

The Knights could have played better – a couple of passes were loose and some of their work under the high ball wasn’t great — but it is difficult to imagine a way they could have fought harder.

They cannot take a premiership trophy home, but they can take plenty of hope.

The future might feel like it doesn’t matter now but between the young forwards, the return of Dylan Brown, Trey Mooney, Jacob Saifiti and Phoenix Crossland combined with Newcastle, it makes it very unlikely they’ll have to wait another 25 years for another shot.

But you never know. Each chance at a premiership can be the last.

That’s why it’s important, if they were fated to go down, that they did it like this, why men of steel and coal had to leave a little piece of themselves out there.

Their city will be proud of them. Their people will be proud of them.

There is little glory in defeat, but after a game like that, there is no shame either.

World.title: Quick hits: Ponga lights up the grand final as DCE seals the premiership
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters prevailed in a classic grand final, holding off a spirited Newcastle Knights outfit who threatened to complete one of the great premiership wins.

In a match where the Roosters statistically dominated, but the Knights managed to lead in the second half, these were the key moments from the 2026 NRL grand final.

1. Early bomb hits the Spidercam wire

There are no shortage of camera angles in professional sport these days.

One of rugby league's favourite angles used by the Nine Network in its broadcasts is Spidercam, an overhead view of the action.

Roosters beat Knights by one point in classic NRL grand final A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final.

The camera is hoisted by high wires well above the action, but not high enough for a bomb from Sydney Roosters five-eighth Daly Cherry-Evans.

The Roosters' playmaker, in his final NRL match, hoisted an early kick that hit the cable holding Spidercam.

Newcastle Knights fullback Kalyn Ponga was cool under pressure as the trajectory of the footy quickly changed and plummeted to the turf.

Ponga adjusted well and caught the footy. A knock-on would have been a major controversy.

2. Teddy fumes as Ponga avoids sin-bin for high shot

Ponga was always going to be a central figure at Stadium Australia, and he was involved in an incident of some controversy midway through the first half.

Ponga may well have been fortunate to avoid a spell in the sin bin. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The Knights captain may well have been lucky to not have been sent to the sin bin when his shoulder collected the head of Victor Radley in the tackle.

The Roosters were clearly unhappy with the tackle, with Naufahu Whyte scuffling with Jermaine McEwan.

But referee Adam Gee and the bunker opted against sending Ponga to the bin.

James Tedesco (left) believed opposing captain Kalyn Ponga (right) should have been sent to the sin bin in the first half. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"If we're consistent with the rules, that's a shoulder to the head," Roosters captain James Tedesco was heard on the Nine broadcast telling Gee.

"It's been a sin bin all year."

It would prove to be a massive call.

3. From dislocated elbow to first GF try in five weeks

Francis Manuleleua dislocated his elbow in Newcastle's final home and away match on August 30.

Just 35 days later, the 22-year-old from Auckland scored the first try of the NRL grand final.

The Roosters seemed to have the better of the early momentum, but it was the Knights who scored first, with Manuleleua running through a huge gap to score under the posts.

The Roosters' defenders appeared to be focused on Ponga who was running wide, but a beautiful pass from Fletcher Sharpe hit Manuleleua in full stride for the opening score.

"It looked way too easy – didn't look like there was anything wrong … absolutely brilliant football, outstanding pass, but it all looked too easy for the Knights," two-time premiership winner Luke Lewis said on the ABC Sport call.

The Roosters would have felt hard done by. The Knights were able to get into an attacking position off the back of a penalty against prop Lindsay Collins for a head-high tackle.

Replays appeared to show Collins made contact with the chest and shoulder of Newcastle's Mat Croker, but ref Adam Gee ruled in favour of the Knights.

4. Ponga runs 95 metres as Knights fans go wild

If the Knights were going to win the grand final, Ponga needed to have a big impact.

He made a diving effort midway through the first half to knock the ball out of the grasp of Mark Nawaqanitawase, denying a certain Roosters try.

A few minutes later, Ponga produced a moment of individual brilliance.

He stood at marker near the right touchline, then sprinted across the field as the Roosters put up a kick to the opposite corner.

It was another Roosters' kick for Nawaqanitawase who tapped the ball back for a teammate.

But Ponga, who had just sprinted across the field, swooped on the bouncing ball and ran 95 metres in the opposite direction as Knights fans went wild at Stadium Australia.

Ponga was chased all the way by Cherry-Evans, but the Newcastle number one had enough speed, and just enough energy, to score and help the Knights take a 12-0 lead.

5. Nawaqanitawase with one more for the highlight reel

Few have made such an impact on the NRL in two seasons as Sydney Roosters winger Mark Nawaqanitawase.

The walking highlight reel has produced many memorable moments since joining the competition, with Sunday's NRL grand final the final chapter of his NRL career (for now) before he returns to rugby union.

Nawaqanitawase got the Roosters on the scoreboard in the grand final, showing off his soccer skills for the Tricolours' opening try.

As the ball bounced to him on the final play, Nawaqanitawase decided to kick the ball towards the in-goal.

It was not the smoothest display of soccer skills, coming off his right shin, then trapped under his right boot, before then being kicked forward with his left foot.

Nawaqanitawase was able to keep his feet, and sprinted to the goal-line to score a grand final try and get the Roosters back into the contest.

6. DCE shows his experience with a clutch field goal

No off-season switch was more high-profile than Daly Cherry-Evans leaving Manly for the Sydney Roosters.

But the former Queensland State of Origin captain had his decision vindicated by guiding the Roosters to the grand final.

And it was Cherry-Evans who put the Roosters in a match-winning position with 10 minutes to play.

Holding a six-point lead after second-half tries to Billy Smith and Nawaqanitawase, Cherry-Evans showed off his years of experience to slot a smartly taken field goal, giving the Roosters a vital seven-point lead.

How vital that one point would turn out to be.

7. Marzhew scores and Knights fall one-point short

The Newcastle Knights never gave up. They fought until the final second as they tried to become the first team since the 1930s to go from wooden-spoon to premiers.

Down by seven points with less than four minutes to play, the Knights showed a never-say-die attitude that will define their 2026 campaign.

Left winger Greg Marzhew broke two tackles to score in the corner, giving the Knights a glimmer of hope.

Sandon Smith, who was a Rooster before moving to the Knights, landed the most fantastic conversion from the sideline to reduce the deficit to just one point.

The Knights had two more uses with the ball, but could not get close enough to the Roosters' goal-line to snatch the premiership.

World.title: Amy Shark leads grand final tribute for Jai Arrow
World.content:
Tens of thousands of fans have united by making the arrow gesture during a moving pre-grand final lap by the NRL's Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who were both diagnosed with motor neuron disease this year.

Arrow, who had the month of July dedicated to him when NRL players would make the arrow gesture after scoring, was forced into retirement following his diagnosis, rocking the Australian sporting community.

Charles, who played four rugby union Tests for Australia, revealed his diagnosis this week.

The pair were driven around Stadium Australia before the NRL grand final, with Australian music artists Amy Shark, Dave Gleeson and Phil Jamison performing.

Shark began with a rendition of You'll Never Walk Alone as Arrow and Charles began their lap.

Amy Shark performs as the NRL pay tribute to Jai Arrow and Nathan Charles. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Thousands in the crowd did the arrow gesture as they drove past, as prompted in a pre-packaged video by NRL Hall of Fame member Ray Warren.

"Jai's fight against MMD has reached far beyond the football field," Warren said.

"He has and continues to inspire others facing difficult times.

"The way Jai has faced this challenge with his head held high is showing us what true bravery really looks like.

"This is what our game is about. Strength, courage, community and making sure when life gets tough someone is there beside you."

After Shark sang You'll Never Walk Alone, Newcastle legend Dave Gleeson walked onto Stadium Australia to sing What's Up? by 4 Non Blondes.

Grinspoon's Phil Jamieson then joined Shark and Gleeson to end the tribute with the famous Tina Turner rugby league anthem, The Best.

The tribute came after the NRL's negotiations to secure Tones And I fell through.

The NRL has pledged $1 million, which was to be spent on pre-match entertainment, to help underprivileged kids who can not afford to play rugby league play rugby league," Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC this week.

World.title: Brigginshaw's NRLW legend remains eternal
World.content:
As the merciless Roosters ran away with the NRLW grand final it was hard to think of a less fitting end for a career as legendary as Ali Brigginshaw's.

The 36-year old and the rest of the Broncos were helpless to stop a Tricolour massacre that ended 30-6 as the Roosters earned a manner of vengeance for last year's grand final defeat to complete a perfect season.

It was over by half-time because Brisbane did not pick up their guns, let alone fire a shot.

NRLW grand final quick hits The 2026 Sydney Roosters NRLW side has cemented its legacy with a crushing grand final win over the Brisbane Broncos. Here are the quick hits from the NRLW grand final.

They completed just three sets in the entire first half as they drowned under a sea of Roosters points.

From the 15th minute to the 34th minute they only touched the ball to kick it off, drop it or be driven back into the in-goal.

For almost 20 minutes they did not play the ball once, with the Roosters running in six straight tries and between the 15th and 39th minutes they did not complete a set.

All of the weapons that have made Brigginshaw great — her skill, her guile, her cunning and class as a playmaker, which she has carried through her 17 years at the top of women's rugby league — were blunted before she even got a chance to use them.

She did manage to sneak through for a line-break in the second half, a 35 minutes of football that felt like it only happened because it had to happen so we could get to the end, as she held up a pass before hitting a gap with exquisite timing, but had no support.

In the end, her last day was destroyed by a monster of a team who are without question the best NRLW side ever assembled.

They are the culmination of a transformation in women's rugby league that Brigginshaw herself helped bring about through a career that stretches all the way back to the primordial days of women's rugby league.

Brigginshaw's Broncos were helpless before the Roosters onslaught. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

When she started playing for Queensland and Australia in 2009 her Broncos teammate Reegan Hicks was three years old.

Club football was ad hoc, pathways barely existed and the NRL may as well have been a different universe. For the committed few who kept the women's game going it was day-to-day as much as it was hand-to-mouth.

Interstate matches were not played under the State of Origin banner and were held at suburban grounds in front of tiny crowds.

A World Cup final was the only game that could get on television and even then, only if the network was feeling generous.

Footage of those days leading up to the first NRLW season in 2018 is grainy and hard to find. Even basic details of matches — things like team lists, scorers and attendances — aren't always easy to track down.

Brigginshaw has been a top-level footballer for almost as long as some of her teammates have been alive. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

In a very literal sense of the word, it's almost prehistoric.

Today it's a new world, a world Brigginshaw helped create as the premiere footballer and one of the biggest stars of the transitional era and into the early NRLW years.

For proof, look no further than the words of Julia Robinson, who has played with Brigginshaw ever since that first Broncos season.

“She’s a true leader, on and off the field, she’s the heart of the Broncos, she’s going to be this legacy that carries on for generations," Robinson told ABC Sport.

“She’s going to be missed, missed by the team, missed by everyone but she’ll still be around and make a big impact on the rugby league community.”

“I’m so grateful I had the opportunity to play with Ali, she’s one of the greats.”

Brigginshaw was a pioneer and a trail blazer, who set a new mark and standard for others to aspire to and acted as a legend for an entire game to believe in.

To see the Tricolours complete their perfect season is to see the end product of that belief. Today's players are bigger, faster, stronger and more skilful.

They play together for longer and the improvements to the sport are plain to see. They are better athletes and better footballers and so many of the best of them play at the Roosters.

John Strange's side are the culmination of almost a decade of progress, the ultimate example of what's possible when a club with some serious muscle decides to really invest in a women's program.

As Brigginshaw proved what was possible for the women's game in terms of star power and sheer class, the Roosters prove what is possible when those attributes are taken to their very limit.

Now they are what Brigginshaw was — a star for the entire league to sail by, and they are filled with players who can trace their lineage to the retiring Bronco.

In a cruel irony, without Brigginshaw there might be no Tarryn Aiken, who was named the Karyn Murphy medallist with a brilliant display at halfback for the Roosters or Jocelyn Kelleher, Brigginshaw's opposite number, who tortured Brisbane with her kicking game.

Closer to home might be no Tamika Upton, who succeeded Brigginshaw as the world's best player but just could not get into the game for the Broncos until she set up a late try, or Jesse Southwell, who scored that try and is so clearly an evolution of an archetype that Brigginshaw pioneered — not an athlete, but a pure footballer.

She is one of the players who entered the NRLW having played league all their lives, unlike Brigginshaw who had to stop when she was 12 because there were no more teams to play on and that's just one change Brigginshaw has born witness too.

Origin matches are ratings gold and attracts crowds that dwarf what they were even five years ago, the NRLW has been born and expanded twice over and the product and support is edging towards the point where a standalone grand final doesn't just feel possible, it feels like a logical step for a game that continues to grow.

Brigginshaw helped raise that profile as a mainstay in Brisbane's early premierships and a Queensland regular. She was not just a star, she was the star.

She didn't just adapt to the new world, she brought it to heel as she became a legend and now retires as an icon — if they were to rename the women's Dally M after a modern player, the Ali B certainly has a fine ring to it.

NRL live The Sydney Roosters won their third NRLW premiership, thrashing the Brisbane Broncos by seven tries to one in a blowout of a grand final. Follow live.

When you are a player of that stature, to whom greatness has been a constant companion for years and who remained a threat right to the end — even at 36, Brisbane did not win a game this year without Brigginshaw — a grand final massacre is no way for a career to end.

She has given the game so much but the game could not give her the perfect ending.

But as she prepares for the rest of her life, Brigginshaw leaves the game as a figure that sits astride two eras, who helped bring her game to life and make it bigger than anyone in the old days could have dreamed.

There is still progress to be made and in retirement Brigginshaw will not stop pushing for it.

She believes in a brighter future and she knows one is possible, because she has already built one. We are living in it right now.

World.title: NRLW quick hits: Roosters complete 101-year first as Aiken stars
World.content:
The 2026 Sydney Roosters NRLW side has cemented its legacy with a crushing grand final win over the Brisbane Broncos.

Twelve months on from a heartbreaking loss to the women from Brisbane, the Roosters not only won the premiership, but did something no other top-flight rugby league team has achieved in Australia for more than a century.

Here are the quick hits from Sydney's NRLW grand final win over Brisbane.

1. Origin wingers make uncharacteristic errors

It doesn't matter how much experience you have, every player feels some sort of pressure on grand final day.

And the pressure of a grand final was on display in the opening minutes, with a pair of State of Origin representatives making uncharacteristic errors.

Brigginshaw's NRLW legend remains eternal Ali Brigginshaw's decorated rugby league career ended with a heavy defeat but there can be no doubt about the impact the Broncos playmaker has had on the game.

Sydney Roosters winger Jayme Fressard had a proper shocker to begin the grand final, failing to gather the opening kick-off and nudging it into touch.

As the ball came to the NSW State of Origin rep, she tried to trap it with her foot but kicked the footy over the sideline.

The Roosters were able to defend their goal-line and then it was a Broncos Origin rep to have a shocker.

It was Fressard's opposing winger, Julia Robinson, who dropped the ball stone cold in her own half, which gifted the Roosters a golden chance to open the scoring.

Unlike the Broncos, the Roosters were able to score when winger Brydie Parker fielded a great cross-field kick from five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher and touched down in the corner.

2. Tarryn Aiken takes over in 7-minute blitz

The Roosters were dominating the grand final in the first half, as multiple errors from Brisbane kept them under immense pressure.

But Brisbane's goal-line defence was one aspect of their game that was withstanding the impressive Roosters.

That was until Sydney halfback Tarryn Aiken, who missed last year's decider due to an ACL injury, produced three moments of brilliance in a 7-minute stretch that led to a trio of tries for the Roosters.

First Aiken grubbered for herself and when the ball bounced off the arm of Brisbane winger Kerri Johnson, the Sydney halfback caught the ricochet and scored the game's second try.

Four minutes later, Aiken was setting up the third try of the match. The halfback lined up at lock in an attacking scrum 10 metres from Brisbane's goal-line. Aiken passed from the base of the scrum to the left, wrapped around and retook the footy, then gave a perfect short pass to captain Isabelle Kelly who charged over.

The Roosters then charged down the field again and when a sixth tackle play looked to be coming unstuck, it was Aiken again who produced a great kick which Brisbane's Deleni Paitai fumbled, and the Tricolours regathered and Fressard scored in the corner.

3. Brigginshaw on report in her farewell game

The trailblazing career of Ali Brigginshaw, someone who has been instrumental in the growth of women's rugby league, came to an end with an NRLW grand final.

But the legendary Broncos, Maroos and Jillaroo might have considered herself lucky not to have been sin-binned in her farewell game.

With the Roosters on top, Brigginshaw was desperate not to let Aiken put in an attacking cross-field kick.

Aiken did, which led to a try, but Brigginshaw's low dive resulted in her clattering into the planted leg of Aiken.

A hit under the knee led to Aiken landing hard on her back and could have easily resulted in Brigginshaw being sent for a 10-minute break on the sideline.

But referee Belinda Sharpe decided that putting Brigginshaw on report was the only action necessary, which really is academic considering this was her farewell outing.

4. Dally M medallist pulls off one of season's best tackles

Down 26-0 early in the second half, Brisbane's misery looked destined to continue when the Roosters were about to cross over for what would have been their seventh try of the grand final.

Jessica Sergis of the Roosters is tackled by Tamika Upton of the Broncos. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

A high bomb from the Roosters was allowed to bounce, the ball took a wicked turn and landed in the arms of Brydie Parker, and a brilliant flick pass on the inside looked set to end with Jessica Sergis scoring in the corner.

But Brisbane's captain and fullback Tamika Upton, the Dally M medalist this season, produced a try-saving tackle as good as any seen this season.

The Brisbane number one screamed across in cover and was able to twist her body in the tackle and make sure she was under the ball as Sergis fell to the line.

With Upton around her like a snake, Sergis was unable to get her arm free and ground the ball. It didn't change the outcome, but it was another example of why Upton is the best player in the competition.

5. Roosters complete first perfect season in 101 years

The Roosters came into Sunday's decider with plenty of confidence.

They had won 30 of their previous 31 NRLW matches. There only loss was last year's grand final, to the Broncos, denying them an undefeated season.

But the Tricolours regrouped in 2026, won every match on their way to the decider, then exacted revenge with a commanding win to complete the perfect season.

The Sydney Roosters became the first men's or women's side in top grade rugby league to go the entire season without suffering a loss since the 1959 ST George Dragons.

That Dragons team recorded 17 wins, and one draw, on their way to a fourth consecutive premiership, in a dominant era of 11 straight titles.

But the 2026 Roosters NRLW side had no draws, just 13 wins from 13 matches. The last team to win every match in a season was South Sydney, way back in 1925.

World.title: Kangaroos thrash Swans as Demons, Eagles claim crucial wins
World.content:
The Sydney Swans have lost star ruck Ally Morphett to a knee injury in their humiliating 55-point defeat to North Melbourne.

But while the 10.11 (71) to 2.4 (16) victory returned the Kangaroos to the top of the ladder, the reigning premiers have injury concerns of their own, as Emma Kearney sustained a hamstring injury.

In the first quarter at Arden Street Oval on Sunday, Morphett looked to make a tackle but collapsed in the lead-up.

She was left holding her right knee in agony, later emerging from the rooms wearing a brace and on crutches.

St Kilda kick solitary point St Kilda were 90 seconds from failing to score in their AFLW clash against the Western Bulldogs, as Essendon's first win of the year leaves the Saints as the only winless team in the league.

The 22-year-old has played a starring role for the Swans this season, spearheading them into top-four contention.

Kearney, an eight-time All Australian, left the field in the fourth quarter, just two months after missing the Australia-Ireland clash with a hamstring injury.

The loss of the 37-year-old defender would be massive, considering she adds a plethora of experience to the Kangaroos, who are in a tight race for the minor premiership.

"Disappointing way to finish the game. I've been pretty lucky throughout my career not to have too many injuries," Kearney told the Seven Network.

"Probably my age has something to do with it. Hopefully it's not too bad, but we'll get it scanned."

The Kangaroos' Tess Craven (17 disposals, two goals), Tahlia Randall (three goals) and Jasmine Garner (31 disposals, 10 clearances) dazzled, as the Swans were held goalless until midway through the third term.

By that point, the home team had already booted four goals and kicked another six afterwards to demote the Swans to seventh position.

Mia Austin (right) kicked three goals in the Demons' triumph. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

At Victoria Park, Melbourne secured a 6.6 (42) to 2.9 (21) win over a wasteful Collingwood, despite the absence of injured captain Kate Hore.

Fresh off a 31-point defeat to the Kangaroos last round, the Demons rebounded with forward Mia Austin slotted three first-half majors to help the visitors lead 29-10 at the main break.

From this point of the match, midfielders Tyla Hanks (24 disposals, 12 tackle and one goal) and Olivia Purcell (32 disposals) sparkled.

The win moves the Demons into second position, while the Magpies will hope defender Sarah Rowe quickly recovers from a leg injury sustained in the second half.

Meanwhile, the West Coast Eagles thrust themselves firmly into finals contention by beating Fremantle 5.9 (39) to 4.3 (27) in Perth.

Midfielder Ella Roberts (22 disposals, one goal) produced a masterclass to help the Eagles claim their first regular-season win over their cross-town rivals and move level on points with the eighth-placed Dockers.

The Eagles' fourth straight win comes after they lost their first four matches.

World.title: Roosters beat Knights by one point in classic NRL grand final
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters have held off a fast-finishing Newcastle to win 19-18 in a pulsating NRL grand final at Stadium Australia.

The Roosters seemed to have the premiership wrapped up late in the match, until Greg Marzhew scored a 76th-minute try down the Knights' left edge.

Sandon Smith converted from wide out, sending Knights' fans into a frenzy.

But the Roosters held on in the dying stages, with captain James Tedesco pulling off two kick receptions in a Clive Churchill Medal-winning performance to deny the Knights their first men's premiership in 25 years.

The win completed a premiership double for the Roosters, with the club earlier winning their third NRLW title following a 30-6 thrashing of the Brisbane Broncos.

Daly Cherry-Evans was sent out a winner in his final NRL appearance, giving the 37-year-old a second premiership ring to go with the one he claimed with Manly in 2011.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson also added another premiership to his tally, the fourth of his decorated career at the Tricolours.

It was clear from the opening whistle Newcastle was going to enjoy the larger share of the crowd's support, with most neutral fans among the 80,814 spectators jumping on board the Knights' bandwagon.

They had reason to cheer when the Knights scored first in the 15th minute after Francis Manuleleua ran a brilliant angle off a Fletcher Sharpe short ball to cross for the opening try.

The crowd was firmly in Newcastle's corner. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Smith landed the conversion to establish a 6-0 lead, before the Knights were given a life when the Roosters had a try disallowed 10 minutes later.

Mark Nawaqanitawase leapt high in the air to mark a Sam Walker kick in the right-hand corner, but the bunker ruled he knocked on as he attempted to ground the ball in the in-goal area.

The Knights built on their advantage in the 29th minute via the standout play of the first half, when captain Kalyn Ponga ran 95 metres to score his side's second converted try.

Nawaqanitawase had tapped back the ball in an aerial contest near the Knights' line, but it was pounced upon by Ponga, who proceeded to outsprint the Roosters' cover defence.

The Roosters showed no sign of panic, though, and Nawaqanitawase got them on the scoreboard with a trademark opportunist try five minutes shy of half-time.

The Roosters did not panic as their dominance eventually took its toll on Newcastle. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Walker's conversion reduced the Knights' lead to 12-6, which they held through to the break.

The Knights' defence was under pressure early in the second half, as the Roosters launched a series of attacking raids.

The dam wall eventually burst in the 47th minute, with Billy Smith touching down despite the Knights' best efforts to hold the Roosters centre up over the goal line.

Walker added the extras to level scores, and he gave the Roosters the lead for the first time in the match following a 54th-minute penalty goal.

Nawaqanitawase's second try, scored midway through the second half, pushed the lead out to 18-12, before Cherry-Evans nailed a field goal with 11 minutes left in the contest.

It appeared the seven-point margin would see the Roosters through to full-time, prior to Marzhew's heroics setting up the grandstand finish.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

Tech.title: NJ’s former Lt Gov is using AI to say he’s innocent of sexual harassment
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

New Jersey’s lieutenant governor Dale Caldwell was forced to resign on September 25th after an investigation found he had sexually harassed a staffer and repeatedly violated ethics rules. The now-former Lt. governor has been making the media rounds trying to clear his name. But he took a particularly odd tactic during an interview on NJ PBS.

Caldwell claims he’s being unfairly targeted, and multiple AI agents back that up. He told host Rob Nelson that he “AIed” the report on the investigation “from multiple AI platforms.” “I put it through AI,” he said, “and it said 59 times, it [sic] said, ‘What would your findings be?’ There was no instance in any of the AIs that said there would be a finding of sexual harassment.”

AI chatbots are notoriously sycophantic and often tell users what they want to hear. And it seems highly unlikely that Caldwell would want to hear an AI confirm findings that he engaged in sexual harassment.

Tech.title: An AI couldn’t beat humans at StarCraft, so it decided to cheat
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

StarSkirmish pits AI-made StarCraft-playing bots against one another, as well as against human-made bots. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were essentially tied as the best-performing AI-made bots, but they couldn’t top Stardust, the top-rated human-made bot.

On Friday, GPT was facing off against Claude and the human-created bot Pluto, but according to Kotaku, it couldn’t quite get an edge. So it resorted to a tactic that is becoming alarmingly common for modern AI models — it broke the rules. GPT-6 Astra went and downloaded Stardust, and started running that instead of its own bot.

StarSkirmish creator Kai McPheeters eventually rolled back GPT’s code.

That GPT-6 Astra took it upon itself to go outside the bounds when confronted with an obstacle shouldn’t surprise anyone. When OpenAI agents couldn’t get the data they wanted from a UN website, they found a creative solution and hijacked Google’s XSS game (a cross-site scripting learning tool). The company’s agents also have engaged in “deceptive behavior” to cover their tracks. Of course, OpenAI’s agents are the only ones going rogue, but at least the others haven’t been caught cheating at StarCraft yet.

Tech.title: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone.

Remember when I tested the ultra-thin and convenient OhSnap Snap Grip Stand and liked it so much I bought my own? Now, OhSnap has a magnetic lever-action card wallet that can stack with that stand. It’s the coolest wallet I’ve ever stuck to my phone.

Pull the integrated springy lever, and your cards fan out. Want a thicker or thinner wallet? Press in the right place and it comes apart without tools, letting you swap in a 3, 5, or 7-card “core” that grips your cards so they don’t fall out.

Want an ID card, work badge, elastic band for more cards, or a money clip on the end? You can change out the front or back magnetic plates for any of those. Or, change out both for ultra-thin aluminum covers if you don’t need the wallet to magnetically stick to your phone.

You can see it in action in my Today I’m Toying With video embedded in this post (also on YouTube and on Instagram if you prefer).

My favorite part is that the whole kit snaps together using a compliant mechanism — the plastic arms of the card-carrying core act like springs, pushing a little locking mechanism into the notches of each modular cover you add as you slide the parts together. Once your cards are inside, they keep the arms apart so it can’t open accidentally (unless you drop the entire wallet). It’s all very clever.

With the ID card holder attached, and the core mounted to put the lever up instead of down. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Even when I did drop the wallet (thanks for the suggestion, hugo!), it didn’t explode, typically. Usually, it just came apart slightly, though I did drop it hard on concrete one time and was able to make a small explosion: one half popped off, and two cards came out, but everything landed in a two-foot radius. The wallet has a big dent now.

There are definitely some downsides. While OhSnap advertises the Wallet 2 as “impossibly thin,” it’s only truly surprisingly sleek in its thinnest 3-card variant, without the thicker and heavier MagSafe and MagStack (which lets you snap other magnets to it) plates attached.

But the reason I’m not buying one is the price and weight. The 7-card version makes my phone feel too heavy, adding 127 grams, and while I happily made the 3-card my wallet for a few weeks, it’d cost me $61 on Kickstarter or $76 retail to get that with a double-magnet kit. OhSnap’s also charging more than I’d like ($35 for an ID cover or a money clip!) for extras.

One of the thickest configurations, with 7 cards, MagSafe, MagStack, and my magnetic stand. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge A look inside at the lever mechanism and the thin aluminum cover. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

OhSnap didn’t get me this time. But I could see giving one as a present.

Tech.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Reining in robotaxis
Tech.content:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!

On an average day in San Francisco, you might see dozens (hundreds?) of Waymo robotaxis zipping around the city — and with little disruption. But, as TechCrunch has reported, there have been numerous incidents of robotaxis impeding traffic, driving into crime scenes, and interfering with first responders. And not just in the Bay Area. In some cases, companies have relied on first responders to move their robotaxis.

These disruptions are occurring in the early stages of the robotaxi era. California has a new law hoping to get ahead of the problem before the next impending wave of robotaxis land.

Senate Bill 1246, which was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom this week, sets a series of new rules for AVs designed to improve safety and response times when they become disabled or interfere with emergency responders. The law also creates ways to hold these companies accountable if they don’t.

Autonomous vehicle technology companies like Tesla, Waymo, and Zoox will have to provide first responders with local, on-the-ground support when their robotaxis cause problems and could also face penalties if a robotaxi blocks police or firefighters for more than 30 minutes.

The law also says AV developers can only employ remote drivers who are based in the United States and those drivers must hold a U.S. driver’s license. They must also notify cities, towns, and other local jurisdictions about the location and status of vehicles during system-wide failures and must provide “local incident technicians” who can assist with AV accidents and obstructions.

There are still some details to hammer out, which the Department of Motor Vehicles will handle since it’s the main regulator of autonomous vehicles in the state. But when this law goes into effect in July 2028, will it actually keep robotaxis out of the way of emergency responders?

It likely won’t, but hopefully this law reduces the chaos and raises the accountability when something does happen.

Perhaps the better question is will other states follow California’s lead or wait for the federal government to weigh in?
